0.title: Remember and Obey: The Book of Deuteronomy
0.overview:
On the plains of Moab, within sight of a land he would never enter, Moses preaches the greatest sermon of his life. Deuteronomy, from the Greek for “second law,” is not a new law but the law renewed and pressed home on a new generation. Their parents are dead; they stand at the edge of Canaan. With the urgency of a dying father, Moses calls them to remember the God who redeemed them and to obey him with all their heart.

The book is shaped like an ancient covenant treaty (a covenant is a binding relationship sealed by oath): a historical prologue rehearsing God’s gracious acts (chs. 1–4), the covenant stipulations (chs. 5–26), blessings and curses (chs. 27–28), and witnesses, succession and ratification (chs. 29–34). The order itself preaches: grace is recited before a single law is given. And the book pulses with love: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart” (6:4–5), the verse Jesus called the greatest commandment.

Did Moses write Deuteronomy? Many scholars hold that it was written in the seventh century and “found” under Josiah (2 Kings 22) to support his reforms. But the book says Moses wrote this law (31:9, 24), a good number find its shape closest to Hittite treaties of the second millennium BC (others point to Assyrian treaties of the seventh century, and the debate continues), and Jesus quotes it as Moses’ (Mark 10:3–5). This commentary takes what Josiah found to be a neglected copy of an older book, which would explain why its words terrified him. The account of Moses’ death (ch. 34) was added by a later inspired hand, perhaps Joshua, and a few explanatory notes (such as 2:10–12) suggest inspired updating in places.

The New Testament quotes it constantly. Jesus answered every wilderness temptation from it (Matthew 4); Paul drew from it that “the word is near you” (Romans 10:8), and that Christ became a curse for us to redeem us from the curse of its law (Gal 3:13). Moses promised a prophet like him (18:15–18), and Peter and Stephen say plainly that this Prophet is Jesus (Acts 3:22–26; 7:37). To read Deuteronomy is to walk in the footsteps of our Lord and to hear the gospel in shadow and promise.

And Deuteronomy ends with Moses’ death. The mediator of the old covenant, the greatest prophet Israel had known, cannot bring the people in; he can only point. It falls to Joshua (Yeshua, the Hebrew name behind Jesus) to lead them. The law cannot save; it shows us our need, and Deuteronomy itself admits that Israel’s heart would need circumcising by God (30:6). Christ alone brings us home, and his Spirit writes the law on the heart. Remember, then, and obey: not to earn the land, but because grace has already given it.

1.title: Looking Back: The God Who Was Faithful Though We Failed
1.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan in the wilderness, in the Arabah opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab.<sup>2</sup>It is eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea.<sup>3</sup>In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month, Moses spoke to the people of Israel according to all that the LORD had given him in commandment to them,<sup>4</sup>after he had defeated Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, and Og the king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth and in Edrei.<sup>5</sup>Beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab, Moses undertook to explain this law, saying,<sup>6</sup>"The LORD our God said to us in Horeb, 'You have stayed long enough at this mountain.<sup>7</sup>Turn and take your journey, and go to the hill country of the Amorites and to all their neighbors in the Arabah, in the hill country and in the lowland and in the Negeb and by the seacoast, the land of the Canaanites, and Lebanon, as far as the great river, the river Euphrates.<sup>8</sup>See, I have set the land before you. Go in and take possession of the land that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give to them and to their offspring after them.'<sup>9</sup>"At that time I said to you, 'I am not able to bear you by myself.<sup>10</sup>The LORD your God has multiplied you, and behold, you are today as numerous as the stars of heaven.<sup>11</sup>May the LORD, the God of your fathers, make you a thousand times as many as you are and bless you, as he has promised you!<sup>12</sup>How can I bear by myself the weight and burden of you and your strife?<sup>13</sup>Choose for your tribes wise, understanding, and experienced men, and I will appoint them as your heads.'<sup>14</sup>And you answered me, 'The thing that you have spoken is good for us to do.'<sup>15</sup>So I took the heads of your tribes, wise and experienced men, and set them as heads over you, commanders of thousands, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifties, commanders of tens, and officers, throughout your tribes.<sup>16</sup>And I charged your judges at that time, 'Hear the cases between your brothers, and judge righteously between a man and his brother or the alien who is with him.<sup>17</sup>You shall not be partial in judgment. You shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be intimidated by anyone, for the judgment is God's. And the case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.'<sup>18</sup>And I commanded you at that time all the things that you should do.<sup>19</sup>"Then we set out from Horeb and went through all that great and terrifying wilderness that you saw, on the way to the hill country of the Amorites, as the LORD our God commanded us. And we came to Kadesh-barnea.<sup>20</sup>And I said to you, 'You have come to the hill country of the Amorites, which the LORD our God is giving us.<sup>21</sup>See, the LORD your God has set the land before you. Go up, take possession, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has told you. Do not fear or be dismayed.'<sup>22</sup>Then all of you came near me and said, 'Let us send men before us, that they may explore the land for us and bring us word again of the way by which we must go up and the cities into which we shall come.'<sup>23</sup>The thing seemed good to me, and I took twelve men from you, one man from each tribe.<sup>24</sup>And they turned and went up into the hill country, and came to the Valley of Eshcol and spied it out.<sup>25</sup>And they took in their hands some of the fruit of the land and brought it down to us, and brought us word again and said, 'It is a good land that the LORD our God is giving us.'<sup>26</sup>"Yet you would not go up, but rebelled against the command of the LORD your God.<sup>27</sup>And you murmured in your tents and said, 'Because the LORD hated us he has brought us out of the land of Egypt, to give us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us.<sup>28</sup>Where are we going up? Our brothers have made our hearts melt, saying, "The people are greater and taller than we. The cities are great and fortified up to heaven. And besides, we have seen the sons of the Anakim there."'<sup>29</sup>Then I said to you, 'Do not be in dread or afraid of them.<sup>30</sup>The LORD your God who goes before you will himself fight for you, just as he did for you in Egypt before your eyes,<sup>31</sup>and in the wilderness, where you have seen how the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went until you came to this place.'<sup>32</sup>Yet in spite of this word you did not believe the LORD your God,<sup>33</sup>who went before you in the way to seek you out a place to pitch your tents, in fire by night and in the cloud by day, to show you by what way you should go.<sup>34</sup>"And the LORD heard your words and was angered, and he swore,<sup>35</sup>'Not one of these men of this evil generation shall see the good land that I swore to give to your fathers,<sup>36</sup>except Caleb the son of Jephunneh. He shall see it, and to him and to his children I will give the land on which he has trodden, because he has wholly followed the LORD!'<sup>37</sup>Even with me the LORD was angry on your account and said, 'You also shall not go in there.<sup>38</sup>Joshua the son of Nun, who stands before you, he shall enter. Encourage him, for he shall cause Israel to inherit it.<sup>39</sup>And as for your little ones, who you said would become a prey, and your children, who today have no knowledge of good or evil, they shall go in there. And to them I will give it, and they shall possess it.<sup>40</sup>But as for you, turn, and journey into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea.'<sup>41</sup>"Then you answered me, 'We have sinned against the LORD. We ourselves will go up and fight, just as the LORD our God commanded us.' And every one of you fastened on his weapons of war and thought it easy to go up into the hill country.<sup>42</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'Say to them, Do not go up or fight, for I am not in your midst, lest you be defeated before your enemies.'<sup>43</sup>So I spoke to you, and you would not listen; but you rebelled against the command of the LORD and presumptuously went up into the hill country.<sup>44</sup>Then the Amorites who lived in that hill country came out against you and chased you as bees do and beat you down in Seir as far as Hormah.<sup>45</sup>And you returned and wept before the LORD, but the LORD did not listen to your voice or give ear to you.<sup>46</sup>So you remained at Kadesh many days, the days that you remained there.
1.overview:
Deuteronomy opens not with commands but with memory. Before Moses tells Israel what to do, he tells them what God has done. The first address (chs. 1–4) is a sermon of remembrance, and chapter 1 begins at the nation’s worst wound: Kadesh-barnea, where a generation forfeited the land through unbelief.

God had given them everything: his presence, his promise, leaders to share the burden, the land laid open. Instead they listened to fear and rebelled. Yet grace shines even here, in God’s patience and in his preservation of the children, the very generation now listening. The chapter is a mirror for us too, and behind it stands Christ, who believed where we did not and entered the rest on our behalf.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Word at Horeb: ‘Go, Take Possession’
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sets the scene on the plains of Moab and recalls how God, after Sinai, commanded Israel to break camp and take the land he had sworn to the patriarchs.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s promises are grounded in his oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The land is a gift, secured by covenant and not earned by merit.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel stood on the threshold of an inheritance already sworn to them. Every believer stands before promises God has already sworn to give in Christ, and the call is the same: go forward in faith.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan in the wilderness, in the Arabah opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Hebrew Bible names its books from their opening line, and this one is Debarim, “Words.” Our title comes by a longer road: the Greek translators rendered a phrase in 17:18 as deuteronomion, a second law. It is a little misleading. This is not a second law but the first law preached, the same commandments pressed home to a congregation, which is why Deuteronomy reads more like a sermon than anything else in the Pentateuch.

Picture the preacher: a hundred and twenty years old, knowing his death is near, speaking to the children of the people he began with, almost none of whom remember Egypt. He will not cross the river with them. He might settle scores, secure a legacy, or go quiet. Instead everything from here to the end of the book is one old man trying to get the truth into a generation he will not see again.

And note who is listening: all Israel. Not the elders or the men who could read, but the whole people, hearing the law of God for themselves. That is a decision about how God deals with people, and it has never been reversed.
verseByVerse.note: Moses’ farewell sermons, given on the plains of Moab in the fortieth year (1:3).

verseByVerse.quote: It is eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea. In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month, Moses spoke to the people of Israel according to all that the LORD had given him in commandment to them, after he had defeated Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, and Og the king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth and in Edrei. Beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab, Moses undertook to explain this law, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The opening sentence is the narrator, leaning in before the sermon starts. Eleven days: something like a hundred and fifty miles, a fortnight’s march for a family with animals, from the mountain of the law to the border of the promise. Then verse 3: In the fortieth year.

Set the figures side by side and you have Deuteronomy in miniature. Nothing was wrong with the route, the provisions or the God leading. A fortnight’s journey took four decades, and every year has a grave in it.

Most lives have an eleven-day journey that has been taking years: a conversation that should have happened, a sin that should have been confessed once, a clear step of obedience postponed until postponing became the shape of things. The distance never grows; only the years do. But this sermon is preached to people on the far side of such years, by a God who had carried them through all of it, and the door is still open. The way out of a forty-year delay is not a grand resolution but to confess it to the God who has not given up on you, and take the next step he shows.

Verse 5 says what Moses is doing: he undertook to explain this law, to make it plain. Not new revelation, but what God has already said, cut deep enough that a new generation cannot miss it.
verseByVerse.note: Horeb is Sinai; Kadesh-barnea was the oasis on Canaan’s southern border. The years from leaving Kadesh to crossing the brook Zered were thirty-eight (2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD our God said to us in Horeb, 'You have stayed long enough at this mountain. Turn and take your journey, and go to the hill country of the Amorites and to all their neighbors in the Arabah, in the hill country and in the lowland and in the Negeb and by the seacoast, the land of the Canaanites, and Lebanon, as far as the great river, the river Euphrates. See, I have set the land before you. Go in and take possession of the land that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give to them and to their offspring after them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They had been at Sinai about eleven months, and nothing in history compares with what happened there: the mountain burning, God speaking to a whole nation, the covenant cut, the glory filling the tabernacle. If any place deserved permanent settlement, it was that one. And God says: enough. Break camp.

Some Christians want to live at the site of their best experience of God, the conference, the conversion, the year everything was clear, and measure every later season against it. Sinai was no small experience, yet God moved them on within the year, because the mountain was never the destination. It was where they were made ready to go somewhere.

Then the commission, whose grammar repays attention: I have set the land before you. Go in and take possession. The first verb is finished; the second is a command. The land is already given and still has to be walked into. Grace does not cancel effort; it is the only thing that makes effort anything other than futile.

And underneath stands an oath older than anyone present: the land that the LORD swore to your fathers. Centuries earlier God bound himself to a childless man. Nothing Israel did at Kadesh put that oath at risk. It never rested on them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–18 — Leaders Appointed: Sharing the Burden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses recalls how, as the people multiplied according to God’s promise, he appointed wise and able men to share the burden of judging, charging them to judge justly and without partiality.
verseByVerse.theology: God multiplies his people and provides leaders to care for them. Because justice belongs to God, judges act in his name and must show no partiality.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel grew too numerous for one man, and the load was shared. Christ gives shepherds and elders to his church (Eph 4) in the same way: leadership is shared stewardship under the Chief Shepherd, not one person carrying everything.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time I said to you, 'I am not able to bear you by myself. The LORD your God has multiplied you, and behold, you are today as numerous as the stars of heaven. May the LORD, the God of your fathers, make you a thousand times as many as you are and bless you, as he has promised you! How can I bear by myself the weight and burden of you and your strife? Choose for your tribes wise, understanding, and experienced men, and I will appoint them as your heads.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is candid about the day the work became too big: I am not able to bear you by myself. But in the same breath he says why: Israel is now as numerous as the stars of heaven, the promise God made to a childless Abraham (Gen. 15:5).

So the thing crushing Moses is God’s fulfilled promise. The weight is answered prayer. The ministry that has outgrown you, the family bigger than your energy, the responsibility that came because something went well: not every burden means something has gone wrong. Some are what blessing feels like from underneath.

Then the sentence that shows the man: May the LORD… make you a thousand times as many as you are and bless you. Flattened by the size of this nation, he asks God to multiply it by a thousand. Most of us can pray for relief. Praying for more of the very thing that is breaking you is possible only if you believe it is good and God gave it, which is exactly what Moses believed, and why God could trust him with it.

His solution is not to work harder but to share the load, with men wise, understanding, and experienced: character and judgment, not force of personality. The apostles reached for the same remedy when the church outgrew them (Acts 6:2–4).

verseByVerse.quote: And you answered me, 'The thing that you have spoken is good for us to do.' So I took the heads of your tribes, wise and experienced men, and set them as heads over you, commanders of thousands, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifties, commanders of tens, and officers, throughout your tribes. And I charged your judges at that time, 'Hear the cases between your brothers, and judge righteously between a man and his brother or the alien who is with him. You shall not be partial in judgment. You shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be intimidated by anyone, for the judgment is God's. And the case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.' And I commanded you at that time all the things that you should do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge to the judges is short, and every clause has teeth. The foreigner gets the same court as a man with a tribe behind him.

You shall not be partial in judgment: the Hebrew idiom is not to recognise faces. In the ancient world law bent toward wealth as water runs downhill; this forbids the tilt either way, and Leviticus makes the second half explicit: you shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great (Lev. 19:15). Sympathy can corrupt a verdict as surely as a bribe.

A judge afraid of the man in front of him cannot do justice, and the cure for that fear is the clause that follows: For the judgment is God’s. The judge administers a verdict that belongs to someone else and will answer for it. That is why he need not fear the powerful, and why he dare not favour them.

And one more, easily missed: the case too hard for you is brought to Moses. Even the appointed men are allowed a limit. There is no shame in a man in authority saying this one is beyond me, and considerable danger in a man who never does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–33 — Kadesh-barnea: The Tragedy of Unbelief
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses recounts the journey to Kadesh, the spies, and the people’s refusal to go up, grumbling against the LORD who had carried them all the way.
verseByVerse.theology: Unbelief is the root sin: it calls God a liar and recasts his love as hatred, even while he is carrying his people like a father.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel saw the giants and forgot the God who split the sea. We do the same when we let our obstacles grow larger in our minds than the God who has already carried us through worse.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then we set out from Horeb and went through all that great and terrifying wilderness that you saw, on the way to the hill country of the Amorites, as the LORD our God commanded us. And we came to Kadesh-barnea. And I said to you, 'You have come to the hill country of the Amorites, which the LORD our God is giving us. See, the LORD your God has set the land before you. Go up, take possession, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has told you. Do not fear or be dismayed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses does not tidy the journey up. The wilderness was great and terrifying, and his hearers had seen it. He builds his case not by minimising what God asked but the other way: they went through that and came out the other side. The wilderness they survived is the evidence he will hold up against their fear.

Then the moment at the border, packed into two verses: a gift already given, a command to act, and an explicit word about their emotions, do not fear or be dismayed, spoken before anybody had said they were afraid. God addressed the fear in advance rather than waiting to rebuke it.

Everything they needed was in Moses’ mouth that morning. Whatever happens next cannot be blamed on insufficient information.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all of you came near me and said, 'Let us send men before us, that they may explore the land for us and bring us word again of the way by which we must go up and the cities into which we shall come.' The thing seemed good to me, and I took twelve men from you, one man from each tribe. And they turned and went up into the hill country, and came to the Valley of Eshcol and spied it out. And they took in their hands some of the fruit of the land and brought it down to us, and brought us word again and said, 'It is a good land that the LORD our God is giving us.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Numbers the command to send spies comes from God (Num. 13:1–2); here the people asked. Both are true: the request came from below and God permitted it. And Moses does not shelter behind that: The thing seemed good to me. Forty years later he puts his own judgment on the record.

Then the report as he gives it: the fruit in their hands and It is a good land. That is all. No giants, no fortified cities, no ten against two. Moses knows what else was said (he quotes the fear in verse 28), but when he sets out what the spies reported, he gives the good land and stops.

He is not misremembering; he is preaching. From where he stands, the bad report was never the substance; it was noise. The land was good, God was giving it, they had the fruit in their hands, and they would not go. Strip out the excuse and the refusal stands with nothing in front of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet you would not go up, but rebelled against the command of the LORD your God. And you murmured in your tents and said, 'Because the LORD hated us he has brought us out of the land of Egypt, to give us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us. Where are we going up? Our brothers have made our hearts melt, saying, "The people are greater and taller than we. The cities are great and fortified up to heaven. And besides, we have seen the sons of the Anakim there."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In your tents. Not at the tabernacle or to Moses’ face, where it could be answered, but in the dark, at home, to the family, which is where this always incubates, because it needs privacy to grow and dies in daylight.

And what came out was Because the LORD hated us. The God who broke Egypt for them, opened a sea, drowned an army, fed them every morning and stood over their camp in fire every night had, they said, done all of it to get them somewhere quiet enough to kill them.

Unbelief cannot leave God’s character alone. It never stops at “I am not sure this will work”; it goes on to “he does not mean me well,” because a God who is good and able leaves no room for the refusal. It is the serpent’s oldest lie: God knows that when you eat of it… you will be like God (Gen. 3:5), that is, he is keeping something from you.

If you have lain awake after a diagnosis or a bereavement and felt the thought forming that God is against you, that thought has a history, and this is where it is recorded. It is answered much later, not with an argument: He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Rom. 8:32). You cannot hold that sentence and the whisper in the tent at the same time.

And see what fear does to measurement. Cities fortified up to heaven is not a report but a feeling with numbers on it. Nobody had measured a wall.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said to you, 'Do not be in dread or afraid of them. The LORD your God who goes before you will himself fight for you, just as he did for you in Egypt before your eyes, and in the wilderness, where you have seen how the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went until you came to this place.' Yet in spite of this word you did not believe the LORD your God, who went before you in the way to seek you out a place to pitch your tents, in fire by night and in the cloud by day, to show you by what way you should go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses answers their terror not with encouragement but with evidence, in three pieces: the God who goes before them now, what he did in Egypt before your eyes, and, deepest, the wilderness, where the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son.

It is one of the tenderest images in the Old Testament, placed here on purpose. A father at the end of a long walk with a child who cannot go another step: the child up on his shoulder, asleep, arms round his neck, contributing nothing whatever and getting there anyway. That is what the forty years had been. The people who said the LORD hated us had been carried the whole way by the one they accused.

Then verse 32 falls like a stone: you did not believe the LORD your God. Not “you were outnumbered,” not “the giants were real.” They did not believe him. Hebrews hands this to the church as the standing warning: So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief (Heb. 3:19).

Verse 33 adds the last, quietly devastating piece: he went ahead to seek you out a place to pitch your tents. While they decided he meant to destroy them, he was out ahead of them, in the dark, looking for somewhere they could sleep.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–46 — The Sentence and the Stubborn Presumption
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God swears that the unbelieving generation will not see the land, sparing Caleb and Joshua; then, when Israel presumptuously tries to go up after all, they are defeated, for the LORD is not among them.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s discipline is real and his oath is sure. Presumption is as deadly as cowardice, and true faith waits on God’s timing rather than acting on its own remorse.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel wept too late and fought without God. Religion that ignores God’s word, however zealous it feels, ends in defeat; only faith that listens to him, worked in us by the Spirit, prevails.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the LORD heard your words and was angered, and he swore, 'Not one of these men of this evil generation shall see the good land that I swore to give to your fathers, except Caleb the son of Jephunneh. He shall see it, and to him and to his children I will give the land on which he has trodden, because he has wholly followed the LORD!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He heard them. The murmuring in the tents was private only from Moses. And God answers with an oath, the same form by which he bound himself to Abraham; the second oath closes, for these men, what the first had opened.

Resist the modern instinct to explain God’s anger away. It is not a loss of temper or disproportionate. It is what love looks like when told, by people it carried through a desert, that it is hatred.

Then, mid-sentence, one name: Caleb, because he has wholly followed the LORD. The Hebrew is more concrete: he filled up after the LORD, went all the way behind him, left no gap. The rest followed partially and stopped where it got frightening.

Caleb, with Joshua, was one of two men in six hundred thousand. He had seen the same walls and stood before a crowd that wanted to stone them (Numbers 14:6–10). It changed nothing for anybody else, and God took his name out of the general sentence and wrote it into the promise. Faithfulness in a faithless generation is not wasted, and it is seldom noticed at the time except by God, which turns out to be enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Even with me the LORD was angry on your account and said, 'You also shall not go in there. Joshua the son of Nun, who stands before you, he shall enter. Encourage him, for he shall cause Israel to inherit it. And as for your little ones, who you said would become a prey, and your children, who today have no knowledge of good or evil, they shall go in there. And to them I will give it, and they shall possess it. But as for you, turn, and journey into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses says three times that God was angry with him on your account (1:37; 3:26; 4:21). It raises a fair question, because Numbers is specific that Moses lost the land for his own failure at Meribah, striking the rock in temper (Num. 20:10–12).

Both are true. The sin was his, and God named it. The context was theirs: forty years of being ground down, in an argument they started, about water they blamed him for. Anyone who has snapped after years of provocation knows both can be true at once, and that the second does not excuse the first, which is why Moses, though he once pleaded to cross (3:23–25), never disputes that the sin was his.

Then the succession. The name Joshua is Yehoshua, which comes into Greek as Iesous, Jesus. The law-giver dies outside the land; the man who bears the name of Jesus takes the people in. Hebrews makes the point and leaves it hanging on purpose: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on (Heb. 4:8). One Joshua brought them into Canaan. That was never going to be the end of it.

And a small instruction: Encourage him. The man God has chosen still needs strengthening from those he leads. Nobody is so appointed that he can do without that.

Does “no knowledge of good or evil” teach an age of accountability? It means children too young to share the guilt of Kadesh, and so they inherited the land. Scripture does not set an age. But it gives hope for little ones who die, that God deals with them in mercy (2 Sam 12:23), and Christians may rest them in the hands of the Judge who does right.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then you answered me, 'We have sinned against the LORD. We ourselves will go up and fight, just as the LORD our God commanded us.' And every one of you fastened on his weapons of war and thought it easy to go up into the hill country. And the LORD said to me, 'Say to them, Do not go up or fight, for I am not in your midst, lest you be defeated before your enemies.' So I spoke to you, and you would not listen; but you rebelled against the command of the LORD and presumptuously went up into the hill country. Then the Amorites who lived in that hill country came out against you and chased you as bees do and beat you down in Seir as far as Hormah. And you returned and wept before the LORD, but the LORD did not listen to your voice or give ear to you. So you remained at Kadesh many days, the days that you remained there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The strangest turn comes last. Told the door is shut, Israel suddenly wants to go in, and they thought it easy to go up into the hill country.

It sounds like repentance and is not. Yesterday God said go and they would not. Today he says do not go up or fight, for I am not in your midst, and they go. The direction has reversed; the disposition has not moved an inch. Both times what God said was the thing to be got round.

There are two ways to refuse God, and the second looks like zeal. A man can disobey by hanging back or by charging ahead, and the second is more dangerous because it feels like courage and can be mistaken for faith by everyone watching, including himself. I am not in your midst is the only difference that matters, and it is invisible until the fighting starts.

Then the humiliation: the Amorites chased you as bees do, a rout, men running from something small and furious and everywhere at once. And the saddest line: they wept before the LORD, but the LORD did not listen. That was grief at the consequences, not repentance, and God can tell the difference.

What, then, should they have done? Exactly what they were told in verse 40: turn, and journey into the wilderness. Accept the discipline. Go the long way. Wait for God to open the door again, without knowing whether he would. And the extraordinary thing is that he did: the whole of Deuteronomy is being preached at the foot of that reopened door, to the children of the men who were chased down that hill. If you have missed a window God opened, the answer is not a self-willed charge at it. It is to submit to the wilderness and wait for him to speak again, because he is the God who gave a second generation the land their fathers threw away.

1.theology:
Unbelief as the root sin. Israel’s catastrophe was not military but spiritual (1:32), and Hebrews 3–4 makes it the great warning for the church. Unbelief always slanders God’s character, recasting his love as hatred (1:27).

The faithfulness of God to his oath. He swore the land to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (1:8), and though a generation perishes, the promise passes to their children. Against the backdrop of Israel’s failure, God’s covenant fidelity blazes: grace outlasts and outruns human sin.

The mediator who cannot bring them in. Moses is barred from the land (1:37), and Joshua, whose name is the Hebrew form of Jesus, is appointed to lead Israel in (1:38). The law shows the land; only the Saviour carries us across into rest.
1.examples:
Then: at Kadesh-barnea, with the fruit of the land in their hands, Israel looked at the giants instead of God, grumbled in their tents and turned a fortnight’s journey into forty years of graves.

Now: we do the same whenever we magnify our obstacles and shrink our God, or rush into self-willed action when he says wait. The cure is remembrance, rehearsing how God has carried us (1:31), and resting in Christ, who believed where we failed, entered the rest on our behalf, and by his Spirit leads us through death into the everlasting land.

2.title: The Journey Around Edom and Moab: The Sovereign Lord of All Nations
2.text: <sup>1</sup>"Then we turned and journeyed into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea, as the LORD told me. And for many days we traveled around Mount Seir.<sup>2</sup>Then the LORD said to me,<sup>3</sup>'You have been traveling around this mountain country long enough. Turn northward<sup>4</sup>and command the people, "You are about to pass through the territory of your brothers, the people of Esau, who live in Seir; and they will be afraid of you. So be very careful.<sup>5</sup>Do not contend with them, for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession.<sup>6</sup>You shall purchase food from them with money, that you may eat, and you shall also buy water from them with money, that you may drink.<sup>7</sup>For the LORD your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands. He knows your going through this great wilderness. These forty years the LORD your God has been with you. You have lacked nothing."'<sup>8</sup>So we went on, away from our brothers, the people of Esau, who live in Seir, away from the Arabah road from Elath and Ezion-geber. "And we turned and went in the direction of the wilderness of Moab.<sup>9</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle, for I will not give you any of their land for a possession, because I have given Ar to the people of Lot for a possession.'<sup>10</sup>(The Emim formerly lived there, a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim.<sup>11</sup>Like the Anakim they are also counted as Rephaim, but the Moabites call them Emim.<sup>12</sup>The Horites also lived in Seir formerly, but the people of Esau dispossessed them and destroyed them from before them and settled in their place, as Israel did to the land of their possession, which the LORD gave to them.)<sup>13</sup>'Now rise up and go over the brook Zered.' So we went over the brook Zered.<sup>14</sup>And the time from our leaving Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation, that is, the men of war, had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them.<sup>15</sup>For indeed the hand of the LORD was against them, to destroy them from the camp, until they had perished.<sup>16</sup>"So as soon as all the men of war had perished and were dead from among the people,<sup>17</sup>the LORD said to me,<sup>18</sup>'Today you are to cross the border of Moab at Ar.<sup>19</sup>And when you approach the territory of the people of Ammon, do not harass them or contend with them, for I will not give you any of the land of the people of Ammon as a possession, because I have given it to the sons of Lot for a possession.'<sup>20</sup>(It is also counted as a land of Rephaim. Rephaim formerly lived there—but the Ammonites call them Zamzummim—<sup>21</sup>a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim; but the LORD destroyed them before the Ammonites, and they dispossessed them and settled in their place,<sup>22</sup>as he did for the people of Esau, who live in Seir, when he destroyed the Horites before them and they dispossessed them and settled in their place even to this day.<sup>23</sup>As for the Avvim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, the Caphtorim, who came from Caphtor, destroyed them and settled in their place.)<sup>24</sup>'Rise up, set out on your journey and go over the Valley of the Arnon. Behold, I have given into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land. Begin to take possession, and contend with him in battle.<sup>25</sup>This day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you on the peoples who are under the whole heaven, who shall hear the report of you and shall tremble and be in anguish because of you.'<sup>26</sup>"So I sent messengers from the wilderness of Kedemoth to Sihon the king of Heshbon, with words of peace, saying,<sup>27</sup>'Let me pass through your land. I will go only by the road; I will turn aside neither to the right nor to the left.<sup>28</sup>You shall sell me food for money, that I may eat, and give me water for money, that I may drink. Only let me pass through on foot,<sup>29</sup>as the sons of Esau who live in Seir and the Moabites who live in Ar did for me, until I go over the Jordan into the land that the LORD our God is giving to us.'<sup>30</sup>But Sihon the king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him, for the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, that he might give him into your hand, as he is this day.<sup>31</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'Behold, I have begun to give Sihon and his land over to you. Begin to take possession, that you may occupy his land.'<sup>32</sup>Then Sihon came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Jahaz.<sup>33</sup>And the LORD our God gave him over to us, and we defeated him and his sons and all his people.<sup>34</sup>And we captured all his cities at that time and devoted to destruction every city, men, women, and children. We left no survivors.<sup>35</sup>Only the livestock we took as spoil for ourselves, with the plunder of the cities that we captured.<sup>36</sup>From Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the city that is in the valley, as far as Gilead, there was not a city too high for us. The LORD our God gave all into our hands.<sup>37</sup>Only to the land of the sons of Ammon you did not draw near, that is, to all the banks of the river Jabbok and the cities of the hill country, whatever the LORD our God had forbidden us.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 carries the sermon from the wasted years to the renewed march. The wilderness generation has died, and the new one moves north. As they go a striking theme emerges: the LORD is not merely Israel’s God but the ruler of all nations. He has given Edom to Esau’s descendants, and Moab and Ammon to Lot’s sons, and Israel must not touch them. It is a stunning expansion of vision: the whole map of the ancient Near East is his handiwork.

The chapter turns at Sihon king of Heshbon, the first enemy God hands over to Israel. The God who restrained Israel from Edom now sends them against the Amorites, for the timing of judgment is his alone.

For us, chapter 2 enlarges our God. He is no tribal deity but the Lord of history, ruling the rise and fall of every people, and his purpose for the spared nations did not end with boundaries: Ruth the Moabitess became an ancestor of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), and Amos foresaw a remnant of Edom called by the LORD’s name, a promise James quotes as fulfilled when Gentiles turned to Christ (Amos 9:11–12; Acts 15:16–17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Passing By Edom: Land You May Not Take
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel skirts the territory of Esau’s descendants, forbidden to provoke them, for the LORD has given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s rule extends to all nations. He grants lands even to peoples outside the covenant line, and holds his own people to respecting them.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel paid for Edom’s food and water rather than seizing them. God’s people still honour boundaries and deal fairly with those they could overpower.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then we turned and journeyed into the wilderness in the direction of the Red Sea, as the LORD told me. And for many days we traveled around Mount Seir. Then the LORD said to me, 'You have been traveling around this mountain country long enough. Turn northward
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirty-eight years in a sentence, and the word around is exactly right: they were not going anywhere. They circled a mountain while a generation died.

Then: You have been traveling around this mountain country long enough. In 1:6 God had said You have stayed long enough at this mountain of Sinai, the place of glory. Here the same words are spoken over a wilderness of failure: God ends both seasons with the identical sentence. He will not let his people settle permanently on their highest day, and he will not leave them permanently in their worst one.

The wandering had a term. From inside, every year looked like the last, and nobody could have said how much longer. But God knew the day he would say turn northward, and he said it. Anyone in a season that seems to have no edge should notice that this verse exists. The circling was not aimless to God, even when it was indistinguishable from aimless to them.

verseByVerse.quote: and command the people, "You are about to pass through the territory of your brothers, the people of Esau, who live in Seir; and they will be afraid of you. So be very careful. Do not contend with them, for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession. You shall purchase food from them with money, that you may eat, and you shall also buy water from them with money, that you may drink. For the LORD your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands. He knows your going through this great wilderness. These forty years the LORD your God has been with you. You have lacked nothing."' So we went on, away from our brothers, the people of Esau, who live in Seir, away from the Arabah road from Elath and Ezion-geber. "And we turned and went in the direction of the wilderness of Moab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first order to the newly turned nation is a restraint: not so much ground as for the sole of the foot to tread on. Six hundred thousand fighting men may not take a single pace of Edomite ground. And they pay for food and water: the nation on its way to conquer Canaan walks past the brother who had refused them the road (Num. 20:18–21) and buys its dinner at the going rate.

Consider whose land this is. Esau despised his birthright (Heb. 12:16), and God gave him a country and defends his title against the covenant people. The Lord who chooses is not careless of those he did not choose. He made from one man every nation of mankind… having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place (Acts 17:26). No square mile on earth is the business of its inhabitants alone.

And in the middle sits an extraordinary sentence: You have lacked nothing. Forty years of judgment, and he says they lacked nothing. That is a hard thing to say over a generation of funerals, and it is true. The discipline was real; so was the daily bread, all the way through.
verseByVerse.note: Edom, Moab and Ammon were Israel’s relatives, descended from Esau and Lot; Israel was not to take their land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Passing By Moab: The Old Giants Displaced
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is likewise forbidden to harass Moab, whose land God gave to Lot’s descendants, and Moses notes how God had earlier displaced the giant Emim and other ancient peoples to settle these nations.
verseByVerse.theology: God displaces one people to settle another according to purposes he does not always explain, and the death of the wilderness generation keeps his solemn oath (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.examples: God moved the old giants out to make room for nations that had no covenant with him. When the movements of nations bewilder us, we can trust the same God to be ruling them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, 'Do not harass Moab or contend with them in battle, for I will not give you any of their land for a possession, because I have given Ar to the people of Lot for a possession.' (The Emim formerly lived there, a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim. Like the Anakim they are also counted as Rephaim, but the Moabites call them Emim. The Horites also lived in Seir formerly, but the people of Esau dispossessed them and destroyed them from before them and settled in their place, as Israel did to the land of their possession, which the LORD gave to them.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab next, the people of Lot: Abraham’s nephew, who chose the well-watered plain and ended in Sodom, and whose line came out of a cave and a drunken night that Scripture reports without approval (Gen. 19:30–38). That family gets a country too, and God will not have it touched.

Then a historian’s aside doing serious work. The Emim were giants, the text says, of the same stock as the Anakim whose name made the spies at Kadesh go to pieces. And God cleared them out of Moab for Lot’s descendants.

While Israel’s fathers stood at Kadesh saying the giants were too big, God had been dispossessing giants routinely, for centuries, in that very neighbourhood, for nations with no covenant and no promise. The thing that paralysed the people of God had never once given him any trouble at all.

Were these literally giants? They were peoples remembered as unusually tall and strong, like the Anakim (compare Goliath, 1 Samuel 17:4). The text describes men, not monsters, and names such as Emim and Zamzummim were what their neighbours called them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Now rise up and go over the brook Zered.' So we went over the brook Zered. And the time from our leaving Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation, that is, the men of war, had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them. For indeed the hand of the LORD was against them, to destroy them from the camp, until they had perished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A brook, not a river: a seasonal stream a man steps over. That is the boundary God set for the end of a generation, and it took thirty-eight years to reach it.

Verse 15 should not be softened: the hand of the LORD was against them. Every funeral in that camp was the hand of God, and Moses says so to their children’s faces. Modern readers want to reword it; it should stand, because Scripture never treats God’s judgments as an embarrassment to be managed.

But look who is being told. The listeners are the boys who dug those graves, now told what it meant. God buried a generation of redeemed people who would not trust him, and then walked their sons across the stream. Both halves are the same God, and the New Testament puts them in one sentence: Note then the kindness and the severity of God (Rom. 11:22).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–25 — The Command to Begin: Ammon Spared, Sihon Devoted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After sparing Ammon too, God commands Israel to begin taking possession, starting with Sihon king of Heshbon, and promises to put dread of Israel upon the peoples.
verseByVerse.theology: God alone sets the time for judgment and conquest. He goes before his people, and the fear of him reaches the nations before they do.
verseByVerse.examples: God said, This day I will begin (v. 25). His kingdom still advances on his timetable, not ours, and he still goes ahead of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: "So as soon as all the men of war had perished and were dead from among the people, the LORD said to me, 'Today you are to cross the border of Moab at Ar. And when you approach the territory of the people of Ammon, do not harass them or contend with them, for I will not give you any of the land of the people of Ammon as a possession, because I have given it to the sons of Lot for a possession.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A third nation placed out of reach: Edom, Moab, Ammon. Not yours; I gave it to somebody else. The repetition is the point, because Israel is about to be told to take a country by force, and God first establishes that this is no licence for acquisition. A land-grab does not begin by ruling out three softer targets on the way. Israel took the ground God gave and no other, and the boundary was not drawn by what she could reach.

There is a quieter application. Much of a Christian’s life consists of walking past things genuinely good and obtainable, because they were assigned to somebody else. The tenth commandment exists for this. So does contentment, which is not the belief that others’ portions are worthless but the settled conviction that God has allotted them on purpose, and has given us in Christ more than any field. Paul learned it as a secret, through the one who strengthens me (Phil. 4:13), and it is learned the same way still.

verseByVerse.quote: (It is also counted as a land of Rephaim. Rephaim formerly lived there—but the Ammonites call them Zamzummim— a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim; but the LORD destroyed them before the Ammonites, and they dispossessed them and settled in their place, as he did for the people of Esau, who live in Seir, when he destroyed the Horites before them and they dispossessed them and settled in their place even to this day. As for the Avvim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, the Caphtorim, who came from Caphtor, destroyed them and settled in their place.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another parenthesis, the same drumbeat: Rephaim, Zamzummim, Avvim, Caphtorim, people after people displaced by God in four verses, none of it Israel’s doing.

The cumulative effect is a view of history. The map that looked to everyone on it like the permanent shape of things was being redrawn constantly by a God most of those nations had never heard of. Empires think they are the subject of the sentence. In Scripture they are the object.

That steadies any century: It is he who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers… who brings princes to nothing, and makes the rulers of the earth as emptiness (Isa. 40:22–23). The Zamzummim were the great power of their valley, and we cannot even pronounce their name with confidence.
verseByVerse.note: The Rephaim were a people remembered for their great height.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Rise up, set out on your journey and go over the Valley of the Arnon. Behold, I have given into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land. Begin to take possession, and contend with him in battle. This day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you on the peoples who are under the whole heaven, who shall hear the report of you and shall tremble and be in anguish because of you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
After all the restraint, the word changes. Begin. After forty years of not beginning, the first real order to advance.

The order of the clauses governs everything that follows: I have given comes before begin to take. The gift is announced in the past tense before a sword is drawn. Israel is not fighting to obtain something but to take up something already handed over: the difference between an army hoping and an army collecting.

The same grammar runs through the New Testament and grounds Christian effort: Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Phil. 2:12–13). The working out is real and strenuous. It is never the means of getting what God has not already given, and the power for it is his own, working within.

Then the promise widens: God will put the dread of Israel on the peoples. He fights this war in the minds of Canaan before Israel arrives, and Rahab will soon describe it from the inside: our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man (Josh. 2:11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–37 — The Defeat of Sihon: The First Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses offers Sihon peace, but God hardens his heart; he comes out to battle and is defeated, the first fruits of the conquest.
verseByVerse.theology: God offers terms of peace and also hardens hearts to carry out his judgment; how the two fit together is taken up at verses 26–30.
verseByVerse.examples: Sihon’s refusal of peace sealed his doom. The gospel goes out with a genuine offer of peace, and it is the refusal of that offer, not any lack of welcome in it, that ripens into judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "So I sent messengers from the wilderness of Kedemoth to Sihon the king of Heshbon, with words of peace, saying, 'Let me pass through your land. I will go only by the road; I will turn aside neither to the right nor to the left. You shall sell me food for money, that I may eat, and give me water for money, that I may drink. Only let me pass through on foot, as the sons of Esau who live in Seir and the Moabites who live in Ar did for me, until I go over the Jordan into the land that the LORD our God is giving to us.' But Sihon the king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him, for the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, that he might give him into your hand, as he is this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s first war opens with an offer of peace: the same modest, genuine request Edom refused. Sihon says no, and the text says something that stops every honest reader: the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate. Here Deuteronomy first raises the hardest question about the will of God and the will of man, and we should not pretend it is simple.

Begin with what Scripture does not say. It never says God put a desire for evil into a good man. Sihon was an Amorite warlord who had taken Heshbon by conquest (Num. 21:26) and marched out to attack a nation that had asked to use a road. What God hardened was already there.

The parallel case is handled carefully. Of Pharaoh, Exodus says God will harden his heart (Exod. 4:21), Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exod. 8:15), and God hardened it (Exod. 9:12): both asserted, without embarrassment and without resolution. Paul sharpens it rather than smoothing it: So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills, and voices our objection, Why does he still find fault? (Rom. 9:18–19).

What can be said with confidence: God never makes a man sin; every man hardened is hardened in what he already wanted. And God is no spectator of wickedness; he governs it, and it serves his purposes. Both truths stand, and the line where they meet is not shown us. Anyone who has tidied this into a system has almost certainly dropped half of what the text says.

Verse 29 says Edom sold Israel food, while Numbers says Edom refused passage (Num 20:14–21). Both are true: Edom refused the main road through its land, so Israel went round its borders, and along the edge Edom and Moab sold them food and water.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, 'Behold, I have begun to give Sihon and his land over to you. Begin to take possession, that you may occupy his land.' Then Sihon came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Jahaz. And the LORD our God gave him over to us, and we defeated him and his sons and all his people. And we captured all his cities at that time and devoted to destruction every city, men, women, and children. We left no survivors. Only the livestock we took as spoil for ourselves, with the plunder of the cities that we captured. From Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the city that is in the valley, as far as Gilead, there was not a city too high for us. The LORD our God gave all into our hands. Only to the land of the sons of Ammon you did not draw near, that is, to all the banks of the river Jabbok and the cities of the hill country, whatever the LORD our God had forbidden us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The battle is over in a verse. Israel fought, we defeated him, and the credit is placed with God in the same sentence.

Then the hard part: the cities were devoted to destruction. Deuteronomy sets out the grounds in chapters 7 and 20; two things belong here. The judgment is God’s, executed through Israel at a fixed moment for a stated reason: the Amorites are judged for four centuries of accumulated wickedness, at the end of a delay God imposed while it ripened (Gen. 15:16). And it is no pattern for anybody: no nation since has held that commission, and the New Testament removes the possibility (2 Cor. 10:3–4).

The chapter ends with a boundary: Only to the land of the sons of Ammon you did not draw near. In the flush of a first victory the restraint holds. An army that has tasted success and can still be told “not that” is the difference between a nation under orders and a nation on the make.

But women and children? The judgment fell on a whole people, as the flood and Sodom did, and the Judge of all the earth has the right to take any life (Gen 18:25). Those who turned to the LORD, like Rahab, were spared (Josh 6:25). This was a unique command for that moment, never a pattern: the law itself forbids punishing children for their fathers’ crimes in human courts (24:16).
verseByVerse.note: “Devoted to destruction” means set apart to the LORD for destruction (ESV note).

2.theology:
The sovereignty of God over all nations. Three times God forbids Israel to seize the lands of Edom, Moab, and Ammon, because he himself allotted them (2:5, 9, 19). The God of Israel rules the boundaries of every people (Acts 17:26), raising up and casting down, displacing giants to settle nations according to his hidden counsel.

Divine hardening and human responsibility. Sihon refuses peace of his own pride, yet “the LORD your God hardened his spirit” (2:30). Scripture holds both together, as with Pharaoh: God’s righteous judgment is accomplished even through the free rebellion of the wicked (see vv. 26–30).

The faithful provision of God. Through forty years in “this great wilderness,” God was with his people and “you have lacked nothing” (2:7). The Lord of history is also the shepherd who counts every need of his children.
2.examples:
Then: Israel marched north under restraint, buying food from Edom and sparing Moab and Ammon, until the appointed hour came for Sihon.

Now: We serve the Lord of all nations, whose kingdom advances on his timetable with a genuine offer of peace in the gospel. His people go forward certain that every enemy is already “given over” in Christ, who has disarmed the powers and goes before us to the final victory.

3.title: Victories East of the Jordan: ‘It Is Enough for You’
3.text: <sup>1</sup>"Then we turned and went up the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei.<sup>2</sup>But the LORD said to me, 'Do not fear him, for I have given him and all his people and his land into your hand. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon.'<sup>3</sup>So the LORD our God gave into our hand Og also, the king of Bashan, and all his people, and we struck him down until he had no survivor left.<sup>4</sup>And we took all his cities at that time—there was not a city that we did not take from them—sixty cities, the whole region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan.<sup>5</sup>All these were cities fortified with high walls, gates, and bars, besides very many unwalled villages.<sup>6</sup>And we devoted them to destruction, as we did to Sihon the king of Heshbon, devoting to destruction every city, men, women, and children.<sup>7</sup>But all the livestock and the spoil of the cities we took as our plunder.<sup>8</sup>So we took the land at that time out of the hand of the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon<sup>9</sup>(the Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, while the Amorites call it Senir),<sup>10</sup>all the cities of the tableland and all Gilead and all Bashan, as far as Salecah and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan.<sup>11</sup>(For only Og the king of Bashan was left of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bed was a bed of iron. Is it not in Rabbah of the Ammonites? Nine cubits was its length, and four cubits its breadth, according to the common cubit.)<sup>12</sup>"When we took possession of this land at that time, I gave to the Reubenites and the Gadites the territory beginning at Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and half the hill country of Gilead with its cities.<sup>13</sup>The rest of Gilead, and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og, that is, all the region of Argob, I gave to the half-tribe of Manasseh. (All that portion of Bashan is called the land of Rephaim.<sup>14</sup>Jair the Manassite took all the region of Argob, that is, Bashan, as far as the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and called the villages after his own name, Havvoth-jair, as it is to this day.)<sup>15</sup>To Machir I gave Gilead,<sup>16</sup>and to the Reubenites and the Gadites I gave the territory from Gilead as far as the Valley of the Arnon, with the middle of the valley as a border, as far over as the river Jabbok, the border of the Ammonites;<sup>17</sup>the Arabah also, with the Jordan as the border, from Chinnereth as far as the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, under the slopes of Pisgah on the east.<sup>18</sup>"And I commanded you at that time, saying, 'The LORD your God has given you this land to possess. All your men of valor shall cross over armed before your brothers, the people of Israel.<sup>19</sup>Only your wives, your little ones, and your livestock (I know that you have much livestock) shall remain in the cities that I have given you,<sup>20</sup>until the LORD gives rest to your brothers, as to you, and they also occupy the land that the LORD your God gives them beyond the Jordan. Then each of you may return to his possession which I have given you.'<sup>21</sup>And I commanded Joshua at that time, 'Your eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings. So will the LORD do to all the kingdoms into which you are crossing.<sup>22</sup>You shall not fear them, for it is the LORD your God who fights for you.'<sup>23</sup>"And I pleaded with the LORD at that time, saying,<sup>24</sup>'O Lord GOD, you have only begun to show your servant your greatness and your mighty hand. For what god is there in heaven or on earth who can do such works and mighty acts as yours?<sup>25</sup>Please let me go over and see the good land beyond the Jordan, that good hill country and Lebanon.'<sup>26</sup>But the LORD was angry with me because of you and would not listen to me. And the LORD said to me, 'Enough from you; do not speak to me of this matter again.<sup>27</sup>Go up to the top of Pisgah and lift up your eyes westward and northward and southward and eastward, and look at it with your eyes, for you shall not go over this Jordan.<sup>28</sup>But charge Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him, for he shall go over at the head of this people, and he shall put them in possession of the land that you shall see.'<sup>29</sup>So we remained in the valley opposite Beth-peor.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 completes the eastern conquests with the defeat of Og king of Bashan, the last of the giants, and the allotment of his land to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. Og’s great iron bed, kept as a curiosity, testifies to the size of the foe and the greatness of the God who felled him.

Then the chapter turns personal. Moses pleads to cross the Jordan and see the good land, one of the most poignant prayers in Scripture, and God’s answer is a firm no. Yet even the refusal comes with gifts: Moses may see the land from Pisgah, and he is to commission and encourage Joshua.

The book’s great theme deepens: the mediator of the law cannot bring the people into the inheritance. Hebrews adds that even Joshua did not give the final rest (Hebrews 4:8); that was kept for the greater Joshua, whose Hebrew name is the same. The chapter holds both the triumph of a God who fights for us and the hard mystery of a prayer refused, where God’s “no” is itself wrapped in fatherly love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Defeat of Og: The Last of the Giants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel defeats Og king of Bashan, the last of the Rephaim, and takes his fortified cities, as with Sihon.
verseByVerse.theology: No enemy, however great, can stand before the LORD who fights for his people; the giants of legend fall before him.
verseByVerse.examples: The fear that broke the fathers was overcome by their sons. What once terrified us, and what God has since brought us through, is evidence to hold up against the next fear.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then we turned and went up the way to Bashan. And Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei. But the LORD said to me, 'Do not fear him, for I have given him and all his people and his land into your hand. And you shall do to him as you did to Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon.' So the LORD our God gave into our hand Og also, the king of Bashan, and all his people, and we struck him down until he had no survivor left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of all the enemies Israel could have met first, this is the worst. Og was the last of the Rephaim, the giant stock that made the spies at Kadesh say we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers (Num. 13:33). The terror that destroyed their parents comes down the road at them in person, in the first campaign of their lives.

Look at God’s argument. Not “he is smaller than he looks,” not “you are stronger than you think,” but: you have just seen me do this to Sihon. The cure for fear is not a reassessment of the enemy but a memory of God.

And it worked. The fathers ran from giants they had only heard described; their sons killed one. Nothing had changed about the giants.

verseByVerse.quote: And we took all his cities at that time—there was not a city that we did not take from them—sixty cities, the whole region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan. All these were cities fortified with high walls, gates, and bars, besides very many unwalled villages. And we devoted them to destruction, as we did to Sihon the king of Heshbon, devoting to destruction every city, men, women, and children. But all the livestock and the spoil of the cities we took as our plunder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read 1:28 beside this. The report that broke the nation at Kadesh was The cities are great and fortified up to heaven. Here are sixty of them, fortified with high walls, gates, and bars, and the summary is that not one was left untaken. What their fathers called insurmountable their sons list like an inventory.

The walls had not got lower; the text insists on how strong Bashan’s cities were. What changed was that this generation went up when God said go. Most Christians spend much of life in front of some wall. The question is almost never whether the obstacle is real. Israel’s fathers were right about the walls and wrong about God, and being right about the walls did not save them.

As with Sihon (2:34), this was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened, carried out once through Israel. Those who turned to the LORD were spared, and it is no pattern for any later war.

verseByVerse.quote: So we took the land at that time out of the hand of the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon (the Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, while the Amorites call it Senir), all the cities of the tableland and all Gilead and all Bashan, as far as Salecah and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan. (For only Og the king of Bashan was left of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bed was a bed of iron. Is it not in Rabbah of the Ammonites? Nine cubits was its length, and four cubits its breadth, according to the common cubit.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator stops for a museum note, a strange and human touch. Nine cubits by four, something over thirteen feet by six, and iron, rare and costly in that age. And the aside is almost conversational: Is it not in Rabbah? You can go and look at it.

Some think the “bed” was a basalt coffin; either way the point is the same. Before long the only thing left of the last of the Rephaim was a piece of furniture for tourists to stare at. The man who came out at Edrei with an army had become an exhibit.

Scripture does this repeatedly with what frightens people. It does not deny they were frightening; it tells you what became of them. Pharaoh’s chariots are on the sea floor. Og’s bed is in a museum. And the last enemy is described in the same register: O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting? (1 Cor. 15:55).
verseByVerse.note: Rabbah was the Ammonite capital, on the site of modern Amman.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — The Land Allotted; ‘The LORD Fights for You’
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses allots the eastern land to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, charging their fighting men to cross and help their brothers first, for the LORD fights for them.
verseByVerse.theology: The people of God are one body: no tribe may rest in its own inheritance while its brothers still fight for theirs.
verseByVerse.examples: The eastern tribes had to fight for their brothers before enjoying their own land. Christians cannot settle into private comfort while the rest of the body still labours.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we took possession of this land at that time, I gave to the Reubenites and the Gadites the territory beginning at Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and half the hill country of Gilead with its cities. The rest of Gilead, and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og, that is, all the region of Argob, I gave to the half-tribe of Manasseh. (All that portion of Bashan is called the land of Rephaim. Jair the Manassite took all the region of Argob, that is, Bashan, as far as the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and called the villages after his own name, Havvoth-jair, as it is to this day.) To Machir I gave Gilead, and to the Reubenites and the Gadites I gave the territory from Gilead as far as the Valley of the Arnon, with the middle of the valley as a border, as far over as the river Jabbok, the border of the Ammonites; the Arabah also, with the Jordan as the border, from Chinnereth as far as the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, under the slopes of Pisgah on the east.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six verses of surveying, here because this is the first land any Israelite has owned since Egypt: four centuries there, forty years of tents, and now somebody has a deed. God’s gifts are not received in a heap but measured out and written down.

It also proves something. Moses is about to ask them to trust God for a country across a river, and the argument is not theoretical: they can walk out of the assembly and stand on the first instalment.

God often works that way. The full inheritance is still across the water, but something is already in hand as a pledge. Paul calls the Spirit exactly that: the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it (Eph. 1:14).

verseByVerse.quote: "And I commanded you at that time, saying, 'The LORD your God has given you this land to possess. All your men of valor shall cross over armed before your brothers, the people of Israel. Only your wives, your little ones, and your livestock (I know that you have much livestock) shall remain in the cities that I have given you, until the LORD gives rest to your brothers, as to you, and they also occupy the land that the LORD your God gives them beyond the Jordan. Then each of you may return to his possession which I have given you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eastern tribes have their land, and at once the condition: their fighting men go over the Jordan in the front rank, into a war they have nothing to gain from, until the LORD gives rest to your brothers, as to you.

Rest is one of the great words of this book: not merely the end of fighting but a people settled at home, everyone on his own ground. It is what the exodus was for. And nobody gets it early. That is the force of as to you. In God’s reckoning rest is one thing belonging to one people, not a private arrangement each family reaches separately.

Hebrews builds a whole argument on the word, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God (Heb. 4:9), and keeps its corporate shape. No Christian arrives home alone. The command is a description of belonging to God’s people: you do not sit down while your brothers are still fighting. And the pattern is Christ’s before it is ours: he who had every right to rest crossed over for brothers who could not win their own inheritance, and his Spirit now makes his people willing to do the same for one another.

verseByVerse.quote: And I commanded Joshua at that time, 'Your eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings. So will the LORD do to all the kingdoms into which you are crossing. You shall not fear them, for it is the LORD your God who fights for you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge to Joshua makes three moves, and the order matters. First, what he has seen with his own eyes, not been told, in Sihon and Og. Second, the inference: So will the LORD do to everything across the river. Third, the conclusion for the heart: You shall not fear them.

That is how Scripture deals with fear. It does not tell a man to feel braver. It points him to something God has actually done in his own past and reasons forward from it. Faith here is not a mood; it is an argument with a memory in the first premise.

And the last clause takes the weight off Joshua entirely: it is the LORD your God who fights for you. He is handed a nation and a war and told the outcome does not finally rest on him. Every leader who has lain awake over something too big should notice that this is the last thing Moses says to his successor before he prays about his own death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — Moses’ Plea Denied: ‘It Is Enough for You’
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses pleads to cross over and see the land, but the LORD refuses, telling him to view it from Pisgah and commission Joshua.
verseByVerse.theology: Even the greatest mediator of the old covenant cannot bring God’s people into the inheritance, and God’s refusal of his servant is not the end of his kindness to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses saw the land but could not enter it. When our own prayers meet a closed door we are not abandoned, and the One who brings God’s people home is greater than Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I pleaded with the LORD at that time, saying, 'O Lord GOD, you have only begun to show your servant your greatness and your mighty hand. For what god is there in heaven or on earth who can do such works and mighty acts as yours? Please let me go over and see the good land beyond the Jordan, that good hill country and Lebanon.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the most affecting prayers in the Old Testament. The verb pleaded is the one used for asking for grace: the plea of a man with no claim who asks anyway.

Moses is nearly a hundred and twenty. He has seen the bush burn, the sea open, the mountain shake, the glory fill the tent, bread fall from the sky for forty years, and has spoken with God as a man with his friend. And he calls it only begun. There is no trace in him of a man who feels he has seen enough. Long acquaintance with God has not dulled the appetite. The old man is the hungriest believer in the camp.

And the request is almost childlike. He does not ask to lead the conquest or have Meribah reversed on the record. He asks to cross a river and look at some hills. Forty years of carrying this nation, and what he wants is to see the place he has been walking toward.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD was angry with me because of you and would not listen to me. And the LORD said to me, 'Enough from you; do not speak to me of this matter again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God says no, and then tells Moses to stop asking. There is no way to make that comfortable, and it should not be attempted. The friend of God prays a humble, modest, good request, and the answer is a closed door.

Anyone who has prayed for years about one thing knows the size of this verse. Scripture does not hide such cases. Paul asked three times for a thorn to be removed and was told My grace is sufficient for you (2 Cor. 12:8–9). David fasted seven days for a child who died (2 Sam. 12:16–18). And the Lord Jesus in Gethsemane asked three times for a cup to pass, and drank it (Matt. 26:39–44). No one is exempt, including him.

Two things must be held together. God’s refusals are real refusals, and pretending otherwise wrecks faith when the answer comes back no. And God’s refusals are not the last word about the person refused.
