Because the end of this is not on the far side of the Jordan. Some fourteen centuries later, three disciples woke on a mountain in that country and saw two men talking with Jesus, and one was Moses (Luke 9:30–31). He got into the land. He came in through the front door, in glory, in company with the Christ he had served: not because the no was reversed, but because it was never the whole account. What God refused him was a walk among some hills. What God had in mind was standing next to his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Go up to the top of Pisgah and lift up your eyes westward and northward and southward and eastward, and look at it with your eyes, for you shall not go over this Jordan. But charge Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him, for he shall go over at the head of this people, and he shall put them in possession of the land that you shall see.' So we remained in the valley opposite Beth-peor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The no is not bare. Three things come with it.

First, a sight: Moses is to look in all four directions from Pisgah and take in the whole land. God will not let him enter, and will not let him die without seeing. That kindness cost nothing to withhold, and God gives it anyway.

Second, a task: to strengthen Joshua, who will do the very thing Moses has just been forbidden, in the land that you shall see. There is no hint that he resented it. His last months are spent making his successor braver.

Third, easily missed, the location: opposite Beth-peor, the shadow of Numbers 25, where twenty-four thousand died over Baal of Peor. Deuteronomy is preached from a valley facing Israel’s worst failure, and the whole book pleads with them not to do it again. When Moses dies, God buries him there (Deut. 34:6), in sight of the place where his people betrayed their God, by the God who never once betrayed them.
verseByVerse.note: Pisgah is the ridge of Mount Nebo, overlooking the Jordan valley.

3.theology:
The LORD fights for his people. The defeat of Og and the charge to Joshua rest on one truth: it is the LORD your God who fights for you (3:22). Faith for the future is built on God’s remembered faithfulness in the past; the giants behind us assure us of victory over the giants ahead.

The mediator who cannot bring them in. Moses pleads to enter the land and is refused (3:26). The greatest prophet of the old covenant dies outside, for the law cannot carry anyone into the rest; that is left to the One the law points to.

God’s refusals. God’s no to Moses was real, and Scripture does not soften it. But it was not cruelty, and it was not the last word: Moses would yet stand in the land beside Christ (see v. 26). A believer whose prayer has been refused may grieve honestly and still trust the One who sees what we cannot.
3.examples:
Then: Israel watched the last giant fall and the eastern land divided, while Moses climbed Pisgah to see a land he would never enter and handed the work to Joshua.

Now: we face our own giants knowing the Lord fights for us, and remembering what he has already brought us through. We pray boldly, and when the answer is no, we may grieve it, as Moses did, without letting go of God. And we rest our hope not in the law that brings us to the border but in Jesus, who carries us across into the everlasting inheritance.

4.title: The God Who Speaks: ‘What Great Nation Has a God So Near?’
4.text: <sup>1</sup>"And now, O Israel, listen to the statutes and the rules that I am teaching you, and do them, that you may live, and go in and take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, is giving you.<sup>2</sup>You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it, that you may keep the commandments of the LORD your God that I command you.<sup>3</sup>Your eyes have seen what the LORD did at Baal-peor, for the LORD your God destroyed from among you all the men who followed the Baal of Peor.<sup>4</sup>But you who held fast to the LORD your God are all alive today.<sup>5</sup>See, I have taught you statutes and rules, as the LORD my God commanded me, that you should do them in the land that you are entering to take possession of it.<sup>6</sup>Keep them and do them, for that will be your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples, who, when they hear all these statutes, will say, 'Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.'<sup>7</sup>For what great nation is there that has a god so near to it as the LORD our God is to us, whenever we call upon him?<sup>8</sup>And what great nation is there, that has statutes and rules so righteous as all this law that I set before you today?<sup>9</sup>"Only take care, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things that your eyes have seen, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life. Make them known to your children and your children's children—<sup>10</sup>how on the day that you stood before the LORD your God at Horeb, the LORD said to me, 'Gather the people to me, that I may let them hear my words, so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so.'<sup>11</sup>And you came near and stood at the foot of the mountain, while the mountain burned with fire to the heart of heaven, wrapped in darkness, cloud, and gloom.<sup>12</sup>Then the LORD spoke to you out of the midst of the fire. You heard the sound of words, but saw no form; there was only a voice.<sup>13</sup>And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, that is, the Ten Commandments, and he wrote them on two tablets of stone.<sup>14</sup>And the LORD commanded me at that time to teach you statutes and rules, that you might do them in the land that you are going over to possess.<sup>15</sup>"Therefore watch yourselves very carefully. Since you saw no form on the day that the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the midst of the fire,<sup>16</sup>beware lest you act corruptly by making a carved image for yourselves, in the form of any figure, the likeness of male or female,<sup>17</sup>the likeness of any animal that is on the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies in the air,<sup>18</sup>the likeness of anything that creeps on the ground, the likeness of any fish that is in the water under the earth.<sup>19</sup>And beware lest you raise your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, you be drawn away and bow down to them and serve them, things that the LORD your God has allotted to all the peoples under the whole heaven.<sup>20</sup>But the LORD has taken you and brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be a people of his own inheritance, as you are this day.<sup>21</sup>Furthermore, the LORD was angry with me because of you, and he swore that I should not cross the Jordan, and that I should not enter the good land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.<sup>22</sup>For I must die in this land; I must not go over the Jordan. But you shall go over and take possession of that good land.<sup>23</sup>Take care, lest you forget the covenant of the LORD your God, which he made with you, and make a carved image, the form of anything that the LORD your God has forbidden you.<sup>24</sup>For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.<sup>25</sup>"When you father children and children's children, and have grown old in the land, and you act corruptly by making a carved image in the form of anything, and by doing what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God, so as to provoke him to anger,<sup>26</sup>I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that you will soon utterly perish from the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess. You will not live long in it, but will be utterly destroyed.<sup>27</sup>And the LORD will scatter you among the peoples, and you will be left few in number among the nations where the LORD will drive you.<sup>28</sup>And there you will serve gods of wood and stone, the work of human hands, that neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.<sup>29</sup>But from there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul.<sup>30</sup>When you are in tribulation, and all these things come upon you in the latter days, you will return to the LORD your God and obey his voice.<sup>31</sup>For the LORD your God is a merciful God. He will not leave you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers that he swore to them.<sup>32</sup>"For ask now of the days that are past, which were before you, since the day that God created man on the earth, and ask from one end of heaven to the other, whether such a great thing as this has ever happened or was ever heard of.<sup>33</sup>Did any people ever hear the voice of a god speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and still live?<sup>34</sup>Or has any god ever attempted to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, and by war, by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and by great deeds of terror, all of which the LORD your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?<sup>35</sup>To you it was shown, that you might know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides him.<sup>36</sup>Out of heaven he let you hear his voice, that he might discipline you. And on earth he let you see his great fire, and you heard his words out of the midst of the fire.<sup>37</sup>And because he loved your fathers and chose their offspring after them and brought you out of Egypt with his own presence, by his great power,<sup>38</sup>driving out before you nations greater and mightier than you, to bring you in, to give you their land for an inheritance, as it is this day,<sup>39</sup>know therefore today, and lay it to your heart, that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other.<sup>40</sup>Therefore you shall keep his statutes and his commandments, which I command you today, that it may go well with you and with your children after you, and that you may prolong your days in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for all time."<sup>41</sup>Then Moses set apart three cities in the east beyond the Jordan,<sup>42</sup>that the manslayer might flee there, anyone who kills his neighbor unintentionally, without being at enmity with him in time past; he may flee to one of these cities and save his life:<sup>43</sup>Bezer in the wilderness on the tableland for the Reubenites, Ramoth in Gilead for the Gadites, and Golan in Bashan for the Manassites.<sup>44</sup>This is the law that Moses set before the people of Israel.<sup>45</sup>These are the testimonies, the statutes, and the rules, which Moses spoke to the people of Israel when they came out of Egypt,<sup>46</sup>beyond the Jordan in the valley opposite Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon, whom Moses and the people of Israel defeated when they came out of Egypt.<sup>47</sup>And they took possession of his land and the land of Og, the king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites, who lived to the east beyond the Jordan;<sup>48</sup>from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, as far as Mount Sirion (that is, Hermon),<sup>49</sup>together with all the Arabah on the east side of the Jordan as far as the Sea of the Arabah, under the slopes of Pisgah.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the climax of Moses’ first address. Having rehearsed the history, he presses home its meaning: the God who has done all this is utterly unique, and Israel’s response must be wholehearted obedience and exclusive worship. No other nation has laws so righteous, a God so near, a redemption so mighty.

At Sinai Israel heard words but saw no form (4:12). This is the foundation of the second commandment and of true worship: God revealed himself by his Word, not by an image. Moses warns with fierce tenderness against idolatry, knowing it will be Israel’s besetting sin and the cause of exile.

Yet even the warning of exile ends in hope: “from there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him” (4:29). The “consuming fire” and “jealous God” is also the merciful God who will not abandon his covenant. The chapter closes with cities of refuge and the confession that frames Israel’s faith: “the LORD is God; there is no other besides him” (4:35, 39). To know this God who speaks, and to obey his Word, is the highest privilege a creature can have.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Privilege of God’s Law and Nearness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses calls Israel to obey God’s statutes without adding or subtracting, for their obedience will display wisdom to the nations and reflect the unique privilege of a God so near and laws so righteous.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s law is a gift and a privilege, not a burden. Obeying it displays his wisdom and the nearness of a God unlike any other.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel’s obedience was meant to make the nations marvel at her God. The church’s holy life still commends the gospel to those who are watching.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O Israel, listen to the statutes and the rules that I am teaching you, and do them, that you may live, and go in and take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, is giving you. You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it, that you may keep the commandments of the LORD your God that I command you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three chapters of history end, and the sermon turns: And now. Moses has shown what God did; from here he shows what Israel is to do about it, and Scripture never reverses that order. Grace first, then the response.

Note the joint: do them, that you may live. Obedience is not the price of life; they are already redeemed, already carried, already on the border. It is the path of it. A man does not obey in order to be brought out of Egypt. He obeys because he has been. And the Old Testament itself promises where the power for that path will come from: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes and be careful to obey my rules (Ezek. 36:27).

Then a sentence that has shaped the doctrine of Scripture: You shall not add to the word… nor take from it. We usually fear only one direction. Taking away is the obvious sin. But adding is named first, and it is the one religious people commit. The Pharisees did not delete the law; they fenced it until the fence was heavier than what it protected, and Jesus told them the result: you leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men (Mark 7:8). Every generation adds something and then requires it, and the addition ends up obscuring what it was meant to guard. The last book of the Bible closes with the same guard at both ends (Rev. 22:18–19). God’s word is sufficient, and it is finished, and the reverence that will not subtract from it must also refuse to improve it.

Does this forbid the rest of the Bible? No. It forbids human additions or subtractions; God himself added his word through the prophets and apostles, and the canon closed with them (Rev 22:18–19). It also forbids raising church traditions to the level of God’s commands (Mark 7:7–8).

verseByVerse.quote: Your eyes have seen what the LORD did at Baal-peor, for the LORD your God destroyed from among you all the men who followed the Baal of Peor. But you who held fast to the LORD your God are all alive today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is not arguing from theory; he is pointing across the valley. Beth-peor is in sight, the graves are recent, and every man listening knows somebody in them (Num. 25:9).

Two verbs divide the living from the dead: some followed the Baal of Peor; others held fast to the LORD. The second is dabaq, to cling, to be glued to, what a man does to his wife when the two become one flesh (Gen. 2:24). It describes not an opinion but a grip.

The difference between the men in the graves and the men in the congregation was not intelligence, courage, upbringing or knowledge of the law. They grew up in the same camp and ate the same manna. What separated them was what they were holding on to when the invitation came. Anyone who has watched someone he respected fall a long way should notice: it was seldom a failure of information. And the grip itself is a gift: those who held fast were held first by the God who had carried them for forty years.

verseByVerse.quote: See, I have taught you statutes and rules, as the LORD my God commanded me, that you should do them in the land that you are entering to take possession of it. Keep them and do them, for that will be your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples, who, when they hear all these statutes, will say, 'Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s obedience is not private. It is evidence, and the nations are the jury.

What would the watching world see? Not a temple, an army, art or a great city. They would see how these people treated their poor, slaves, foreigners, debtors, animals and enemies, and the verdict, Moses says, will be wise. In the ancient world greatness was measured by what a nation could take. Moses says the peoples will look at a code that protects the widow, cancels debts every seventh year and orders you to return your enemy’s stray ox, and conclude that these people know how to live.

The same logic governs the church: let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16). Nobody is asked to argue the world into the kingdom. They are asked to live in a way that raises the question.

verseByVerse.quote: For what great nation is there that has a god so near to it as the LORD our God is to us, whenever we call upon him? And what great nation is there, that has statutes and rules so righteous as all this law that I set before you today?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two questions to the nations of the earth, never answered, and two boasts, the only ones Israel had: not size or power, but nearness and righteousness.

The gods of the ancient world were far off by definition: up a mountain, inside a temple only a priest could enter, reachable through ritual if you knew the procedure and could pay. Nobody expected a god to be near whenever we call upon him, with no conditions on the hour or the mood or the man.

And look who says it: former brick-makers in a valley with no country, capital, king or temple, told to name a nation better off. By every Moabite measure they had nothing. The claim is not that God had made them comfortable, but that he was close.

Fifteen centuries later a church of Gentiles was told, But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Eph. 2:13), and then invited: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb. 4:16). Israel could call whenever she liked, and God was near. The church is nearer still, and the distance was closed from his side, at his cost. Few religions make nearness their central boast. Most are about the climb.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — Remember Horeb: The God You Heard but Did Not See
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses urges Israel never to forget the day at Horeb when God spoke from the fire, and to teach it to their children, for they heard a voice but saw no form.
verseByVerse.theology: God makes himself known by his word rather than by any visible form, which is why hearing comes before seeing in true worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel was to tell her children what she had heard at the mountain. Christian parents still pass on the faith mostly by talking: about what God has said and what he has done.

verseByVerse.quote: "Only take care, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things that your eyes have seen, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life. Make them known to your children and your children's children— how on the day that you stood before the LORD your God at Horeb, the LORD said to me, 'Gather the people to me, that I may let them hear my words, so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great enemy in Deuteronomy is not persecution but forgetting, and Moses treats it as something to be actively guarded against. Keep your soul diligently is the language of a watchman on a wall.

Memory does not fail suddenly. It thins. The story gets shorter, the wonder becomes information, and one day a man finds he can recite what God did for him without any of it touching him. Nobody decides to forget; it is what happens to everything not deliberately kept.

And the timescale is your children and your children’s children: getting something across two handovers to people not yet born. The exodus generation saw the sea; their children saw the wilderness; their grandchildren would see only a settled country and hear what they were told. Israel’s knowledge of God depended on whether ordinary parents kept talking.

The purpose is not information transfer but that they may learn to fear me, reverent awe, and the proof it landed is that the next generation passes it on. Parents who have failed at this, as all have in part, should hear that the God of this chapter keeps his own covenant to a thousand generations; the telling is ours, but the giving of faith is his.

verseByVerse.quote: And you came near and stood at the foot of the mountain, while the mountain burned with fire to the heart of heaven, wrapped in darkness, cloud, and gloom. Then the LORD spoke to you out of the midst of the fire. You heard the sound of words, but saw no form; there was only a voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the theological centre of the chapter. Everything about the scene overwhelms the eye: a mountain on fire to the heart of heaven, wrapped in darkness, cloud and gloom, three words piled up. One of the most spectacular events in religious history, and the deliberate effect of the darkness is that there was nothing to look at. There was only a voice.

God revealed himself by speaking: not by a shape or a vision with edges, but by words, the way one person makes himself known to another. That fact grounds the second commandment, explains why Israel’s worship had no image at its centre when every other nation’s did, and why the Christian faith has been carried by preaching rather than spectacle. Faith comes from hearing (Rom. 10:17), because of Horeb.

But the New Testament does something with this no one at Sinai could have anticipated: No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known (John 1:18); the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). At the mountain there was a voice and no form. In Bethlehem the voice took a form. The God who would not be represented by anything he had made represented himself, in a body, once, and men who had eaten fish with him wrote of what we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands (1 John 1:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, that is, the Ten Commandments, and he wrote them on two tablets of stone. And the LORD commanded me at that time to teach you statutes and rules, that you might do them in the land that you are going over to possess.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two details mark the Ten Commandments off from the rest of the law. God spoke them directly to the whole nation, with no mediator; and he wrote them himself, on stone (Exod. 31:18), while Moses wrote the rest in a book (31:9, 24). Nothing else in Scripture was delivered like that. Whatever else the Ten Commandments are, they are the part of God’s law that he took the trouble to say out loud to everybody and to carve in rock. Verse 14 marks the distinction from the other side: the statutes and rules came through Moses. Both are God’s word; the manner of their giving differs, and the text is careful about it.

The key word is covenant. These are not ten pieces of advice or a moral system detached from a relationship. They are the terms of a bond between a God who had already rescued this people and a people who now belonged to him, which is why the first thing the fire said was not a command but a reminder: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.note: “The Ten Commandments” is literally “the ten words” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Warning Against Idolatry: A Consuming Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because they saw no form, Israel must make no idol; God is a jealous, consuming fire, and idolatry will bring exile.
verseByVerse.theology: Because God showed no form, any image of him is a lie about him, and turning to idols is unfaithfulness to the God who has bound himself to his people.
verseByVerse.examples: Few of us are tempted by carved images, but every heart makes idols of its own: good things loved in God’s place, and false pictures of God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore watch yourselves very carefully. Since you saw no form on the day that the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the midst of the fire, beware lest you act corruptly by making a carved image for yourselves, in the form of any figure, the likeness of male or female, the likeness of any animal that is on the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies in the air, the likeness of anything that creeps on the ground, the likeness of any fish that is in the water under the earth. And beware lest you raise your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, you be drawn away and bow down to them and serve them, things that the LORD your God has allotted to all the peoples under the whole heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The argument hangs on one word: since. Because God showed no shape, to give him a shape is to say something false about him. That is what an idol is: not primarily a rival to God but a lie about him, a statement in wood or stone that he is like this, when he never said so.

The catalogue runs in a particular order: male or female, beast, bird, creeping thing, fish, roughly reversing Genesis 1. Moses walks back down the ladder of creation, ruling out every rung, because every idol is a piece of creation promoted. Then he raises his eyes to sun, moon and stars, the cleanest things in the visible world and worshipped by nearly every ancient civilisation. They too are on the wrong side of the line; they were made on the fourth day.

Readers stumble over the phrase that these are allotted to all the peoples. The most natural sense is that God gave the heavenly lights to all mankind, for light and seasons (Gen. 1:14). He gave them not as gods but as lamps, to everybody.

Almost nobody reading this owns a carved image. The commandment is really about the picture of God a man carries in his head, assembled from his father, temperament, culture and preferences, and then treated as the real thing. That is a carved image, carved where you cannot see it. The test is the same as at Horeb: has God said he is like that, or have you decided it?

Does this forbid pictures of Jesus or religious art? It forbids any image made to represent God or to be used in worship, since Israel saw no form (Deut 4:15). God himself commanded art for the tabernacle, including cherubim (Exod 25:18), so art as such is not forbidden. Christians differ over pictures of Christ: many hold that since he took a real body he may be depicted, especially for teaching; the Reformed confessions (the Westminster Larger Catechism, question 109, for example) answer that no image can show the person who is God and man, and that images used in worship break this commandment. The Reformed caution is the safer course: no image of Christ in worship or as an aid to prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD has taken you and brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be a people of his own inheritance, as you are this day. Furthermore, the LORD was angry with me because of you, and he swore that I should not cross the Jordan, and that I should not enter the good land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance. For I must die in this land; I must not go over the Jordan. But you shall go over and take possession of that good land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The iron furnace is a smelting furnace, the fierce enclosed heat in which ore is melted: a brutal image for four hundred years. Egypt was not merely captivity; it was a fire.

The chapter is organised around fire: the fire of Egypt, which was slavery; the fire on the mountain, which was revelation; and in three verses, the fire God himself is. He brought his people out of one into the presence of another.

And he brought them out to be a people of his own inheritance. An inheritance is the thing of lasting value that is properly a man’s own. Israel was not God’s workforce but his portion. Paul prays Christians would grasp the same: the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints (Eph. 1:18). The inheritance is us.

Then Moses mentions his own exclusion a third time (1:37; 3:26; 4:21). It is not self-pity; each time it comes in the middle of a warning about sin, as the nearest and costliest illustration he has. His last sermon uses his own funeral as an argument.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care, lest you forget the covenant of the LORD your God, which he made with you, and make a carved image, the form of anything that the LORD your God has forbidden you. For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two words modern readers flinch at, and both need explaining rather than softening.

A consuming fire: not a warm hearth. It is the fire that spoke from the mountain, and it will not tolerate a rival in the camp. God’s holiness is not passive; the presence that gives light and warmth to those who belong to him burns what is set up against him. The New Testament quotes this at Christians, not pagans: for our God is a consuming fire (Heb. 12:29).

A jealous God. Jealousy in Scripture is not envy, which wants what belongs to someone else. It is a husband’s rightful refusal to share his wife, the opposite of indifference. A man who watches his wife leave with somebody else and feels nothing does not love her.

God had married this nation at that mountain; covenant language is marriage language, and idolatry in the prophets is adultery. So when Moses says God is jealous, he is telling them how much they are loved, and what it will cost to treat that love as though it did not matter.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses foresees Israel’s idolatry and scattering, yet promises that if they seek the LORD with all their heart from exile, the merciful God will not forsake his covenant.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s judgment on idolatry is certain, but his covenant mercy is greater: he disciplines his people and will not abandon them.
verseByVerse.examples: Exile and return were foretold before Israel had even entered the land. A believer who has wandered far can still come back, for God meets the seeking heart with mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you father children and children's children, and have grown old in the land, and you act corruptly by making a carved image in the form of anything, and by doing what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God, so as to provoke him to anger, I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that you will soon utterly perish from the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess. You will not live long in it, but will be utterly destroyed. And the LORD will scatter you among the peoples, and you will be left few in number among the nations where the LORD will drive you. And there you will serve gods of wood and stone, the work of human hands, that neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses looks down the centuries and describes exactly how this will go wrong. Look at the timing: not the first generation, nor a crisis, but when they have grown old in the land, after the vineyards are producing and nobody remembers a tent. Prosperity, not persecution, is what he expects to undo them. That is the pattern of the Bible and of most Christian lives: few people are argued out of faith, and many are made comfortable out of it.

I call heaven and earth to witness is courtroom language. Ancient treaties named the gods of both parties as witnesses; Israel has no such gods, so Moses summons creation to the stand.

And the punishment fits the crime with terrible precision. You wanted a god you could see, so you will get gods that neither see, nor hear. The Psalms name what this does over time: Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps. 115:8). Whatever a man worships he grows to resemble, whether wood, or money, or Christ, as those who behold his glory are changed into his image (2 Corinthians 3:18), which is the only reason any of us has hope of becoming anything worth being.

Was this written after the exile happened? Scholars who date Deuteronomy late read these verses as written after the event. But exile was a familiar threat long before Babylon: ancient treaties threatened it, and the empires of the region deported conquered peoples as a matter of policy. The verses name no Babylon and give no date. And for a reader who believes the God of this chapter speaks, his foretelling the end from the beginning is no difficulty (Isaiah 46:10).

verseByVerse.quote: But from there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul. When you are in tribulation, and all these things come upon you in the latter days, you will return to the LORD your God and obey his voice. For the LORD your God is a merciful God. He will not leave you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers that he swore to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of the middle of the worst thing Moses has said comes this. From there: not from the land, nor after they have got themselves back, but from exile, from the middle of the consequences, surrounded by the wooden gods they chose. God puts the address in the sentence so that nobody can claim to be too far away.

What is required? Not a sacrifice, pilgrimage or temple; there will be no temple. Only to search after him with all your heart: the whole heart, but nothing they could not do in Babylon.

Then verse 30 shifts from condition to prediction: you will return. Not “you may.” The God who foresees the apostasy foresees the homecoming, and says so before either has happened.

And the ground is not in them: the LORD your God is a merciful God. Rachum is the tender compassion Scripture compares to a mother’s for the child she carried (Isa. 49:15), not a response to anything the child has done. The security is an oath sworn to men centuries dead. Israel’s way home did not depend on Israel’s performance in exile. It rested on a promise made to Abraham and on a mercy that is simply what God is like. This is the comfort for every reader who knows he has broken the commands of this chapter: the way back is to turn and seek, and the welcome rests on God’s faithfulness, which Christ has now sealed by keeping the covenant perfectly in our place.

Jesus told a story with the same shape. A son took everything, went to a far country, ended up feeding pigs, and when he came to himself went home, and his father saw him a long way off and ran (Luke 15:17–20). The road home runs along the line Deuteronomy 4:29 had already drawn.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–40 — There Is No Other: The Incomparable God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No other nation has heard God speak from fire or been redeemed by such acts, all to prove the great confession: the LORD is God, and there is no other.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s unrepeatable acts of revelation and rescue show that he alone is God, and so he alone is to be worshipped.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel’s history was her proof that the LORD alone is God. For the Christian the greatest proof is the resurrection of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "For ask now of the days that are past, which were before you, since the day that God created man on the earth, and ask from one end of heaven to the other, whether such a great thing as this has ever happened or was ever heard of. Did any people ever hear the voice of a god speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and still live? Or has any god ever attempted to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, and by war, by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and by great deeds of terror, all of which the LORD your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A challenge with no limits: search all of time, back to the creation of man, and all of space, and find a parallel.

The second question is the more staggering, and its force is lost on us. Gods belonged to nations; a god of Egypt was for Egyptians, and his fortunes rose and fell with theirs. A god crossing a border into the strongest empire on earth to extract a slave population, the lowest thing in that society, and make them his own, is not a variation on ancient religion. There is no category for it.

And note attempted. Has any god even tried? Not merely succeeded; tried. The gods of the nations did not go and get anybody. They stayed where they were and waited to be fed.

That is the God of the Bible from beginning to end, and at the incarnation it intensifies. He comes down into a foreign country and takes people out of it at his own cost, and Christianity is a footnote to that habit of his.

verseByVerse.quote: To you it was shown, that you might know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides him. Out of heaven he let you hear his voice, that he might discipline you. And on earth he let you see his great fire, and you heard his words out of the midst of the fire. And because he loved your fathers and chose their offspring after them and brought you out of Egypt with his own presence, by his great power, driving out before you nations greater and mightier than you, to bring you in, to give you their land for an inheritance, as it is this day,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the purpose of everything just listed. The plagues, the sea, the fire, the voice, the forty years had one aim: that they should know. God taught a nation of slaves, by means of an entire national history, one fact, and the scale of the teaching shows the difficulty of the lesson.

Verse 36 puts the two halves side by side: a voice from heaven that he might discipline you, and the fire on earth. Yasar is to train, what a father does to a son he means to make into something. Sinai was a classroom with the roof off.

Then verse 37 answers the question the passage raises. Why them? Because he loved your fathers. Not because they were numerous or good; three chapters have just established the opposite. Deuteronomy will say it more bluntly: It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you… but it is because the LORD loves you (7:7–8). The love is its own explanation, with nothing underneath it.

And note the means: with his own presence, literally with his face. He did not send. He came.

verseByVerse.quote: know therefore today, and lay it to your heart, that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other. Therefore you shall keep his statutes and his commandments, which I command you today, that it may go well with you and with your children after you, and that you may prolong your days in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for all time."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two commands, and the second is harder. Know: settle it as fact. Then lay it to your heart: bring it from the head to where decisions are made. Moses did not think the first would produce the second automatically, and he was right.

Every Christian knows the gap. A man can hold without hesitation that God rules heaven and earth, and still lie awake at three in the morning managing the universe on God’s behalf, or decide out of fear of someone who will be dead in forty years. The doctrine is filed correctly and is not running anything. Laying it to heart is the work of a lifetime, and it is the Spirit’s work in us more than ours, done through the word and prayer; it does not happen by learning more.

The claim is comprehensive: in heaven above and on the earth beneath. No jurisdiction he does not hold, which is precisely what no other god of that world ever claimed, and precisely why an Israelite in exile, under Babylon’s gods in Babylon’s land, could still pray.

Then verse 40: Therefore you shall keep his statutes. That therefore is the logic of Deuteronomy. Obedience is not the foundation; it is the roof. First know who he is, then lay it to heart, then keep his commandments, because a command obeyed without the first two is mere compliance, and it never lasts a generation. And when the roof leaks, as in every life it does, the foundation does not move: we are accepted not for our keeping but for Christ’s, whose obedience is counted as ours (Rom. 5:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–43 — The Cities of Refuge East of the Jordan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sets apart three cities of refuge east of the Jordan, where one who kills unintentionally may flee and find safety from the avenger of blood.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides refuge for one who has killed without malice, a picture of Christ as the refuge to whom sinners flee.
verseByVerse.examples: The manslayer fled to a city of refuge; sinners flee to Christ, who shelters them from the judgment they deserve.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses set apart three cities in the east beyond the Jordan, that the manslayer might flee there, anyone who kills his neighbor unintentionally, without being at enmity with him in time past; he may flee to one of these cities and save his life: Bezer in the wilderness on the tableland for the Reubenites, Ramoth in Gilead for the Gadites, and Golan in Bashan for the Manassites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The strangest paragraph in the chapter. Moses has just finished some of the highest theology in the Pentateuch, and the next thing he does is administration: three towns, named, mapped, allocated.

These cities are for a man who has not yet killed anybody, who may not yet be born, whose axe head will fly off a handle some afternoon decades from now in a country Moses will never enter. He is arranging a stranger’s worst day in a future he has no part in.

That is what the theology of verses 32–40 is for. A man who truly believes there is no other God will find himself doing small concrete kindnesses for people he will never meet. Doctrine that does not come down into three named towns on a map has not yet been laid to the heart.

And it is mercy precisely: not a reward for the innocent but shelter for a man who has really taken a life. The chapter that establishes God as a consuming fire ends by building somewhere for the guilty to run.

The avenger of blood was the dead man’s nearest kinsman, who had the duty of executing justice on a murderer (see 19:4–6).
verseByVerse.note: Bezer served Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead served Gad, and Golan in Bashan served the half-tribe of Manasseh (v. 43).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 44–49 — The Setting of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A heading introduces the body of law that follows, located after the defeat of Sihon and Og.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s law is given in real history to a redeemed people, at a real time and place.
verseByVerse.examples: The law was set before Israel on land taken from defeated kings. God’s word still comes to us as history, not as abstract philosophy.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the law that Moses set before the people of Israel. These are the testimonies, the statutes, and the rules, which Moses spoke to the people of Israel when they came out of Egypt, beyond the Jordan in the valley opposite Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon, whom Moses and the people of Israel defeated when they came out of Egypt. And they took possession of his land and the land of Og, the king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites, who lived to the east beyond the Jordan; from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, as far as Mount Sirion (that is, Hermon), together with all the Arabah on the east side of the Jordan as far as the Sea of the Arabah, under the slopes of Pisgah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A heading and a hinge: the first address is over, and from chapter 5 the law itself begins.

The three words are not synonyms piled up. Testimonies are what God has borne witness to about himself; statutes are fixed; rules are a judge’s decisions applied to cases. Together: what God has declared, what he has fixed, and how it works out in ordinary disputes.

Every element of the address is a sermon. Beyond the Jordan: still on the wrong bank. Opposite Beth-peor: facing the nation’s latest and most shameful collapse. In the land of Sihon: standing on ground God had already given.

So the law is delivered to a people camped between their worst failure and their unclaimed inheritance, on land that proves he keeps his promises. That describes where the church stands whenever Scripture is opened: our failures behind us and in plain view, the promise ahead and not yet possessed, and enough already given to make it unreasonable to doubt the rest.

4.theology:
The God who reveals himself by his word. At Horeb Israel heard but did not see (4:12). This grounds the prohibition of images and the priority of hearing in worship, and the speaking God is fully revealed in the Word made flesh (John 1; Heb 1:1–2).

A consuming fire, a jealous God. God’s holiness burns against every rival, and his jealousy is a husband’s love (4:24; Heb 12:29). Yet this same fire fell on Christ at Calvary, so that the redeemed are embraced rather than consumed.

There is no other. The whole sermon aims at one confession (4:35, 39). God’s acts in history prove that he alone is God, supremely now in the resurrection of Christ, and they call for undivided devotion.
4.examples:
Then: Israel was the most privileged nation on earth, and Moses pleaded with her to remember, to shun idols, and to know that the LORD alone is God.

Now: We who have a God nearer than our breath, who hears us “whenever we call,” must still guard our hearts against the idol-factory within and teach God’s mighty acts to our children, and we do it in the power of his Spirit, not our own. The consuming fire is our Father; the jealous God is our faithful husband; and the merciful God meets every seeking heart, however far it has wandered, with the welcome of grace.

5.title: The Ten Commandments Repeated: Grace Before Law
5.text: <sup>1</sup>And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them, "Hear, O Israel, the statutes and the rules that I speak in your hearing today, and you shall learn them and be careful to do them.<sup>2</sup>The LORD our God made a covenant with us in Horeb.<sup>3</sup>Not with our fathers did the LORD make this covenant, but with us, who are all of us here alive today.<sup>4</sup>The LORD spoke with you face to face at the mountain, out of the midst of the fire,<sup>5</sup>while I stood between the LORD and you at that time, to declare to you the word of the LORD. For you were afraid because of the fire, and you did not go up into the mountain. He said:<sup>6</sup>"'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.<sup>7</sup>"'You shall have no other gods before me.<sup>8</sup>"'You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is on the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.<sup>9</sup>You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me,<sup>10</sup>but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.<sup>11</sup>"'You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.<sup>12</sup>"'Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as the LORD your God commanded you.<sup>13</sup>Six days you shall labor and do all your work,<sup>14</sup>but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you or your son or your daughter or your male servant or your female servant, or your ox or your donkey or any of your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates, that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you.<sup>15</sup>You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.<sup>16</sup>"'Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God commanded you, that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>17</sup>"'You shall not murder.<sup>18</sup>"'And you shall not commit adultery.<sup>19</sup>"'And you shall not steal.<sup>20</sup>"'And you shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.<sup>21</sup>"'And you shall not covet your neighbor's wife. And you shall not desire your neighbor's house, his field, or his male servant, or his female servant, his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's.'<sup>22</sup>"These words the LORD spoke to all your assembly at the mountain out of the midst of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness, with a loud voice; and he added no more. And he wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to me.<sup>23</sup>And as soon as you heard the voice out of the midst of the darkness, while the mountain was burning with fire, you came near to me, all the heads of your tribes, and your elders.<sup>24</sup>And you said, 'Behold, the LORD our God has shown us his glory and greatness, and we have heard his voice out of the midst of the fire. This day we have seen God speak with man, and man still live.<sup>25</sup>Now therefore why should we die? For this great fire will consume us. If we hear the voice of the LORD our God any more, we shall die.<sup>26</sup>For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of fire as we have, and has still lived?<sup>27</sup>Go near and hear all that the LORD our God will say, and speak to us all that the LORD our God will speak to you, and we will hear and do it.'<sup>28</sup>"And the LORD heard your words, when you spoke to me. And the LORD said to me, 'I have heard the words of this people, which they have spoken to you. They are right in all that they have spoken.<sup>29</sup>Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear me and to keep all my commandments, that it might go well with them and with their descendants forever!<sup>30</sup>Go and say to them, "Return to your tents."<sup>31</sup>But you, stand here by me, and I will tell you the whole commandment and the statutes and the rules that you shall teach them, that they may do them in the land that I am giving them to possess.'<sup>32</sup>You shall be careful therefore to do as the LORD your God has commanded you. You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.<sup>33</sup>You shall walk in all the way that the LORD your God has commanded you, that you may live, and that it may go well with you, and that you may live long in the land that you shall possess.
5.overview:
Chapter 5 returns to the foundation of the covenant: the Ten Commandments (the “ten words”) God spoke from the fire at Horeb, repeated to a new generation for whom the covenant is present, not past (5:3).

The prologue is pure gospel: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (5:6). God redeems first, then commands; the law is the response of a freed people, never the price of their freedom. Deuteronomy grounds the Sabbath not in creation, as Exodus does, but in that redemption (5:15).

The chapter closes with the people’s terror at God’s voice, their plea for a mediator, and God’s longing that they had such a heart always (5:29), a longing the gospel alone fulfils.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Covenant Is Ours Today
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The covenant made at Horeb binds the living generation, not only their fathers.
verseByVerse.theology: The covenant is present and personal. Each generation has to own it as made with them, rather than leave it in the history books.
verseByVerse.examples: The children of the wilderness generation were told that Horeb was their covenant too. Faith cannot be inherited second-hand: every believer has to receive the gospel for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them, "Hear, O Israel, the statutes and the rules that I speak in your hearing today, and you shall learn them and be careful to do them. The LORD our God made a covenant with us in Horeb. Not with our fathers did the LORD make this covenant, but with us, who are all of us here alive today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, O Israel. The phrase reaches its summit in the next chapter and sets the posture of the whole book: before Israel does anything, she listens.

Not with our fathers. Strictly, the covenant at Horeb was made with their fathers, who now lie dead in the wilderness; the men listening were children then, or unborn. Moses knows it perfectly well; he has just spent three chapters on those graves. He is making a preaching point, one of the most important in Scripture: the covenant is not a title deed handed down from somebody else. It binds the living, and every generation stands at Sinai for itself.

It is possible to be the third generation in a Christian family, to know the language, hold the doctrines, keep the habits, and never once to have dealt with God personally. That is a covenant made with our fathers. Moses will not permit it, and today, one of the great words of this book, sounds through it dozens of times.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke with you face to face at the mountain, out of the midst of the fire, while I stood between the LORD and you at that time, to declare to you the word of the LORD. For you were afraid because of the fire, and you did not go up into the mountain. He said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things are said in one breath and they pull against each other. God spoke face to face, directly, as a man speaks to a friend; and Moses stood between. That tension is the whole situation of fallen man before God. He came near enough to be heard by everybody, without priest or temple, and they could not bear it, so a man stood in the gap and carried the words across.

The Old Testament is arranged around such men: Moses at the mountain, Aaron with a censer in a plague, the high priest behind the curtain once a year. Each was temporary, and each died. The New Testament names the office and adds one word: For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5). One. Not a succession. The man between the fire and the people at Horeb did for a day what Christ does permanently, and unlike Moses, he did not merely carry the words. He was them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any command, God announces what he has already done. Grace comes before law.
verseByVerse.theology: God saves first and commands second, and this order runs through the whole Bible.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians obey, as Israel was meant to, out of thankfulness for a rescue already finished, never to earn it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a single you shall, this. It is the most important structural fact about the Ten Commandments, and it is missed almost every time they are quoted.

Read the commandments from verse 7 and you have a moral code, and a hearer will naturally assume that keeping it is how you get in with God. Read them from verse 6 and they are not entrance conditions but the way a people already rescued now live. God does not say, "Keep these and I will bring you out of Egypt." They are already out. The sea is behind them, the chains are off, and they have been carried through a desert for forty years. He identifies himself as the one who did that, and only then tells them how to live.

This is the shape of the whole Bible: what God has done before what we must do, Romans 1–11 before Romans 12. The difference between religion and the gospel is not in the commandments, which are the same, but in what they are for. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace (Rom. 6:14). Every one of the ten is addressed to ex-slaves by the God who unlocked the door: not new chains, but a description of what free people look like, written by the one who paid to make them free.
verseByVerse.note: Why lists of the Ten differ: Jewish tradition counts this verse as the first of the ten words; Roman Catholics and Lutherans join the images commandment to the first and divide the coveting commandment in two. This commentary follows the numbering used by most Protestant churches.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — The First Table: Loving God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first table governs Israel’s relationship to God: whom she worships, how, with what honour for his name, and with what rest.
verseByVerse.theology: God is to have no rival, no image, no careless use of his name, and his people are to stop and rest because he has set them free.
verseByVerse.examples: These commandments reach past carved idols to the idols of the heart, and past swearing to every way of using God’s name for our own ends.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You shall have no other gods before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Hebrew behind before me is literally before my face (the ESV note offers "besides"). It is not about ranking, as though lesser gods were permitted underneath; it is about location, and the location is everywhere. A man may not keep other gods in the back of the house.

The sentence does not say "there are no other gods," although Deuteronomy says that plainly enough (4:35, 39). The issue is possession: you shall have, what you actually reckon with. A man’s real god is not the one he would name if asked but the one he consults when frightened, obeys when the two conflict, and cannot imagine living without. Grieving a real loss is not idolatry; making something the ground of life in God’s place is. And the command comes from the God who has just rescued his people: he forbids rivals because he offers himself as the one they can lean their whole weight on.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is on the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second commandment governs not whom Israel worships but how. A man may aim at the true God and still worship falsely, if he has made an image and put it in the way.

The threat attached to this commandment troubles many readers, and three things make it clearer. First, the qualifier: of those who hate me. The children in view have taken up their fathers’ hatred and continued in it; Scripture insists the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezek. 18:20). Second, what is described is observable: sin runs in families, the drinking, the temper, the coldness, each generation learning it from the last. God is naming that mechanism, not inventing it. Third, the arithmetic: three or four generations set against thousands, which can be read as thousands of generations. His mercy outweighs his judgment beyond counting, and the line can be broken: anyone who turns to the Lord steps out of those who hate me into the thousands who are loved. That is how he describes himself to Moses: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands (Exod. 34:6–7).

Does this forbid pictures of Jesus or religious art? Not art as such: God commanded carved cherubim for the tabernacle (Exod 25:18). What it forbids is any image made to represent God or to serve in worship, because Israel saw no form (Deut 4:15). Christians differ over pictures of Christ. Many hold that because he took a real body he may be depicted, especially in teaching; the Reformed confessions reply that no picture can show the one person who is both God and man, and that images used in worship break this commandment. This commentary takes the Reformed caution as the safer course: no image of Christ in worship or as an aid to prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verb is lift up or carry, and in vain means emptily, for nothing. Profanity is the least of it: a man who curses with the name of God at least believes it has weight, which is why he reaches for it. The commandment covers the false oath, which makes God the guarantor of a lie; the prayer that uses his name as a formula; and most searchingly, claiming God’s authority for what he has not said, attaching his name to our preferences, our politics, our certainty about somebody else’s motives. That is done most often by people who would never swear.

Israel had the name of God put upon her (Num. 6:27); Christians are called by the name of Christ. To wear that name and live emptily is to take it in vain without a word.

This is the only one of the ten with the clause the LORD will not hold him guiltless, because his name is the revelation of who he is. To handle it carelessly is to handle him carelessly.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as the LORD your God commanded you. Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you or your son or your daughter or your male servant or your female servant, or your ox or your donkey or any of your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates, that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the great difference from the Decalogue of Exodus 20, and it is a deliberate second lesson, not a discrepancy. Exodus grounds the Sabbath in creation (Exod. 20:11); Deuteronomy grounds it in redemption, remember that you were a slave. Creation says rest is woven into the structure of the world, and a man who never stops is fighting its grain. Redemption says rest is what freedom looks like. Slaves in Egypt got no seventh day; every time Israel stopped, she said with her body, "I am not a slave any more."

Deuteronomy also gives the servants’ rest as the purpose: that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you. A man who had been a slave is forbidden to turn his own household into what he came out of, and even the ox gets its day off, a real cost in a farming economy.

The Lord Jesus stood in this tradition when he said The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27), and he is what it was pointing at: So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his (Heb. 4:9–10). The rest itself is a Person, and entering it means giving up the exhausting business of justifying yourself.

Does the Sabbath bind Christians today? Faithful Christians differ here. The Sabbath was the sign of the covenant at Sinai (Exod 31:13), and the New Testament calls Sabbaths a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Col 2:16–17). Many godly brothers, with the Westminster Confession of Faith (21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (22.7–8), hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment, because the pattern of one day in seven goes back to creation; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. This commentary judges that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Heb 4:9–10), because the New Testament repeats and deepens the other nine commandments but names the Sabbath among the shadows, and it leaves the believer free (Rom 14:5): no one may bind another’s conscience about a day. The Lord’s Day is a gift. Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a law with rules about work. And this chapter’s own reason still speaks: a Christian who employs others has every reason to see that they get their rest too.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus 20:8 begins “Remember the Sabbath day”; Deuteronomy begins “Observe the Sabbath day” and keeps the word remember for the slavery in Egypt (5:15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — The Second Table: Loving Neighbor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second table governs our dealings with one another.
verseByVerse.theology: Love for God overflows into love for neighbour. The second table protects a neighbour’s life, marriage, property and good name, and then reaches into the heart.
verseByVerse.examples: The Lord Jesus did not loosen these commands; he took them inward, so that they govern anger, desire and envy as well as deeds.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God commanded you, that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This commandment stands at the hinge of the two tables. Parents sit between God and neighbour because they are the first authority anyone meets, and a child learns submission or defiance long before he thinks about God.

Honor is kabed, a word that elsewhere means heavy: to treat as weighty. It is not agreement, nor affection, which cannot be commanded, but a settled way of treating a person, and it outlasts childhood and survives a parent’s failures. Not everybody had parents who were honourable, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise; the command is not obey but honor, and it is possible to honour a parent who failed badly. Honouring a parent who was abusive never means staying within reach of harm. It can mean speaking of them truthfully and without revenge, praying for them, and caring for them from a safe distance. Abuse is never to be tolerated, and anyone in danger should seek safety at once.

Deuteronomy adds and that it may go well with you, and Paul notes it: “Honor your father and mother” (this is the first commandment with a promise), “that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land” (Eph. 6:2–3). Of all ten, this is the one God chose to attach a promise to.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You shall not murder. "'And you shall not commit adultery. "'And you shall not steal. "'And you shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four commandments in four short lines cover what a neighbour cannot live without: his life, his marriage, his property, and his good name.

The commandment does not touch warfare or judicial execution, which the same law regulates. Its ground is that God made man in his own image (Gen. 9:6): human beings are not merely useful but stamped. Marriage is placed immediately after life, which is its own statement of how seriously God treats it. The ban on stealing assumes that property is real and that a man may rightly own things. And false witness belongs to the courtroom: where testimony cannot be trusted, the weak are the first to suffer.

All four can be kept outwardly by a thoroughly bad man, which is why the Lord Jesus drove them inward: You have heard that it was said… “You shall not murder”… But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment (Matt. 5:21–22). He was not adding to Moses. He refused to let the commandments be reduced to a list of things a man has not done, and the same for adultery and the look that precedes it.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew word for “murder” also covers causing death by negligence (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "'And you shall not covet your neighbor's wife. And you shall not desire your neighbor's house, his field, or his male servant, or his female servant, his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tenth is unlike the other nine, and that is why it is last. Every other commandment can be broken visibly. A man could keep the first nine outwardly for sixty years with a heart like a sewer, and no court could touch him. The tenth takes hold of what nobody can see, and it makes the other nine unkeepable.

Deuteronomy puts the wife first, where Exodus 20:17 begins with the house, and uses a different verb for her than for the property: she is set apart from a man’s goods.

This commandment took Paul apart. He had kept the visible law and counted himself blameless, and then: I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet” (Rom. 7:7). The law was never a ladder. It is a mirror, and the tenth commandment shows you your face rather than your hands. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin (Rom. 3:20).

The mirror is not the end. What no one has done, Christ did: he kept all ten, inside and out, in our place, and by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (Rom. 5:19). So the believer whom the tenth commandment still exposes is not cast off; he confesses and is forgiven (1 John 1:9), and the Spirit who now lives in him writes this law on his heart (Ezek. 36:27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–33 — The People’s Fear and God’s Longing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people beg Moses to stand between them and God; God approves their fear and longs for them to have such a heart always.
verseByVerse.theology: Sinners cannot bear the unmediated presence of a holy God. The law shows the need both for a mediator and for a new heart, and only grace can supply either.
verseByVerse.examples: We draw near through Christ, the greater Mediator, who does what Moses could not: he removes our sin and gives the new heart the law could only ask for.

verseByVerse.quote: "These words the LORD spoke to all your assembly at the mountain out of the midst of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness, with a loud voice; and he added no more. And he wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to me. And as soon as you heard the voice out of the midst of the darkness, while the mountain was burning with fire, you came near to me, all the heads of your tribes, and your elders. And you said, 'Behold, the LORD our God has shown us his glory and greatness, and we have heard his voice out of the midst of the fire. This day we have seen God speak with man, and man still live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He added no more. Everything else in the law came through Moses. These ten God spoke himself, aloud, to the whole nation, and then wrote on stone with his own hand. The rest of Scripture is not less inspired, but the manner of their delivery is part of their meaning, and it is why the Ten have always stood where they do.

Man still live. The people’s astonishment is not that God spoke but that they were still standing afterwards. They had assumed, correctly, that hearing the voice of God would kill them, and they had just survived it and could not get over it. That is a category we have almost entirely lost. Our difficulty with God is that we cannot hear him; theirs was that they had, and were somehow not dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore why should we die? For this great fire will consume us. If we hear the voice of the LORD our God any more, we shall die. For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of fire as we have, and has still lived? Go near and hear all that the LORD our God will say, and speak to us all that the LORD our God will speak to you, and we will hear and do it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the terror catches up with them: why should we die? It is neither superstition nor cowardice but an accurate reading of their situation. Sinful people cannot stand in the unmediated presence of a holy God, and they were right.

So they ask for a go-between. Not less of God, nor a lower standard, but a man who can survive the fire to bring them what is said in it. They are not asking him to go away. It is one of the most spiritually intelligent things this nation ever says, and it is the request every human being has once he understands the problem. The machinery of religion is people trying to solve it with priests, rituals and techniques; Israel at least asked God for the solution instead of inventing one, and the next verses record what he thought of that.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the LORD heard your words, when you spoke to me. And the LORD said to me, 'I have heard the words of this people, which they have spoken to you. They are right in all that they have spoken. Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear me and to keep all my commandments, that it might go well with them and with their descendants forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God endorses their fear. Not "they should be braver," not "they have misunderstood me": their assessment of what it would cost to hear his voice unmediated was correct, and he says so.

Then comes one of the most extraordinary sentences God ever speaks. The Hebrew is an exclamation of wish, literally who will give that they had such a heart. That is longing. The God who needs nothing, who is complete in himself, who has just spoken the universe’s moral law out of a burning mountain, says: if only. We should be careful here, and also honest. This is not a defect in his knowledge, as though he did not see what was coming; this book has already predicted the exile (4:25–28). It reveals his disposition: he genuinely delights in the obedience of his people and genuinely grieves at its absence, and he wants us to know it. Ezekiel says the same thing in the same register: I have no pleasure in the death of anyone (Ezek. 18:32).

And he wishes not for better behaviour but for such a heart. The problem is not in the commandments or the mediator but in them. Twenty-five chapters on comes the answer to God’s own wish: And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live (30:6). That is the whole gospel in the space of one book: God asks for what we cannot produce, and then produces it in us himself. I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezek. 36:26).

verseByVerse.quote: Go and say to them, "Return to your tents." But you, stand here by me, and I will tell you the whole commandment and the statutes and the rules that you shall teach them, that they may do them in the land that I am giving them to possess.' You shall be careful therefore to do as the LORD your God has commanded you. You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left. You shall walk in all the way that the LORD your God has commanded you, that you may live, and that it may go well with you, and that you may live long in the land that you shall possess.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two destinations in one sentence: the people go home; the mediator stays with God. A crowd walks down to the cooking fires and the children, and one man is left on a burning mountain in the dark, being given the rest of the law. Somebody has to remain in the fire so that everybody else can go home, and that is what a mediator is for. There is only one place in Scripture where that pattern is broken, and it is broken by the one who said Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28). He stood in the fire so that we could go home, and then, unlike Moses, he brought us with him.

Neither right nor left. There are two ways off a road. A man can leave God’s way by laxity or by excess of scruple, by loosening what God tied or tying what God left free, and Deuteronomy worries about both, which is why it forbade addition as well as subtraction (4:2). The road runs straight, and the God who brought his people out walks it with them.

5.theology:
Grace before law. The commandments open with what God has done (5:6), so obedience is the grateful answer of a freed people, never the price of freedom. That order governs all of Scripture and reaches its fullness in the cross.

Rest for the redeemed. Deuteronomy ties the Sabbath to the rescue from slavery (5:15), and the rest it promised is found in Christ (Heb 4), entered by faith.

A new heart. God’s own wish in 5:29 exposes the central problem: the law commands a heart it cannot create. What he longs for here he supplies in the new covenant, writing his law on hearts of flesh by the Spirit (Jer 31:33; Ezek 36:26).
5.examples:
For Israel, this chapter was a new generation taking the Horeb covenant as its own: trembling at God’s voice and asking for a man to stand between them and him.

For us it means owning the covenant of grace personally, obeying out of gratitude for a redemption already accomplished, and drawing near through Jesus, who not only brings us God’s word but takes away our sin.

6.title: The Shema and the Great Commandment: Love the LORD with All Your Heart
