6.text: <sup>1</sup>"Now this is the commandment—the statutes and the rules —that the LORD your God commanded me to teach you, that you may do them in the land to which you are going over, to possess it,<sup>2</sup>that you may fear the LORD your God, you and your son and your son's son, by keeping all his statutes and his commandments, which I command you, all the days of your life, and that your days may be long.<sup>3</sup>Hear therefore, O Israel, and be careful to do them, that it may go well with you, and that you may multiply greatly, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you, in a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>4</sup>"Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.<sup>5</sup>You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.<sup>6</sup>And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart.<sup>7</sup>You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.<sup>8</sup>You shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes.<sup>9</sup>You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.<sup>10</sup>"And when the LORD your God brings you into the land that he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give you—with great and good cities that you did not build,<sup>11</sup>and houses full of all good things that you did not fill, and cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant—and when you eat and are full,<sup>12</sup>then take care lest you forget the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.<sup>13</sup>It is the LORD your God you shall fear. Him you shall serve and by his name you shall swear.<sup>14</sup>You shall not go after other gods, the gods of the peoples who are around you—<sup>15</sup>for the LORD your God in your midst is a jealous God— lest the anger of the LORD your God be kindled against you, and he destroy you from off the face of the earth.<sup>16</sup>"You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah.<sup>17</sup>You shall diligently keep the commandments of the LORD your God, and his testimonies and his statutes, which he has commanded you.<sup>18</sup>And you shall do what is right and good in the sight of the LORD, that it may go well with you, and that you may go in and take possession of the good land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers<sup>19</sup>by thrusting out all your enemies from before you, as the LORD has promised.<sup>20</sup>"When your son asks you in time to come, 'What is the meaning of the testimonies and the statutes and the rules that the LORD our God has commanded you?'<sup>21</sup>then you shall say to your son, 'We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.<sup>22</sup>And the LORD showed signs and wonders, great and grievous, against Egypt and against Pharaoh and all his household, before our eyes.<sup>23</sup>And he brought us out from there, that he might bring us in and give us the land that he swore to give to our fathers.<sup>24</sup>And the LORD commanded us to do all these statutes, to fear the LORD our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive, as we are this day.<sup>25</sup>And it will be righteousness for us, if we are careful to do all this commandment before the LORD our God, as he has commanded us.'
6.overview:
Chapter 6 contains the passage Israel has always treated as the centre of its faith, the Shema (from the Hebrew “Hear”): “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (6:4–5).

It commands not merely obedience or correct doctrine but love, filling heart, soul and might, and Moses tells how it is to be handed on: on the heart, taught to children, spoken of at home and on the road. The chapter warns that comfort in the land will tempt Israel to forget the God who gave it, and ends with the story of redemption that parents are to tell their children.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Purpose of the Law: Life and Multiplication
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The commandments are given for life and flourishing across the generations.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s commands are given for our good. Obedience grows out of the fear of the Lord and leads to life.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel was shown the good life in the land God was giving. The redeemed still walk in his ways as the path of life, not the price of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now this is the commandment—the statutes and the rules —that the LORD your God commanded me to teach you, that you may do them in the land to which you are going over, to possess it, that you may fear the LORD your God, you and your son and your son's son, by keeping all his statutes and his commandments, which I command you, all the days of your life, and that your days may be long. Hear therefore, O Israel, and be careful to do them, that it may go well with you, and that you may multiply greatly, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you, in a land flowing with milk and honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the great confession, Moses states what the commands are for: the fear of the LORD for you and your son and your son’s son. Three generations in one verse; nothing here is aimed only at the people in front of him.

The law is said to produce not merit or standing but life, and that it may go well with you. Every command in this book is aimed at the flourishing of a people God has already brought out, a claim the human heart has disbelieved since Eden.

Fear does not mean terror of a God who might turn on you. Deuteronomy sets it always alongside love, service and clinging: the awe of a creature taking the living God seriously, the opposite of treating him as a resource. A man who fears God in this sense is the freest man alive, because nothing else left in the world can frighten him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–5 — The Shema: The Great Commandment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The central confession: the LORD is one, to be loved with all the heart, soul and might.
verseByVerse.theology: Because God is one, he asks for undivided love. True religion is more than ritual or right doctrine: it is love for him with the whole self, which Christ alone has given perfectly and the Spirit now works in us.
verseByVerse.examples: This is still the first and greatest commandment, the measure of every other love.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These six Hebrew words are probably the most repeated sentence in Jewish history: said morning and evening, taught to children before they can read, and on the lips of countless Jews as they died. The whole faith of Israel is compressed into one line.

It opens with a command to listen. Faith begins with somebody speaking and somebody attending. So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17).

The Hebrew is compressed enough that the ESV note offers three renderings (“The LORD our God is one LORD,” “The LORD is our God, the LORD is one,” or “The LORD is our God, the LORD alone”), and it carries two truths. There is only one God, against a world with a god for every city, crop and crisis. And he is one: undivided, consistent, not at war with himself. The gods of the nations were a committee with rival interests, and a man could never know where he stood. Israel’s God has one will and one character, and he is the same on Tuesday as he was on the mountain.

Jewish objectors have always raised this verse against the Trinity, and it should be answered. The word itself does not settle it: the same Hebrew one describes a man and wife who become one flesh (Genesis 2:24), a oneness that is not solitary. The doctrine rests on how the New Testament speaks of Father, Son and Spirit, and it confesses exactly what this verse says, in the words Paul uses when he puts Jesus inside the Shema: yet for us there is one God, the Father… and one Lord, Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 8:6). Paul did not abandon the Shema. He recited it, with a name in it.
verseByVerse.note: Shema is the Hebrew for “Hear,” the first word of verse 4. In Jewish prayer the name covers 6:4–9 together with 11:13–21 and Numbers 15:37–41, recited as one.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of everything God might have required first, sacrifice, obedience, worship, what he asks for is love. Asked for the greatest commandment (the rabbis later counted six hundred and thirteen), the Lord Jesus quoted this verse (Mark 12:29–30).

The three terms are not compartments but a way of saying everything three times. Heart in Hebrew is the whole inner person, above all the thinking and the will. Soul is nephesh, the whole living self. Might is normally an adverb meaning very, so that Israel is to love God with all its very; the rabbis took it to include a man’s property, his energy and capacity, the whole of his muchness.

Which raises the crushing question: who has ever done this, even for a single morning? That is not a reason to lower the command; it is the reason the rest of the book exists. Deuteronomy will state the problem plainly (oh that they had such a heart, 5:29) and then announce the solution (the LORD your God will circumcise your heart… so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart, 30:6). The commandment that exposes us is answered by a promise that God will do in us what he requires of us. Which is why John, who had lain against the chest of the Son of God, wrote the sentence that puts the Shema the right way round for a Christian: We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — These Words on the Heart: Passing Faith to Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s words are to be on the heart first, and then woven into every part of daily life and passed to the children.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith is meant to fill the whole of ordinary life and to be handed on deliberately to the next generation.
verseByVerse.examples: Discipleship happens at the kitchen table and in the car as much as in church.

verseByVerse.quote: And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The order cannot be reversed: first on your heart, then teach them. A parent cannot hand on what he does not have, and children are extraordinarily good at telling what their father believes from what he merely says on Sundays.

Teach diligently is a verb for whetting a blade: repeatedly, with pressure, until an edge forms. And the method is the least formal thing imaginable: sitting, walking, lying down, getting up, the whole of an ordinary day. There is no lesson slot. The faith is transmitted the way a family’s accent is, by constant, unremarkable exposure.

That is a relief and a rebuke. A relief, because a parent who is no teacher can still do it; the qualification is presence and honesty, not eloquence. A rebuke, because it cannot be delegated to a church or school, and the times listed are exactly the ones most of us have handed to a screen. What Moses describes is a household where God comes up in conversation because he is genuinely on the mind of the people who live there; and the God who first put his words on our hearts is the one who keeps them there.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Devout Jews have taken these words literally for over two thousand years: small leather boxes of Scripture bound to arm and forehead for prayer, and the mezuzah on the doorframe. Whatever Moses intended, the four locations are clear. On your hand: what you do. Between your eyes: what you look at and think about. On the doorposts: private life, where nobody is watching. On your gates, where the town’s cases were tried and deals struck: public life and work. There is no fifth category and no area left over.

The Lord Jesus remarked that some make their phylacteries broad (Matt. 23:5), enlarging the boxes so everybody could see. The commandment can be obeyed to the letter and turned into its opposite. The word was meant to go on the hand to shape the hand, not so that people would look at the strap.

Was it meant literally? The same language in Proverbs is plainly figurative, Bind them on your fingers (Proverbs 7:3), and the purpose is that God’s words shape what we do and how we see. Christians are not bound to wear them.
verseByVerse.note: The boxes are called tefillin in Hebrew; phylacteries is the Greek word used in Matthew 23:5.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — The Danger of Prosperity: Do Not Forget
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a good land Israel did not build, she must not forget the LORD who redeemed her.
verseByVerse.theology: Plenty is a particular danger to faith: comfort breeds forgetfulness, and forgetfulness breeds idolatry.
verseByVerse.examples: Affluence still dulls the soul, and the cure is to remember the Giver behind each gift.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the LORD your God brings you into the land that he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give you—with great and good cities that you did not build, and houses full of all good things that you did not fill, and cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant—and when you eat and are full, then take care lest you forget the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That you did not build. Four times Moses hammers the phrase: did not build… did not fill… did not dig… did not plant. Everything Israel is about to own will be second-hand mercy: finished houses, wells somebody else cut through rock, olive trees that took years to bear before they arrived.

Then the great warning of this book: the danger is not adversity but when you eat and are full. This nation survived slavery, plagues, desert, serpents and forty years of funerals with its faith more or less intact. Moses warns them about full stomachs, and he is right: within a few generations of settling they are worshipping Baal.

Hardship drives people to God; comfort quietly persuades them they never needed him. The mechanism is not rebellion but forgetting, which requires no decision at all. A man who prayed daily through an illness stops when he recovers, not because he has changed his mind about God but because the pressure has gone. So gratitude is not a nicety but a survival discipline. Every good thing in your house was given, and most of it was dug by somebody else. What do you have that you did not receive? (1 Cor. 4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: It is the LORD your God you shall fear. Him you shall serve and by his name you shall swear. You shall not go after other gods, the gods of the peoples who are around you— for the LORD your God in your midst is a jealous God— lest the anger of the LORD your God be kindled against you, and he destroy you from off the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some fourteen centuries later, in a wilderness, a starving man quoted this verse to the devil. Offered all the kingdoms of the world for one act of worship, the Lord Jesus answered: Be gone, Satan! For it is written, “You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve” (Matt. 4:10). His other two answers came from 6:16 and 8:3. Under maximum pressure, with no food and no company, what came out of the Son of God was Deuteronomy, quoted and not argued. He did not summon his divine authority; he used the weapon available to any believer, and it was enough. Anyone who thinks memorising Scripture a schoolroom exercise should remember that desert.

Verse 15 gives the reason for the exclusivity in the language of marriage: the LORD your God in your midst is a jealous God, living among them, and he will not share his wife with the gods of the neighbours.

May Christians swear oaths? Jesus forbids the evasive swearing that dodged obligations (Matt 5:33–37); his point is plain honesty. He does not forbid solemn oaths before God: he answered under oath at his trial (Matt 26:63–64), Paul called God to witness (2 Cor 1:23), and God swore by himself (Heb 6:13–17). Marriage vows and oaths in court are lawful; what a Christian promises, he must keep.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — Do Not Put the LORD to the Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must not test the LORD as at Massah, but trust and keep his commandments.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith trusts God rather than demanding proof. To test him is to doubt his goodness and faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: Faith rests on God’s promises instead of asking for signs, and Christ in the wilderness shows what perfect trust looks like.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah. You shall diligently keep the commandments of the LORD your God, and his testimonies and his statutes, which he has commanded you. And you shall do what is right and good in the sight of the LORD, that it may go well with you, and that you may go in and take possession of the good land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers by thrusting out all your enemies from before you, as the LORD has promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Massah there was no water, and the people quarrelled and asked, Is the LORD among us or not? (Exod. 17:7).

Testing is not honest doubt. Scripture is full of hard questions put to God, and lament is never rebuked; the Psalms are largely made of it. Testing demands that God prove himself on our terms, at our moment, by a sign of our choosing, before we will trust him. It puts God in the dock and the man on the bench. And after the sea had opened, Israel’s question was really a verdict that none of it counted.

The Lord Jesus used this verse too, when the devil quoted Scripture at him: Again it is written, “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matt. 4:7). A verse can be quoted accurately and used wickedly, and the defence is not less Scripture but more of it, rightly related. The devil knows the Bible. He does not know it whole.

What counts as testing God? Demanding that he prove himself before we trust him, as Israel did at Massah, or forcing his hand, as Satan urged Jesus to do (Matt 4:7). Gideon’s fleece was weak faith that God bore with, not a model for guidance. Malachi’s put me to the test (Mal 3:10) is God’s own invitation to obey and see his faithfulness, which is different from setting the terms ourselves.
verseByVerse.note: Massah means “testing”; the same place was also called Meribah, “quarrelling” (Exod 17:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — Tell the Story to Your Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When children ask what the commandments mean, parents are to tell the story of redemption.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith is handed on by retelling what God has done. Obedience answers his saving acts; it never causes them.
verseByVerse.examples: Christian parents tell the gospel story, so that their children’s faith rests on what God has done in Christ and not on family rules.

verseByVerse.quote: "When your son asks you in time to come, 'What is the meaning of the testimonies and the statutes and the rules that the LORD our God has commanded you?' then you shall say to your son, 'We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand. And the LORD showed signs and wonders, great and grievous, against Egypt and against Pharaoh and all his household, before our eyes. And he brought us out from there, that he might bring us in and give us the land that he swore to give to our fathers. And the LORD commanded us to do all these statutes, to fear the LORD our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive, as we are this day. And it will be righteousness for us, if we are careful to do all this commandment before the LORD our God, as he has commanded us.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends where the whole book is aimed: at a child’s question. A boy grows up inside habits he did not choose, the feasts, the Sabbath, the laws about gleaning and firstfruits, and one day he asks why. The answer decides whether faith survives a generation, and Moses gives it: not philosophy, not a defence of each statute, but a story. Why do we live like this? Because we were slaves and we were rescued, and everything in this house follows from that one fact.

And the pronoun is we, said by a man whose parents came out of Egypt to a boy two generations further removed. The rescue is not commemorated from a distance; each generation is taught to tell it in the first person.

A Christian family answers the same question the same way: not "these are our standards" or "this is how we were raised," but "we were slaves and were bought, at a price, by somebody who came for us." Any answer without the rescue at the centre has turned the faith into house rules, and house rules do not survive a child leaving home.

Does this teach salvation by works? The obedience comes after redemption: We were Pharaoh’s slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out (v. 21). Righteousness here is the covenant faithfulness of a redeemed people. As a way to earn life, the law demands a perfect obedience no sinner can give (Gal 3:10–12); Christ gave it, and his righteousness is counted to all who believe (Rom 10:4–5).

6.theology:
One God, loved with everything. Because the LORD is one, he claims undivided love (6:4–5). Jesus named this the greatest commandment (Mark 12:30); he alone has kept it, and by his Spirit the love of God is poured into our hearts (Rom 5:5).

Faith handed on. God’s words go on the heart and into the rhythms of the day (6:6–9), anchored in the retold story of redemption (6:20–25). Faith is always one generation from being lost, and the remedy is deliberate, gospel-centred teaching in the home.

The danger of plenty. Moses fears full stomachs more than hunger (6:10–12). Deliberate remembrance and the fear of the Lord guard the heart in prosperity.
6.examples:
Israel was given the Shema as the heart of her faith: love the one God with everything, teach that love to the children, and do not forget him among the gifts of the land.

Christians love God only because he first loved us in Christ, who loved the Father perfectly in our place. So we fill ordinary life with his Word, tell our children the gospel before the rules, resist the dulling pull of affluence, and remember the greater exodus by which Christ brought us out of slavery to sin.

7.title: A Holy Nation: Chosen Not Because You Were Great, but Because He Loved You
7.text: <sup>1</sup>"When the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to take possession of it, and clears away many nations before you, the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, seven nations more numerous and mightier than you,<sup>2</sup>and when the LORD your God gives them over to you, and you defeat them, then you must devote them to complete destruction. You shall make no covenant with them and show no mercy to them.<sup>3</sup>You shall not intermarry with them, giving your daughters to their sons or taking their daughters for your sons,<sup>4</sup>for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods. Then the anger of the LORD would be kindled against you, and he would destroy you quickly.<sup>5</sup>But thus shall you deal with them: you shall break down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and chop down their Asherim and burn their carved images with fire.<sup>6</sup>"For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.<sup>7</sup>It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples,<sup>8</sup>but it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers, that the LORD has brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations,<sup>10</sup>and repays to their face those who hate him, by destroying them. He will not be slack with one who hates him. He will repay him to his face.<sup>11</sup>You shall therefore be careful to do the commandment and the statutes and the rules that I command you today.<sup>12</sup>"And because you listen to these rules and keep and do them, the LORD your God will keep with you the covenant and the steadfast love that he swore to your fathers.<sup>13</sup>He will love you, bless you, and multiply you. He will also bless the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground, your grain and your wine and your oil, the increase of your herds and the young of your flock, in the land that he swore to your fathers to give you.<sup>14</sup>You shall be blessed above all peoples. There shall not be male or female barren among you or among your livestock.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD will take away from you all sickness, and none of the evil diseases of Egypt, which you knew, will he inflict on you, but he will lay them on all who hate you.<sup>16</sup>And you shall consume all the peoples that the LORD your God will give over to you. Your eye shall not pity them, neither shall you serve their gods, for that would be a snare to you.<sup>17</sup>"If you say in your heart, 'These nations are greater than I. How can I dispossess them?'<sup>18</sup>you shall not be afraid of them but you shall remember what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt,<sup>19</sup>the great trials that your eyes saw, the signs, the wonders, the mighty hand, and the outstretched arm, by which the LORD your God brought you out. So will the LORD your God do to all the peoples of whom you are afraid.<sup>20</sup>Moreover, the LORD your God will send hornets among them, until those who are left and hide themselves from you are destroyed.<sup>21</sup>You shall not be in dread of them, for the LORD your God is in your midst, a great and awesome God.<sup>22</sup>The LORD your God will clear away these nations before you little by little. You may not make an end of them at once, lest the wild beasts grow too numerous for you.<sup>23</sup>But the LORD your God will give them over to you and throw them into great confusion, until they are destroyed.<sup>24</sup>And he will give their kings into your hand, and you shall make their name perish from under heaven. No one shall be able to stand against you until you have destroyed them.<sup>25</sup>The carved images of their gods you shall burn with fire. You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves, lest you be ensnared by it, for it is an abomination to the LORD your God.<sup>26</sup>And you shall not bring an abominable thing into your house and become devoted to destruction like it. You shall utterly detest and abhor it, for it is devoted to destruction.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 unfolds election in some of the tenderest words in Scripture. Why did God choose Israel? Not because they were many, for they were the fewest of all peoples, nor because they deserved it, but “because the LORD loves you” (7:8). Election rests on nothing but God’s free, unmerited love. Here is grace stripped of all human pretence.

The chapter opens with the hard command to destroy the seven nations of Canaan and make no covenant or marriage with them: God’s judgment on peoples whose wickedness was complete, and a call to undivided devotion. At its heart is “the faithful God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him” (7:9), and it ends with encouragement against fear: the God who shattered Egypt is “in your midst” (7:21).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must devote the Canaanite nations to destruction and make no treaty or marriage with them.
verseByVerse.theology: God asks for a clean break with idolatry, because compromise with other gods corrupts the heart.
verseByVerse.examples: The church fights no such war, but believers still refuse to be shaped by the idols of their age.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to take possession of it, and clears away many nations before you, the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, seven nations more numerous and mightier than you, and when the LORD your God gives them over to you, and you defeat them, then you must devote them to complete destruction. You shall make no covenant with them and show no mercy to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are among the hardest verses in the Bible, and they should be neither softened nor hurried past.

The Hebrew word is herem: to devote something to God so completely that it is put beyond any human use. Applied to plunder it means burnt rather than kept. Applied to a people it means what it says.

Take first what the text itself supplies. The command is limited to seven named nations in one territory. It is not a policy toward foreigners; the same book commands Israel to love the sojourner (10:19) and forbids her to abhor an Egyptian (23:7). It is bounded by geography, by a list, and by a moment.

Second, the reason, which Deuteronomy states repeatedly and which the reader will meet in full at 9:4–5: this is judicial. Not because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart are you going in to possess their land, but because of the wickedness of these nations the LORD your God is driving them out (9:5). God had told Abraham centuries earlier that his descendants would wait, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete (Gen. 15:16): God delayed judgment for four hundred years while a civilisation ripened. What ripened is described in 12:31: they burned their children.

Third, and this must be said plainly: it is a model for nobody. No nation, church or individual since has held this commission, and the New Testament closes the door explicitly. My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36); the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4). Every use of this chapter to justify violence has been a misuse.

And what remains after all that is still hard, and Scripture does not remove it. What is left is the question of whether God has the right to judge, and when. He does, and he exercises it in every generation without consulting us; what is unusual here is only that we are allowed to watch. Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Gen. 18:25), asked, note, by a man arguing with God about the destruction of cities, and asked as a confidence.

And the Judge does not stand outside the story. Canaan was a small, local preview of a judgment the whole world will face, and the New Testament says the Judge on that day will be Jesus (Acts 17:31). The same Jesus is the refuge from it. Rahab, a Canaanite living under this very sentence, believed and was spared (Joshua 2:9–11; Hebrews 11:31), and every sinner who comes over to him finds the same mercy, because on the cross he bore the judgment himself.

A careful reader will also notice a tension inside the chapter itself. Israel is told to destroy these nations (v. 2), and in the next breath not to marry them (v. 3), and God says he will clear them away little by little (v. 22). Many evangelical scholars think the language of total destruction is partly the stock idiom of ancient war reports, which spoke of complete victory where many survived; Judges 1 shows Canaanites still living in the land. Others take the command more literally. This commentary reads it as a real sentence of judgment, as 9:5 presents it, while granting that the reports of its execution use the sweeping idiom of their day. Either way, its aim was to break Canaan’s religion and its hold on the land, and the door stood open to any Canaanite who turned to Israel’s God.

But women and children? The judgment fell on a whole people, as the flood and Sodom did, and the Judge of all the earth has the right to take any life (Gen 18:25). Those who turned to the LORD were spared with their households (Josh 6:25). This was a unique command for that moment, never a pattern: the law itself forbids punishing children for their fathers’ crimes in human courts (24:16).
verseByVerse.note: The rule is given again in 20:16–18, with the reason this chapter gives in verse 4: that these nations would teach Israel their abominable practices.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not intermarry with them, giving your daughters to their sons or taking their daughters for your sons, for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods. Then the anger of the LORD would be kindled against you, and he would destroy you quickly. But thus shall you deal with them: you shall break down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and chop down their Asherim and burn their carved images with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verses 3 to 5 show what the danger actually was, and it is not military. God gives the reason himself: they would turn away your sons. The prohibition is not racial. Rahab was a Canaanite of Jericho and is in the genealogy of Christ; Ruth was a Moabite and King David’s great-grandmother. Both married Israelites, and Scripture celebrates it, because they had come over to the God of Israel: your people shall be my people, and your God my God (Ruth 1:16).

The danger is religious, and the mechanism is precise: not that the husband will be argued out of his faith, but that his sons will be raised by a mother who worships something else, a warning about the next generation one chapter after a chapter about teaching children. Paul applies the same principle to the church for the same reason, allegiance not ethnicity: a widow may remarry whom she wishes, only in the Lord (1 Cor. 7:39).

Verse 5 shows what the real war was: altars, pillars, Asherim and images are to be destroyed, not looted. Every time Israel left a shrine standing, she ended up kneeling at it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — Chosen in Love: The Heart of Election
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is God’s treasured possession, chosen not for greatness but because he loved her.
verseByVerse.theology: Election rests on God’s free love alone, not on anything in the chosen, and they are kept by his faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: The church is God’s treasured people in the same way, saved not by works but by love it did nothing to earn.

verseByVerse.quote: "For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two words carry this verse. Holy, qadosh, does not first mean morally pure but set apart for a particular use. A holy pot in the tabernacle was not a better-behaved pot; it could not be used for anything else. Israel is holy because God has taken her out of general circulation for himself.

Treasured possession is segullah, a king’s private hoard, kept apart from the national accounts. Everything belongs to God by creation (Ps. 24:1); Israel is his the way a man’s own things are his.

Peter hands the whole verse to mostly Gentile congregations without alteration: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession (1 Pet. 2:9), and gives the purpose: that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.

verseByVerse.quote: It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers, that the LORD has brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the two verses at the heart of the chapter. Moses answers the question every chosen person eventually asks: why me? Not size: Israel was the fewest of all peoples, and says so in its own Scriptures, which is not how nations write about themselves. Nor goodness: two chapters on, you are a stubborn people (9:6).

So what is left? Read the sentence again and watch it close the circle. Because the LORD loves you; and if you ask why he loves them, the answer is that he loves them. There is no term underneath it. God’s love for his people has no cause outside himself, which is precisely why nothing outside himself can end it.

If God had chosen Israel for something in her, that thing would have to be maintained, and the day it failed the choosing would fail with it. Every believer who has lain awake wondering whether God has finally had enough of him is asking whether the ground of his acceptance is in himself. This verse says it never was. God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:8): not when the trend was upward, but when there was nothing in us to explain it.

verseByVerse.quote: Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations, and repays to their face those who hate him, by destroying them. He will not be slack with one who hates him. He will repay him to his face. You shall therefore be careful to do the commandment and the statutes and the rules that I command you today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great covenant words gather here. Faithful, from the root that gives us amen: something you can put your weight on. Steadfast love, chesed: loyal covenant love that keeps going when the other party has given every reason to stop. And the arithmetic of the second commandment again: a thousand generations against judgment within a lifetime. A thousand generations at even twenty-five years apiece is twenty-five thousand years, which is a Hebrew way of saying: for ever, past any horizon you can see.

Verse 10 will not let the picture be sentimental. He repays to their face, directly and personally, those who hate him, and is not slack. A reader who takes only one half has not got the God of the Bible.

Then verse 11: You shall therefore be careful to do the commandment. The therefore is always in the same place. Because he chose you, loves you and is faithful, therefore obey. Never the other way round.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — The Blessings of Covenant Faithfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises to bless his covenant people in family, field and flock.
verseByVerse.theology: God delights to bless the people he has made his own, and his blessings were always meant to reach beyond them.
verseByVerse.examples: The believer’s lasting blessings are secured in Christ, the offspring of Abraham, rather than promised as health and harvests.

verseByVerse.quote: "And because you listen to these rules and keep and do them, the LORD your God will keep with you the covenant and the steadfast love that he swore to your fathers. He will love you, bless you, and multiply you. He will also bless the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground, your grain and your wine and your oil, the increase of your herds and the young of your flock, in the land that he swore to your fathers to give you. You shall be blessed above all peoples. There shall not be male or female barren among you or among your livestock. And the LORD will take away from you all sickness, and none of the evil diseases of Egypt, which you knew, will he inflict on you, but he will lay them on all who hate you. And you shall consume all the peoples that the LORD your God will give over to you. Your eye shall not pity them, neither shall you serve their gods, for that would be a snare to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessings are farm blessings: children, crops, cattle, health, and freedom from the evil diseases of Egypt. God speaks to this people about what actually filled their days, and there is nothing embarrassing about it. He is not offering a religious experience; he is offering rain and babies and a healthy flock.

Two cautions belong here. First, these promises are made to a nation, under a specific covenant, in a specific land, and the New Testament does not simply transfer them to individuals. Job’s friends made that mistake and were rebuked by God (Job 42:7); a Christian who reads verse 15 as a guarantee of health has misread the document he is standing in.

Second, the blessings were always a conduit, never a terminus. Israel is blessed above all peoples because of why this family was called: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Gen. 12:3). The surrounding peoples were meant to look and ask.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–26 — Do Not Be Afraid: Remember What God Did
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Israel fears greater nations, she must remember the exodus and trust the God in her midst.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith overcomes fear by remembering what God has already done. He works gradually, but surely.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians facing odds they cannot meet look back to the cross and the empty tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you say in your heart, 'These nations are greater than I. How can I dispossess them?' you shall not be afraid of them but you shall remember what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt, the great trials that your eyes saw, the signs, the wonders, the mighty hand, and the outstretched arm, by which the LORD your God brought you out. So will the LORD your God do to all the peoples of whom you are afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In your heart. God says aloud the thing Israel has not said aloud: the private thought at three in the morning that the nations are too great, the one nobody admits to. He quotes it back before they have said it, which is its own comfort. And the fear is accurate; verse 1 called these nations more numerous and mightier than you. God never argues that the odds are better than they look.

His answer is a discipline of memory: remember Pharaoh, the signs, the mighty hand, and reason forward from it. That is not positive thinking. Nobody is told to feel differently or to shrink the enemy; they are directed to what God did, which they saw. Faith here is an argument with evidence in it, and the evidence is historical.

The Christian has better evidence still, and Paul draws the same inference: He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Rom. 8:32). If the cross happened, nothing that remains is a serious question.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, the LORD your God will send hornets among them, until those who are left and hide themselves from you are destroyed. You shall not be in dread of them, for the LORD your God is in your midst, a great and awesome God. The LORD your God will clear away these nations before you little by little. You may not make an end of them at once, lest the wild beasts grow too numerous for you. But the LORD your God will give them over to you and throw them into great confusion, until they are destroyed. And he will give their kings into your hand, and you shall make their name perish from under heaven. No one shall be able to stand against you until you have destroyed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to fight, even with hornets, an image of panic and rout, and gives the ground: the LORD your God is in your midst. Not watching from a distance. In the camp.

Little by little. God, who could have emptied Canaan in a week, chooses not to, and the reason is agricultural: a land emptied faster than Israel can occupy it goes back to wilderness, the terraces collapse, and the wild beasts move in. Slow victory is the kindness.

Anyone who has prayed for years about a sin that will not die should hold on to verse 22. God’s usual method with his people is little by little, not for lack of power but because sudden deliverance would leave ground a man has no character to occupy. Sanctification is slow for the same reason, and it is God’s own work: the Spirit who lives in his people goes on clearing the land (Gal. 5:16–17), and every inch is held by the God who promised it.

verseByVerse.quote: The carved images of their gods you shall burn with fire. You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves, lest you be ensnared by it, for it is an abomination to the LORD your God. And you shall not bring an abominable thing into your house and become devoted to destruction like it. You shall utterly detest and abhor it, for it is devoted to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temptation of the gold on the idols is precisely calculated. Nobody in that army would be converted to Baal by looking at a statue. But the statues were plated in silver and gold, and Israel was poor: the idol is destroyed, the metal is neutral, why burn good silver?

God says burn it, lest you be ensnared. A snare is not a wall; it lets you walk in freely and then holds you. A man who kept one piece of it would find years later that he had kept a thread back to the whole thing. So verse 26 is deliberately extreme: utterly detest and abhor it, not admire it as an antique. Achan would take a cloak and some silver at Jericho, bury it under his tent, and destroy his family (Josh. 7:21).

That is how a besetting sin survives in a Christian life. Few people keep the idol; many keep something off it, the friendship, the taste, the door left unlocked. If your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away (Matt. 5:30) is the same instruction, given by the gentlest man who ever lived, to people he had come to save.

7.theology:
Election rests on love. God did not choose Israel for her size or goodness but because he loved her (7:7–8). That is the bedrock of assurance: if he chose us for no reason in us, nothing in us can unchoose us.

The faithful God. The security of the chosen rests not on their shaky faithfulness but on God’s chesed (7:9), which finds its yes and amen in Christ (2 Cor 1:20).

A clean break with idols. Holiness is not a polite distance from sin but the renouncing of it (7:25–26). The believer puts sin to death by the Spirit (Rom 8:13), and where he fails, it is Christ’s perfect obedience, not his own, that stands for him before God.
7.examples:
Israel, the fewest of all peoples, was made God’s treasured possession by sheer love, called to make no alliance with Canaan’s gods and to trust the God who broke Egypt to clear the land before her little by little.

Every believer is loved in the same way: not because we were lovely, but because God set his love on us. So we rest our assurance on his faithfulness, meet fear by remembering what he has done, accept slow growth in holiness as a mercy, and give no room to the idols of the heart.

8.title: Remember the LORD Your God: Man Does Not Live by Bread Alone

because you would not obey the voice of the LORD your God.
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is a meditation on memory and danger. The wilderness was a school: God humbled Israel, let them hunger and fed them with manna, “that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (8:3).

The danger ahead is that the abundance of the land will teach self-sufficiency: “My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth” (8:17). The antidote is memory: “it is he who gives you power to get wealth” (8:18). To forget God is to perish like the nations; to remember him is to find life not in bread but in his Word, supremely in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wilderness was God’s fatherly school of humbling, testing and dependence on his word.
verseByVerse.theology: Hardship in God’s hands is a father’s training, meant to humble and to teach dependence. Trials are a school of faith, not a sign that he has left.
verseByVerse.examples: God still uses hard seasons to wean his children from relying on themselves and to teach them to live by his Word.

verseByVerse.quote: "The whole commandment that I command you today you shall be careful to do, that you may live and multiply, and go in and possess the land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers. And you shall remember the whole way that the LORD your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses says God led them, not that he allowed them to wander. From inside, the wilderness looked like the consequence of disaster at Kadesh, which it was; Moses now says it was also a route, chosen and walked by God at the head of the column. Both are true. The years were judgment and they were itinerary.

And they are to remember the whole way, not just the highlights: the water from the rock and the graves at Kibroth-hattaavah, the manna and the serpents, the days when God was unmistakable and the far greater number of days when nothing happened at all. Israel is to remember the entire road. A memory that keeps only the rescues will not help much when the next stretch is dull.

The test was to know what was in your heart, and testing is not God gathering information he lacks; the test was so that they would know. Nobody discovers what he actually believes while things are comfortable. Pressure does not create character; it reveals it, and then, in God’s hands, changes it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The order of the verbs holds the lesson: he humbled, he let you hunger, then he fed. God engineered the hunger. He brought a vast company into a place with no food (the census figures of Numbers imply some two million, though some scholars think the Hebrew word for thousand there can mean a smaller military unit), let them get genuinely hungry, and only then sent bread, so that they would learn what they could not have learned in a fertile country.

The manna itself taught it: bread that appears overnight, cannot be stored, must be gathered fresh each morning, and stops the day you cross into a land with crops. Israel was fed for forty years by a word, not a harvest. This is not a verse about preferring spiritual things to physical ones; the manna filled real stomachs. The point is the source. Bread keeps a man alive because God says so; take away the word and the bread does nothing.

Centuries later the tempter said to a man forty days without food, If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread, and he answered from this verse (Matt. 4:4). Israel hungered forty years and grumbled; the true Son hungered forty days and kept the lesson Israel failed, in her place and ours. Then he said what no Israelite could have expected: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger (John 6:35).

verseByVerse.quote: Your clothing did not wear out on you and your foot did not swell these forty years. Know then in your heart that, as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Clothing that did not wear out and feet that did not swell are not the miracles anybody would have chosen to record. Not the sea or the fire: forty years of walking in a desert, and the cloak lasted and the feet held up. A man who has done any distance on foot knows how much that matters, and how little anybody thanks God for it. God’s care runs down into things nobody notices, and it is generally the small mercies that go unrecorded. Most Christians could list God’s dramatic answers; very few keep any account of forty years of feet that did not give out.

As a man disciplines his son. The word is yasar, to train or bring up, the word for raising a child rather than punishing a criminal. Israel’s forty years were not a father losing his temper but a father raising a child, and the hunger was part of the upbringing.

Hebrews presses this on suffering Christians: It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons… If you are left without discipline… then you are illegitimate children and not sons (Heb. 12:7–8). Hardship is not evidence that God has withdrawn; it is evidence of the relationship. That does not mean each sorrow is punishment for a particular sin (John 9:3); it means no sorrow lies outside a Father’s hands, and none is wasted.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — The Good Land: Bless the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses describes the good land, where Israel will eat, be full, and bless the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: God is a generous giver, and the right response to plenty is to bless him for it.
verseByVerse.examples: Every good gift, from a meal to a harvest, is an occasion for thanks to the Father who gave it.

verseByVerse.quote: So you shall keep the commandments of the LORD your God by walking in his ways and by fearing him. For the LORD your God is bringing you into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and springs, flowing out in the valleys and hills, a land of wheat and barley, of vines and fig trees and pomegranates, a land of olive trees and honey, a land in which you will eat bread without scarcity, in which you will lack nothing, a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills you can dig copper. And you shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD your God for the good land he has given you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the land, and Moses lets himself go. Every item on the list is chosen for people who have eaten the same thing every morning for forty years: water that comes up out of the ground by itself, bread from a field instead of off the sand, fruit, four kinds of it, named so they can taste them in advance, and then iron and copper. God is not embarrassed to describe the goodness of the material world to his people. He made it, and he is about to give them a great deal of it, and the passage has no trace of the suspicion of physical pleasure that has clung to religion since.

Eat, be full, and bless. Verse 10 is the hinge of the chapter and the defence against the disaster of the next ten verses. Prosperity does not have to ruin a man; it ruins him when it arrives without gratitude, because a full stomach and a short memory are exactly the conditions in which people stop needing God. The Jewish practice of saying grace after the meal, when you are full and least inclined to, comes from this verse, and it is wiser than our habit of thanking God only while still hungry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–20 — The Peril of Plenty: Do Not Forget
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Israel prospers, her heart may be lifted up to forget the LORD and credit her own power.
verseByVerse.theology: Plenty tempts the heart to pride and to forget God; remembering where everything came from keeps it humble.
verseByVerse.examples: The more comfortable a Christian’s life, the more deliberately he needs to remember.

verseByVerse.quote: "Take care lest you forget the LORD your God by not keeping his commandments and his rules and his statutes, which I command you today, lest, when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them, and when your herds and flocks multiply and your silver and gold is multiplied and all that you have is multiplied, then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, who led you through the great and terrifying wilderness, with its fiery serpents and scorpions and thirsty ground where there was no water, who brought you water out of the flinty rock, who fed you in the wilderness with manna that your fathers did not know, that he might humble you and test you, to do you good in the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The catalogue of dangers is a catalogue of blessings: full stomachs, good houses, growing herds, more silver. Everything on it is something God gives, and Moses names it all as the road to ruin. The mechanism is precise: your heart be lifted up, and you forget. First a quiet swelling of self-regard nobody notices in himself, then forgetting, which follows almost automatically. A man who has begun to feel substantial does not decide to stop depending on God. He simply finds one day that he has, and cannot say when. It is not usually rebellion; it is drift.

Against that Moses sets a memory, and chooses the details: serpents, scorpions, thirsty ground, flinty rock, manna. That is what he wants remembered in the good houses, not a general sense of having been helped. Prosperity erases detail first, and the detail is the whole point.

Then one of the tenderest phrases in Deuteronomy: he humbled and tested them to do you good in the end. Not to break them. Not even, finally, to punish them. The whole hard road had a kindness at the end that they could not see from inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.' You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth, that he may confirm his covenant that he swore to your fathers, as it is this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God quotes the sentence back to them before anybody has said it, as he did with their fear in 7:17, so that they will recognise it when they hear themselves think it. It is said in your heart: not a boast at dinner, but the private assessment a man makes when he looks at what he has built and draws a straight line back to himself, all the more dangerous for being unexamined.

The correction is not that Israel did nothing. They did farm and build. It is one step further back: it is he who gives you power to get wealth. The energy, health, intelligence, opportunity and decades of peace were none of them self-generated, and a man who traces the chain honestly runs out of his own contributions very quickly. Even the capacity was a gift. Paul asks a self-congratulating church the same question: What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? (1 Cor. 4:7).

And the reason God gives that power: that he may confirm his covenant that he swore to your fathers. The prosperity is not a reward for performance. It is the keeping of an old promise.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you forget the LORD your God and go after other gods and serve them and worship them, I solemnly warn you today that you shall surely perish. Like the nations that the LORD makes to perish before you, so shall you perish, because you would not obey the voice of the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So shall you perish. The chapter ends without softening. Israel is watching God destroy the Canaanites for idolatry, and Moses says: if you do what they did, you will get what they got. The covenant is not a charm. Centuries later Assyria and Babylon carried both kingdoms off for precisely this sin. Amos put it with brutal compression: You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities (Amos 3:2). Being chosen raised the accountability rather than removing it.

And the root is ordinary: because you would not obey the voice of the LORD your God. The book whose great confession begins Hear, O Israel ends its warnings with a people who would not listen.

Paul hands the chapter to the church: Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction… Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Cor. 10:11–12). The warning was never for Israel only, and the danger it names is not persecution. It is a good house and a full table and a heart that has quietly stopped remembering. Yet the warning is not the last word: the God of this book promised to receive his people when they return to him with all their heart (4:29–31), and the one who has forgotten may still come home.

8.theology:
Not by bread alone. The manna taught that life depends on God’s word, not on the harvest (8:3). Jesus kept that lesson in the wilderness where Israel failed (Matt 4:4), and he is himself the bread of life.

The danger of plenty. The real threat is a full table and a lifted heart (8:14, 17). Self-sufficiency grows out of comfort and ends in forgetting God.

A Father’s discipline. The wilderness was an upbringing, not an abandonment (8:5; cf. Heb 12). God trains only those he has already made his sons, and he aims at their good.
8.examples:
Israel was led through forty years of wilderness to learn dependence on God’s word, and then warned that the good land would tempt her to forget the Giver.

Many of us are among the most prosperous Christians in history, and the same danger stands at our door. We trace every good thing, even the ability to earn, back to a Father’s hand, accept hard seasons as his training, and feed on Christ, helped by the Spirit, whose work is to bring Christ’s words to our remembrance (John 14:26).

9.title: Not Because of Your Righteousness: Grace Alone for a Stubborn People
9.text: <sup>1</sup>"Hear, O Israel: you are to cross over the Jordan today, to go in to dispossess nations greater and mightier than you, cities great and fortified up to heaven,<sup>2</sup>a people great and tall, the sons of the Anakim, whom you know, and of whom you have heard it said, 'Who can stand before the sons of Anak?'<sup>3</sup>Know therefore today that he who goes over before you as a consuming fire is the LORD your God. He will destroy them and subdue them before you. So you shall drive them out and make them perish quickly, as the LORD has promised you.<sup>4</sup>"Do not say in your heart, after the LORD your God has thrust them out before you, 'It is because of my righteousness that the LORD has brought me in to possess this land,' whereas it is because of the wickedness of these nations that the LORD is driving them out before you.<sup>5</sup>Not because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart are you going in to possess their land, but because of the wickedness of these nations the LORD your God is driving them out from before you, and that he may confirm the word that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.<sup>6</sup>"Know, therefore, that the LORD your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people.<sup>7</sup>Remember and do not forget how you provoked the LORD your God to wrath in the wilderness. From the day you came out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place, you have been rebellious against the LORD.<sup>8</sup>Even at Horeb you provoked the LORD to wrath, and the LORD was so angry with you that he was ready to destroy you.<sup>9</sup>When I went up the mountain to receive the tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant that the LORD made with you, I remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD gave me the two tablets of stone written with the finger of God, and on them were all the words that the LORD had spoken with you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly.<sup>11</sup>And at the end of forty days and forty nights the LORD gave me the two tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant.<sup>12</sup>Then the LORD said to me, 'Arise, go down quickly from here, for your people whom you have brought from Egypt have acted corruptly. They have turned aside quickly out of the way that I commanded them; they have made themselves a metal image.'<sup>13</sup>"Furthermore, the LORD said to me, 'I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stubborn people.<sup>14</sup>Let me alone, that I may destroy them and blot out their name from under heaven. And I will make of you a nation mightier and greater than they.'<sup>15</sup>So I turned and came down from the mountain, and the mountain was burning with fire. And the two tablets of the covenant were in my two hands.<sup>16</sup>And I looked, and behold, you had sinned against the LORD your God. You had made yourselves a golden calf. You had turned aside quickly from the way that the LORD had commanded you.<sup>17</sup>So I took hold of the two tablets and threw them out of my two hands and broke them before your eyes.<sup>18</sup>Then I lay prostrate before the LORD as before, forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water, because of all the sin that you had committed, in doing what was evil in the sight of the LORD to provoke him to anger.<sup>19</sup>For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure that the LORD bore against you, so that he was ready to destroy you. But the LORD listened to me that time also.<sup>20</sup>And the LORD was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him. And I prayed for Aaron also at the same time.<sup>21</sup>Then I took the sinful thing, the calf that you had made, and burned it with fire and crushed it, grinding it very small, until it was as fine as dust. And I threw the dust of it into the brook that ran down from the mountain.<sup>22</sup>"At Taberah also, and at Massah and at Kibroth-hattaavah you provoked the LORD to wrath.<sup>23</sup>And when the LORD sent you from Kadesh-barnea, saying, 'Go up and take possession of the land that I have given you,' then you rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God and did not believe him or obey his voice.<sup>24</sup>You have been rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you.<sup>25</sup>"So I lay prostrate before the LORD for these forty days and forty nights, because the LORD had said he would destroy you.<sup>26</sup>And I prayed to the LORD, 'O Lord GOD, do not destroy your people and your heritage, whom you have redeemed through your greatness, whom you have brought out of Egypt with a mighty hand.<sup>27</sup>Remember your servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Do not regard the stubbornness of this people, or their wickedness or their sin,<sup>28</sup>lest the land from which you brought us say, "Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land that he promised them, and because he hated them, he has brought them out to put them to death in the wilderness."<sup>29</sup>For they are your people and your heritage, whom you brought out by your great power and by your outstretched arm.'
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is a sustained assault on self-righteousness. Lest Israel imagine that conquest proved her virtue, Moses says three times (vv. 4–6) that the land is given not for her righteousness but because of the nations’ wickedness and the promise to the fathers.

To prove it he rehearses Israel’s rebellion, climaxing in the golden calf made at the foot of the mountain while the covenant was being written. The chapter’s glory is Moses’ intercession: forty days on his face, pleading not the people’s merit but God’s name, promise and redemption. Moses the mediator stands between the people and the wrath they had earned, a shadow of the greater Mediator to come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Not Because of Your Righteousness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must not credit her own righteousness: the land is given because of the nations’ wickedness and God’s promise.
verseByVerse.theology: Inheritance is a gift of grace, never a reward. God blesses the undeserving for his own name’s sake.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel’s conquest was grace, not wages, and so is the believer’s salvation: it rests on Christ’s righteousness, not ours.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear, O Israel: you are to cross over the Jordan today, to go in to dispossess nations greater and mightier than you, cities great and fortified up to heaven, a people great and tall, the sons of the Anakim, whom you know, and of whom you have heard it said, 'Who can stand before the sons of Anak?' Know therefore today that he who goes over before you as a consuming fire is the LORD your God. He will destroy them and subdue them before you. So you shall drive them out and make them perish quickly, as the LORD has promised you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses quotes the spies’ report back at them: fortified up to heaven is the phrase from 1:28, and the Anakim are the terror that broke the last generation. He does not deny a word of it, and adds the proverb the nations used, who can stand before the sons of Anak? His method is never to shrink the obstacle. He grants the whole report and then sets beside it a consuming fire.

Set the Anakim against Israel and the proverb is right. Set them against a consuming fire and the question does not arise. The last generation did the first sum and got a true answer to the wrong question.

And note: he will destroy them… So you shall drive them out. God will do it; Israel will do it. Both in one sentence, without contradiction, which is how Scripture always speaks of the work of God and the work of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not say in your heart, after the LORD your God has thrust them out before you, 'It is because of my righteousness that the LORD has brought me in to possess this land,' whereas it is because of the wickedness of these nations that the LORD is driving them out before you. Not because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart are you going in to possess their land, but because of the wickedness of these nations the LORD your God is driving them out from before you, and that he may confirm the word that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. "Know, therefore, that the LORD your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the point of the chapter, made three times in three verses because Moses knows what victory does to people. Each time the ground is cut away more sharply, ending in a flat insult: you are a stubborn people, the people Exodus calls stiff-necked (Exod. 32:9), like an ox that will not turn under the yoke.

The temptation comes after God has thrust the nations out. It is success that produces this, as in chapter 8 a full stomach did. A man who has just watched God do something remarkable through him is in more spiritual danger than a man who has just failed, because he is tempted to draw a line from the result back to himself.

The two real reasons are neither of them Israel: the wickedness of these nations, so that this is judgment on Canaan, not reward for Israel; and the oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, men centuries dead. That leaves nothing on Israel’s side of the ledger, and it is the doctrine of grace stated as plainly as Paul states it: not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy (Titus 3:5). Every Christian who has begun to feel that his standing with God depends on how the last few months have gone should read these three verses slowly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — The Golden Calf: Provoking God to Wrath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even at Horeb, while Moses received the covenant, Israel made the golden calf.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin runs deep even in God’s redeemed people, which is why their standing has to rest on grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Even in our most privileged moments we are prone to wander, and that keeps us dependent on mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember and do not forget how you provoked the LORD your God to wrath in the wilderness. From the day you came out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place, you have been rebellious against the LORD. Even at Horeb you provoked the LORD to wrath, and the LORD was so angry with you that he was ready to destroy you. When I went up the mountain to receive the tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant that the LORD made with you, I remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water. And the LORD gave me the two tablets of stone written with the finger of God, and on them were all the words that the LORD had spoken with you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In chapter 8 Moses told them to remember what God had done for them; here, what they had done to God. A memory that keeps only the mercies produces sentimentality, one that keeps only the failures produces despair, and Israel is to hold both. The summary is devastating: rebellious from the day you came out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place. Not a bad patch, the whole history.

And the timing makes it unbearable. Moses spent forty days on the mountain without food while God wrote the covenant with his own finger, and during those same forty days, at the foot of the same mountain, the nation was casting a calf. The covenant was broken while it was being written. Not afterwards, when the memory had faded and the generations had turned, but while the ink was wet, by people who had heard the voice from the fire and who six weeks earlier had said all that the LORD has spoken we will do (Exod. 19:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of forty days and forty nights the LORD gave me the two tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant. Then the LORD said to me, 'Arise, go down quickly from here, for your people whom you have brought from Egypt have acted corruptly. They have turned aside quickly out of the way that I commanded them; they have made themselves a metal image.' "Furthermore, the LORD said to me, 'I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stubborn people. Let me alone, that I may destroy them and blot out their name from under heaven. And I will make of you a nation mightier and greater than they.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s words to Moses are abrupt: your people whom you have brought from Egypt. He hands them back to Moses, the way a father says your son to his wife when the boy has disgraced himself.

Then the offer: I will make of you a nation mightier and greater than they. A fresh start, a nation from Moses’ own line, no more of these people. It is genuine, and it is everything Moses could have wanted; and every leader ground down by the people he leads knows what is being dangled.

Let me alone. Why would the Almighty say that to a man? Nothing restrains God. It is an invitation dressed as a prohibition: to say "do not hold me back" tells somebody that they can, and Moses, who knew God better than anyone alive, immediately began to hold him back. God tells intercessors what he is about to do in terms that all but invite them to plead against it, as Abraham found over Sodom: Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do? (Gen. 18:17).

Does prayer change God’s mind? The threat was real, and God used it to draw out Moses’ intercession (9:18–19; 10:10). His eternal purpose included the prayer as the means by which he spared Israel (cf. Jer 18:7–10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — Moses Breaks the Tablets and Destroys the Calf
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses descends, shatters the tablets before their eyes, and grinds the idol to powder.
verseByVerse.theology: The broken tablets act out the broken covenant, and the ground-up calf shows that God tolerates no rivals.
verseByVerse.examples: A Christian, forgiven in Christ, destroys a cherished idol in the Spirit’s strength rather than merely setting it aside.

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned and came down from the mountain, and the mountain was burning with fire. And the two tablets of the covenant were in my two hands. And I looked, and behold, you had sinned against the LORD your God. You had made yourselves a golden calf. You had turned aside quickly from the way that the LORD had commanded you. So I took hold of the two tablets and threw them out of my two hands and broke them before your eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Picture the descent: a mountain on fire behind him, and in his arms the only stones on earth that God himself had written on. Then you had turned aside quickly. That is the word that stings: not after a generation of drift, but within weeks, while the man who led them out was still up the hill.

Before your eyes. The breaking is often read as Moses losing his temper, and there is anger in it. But he did not drop the tablets where nobody was looking. He smashed them in front of the nation as public testimony, probably because in the ancient world a broken treaty was marked by breaking its tablet. He was showing them what they had already done. The tablets were the marriage certificate, and he tore it up in front of the bride, on the day, while the other man was still in the house.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I lay prostrate before the LORD as before, forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water, because of all the sin that you had committed, in doing what was evil in the sight of the LORD to provoke him to anger. For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure that the LORD bore against you, so that he was ready to destroy you. But the LORD listened to me that time also. And the LORD was so angry with Aaron that he was ready to destroy him. And I prayed for Aaron also at the same time. Then I took the sinful thing, the calf that you had made, and burned it with fire and crushed it, grinding it very small, until it was as fine as dust. And I threw the dust of it into the brook that ran down from the mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Moses does next is the greatest thing about him. Forty more days on his face without food, not for himself and not to receive anything, but because of what they had done. If this was a second forty days, that is eighty days of fasting inside a few months, for people who had betrayed him and God while he was away.

Verse 19 lets us see inside him: he was afraid, not for himself, since God had just offered him a dynasty, but for them. He had seen the fire on the mountain and knew what it could do. Then nine words that carry the chapter: But the LORD listened to me that time also.

Verse 20 adds what is impossible to forget once seen: And I prayed for Aaron also, his own brother, the high priest, the man who made the calf and then lied about it. Aaron, whom the LORD was angry enough to destroy, lived to serve as Israel’s first high priest because Moses prayed for him. He prayed hardest for the man who had wronged him most.

Then the idol: burned, crushed, ground as fine as dust, and thrown into running water so it could not be gathered again. There is a way of dealing with an idol that leaves nothing to come back to, and it is the only way that works.
