verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–29 — Moses’ Great Intercession: For Your Name’s Sake
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses recalls Israel’s rebellions and his prayer, which pleaded God’s name, promise and redemption.
verseByVerse.theology: Prayer that prevails appeals not to our merit but to God’s name, promise and saving work.
verseByVerse.examples: We are heard on the same ground: not our worthiness, but the merit and intercession of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "At Taberah also, and at Massah and at Kibroth-hattaavah you provoked the LORD to wrath. And when the LORD sent you from Kadesh-barnea, saying, 'Go up and take possession of the land that I have given you,' then you rebelled against the commandment of the LORD your God and did not believe him or obey his voice. You have been rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses runs through a geography of failure. Taberah, "burning," where the LORD’s fire fell on the outskirts of the camp. Massah, "testing." Kibroth-hattaavah, "graves of craving," where they demanded meat and were buried in it. Israel’s route across the wilderness is marked by place-names that are all confessions, and every one of them was a place where God had already provided.

Then Kadesh-barnea, in one sentence that reaches the root: they did not believe him or obey his voice. Believe and obey, in that order, with the failure of the first producing the failure of the second.

And Moses’ verdict on forty years together: from the day that I knew you. He is not exaggerating; the previous chapters are the evidence. This honest, unflattering account of God’s own people is what makes the next paragraph what it is. Nobody could read Deuteronomy 9 and conclude that Israel deserved to be saved.

verseByVerse.quote: "So I lay prostrate before the LORD for these forty days and forty nights, because the LORD had said he would destroy you. And I prayed to the LORD, 'O Lord GOD, do not destroy your people and your heritage, whom you have redeemed through your greatness, whom you have brought out of Egypt with a mighty hand. Remember your servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Do not regard the stubbornness of this people, or their wickedness or their sin, lest the land from which you brought us say, "Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land that he promised them, and because he hated them, he has brought them out to put them to death in the wilderness." For they are your people and your heritage, whom you brought out by your great power and by your outstretched arm.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the prayer itself, and it is a masterclass in intercession. Moses does not argue that the people are better than they look, or promise they will improve, or mention his own record or the dynasty he was offered. Every argument he makes is about God.

First, they are God’s heritage, whom you have redeemed: he gives back the pronouns God had taken away, and the whole hinge of the prayer is done in one word. Second, the patriarchs: a promise made centuries before any of these sinners existed. Third, he asks God not to regard their stubbornness. He denies none of it; he asks God not to look at it, which is what a man asks when he has no case at all. Fourth, and most boldly, he puts God’s reputation on the table: Egypt will conclude either that the LORD could not finish what he started, or that he never loved them.

Every one of those arguments was available to Moses only because of what God had already said and done. That is how a man prays with nothing to plead on his side of the account: he appeals to what God has done, what God has promised, and who God is, and it works, because those are the only things that ever have. A greater Intercessor prays on the same ground, not that we deserve to be kept, but that we were bought. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25).

9.theology:
Grace, not righteousness. Moses leaves nothing on Israel’s side of the ledger (9:4–6). This is the Old Testament ground of justification by grace, which the gospel states outright: “not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:9).

The depth of sin. Israel’s whole history was rebellion (9:24), and honest remembrance of it guards against pride. We are more sinful than we dare admit, and more loved than we dare hope.

The mediator. Moses pleaded God’s name, promise and redemption (9:18, 25–29), foreshadowing Christ, who intercedes for his people on the ground of his own sacrifice (Heb 7:25).
9.examples:
On the brink of conquest, Israel was warned never to credit her own righteousness, since she had survived only because Moses pleaded for her.

Christians remember their own rebellion honestly, which keeps them humble and grateful; they grind their idols to dust rather than negotiate with them; and they pray with confidence, not because they deserve a hearing but because Christ’s finished work stands for them.

10.title: Circumcise Your Hearts: What Does the LORD Require of You?
10.text: <sup>1</sup>"At that time the LORD said to me, 'Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and come up to me on the mountain and make an ark of wood.<sup>2</sup>And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets that you broke, and you shall put them in the ark.'<sup>3</sup>So I made an ark of acacia wood, and cut two tablets of stone like the first, and went up the mountain with the two tablets in my hand.<sup>4</sup>And he wrote on the tablets, in the same writing as before, the Ten Commandments that the LORD had spoken to you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly. And the LORD gave them to me.<sup>5</sup>Then I turned and came down from the mountain and put the tablets in the ark that I had made. And there they are, as the LORD commanded me."<sup>6</sup>(The people of Israel journeyed from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Moserah. There Aaron died, and there he was buried. And his son Eleazar ministered as priest in his place.<sup>7</sup>From there they journeyed to Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah to Jotbathah, a land with brooks of water.<sup>8</sup>At that time the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD to stand before the LORD to minister to him and to bless in his name, to this day.<sup>9</sup>Therefore Levi has no portion or inheritance with his brothers. The LORD is his inheritance, as the LORD your God said to him.)<sup>10</sup>"I myself stayed on the mountain, as at the first time, forty days and forty nights, and the LORD listened to me that time also. The LORD was unwilling to destroy you.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'Arise, go on your journey at the head of the people, so that they may go in and possess the land, which I swore to their fathers to give them.'<sup>12</sup>"And now, Israel, what does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul,<sup>13</sup>and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD, which I am commanding you today for your good?<sup>14</sup>Behold, to the LORD your God belong heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth with all that is in it.<sup>15</sup>Yet the LORD set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them, you above all peoples, as you are this day.<sup>16</sup>Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn.<sup>17</sup>For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who is not partial and takes no bribe.<sup>18</sup>He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing.<sup>19</sup>Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.<sup>20</sup>You shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him, and by his name you shall swear.<sup>21</sup>He is your praise. He is your God, who has done for you these great and terrifying things that your eyes have seen.<sup>22</sup>Your fathers went down to Egypt seventy persons, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars of heaven.
10.overview:
Chapter 10 moves from rebellion to renewal. God gives new tablets, restoring the covenant Israel had shattered, a picture of grace rewriting what sin destroyed; the ark is made to hold them, and the Levites are set apart.

Then one of the great summaries of true religion: what does the LORD require of you (10:12), a question Micah 6:8 will echo. At the centre stands a command the whole Bible unfolds: “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart” (10:16), a cry the new covenant answers (30:6). And the God who owns heaven and earth loves the sojourner and defends the fatherless and the widow; his people are to love as he loves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — New Tablets: Grace Rewrites the Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rewrites the Ten Commandments on new tablets, restoring the broken covenant.
verseByVerse.theology: Grace rewrites what sin destroyed: God restores the covenant his people broke and keeps his word among them.
verseByVerse.examples: In Christ, God restores what our sin breaks and writes his law on hearts of flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time the LORD said to me, 'Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and come up to me on the mountain and make an ark of wood. And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets that you broke, and you shall put them in the ark.' So I made an ark of acacia wood, and cut two tablets of stone like the first, and went up the mountain with the two tablets in my hand. And he wrote on the tablets, in the same writing as before, the Ten Commandments that the LORD had spoken to you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly. And the LORD gave them to me. Then I turned and came down from the mountain and put the tablets in the ark that I had made. And there they are, as the LORD commanded me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 9 ended with a smashed covenant and a man on his face for forty days. Chapter 10 opens with God’s answer, the plainest picture of grace in the Pentateuch. Israel broke the covenant while it was being written; Moses broke the tablets to show what they had done; and God says: cut two more, and I will write the same words again.

Not different words, not a lower standard for a people who have proved they cannot keep the higher one. God begins again at exactly the point where they failed. And Moses cuts the stone; God does the writing. Man can prepare the tablets; only God can put anything on them worth having, a distinction that matters eleven verses on, when the subject changes from stone to hearts.

Then the ark, a plain wooden box for the second tablets. The most sacred object in Israel existed to house a covenant broken before the ink dried, and God chose to sit above it on the mercy seat and speak from there (Num. 7:89). The law Israel had broken, kept under the blood-sprinkled lid, is the whole gospel in a piece of furniture. Paul uses the Greek Old Testament’s word for that lid when he says God put Christ forward as a propitiation, a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath, by his blood (Romans 3:25; compare Hebrews 9:5).

Moses says he made the ark before going up; Exodus has Bezalel make it later (Exod 37:1). Moses is summarising, not giving a timetable: he is telling what was done under his command. And Aaron died near Moserah (v. 6), probably the camp area near Mount Hor where Numbers says he died (Num 20:28; 33:30, 38).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — The Levites Set Apart; Moses Prevails
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A travel note records Aaron’s death and the setting apart of the Levites, whose inheritance is the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides servants to carry his word and bless his people, and their true inheritance is God himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Those who serve the church in the word are not promised much on earth, but they are promised the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: (The people of Israel journeyed from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Moserah. There Aaron died, and there he was buried. And his son Eleazar ministered as priest in his place. From there they journeyed to Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah to Jotbathah, a land with brooks of water. At that time the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD to stand before the LORD to minister to him and to bless in his name, to this day. Therefore Levi has no portion or inheritance with his brothers. The LORD is his inheritance, as the LORD your God said to him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A short travel note interrupts the sermon, Aaron’s death and Eleazar’s succession, and then, almost in passing, one of the great sentences of the Old Testament: The LORD is his inheritance.

Levi has three duties: carry the ark on the road, stand before God when the camp settles, and bless the people in his name. And therefore Levi gets no land. On the day the country was divided, eleven tribes walked away holding a map: this ridge, that valley, the olive terraces, the boundary stone with a grandfather’s name cut into it. Levi was handed nothing to leave a son, and instead was given God.

That invites a searching question. Suppose you were given everything you have ever wanted, the health returned, the debts cleared, and God himself were not there: would that be heaven? Most of us would have to think about it, and the hesitation shows where our hearts have drifted. The answer is not to love God’s gifts less, but to find that the Giver is the one portion that holds all the rest, and Levi’s portion is offered to every believer. Asaph came to the answer after nearly losing his faith over the prosperity of the wicked: Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you… God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (Ps. 73:25–26).

And every acre the eleven tribes received could be taken, and eventually was, by drought, debt, Assyria and time. A portion that is God cannot be repossessed. Levi held the only inheritance in Israel that no invading army could reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "I myself stayed on the mountain, as at the first time, forty days and forty nights, and the LORD listened to me that time also. The LORD was unwilling to destroy you. And the LORD said to me, 'Arise, go on your journey at the head of the people, so that they may go in and possess the land, which I swore to their fathers to give them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD was unwilling. Put the two halves side by side. On the mountain God had said, let me alone, that I may destroy them; now he says, get up and lead them into the land I promised. Nothing about the people has changed. The calf is still ground to powder in a stream; the same men are still in the camp. What stands between the two sentences is forty days of a man on his face.

Not "unable," and not "persuaded against his will": unwilling. When it came to it, he did not want to. The intercession was real and God answered it, and behind the answer was a disposition that had been there all along. That is the God Moses knew, and the reason he dared to pray as he did. A man does not lie on the ground for forty days pleading with somebody he thinks is looking for an excuse to destroy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–13 — What Does the LORD Require?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sums up covenant life: fear, walk, love, serve and keep, all for Israel’s good.
verseByVerse.theology: True religion is wholehearted, reverent love for God, and his commandments are for our good.
verseByVerse.examples: The same call to fear, walk, love, serve and keep describes the Christian life, now lived in love for God in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Israel, what does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD, which I am commanding you today for your good?
verseByVerse.commentary:
After all the history and warnings, Moses asks the question directly and answers it in one sentence, one of the great summaries of the Old Testament, to which Micah will write a companion (Mic. 6:8).

The list runs from the heart’s posture, fear, reverent awe, to actual obedience, keep the commandments, and in the middle, holding the two together, love him and serve him with all the heart and soul. Deuteronomy will not let them be separated. Awe without love is terror; love without obedience is sentiment; obedience without either is drudgery.

For your good. That is God’s own account of why he gives commandments: not to establish his authority, which needs no establishing, or to make life narrow, but for their flourishing, the precise point the serpent contradicted in Eden. And require is no fee. Read with verse 13 attached, the question becomes: what does God ask of you, other than the things that are for your good? And he asks it of a people he has just forgiven and restored.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–15 — Heaven Belongs to God, Yet He Set His Love on You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who owns heaven and earth set his love on Israel’s fathers.
verseByVerse.theology: The God who owns all things freely chose to love a particular people, and the wonder of election is how low he stooped.
verseByVerse.examples: The God who needs nothing has set his love on us in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, to the LORD your God belong heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth with all that is in it. Yet the LORD set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them, you above all peoples, as you are this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A sentence whose logic takes the breath away. The heaven of heavens is a Hebrew superlative, everything above and beyond what anybody can see, and all of it is his, with the earth and all in it. He lacks nothing and needs nobody.

And yet the God who owns the heaven of heavens set his heart on a family of nomads and their descendants. Not because he needed them, which verse 14 rules out; not because they were impressive, which chapter 9 rules out. Set his heart is a word of attachment, of desire, of being drawn.

Here election stops being an abstraction. People fear that God chose arbitrarily, like a man picking a number. Deuteronomy says he chose in love, which is not arbitrary but is also not explained by anything in the chosen. That is what love is like when it is not a response to merit; nobody asks a man why he loves his own child and expects a list of the child’s qualifications. The New Testament has the same astonishment: See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are (1 John 3:1). The wonder is not that God is loving in general, but that he settled it on these particular people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–22 — Circumcise Your Hearts; Love as God Loves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is to circumcise her heart and love the sojourner as her just and compassionate God does.
verseByVerse.theology: Outward religion is not enough; the heart itself must be cut and changed. God’s own justice and compassion are the pattern for his people’s love.
verseByVerse.examples: The new covenant gives the changed heart, and Christians welcome the outsider because God first welcomed them.

verseByVerse.quote: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Circumcision was the physical mark of the covenant, cut into every Israelite male on the eighth day, the sign that he belonged to God’s people. Moses turns it inward. There is something in the human heart like an uncircumcised foreskin, a covering and hardness that has to be cut away before there can be real belonging. Israel had the outward mark and was stubborn. A man may bear every external sign of covenant membership and be untouched underneath.

That is the burden of the prophets afterwards: all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart (Jer. 9:26). Paul says it to people trusting their pedigree: no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly… circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter (Rom. 2:28–29).

But feel the impossibility of the command. A man can be circumcised in the flesh by somebody else before he can consent to anything; he cannot reach his own heart, or cut away his hardness with the very organ that is hard. Deuteronomy knows it. Twenty chapters later the same verb has a different subject: And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart (30:6). Here it is commanded; there it is promised. The command exposes what we cannot do, and the promise announces that God will do it, which is why Ezekiel’s great sentence sounds like the answer to this verse, because it is: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezek. 36:26).

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who is not partial and takes no bribe. He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing. Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five titles piled up, and then two negatives that do the work. The God of gods is not partial, literally he does not lift up faces, and takes no bribe, unlike the gods of the nations, who were thought to be won over by gifts.

And what he does with his impartiality is not what anyone expects. The God of gods and Lord of lords, who cannot be bribed or impressed, spends his attention on the orphan, the widow and the foreigner, the three groups with no legal standing, no advocate and no leverage, which is exactly why the God who is not impressed by leverage takes them up. His impartiality is not cool neutrality; it is why he ends up on the side of the people nobody else is on the side of. And it is practical: food and clothing, not sympathy only but dinner and a coat.

The inference for Israel is not "therefore admire him" but Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt. You were one, and somebody came and got you. God’s people treat the outsider as God treated them when they were outside, which is the logic of Christian mercy in one line, and the reason the parable of the unforgiving servant ends the way it does.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him, and by his name you shall swear. He is your praise. He is your God, who has done for you these great and terrifying things that your eyes have seen. Your fathers went down to Egypt seventy persons, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hold fast. Dabaq, the word of 4:4 again: cling, stick, be glued to. At Peor those who clung to God were alive and those who followed Baal were in the ground. It is not a word about opinions. It is a word about grip.

He is your praise. Not "he deserves your praise": he is it, the whole content of anything Israel could boast of. A small nation with no standing army and no land of its own had exactly one distinction, and it was not theirs.

Seventy persons. That is a village, one extended family listed in Genesis 46, going down into Egypt to escape a famine. (Stephen’s seventy-five in Acts 7:14 follows the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 46:27, which counts some further descendants of Joseph.) Four centuries later, a nation nobody can count, on the border of a country God promised to a childless man once told to try counting the stars. Seventy people and a promise: that is all God started with, and he has never needed more. The church began the same way, a hundred and twenty in an upstairs room, and a promise.

10.theology:
A circumcised heart. The stubborn heart itself must be cut and changed (10:16). The command exposes a need it cannot meet, but what is commanded here is promised in 30:6 and given in the new covenant, where God himself changes the heart by the Spirit (Jer 31:33; Rom 2:29).

What the LORD requires. Covenant life comes down to fearing, walking, loving, serving and keeping, all for your good (10:12–13). Christ met this demand perfectly, and the Spirit works it in us.

The God who loves the lowly. The Lord of heaven, who needs nothing, set his love on a small, undeserving people (10:14–15) and defends the fatherless, the widow and the sojourner (10:17–19). His people love the outsider because they were once outsiders loved by grace.
10.examples:
God rewrote the covenant Israel had broken, gave the Levites himself as their inheritance, and called his people to circumcise their hearts and love the sojourner as he had loved them.

In Christ, God restores what our sin breaks and by his Spirit does the heart-work we could never do. We hold fast to him as our portion and our praise, and we love the outsider and the vulnerable because we were strangers brought near by grace.

11.title: Love and Obey: The Blessing and the Curse Set Before You
11.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall therefore love the LORD your God and keep his charge, his statutes, his rules, and his commandments always.<sup>2</sup>And consider today (since I am not speaking to your children who have not known or seen it), consider the discipline of the LORD your God, his greatness, his mighty hand and his outstretched arm,<sup>3</sup>his signs and his deeds that he did in Egypt to Pharaoh the king of Egypt and to all his land,<sup>4</sup>and what he did to the army of Egypt, to their horses and to their chariots, how he made the water of the Red Sea flow over them as they pursued after you, and how the LORD has destroyed them to this day,<sup>5</sup>and what he did to you in the wilderness, until you came to this place,<sup>6</sup>and what he did to Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, son of Reuben, how the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households, their tents, and every living thing that followed them, in the midst of all Israel.<sup>7</sup>For your eyes have seen all the great work of the LORD that he did.<sup>8</sup>"You shall therefore keep the whole commandment that I command you today, that you may be strong, and go in and take possession of the land that you are going over to possess,<sup>9</sup>and that you may live long in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give to them and to their offspring, a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>10</sup>For the land that you are entering to take possession of it is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come, where you sowed your seed and irrigated it, like a garden of vegetables.<sup>11</sup>But the land that you are going over to possess is a land of hills and valleys, which drinks water by the rain from heaven,<sup>12</sup>a land that the LORD your God cares for. The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year.<sup>13</sup>"And if you will indeed obey my commandments that I command you today, to love the LORD your God, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul,<sup>14</sup>he will give the rain for your land in its season, the early rain and the later rain, that you may gather in your grain and your wine and your oil.<sup>15</sup>And he will give grass in your fields for your livestock, and you shall eat and be full.<sup>16</sup>Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods and worship them;<sup>17</sup>then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain, and the land will yield no fruit, and you will perish quickly off the good land that the LORD is giving you.<sup>18</sup>"You shall therefore lay up these words of mine in your heart and in your soul, and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes.<sup>19</sup>You shall teach them to your children, talking of them when you are sitting in your house, and when you are walking by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.<sup>20</sup>You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates,<sup>21</sup>that your days and the days of your children may be multiplied in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give them, as long as the heavens are above the earth.<sup>22</sup>For if you will be careful to do all this commandment that I command you to do, loving the LORD your God, walking in all his ways, and holding fast to him,<sup>23</sup>then the LORD will drive out all these nations before you, and you will dispossess nations greater and mightier than you.<sup>24</sup>Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours. Your territory shall be from the wilderness to the Lebanon, and from the River, the river Euphrates, to the western sea.<sup>25</sup>No one shall be able to stand against you. The LORD your God will lay the fear of you and the dread of you on all the land that you shall tread, as he promised you.<sup>26</sup>"See, I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse:<sup>27</sup>the blessing, if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God, which I command you today,<sup>28</sup>and the curse, if you do not obey the commandments of the LORD your God, but turn aside from the way that I am commanding you today, to go after other gods that you have not known.<sup>29</sup>And when the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to take possession of it, you shall set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal.<sup>30</sup>Are they not beyond the Jordan, west of the road, toward the going down of the sun, in the land of the Canaanites who live in the Arabah, opposite Gilgal, beside the oak of Moreh?<sup>31</sup>For you are to cross over the Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you. And when you possess it and live in it,<sup>32</sup>you shall be careful to do all the statutes and the rules that I am setting before you today.
11.overview:
Chapter 11 closes Moses’ second address (chs. 5–11) and leads into the detailed laws. Its theme is the bond of love and obedience: “You shall therefore love the LORD your God and keep his charge… always” (11:1), urged by what Israel’s own eyes have seen of God’s mighty acts.

Moses contrasts the land with Egypt: not watered by human effort but “a land that the LORD your God cares for. The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it” (11:12). And the chapter ends with the choice that runs through the whole book: “See, I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse” (11:26), to be proclaimed from Gerizim and Ebal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Your Eyes Have Seen: Obey Because You Remember
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses appeals to what Israel’s own eyes have seen of God’s discipline and mighty acts.
verseByVerse.theology: Obedience grows out of remembering what God has done; those who have seen his power have no excuse for unbelief.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians obey in the light of what they have seen of God’s grace in Christ and in their own lives.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall therefore love the LORD your God and keep his charge, his statutes, his rules, and his commandments always. And consider today (since I am not speaking to your children who have not known or seen it), consider the discipline of the LORD your God, his greatness, his mighty hand and his outstretched arm, his signs and his deeds that he did in Egypt to Pharaoh the king of Egypt and to all his land, and what he did to the army of Egypt, to their horses and to their chariots, how he made the water of the Red Sea flow over them as they pursued after you, and how the LORD has destroyed them to this day, and what he did to you in the wilderness, until you came to this place, and what he did to Dathan and Abiram the sons of Eliab, son of Reuben, how the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, with their households, their tents, and every living thing that followed them, in the midst of all Israel. For your eyes have seen all the great work of the LORD that he did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love and obedience are bound in a single sentence, and Deuteronomy never separates them. Love that does not obey is sentiment; obedience that does not love is drudgery. The Lord Jesus said the same: If you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15).

Moses addresses the men old enough to remember, not their children who have not known or seen it, and tells them their memories are an obligation. They saw Egypt, the sea closing over Pharaoh’s army, the wilderness, the ground opening under Dathan and Abiram; nobody in the coming generations will. What they do with that is the difference between a nation that knows God and one that has heard about him.

The list is not all mercies. Pharaoh’s army and Dathan are acts of judgment, set in the same sentence as the deliverance, and both are grounds for love. A God who never acted against evil would not be worth loving.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — The Land God Cares For
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The land, unlike Egypt, drinks rain from heaven under God’s constant care.
verseByVerse.theology: God watches over his people’s land without a break, and daily dependence on him is the rhythm of covenant life.
verseByVerse.examples: The believer looks to heaven for every good gift, including the ones that seem to come by our own effort.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall therefore keep the whole commandment that I command you today, that you may be strong, and go in and take possession of the land that you are going over to possess, and that you may live long in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give to them and to their offspring, a land flowing with milk and honey. For the land that you are entering to take possession of it is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come, where you sowed your seed and irrigated it, like a garden of vegetables. But the land that you are going over to possess is a land of hills and valleys, which drinks water by the rain from heaven, a land that the LORD your God cares for. The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now one of the loveliest contrasts in the Old Testament, and it turns on how two countries get their water. Egypt was watered by the Nile, a river that floods on schedule, and by channels opened and closed with the foot. An Egyptian farmer did not pray for rain. He dug, and the river came. Water was a matter of engineering.

Canaan is hills. The water falls out of the sky or it does not, and no digging will produce a drop. A farmer there looked up rather than across, twice a year, and could do nothing whatever about it.

God is deliberately moving his people from a country where they could manage their own supply to one where they could not. That is not a downgrade; he calls it care: The eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year. Israel is moved into permanent dependence and told that this is what being cared for looks like. Anyone whose circumstances have become less controllable than they used to be should hold on to that. The Nile is easier. The hills are where you learn to look up.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew says Israel watered Egypt “with your foot” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "And if you will indeed obey my commandments that I command you today, to love the LORD your God, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul, he will give the rain for your land in its season, the early rain and the later rain, that you may gather in your grain and your wine and your oil. And he will give grass in your fields for your livestock, and you shall eat and be full. Take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods and worship them; then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain, and the land will yield no fruit, and you will perish quickly off the good land that the LORD is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise is rain in its season: the autumn rain that softened the ground for ploughing and the spring rain that filled the grain. Miss either and the year fails.

The warning is calibrated to that geography: turn to other gods and he will shut up the heavens. The gods of Canaan were fertility gods, and Baal was the storm god, the lord of rain; every Canaanite farmer knew what you did in a dry spring. So God says: the rain is mine, and if you go to Baal for it I will stop it. He meets them on the exact ground of the temptation. Centuries later Elijah told Ahab there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word (1 Kgs. 17:1), and the prophets of Baal spent a whole day on Carmel trying to get their storm god to light a fire. Deuteronomy 11:17 is the text Elijah stood on.

Lest your heart be deceived. Not "lest you rebel." Nobody meant to abandon God for Baal; they meant to keep both, with a little insurance for the harvest. Idolatry usually arrives as a supplement rather than a replacement.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah 5:24 and Joel 2:23 also name these two rains, autumn and spring, as God’s gift.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Lay Up These Words; Teach Your Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses repeats the Shema’s call to lay up God’s words in heart and home.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s word is meant to fill heart and home across the generations.
verseByVerse.examples: Faith is still handed on chiefly at home, in ordinary conversation.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall therefore lay up these words of mine in your heart and in your soul, and you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. You shall teach them to your children, talking of them when you are sitting in your house, and when you are walking by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise. You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates, that your days and the days of your children may be multiplied in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give them, as long as the heavens are above the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses repeats the instructions of the Shema almost word for word, five chapters on. A preacher who repeats himself at that length is not running out of material; he is doing what he told them to do, going over the same edge again.

One addition comes at the end: as long as the heavens are above the earth. The promise is measured against the permanence of the sky, and the means by which it reaches that far is not a monument or an institution but parents talking to children in the kitchen and on the road. God has tied his people’s future to the most fragile-looking arrangement imaginable, and it is not fragile; it is the only thing that has ever worked. Institutions preserve documents. Families transmit faith.

Are these signs literal? The language is figurative, as in Proverbs 7:3: God’s words are to govern what we do and how we see. Jewish practice took it literally with tefillin and the mezuzah; Christians are free but not bound to do the same.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you will be careful to do all this commandment that I command you to do, loving the LORD your God, walking in all his ways, and holding fast to him, then the LORD will drive out all these nations before you, and you will dispossess nations greater and mightier than you. Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours. Your territory shall be from the wilderness to the Lebanon, and from the River, the river Euphrates, to the western sea. No one shall be able to stand against you. The LORD your God will lay the fear of you and the dread of you on all the land that you shall tread, as he promised you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three verbs recur through this book like a refrain: loving, walking, holding fast. Affection, direction, and grip. Take away the first and you have mere religion; the second, feeling without a life; the third, somebody who lets go the moment it costs.

The promise is extravagant: territory measured by where the soles of their feet tread. God gives it, and they still have to put their feet on it; Israel’s rule reached these borders under Solomon (1 Kgs 4:21). And the war would be won in Canaan’s mind before Israel arrived, as Rahab confirms from inside: the fear of you has fallen upon us… our hearts melted (Josh. 2:9, 11).

This is a national promise under a specific covenant, not a formula for a Christian’s circumstances. God has not undertaken that every enemy will retreat before the believer; the New Testament says something rather different, and many of the men who wrote it were put to death. What carries across is that the outcome does not finally depend on the size of what is in front of you.

Does the land promise still belong to the Jewish people and modern Israel? Dispensationalists hold that it does: God’s promise to Abraham’s physical descendants remains literal, with its borders, and awaits fulfilment. But Joshua says that Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed (Josh 21:45), and the New Testament widens the promise: Abraham was to be heir of the world (Rom 4:13), and the patriarchs looked for a better country, that is, a heavenly one (Heb 11:16). The land is fulfilled in Christ and the new creation his people will inherit (Matt 5:5). Faithful Christians differ here, and charitably: dispensational believers read the promises as still awaiting literal fulfilment for the Jewish people, and many who do not expect a return to the land still expect a great turning of Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25–29).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–32 — The Blessing and the Curse Set Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sets before Israel the blessing and the curse, to be proclaimed at Gerizim and Ebal.
verseByVerse.theology: Every generation faces the choice between blessing and curse, and the curse for disobedience is finally borne by Christ (Gal 3:13).
verseByVerse.examples: The gospel sets life before us in Christ, who bore the curse so that we might receive the blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: "See, I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse: the blessing, if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God, which I command you today, and the curse, if you do not obey the commandments of the LORD your God, but turn aside from the way that I am commanding you today, to go after other gods that you have not known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the spine of the book, running to chapter 30, where Moses says it for the last time: I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life (30:19).

See: Moses is not describing an abstraction but holding two things up in front of a crowd. And there is no third option, no comfortable middle where a person might live without deciding. Whoever is not with me is against me (Matt. 12:30) is the same sentence in a different century.

The curse is attached to going after other gods that you have not known. A man who turns aside from the way does not stand still in an empty field; he goes after something, gods with no track record with him at all, chosen precisely because they are new.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to take possession of it, you shall set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. Are they not beyond the Jordan, west of the road, toward the going down of the sun, in the land of the Canaanites who live in the Arabah, opposite Gilgal, beside the oak of Moreh? For you are to cross over the Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you. And when you possess it and live in it, you shall be careful to do all the statutes and the rules that I am setting before you today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with staging instructions for a ceremony years away. Gerizim and Ebal face each other with Shechem in the valley, and travellers have long reported that the acoustics carry a voice across it. The ceremony is described in chapter 27 and carried out in Joshua 8:33–35: half the tribes on one slope for the blessing, half on the other for the curse, the ark and priests between, and the words read out to all.

Not a document filed with the elders, but a nation standing on one side or the other of a valley while the covenant was shouted across it. God does not deal with his people only in propositions. He builds things they have to stand in, walk through and taste: a Passover meal, a rainbow, water, bread and wine. This was a covenant you had to climb a hill to hear.

And the last verse: you shall be careful to do all the statutes. Not admire them, not agree with them. Do them, which is where chapter 12 and the law proper begin.
verseByVerse.note: Shechem, in the valley between them, is where God first promised the land to Abraham (Gen 12:6–7).

11.theology:
Love shown in obedience. Love and obedience are inseparable (11:1; John 14:15). Such love is not the price of God’s favour but the answer to it. Only Christ has loved and obeyed wholly, and he did it in our place; the Spirit who pours God’s love into our hearts (Rom 5:5) makes it possible in us.

The land God cares for. God designed a life of daily, upward dependence in a land on which his eyes never close (11:11–12; cf. Ps 121).

Blessing and curse. Every generation faces this choice, and there is no neutral ground (11:26). The curse fell in the exile, but the gospel’s glory is that Christ redeemed us by “becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), so that all who trust him receive the blessing.
11.examples:
Israel, having seen God’s mighty acts, was called to love and obey him, to depend on the rain of a land he watched over, to fill home and heart with his word, and to choose between blessing and curse.

We obey in the light of God’s grace in Christ, live in daily dependence on the Father who watches over us, hand the gospel to our children, and rejoice that the curse we earned has been borne on the tree, so that we stand on the mountain of blessing.

12.title: The Central Sanctuary: Worship God His Way, Not Ours
12.text: <sup>1</sup>"These are the statutes and rules that you shall be careful to do in the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you to possess, all the days that you live on the earth.<sup>2</sup>You shall surely destroy all the places where the nations whom you shall dispossess served their gods, on the high mountains and on the hills and under every green tree.<sup>3</sup>You shall tear down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and burn their Asherim with fire. You shall chop down the carved images of their gods and destroy their name out of that place.<sup>4</sup>You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way.<sup>5</sup>But you shall seek the place that the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there. There you shall go,<sup>6</sup>and there you shall bring your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, your vow offerings, your freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your herd and of your flock.<sup>7</sup>And there you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your households, in all that you undertake, in which the LORD your God has blessed you.<sup>8</sup>"You shall not do according to all that we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes,<sup>9</sup>for you have not as yet come to the rest and to the inheritance that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>10</sup>But when you go over the Jordan and live in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to inherit, and when he gives you rest from all your enemies around, so that you live in safety,<sup>11</sup>then to the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there, there you shall bring all that I command you: your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, and all your finest vow offerings that you vow to the LORD.<sup>12</sup>And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your sons and your daughters, your male servants and your female servants, and the Levite that is within your towns, since he has no portion or inheritance with you.<sup>13</sup>Take care that you do not offer your burnt offerings at any place that you see,<sup>14</sup>but at the place that the LORD will choose in one of your tribes, there you shall offer your burnt offerings, and there you shall do all that I am commanding you.<sup>15</sup>"However, you may slaughter and eat meat within any of your towns, as much as you desire, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you. The unclean and the clean may eat of it, as of the gazelle and as of the deer.<sup>16</sup>Only you shall not eat the blood; you shall pour it out on the earth like water.<sup>17</sup>You may not eat within your towns the tithe of your grain or of your wine or of your oil, or the firstborn of your herd or of your flock, or any of your vow offerings that you vow, or your freewill offerings or the contribution that you present,<sup>18</sup>but you shall eat them before the LORD your God in the place that the LORD your God will choose, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite who is within your towns. And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God in all that you undertake.<sup>19</sup>Take care that you do not neglect the Levite as long as you live in your land.<sup>20</sup>"When the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as he has promised you, and you say, 'I will eat meat,' because you crave meat, you may eat meat whenever you desire.<sup>21</sup>If the place that the LORD your God will choose to put his name there is too far from you, then you may kill any of your herd or your flock, which the LORD has given you, as I have commanded you, and you may eat within your towns whenever you desire.<sup>22</sup>Just as the gazelle or the deer is eaten, so you may eat of it. The unclean and the clean alike may eat of it.<sup>23</sup>Only be sure that you do not eat the blood, for the blood is the life, and you shall not eat the life with the flesh.<sup>24</sup>You shall not eat it; you shall pour it out on the earth like water.<sup>25</sup>You shall not eat it, that all may go well with you and with your children after you, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD.<sup>26</sup>But the holy things that are due from you, and your vow offerings, you shall take, and you shall go to the place that the LORD will choose,<sup>27</sup>and offer your burnt offerings, the flesh and the blood, on the altar of the LORD your God. The blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out on the altar of the LORD your God, but the flesh you may eat.<sup>28</sup>Be careful to obey all these words that I command you, that it may go well with you and with your children after you forever, when you do what is good and right in the sight of the LORD your God.<sup>29</sup>"When the LORD your God cuts off before you the nations whom you go in to dispossess, and you dispossess them and dwell in their land,<sup>30</sup>take care that you be not ensnared to follow them, after they have been destroyed before you, and that you do not inquire about their gods, saying, 'How did these nations serve their gods?—that I also may do the same.'<sup>31</sup>You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way, for every abominable thing that the LORD hates they have done for their gods, for they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods.<sup>32</sup>"Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do. You shall not add to it or take from it.
12.overview:
Chapter 12 opens the detailed covenant code (chs. 12–26), and it begins with worship. God is to be worshiped at the place he chooses, in the way he prescribes, not as the nations worship their gods and not by human invention: the principle Reformed theology calls the regulative principle of worship.

Israel is to destroy the Canaanite high places and seek “the place that the LORD your God will choose” (12:5), rejoicing there before him. The chapter warns against doing “whatever is right in his own eyes” (12:8) and against copying the nations (12:30–31), and closes: “You shall not add to it or take from it” (12:32). To worship God his way is the first duty and the highest joy of the redeemed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Destroy the Places of Idolatry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must destroy the Canaanite places of worship and not worship the LORD in their way.
verseByVerse.theology: God will not be worshipped in the manner of false gods, so their shrines had to go.
verseByVerse.examples: Believers, bought by Christ, refuse to worship God by borrowed methods, however attractive the setting.

verseByVerse.quote: "These are the statutes and rules that you shall be careful to do in the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you to possess, all the days that you live on the earth. You shall surely destroy all the places where the nations whom you shall dispossess served their gods, on the high mountains and on the hills and under every green tree. You shall tear down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and burn their Asherim with fire. You shall chop down the carved images of their gods and destroy their name out of that place. You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law proper begins with worship, and worship begins with demolition: altars torn down, pillars broken, Asherim burnt, images cut to pieces, the very names of the places wiped out. Before Israel is told how to worship, she is told what to knock down.

The shrines stood on hilltops and under great trees. Canaanite worship was set in beautiful places, and that was part of its power. False religion has almost always understood atmosphere better than true religion, and a site can do a great deal of a god’s work for him.

Not in that way. Verse 4 is the hinge, and it is not what the paragraph seemed to be about. The danger is not that Israel will worship Baal but that she will worship the LORD in Baal’s manner: right God, borrowed method. That is a subtler failure than idolatry and a commoner one, and the rest of the chapter is built on it.

Does verse 32 (or v. 4) mean the church may do in worship only what Scripture commands? The Reformed tradition holds the regulative principle: God is to be worshipped only in the ways he has appointed in his word. Lutherans and Anglicans hold the normative principle: what Scripture does not forbid is allowed if it edifies. The regulative principle is the better reading of passages like this and Leviticus 10: the elements of worship are reading and preaching the word, prayer, singing, and the sacraments, while circumstances such as time and place are left to wisdom. Christians in the other traditions also want to honour Scripture; the difference is over how far its silence binds, and even Reformed churches apply the principle differently, for example on hymns and instruments.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — The Place the LORD Will Choose
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is to seek the one place God chooses for his name, and rejoice there.
verseByVerse.theology: God decides where and how he is to be met. One chosen place guarded the purity and unity of Israel’s worship, and it points to Christ, the true meeting place with God.
verseByVerse.examples: We come to God through Christ, the true temple and only mediator, not by paths of our own devising.

verseByVerse.quote: But you shall seek the place that the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there. There you shall go, and there you shall bring your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, your vow offerings, your freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your herd and of your flock. And there you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your households, in all that you undertake, in which the LORD your God has blessed you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Over against the shrines on every hill, God appoints one address, and does not name it. Deuteronomy says the place that the LORD your God will choose, or words very like it, some twenty times and never once says where. Israel is to go where God decides and find out later where that is. The choosing is God’s, and withholding the name keeps it his.

Many critical scholars think this chapter was written in King Josiah’s day, some six or seven centuries after Moses, to support his drive to centralise worship in Jerusalem (2 Kings 23). The question is still debated. But it would be strange for a law written to promote Jerusalem to leave it unnamed, and the earlier sanctuary at Shiloh, where God first made his name dwell (Jeremiah 7:12), fits a command given before the place was known.

What he puts there is his name, the language of ownership and presence: Israel’s worship was to happen at the one spot on earth God had signed.

Then a surprise in a chapter about demolition: there you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice. The centre of Israel’s worship is not a rite performed at a distance by a specialist but a family meal eaten in God’s presence with gladness. That is what the one place was for. Whatever else the restriction of this chapter is, it is not miserly. God narrows the location of worship and then fills it with roast meat, wine, family and joy, which is how the story finishes: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9).
verseByVerse.note: God’s name dwelt first at Shiloh and finally at Jerusalem, where Solomon’s prayer at the temple’s dedication recalls this promise (1 Kgs 8:29).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not do according to all that we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes, for you have not as yet come to the rest and to the inheritance that the LORD your God is giving you. But when you go over the Jordan and live in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to inherit, and when he gives you rest from all your enemies around, so that you live in safety, then to the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there, there you shall bring all that I command you: your burnt offerings and your sacrifices, your tithes and the contribution that you present, and all your finest vow offerings that you vow to the LORD. And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your sons and your daughters, your male servants and your female servants, and the Levite that is within your towns, since he has no portion or inheritance with you. Take care that you do not offer your burnt offerings at any place that you see, but at the place that the LORD will choose in one of your tribes, there you shall offer your burnt offerings, and there you shall do all that I am commanding you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever is right in his own eyes is the phrase Judges uses to explain its own horrors: there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes (Judg. 17:6; 21:25), written just before the worst chapters in the Old Testament.

The wilderness arrangement was improvised; a moving camp could not have a fixed sanctuary. Settled in the land, the same habit would become anarchy, each family with a hilltop and a preference. The point is not that everyone was doing what was wrong in his own eyes but that his own eyes had become the standard. Sincerity is not the issue; the reference point is. A man can be perfectly earnest and entirely his own authority, and three generations later the result is Judges.

The corrective is rest, given by God, and a place God chooses rather than one they like the look of. Which is why the New Testament, for all its freedom about location, insists that worship is not a private construction: God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth (John 4:24). The place has changed. The principle has not moved an inch.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–28 — Eating Meat, Blood, and Bringing Offerings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Meat may be eaten in any town, but the blood must be poured out and holy offerings brought to the chosen place.
verseByVerse.theology: Life belongs to God, as the poured-out blood showed, while his ordinary gifts are to be enjoyed with thanks.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians honour the blood of Christ, by which life is given, and eat their daily bread with gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: "However, you may slaughter and eat meat within any of your towns, as much as you desire, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you. The unclean and the clean may eat of it, as of the gazelle and as of the deer. Only you shall not eat the blood; you shall pour it out on the earth like water. You may not eat within your towns the tithe of your grain or of your wine or of your oil, or the firstborn of your herd or of your flock, or any of your vow offerings that you vow, or your freewill offerings or the contribution that you present, but you shall eat them before the LORD your God in the place that the LORD your God will choose, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite who is within your towns. And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God in all that you undertake. Take care that you do not neglect the Levite as long as you live in your land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a generous concession. In the wilderness, killing an animal for food was a sacrificial act done at the tent; spread over a hundred miles of settled country, that would be impossible. So God releases it: meat in any town, as much as you desire. The chapter that restricts sacrifice frees ordinary eating, in warm language. God is not a minimalist about his people’s dinner tables.

Two things are pinned down: the blood poured out on the ground, and the tithes and offerings still eaten at the chosen place, with the whole household, servants included, and the Levite.

Then verse 19: Take care that you do not neglect the Levite. The Levite had no field and would prosper only if people remembered him, and there is nothing automatic about being remembered. God does not leave the support of his servants to spontaneous goodwill; he commands it, by name, in a paragraph about meat, because the people most likely to be forgotten are the ones with no way of pressing their case.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as he has promised you, and you say, 'I will eat meat,' because you crave meat, you may eat meat whenever you desire. If the place that the LORD your God will choose to put his name there is too far from you, then you may kill any of your herd or your flock, which the LORD has given you, as I have commanded you, and you may eat within your towns whenever you desire. Just as the gazelle or the deer is eaten, so you may eat of it. The unclean and the clean alike may eat of it. Only be sure that you do not eat the blood, for the blood is the life, and you shall not eat the life with the flesh. You shall not eat it; you shall pour it out on the earth like water. You shall not eat it, that all may go well with you and with your children after you, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD. But the holy things that are due from you, and your vow offerings, you shall take, and you shall go to the place that the LORD will choose, and offer your burnt offerings, the flesh and the blood, on the altar of the LORD your God. The blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out on the altar of the LORD your God, but the flesh you may eat. Be careful to obey all these words that I command you, that it may go well with you and with your children after you forever, when you do what is good and right in the sight of the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one restriction comes with a reason: the blood is the life. Blood is treated in Scripture as the carrier of life, and life belongs to God. Pouring the blood on the ground handed back to him what was his and acknowledged that the animal’s death was real, not a triviality. Israel’s cooks were made to think, every time, about the cost of the meal.

The principle runs straight to the one place where God does the opposite: Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life (John 6:54). That was shocking to its first hearers precisely because of this verse. The life never to be consumed is offered to be received.

Even a rule about draining a carcass is framed for the good of a family two generations on: that all may go well with you and with your children after you.

Does the ban on eating blood still bind? It was given to Noah before Israel (Gen 9:4), and the Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to keep it for the sake of fellowship with Jewish Christians (Acts 15:20, 29). But the New Testament declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19; 1 Tim 4:4), and most Christians have concluded that the principle, reverence for the life God gives, remains, while eating meat that is not fully drained is not sin. The command concerns eating, not medicine; a blood transfusion gives life and does not break it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–32 — Do Not Inquire How the Nations Worship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must not copy how the nations served their gods, but worship only as God commands.
verseByVerse.theology: Worship is governed by what God has said, and the curiosity that copies pagan worship ends in horror.
verseByVerse.examples: The church worships by God’s word, neither borrowing the world’s methods nor inventing its own.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD your God cuts off before you the nations whom you go in to dispossess, and you dispossess them and dwell in their land, take care that you be not ensnared to follow them, after they have been destroyed before you, and that you do not inquire about their gods, saying, 'How did these nations serve their gods?—that I also may do the same.' You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way, for every abominable thing that the LORD hates they have done for their gods, for they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods. "Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do. You shall not add to it or take from it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with a particular temptation, and it is not the one you would expect. The man in verse 30 has not stopped believing in the LORD; he intends to worship him. He is curious about method, what the neighbours did, what worked, what their ceremonies looked like, and he wants to borrow it. God calls that a snare and forbids it absolutely.

The reason is the darkest sentence in the chapter: they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire. That is where borrowed method ends. Nobody arrives at child sacrifice in one step; it is reached by a long series of small adoptions, each of which seemed a matter of form rather than substance, and Israel did arrive there, in the valley of Hinnom, centuries later (Jer. 7:31).

Verse 32 forbids both adding and taking away, as at 4:2, and here specifically about worship. God is not a blank space his people fill in according to taste. He has said how he will be approached, and the question in every generation is not whether a form is beautiful, effective or moving, but whether he asked for it. He asks it of a people he has already brought in to eat and rejoice before him: careful worship is the answer of the welcomed, not the fee for entry.

12.theology:
Worship on God’s terms. God will not be approached by the methods of the nations (12:31) or by whatever seems right to us (12:8), and nothing may be added to his commands or taken from them (12:32). None of us worships as purely as this; our acceptance rests on Christ, who gave the Father perfect worship in our place, and by his Spirit we now draw near.

The one chosen place. The single sanctuary points to Christ, the true temple (John 2:19–21), in whom we worship “in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

The blood is the life. The ban on eating blood (12:23) teaches reverence for life as God’s gift and points towards atonement, fulfilled in the precious blood of Christ, poured out for the forgiveness of sins, by which alone we have life.
12.examples:
Entering the land, Israel was to tear down every shrine, feast at the one place God chose, treat the blood as belonging to God, and refuse to worship the LORD by the methods of the nations.

We come to God not at a building but through Christ. We honour the blood by which we have life, enjoy God’s gifts with thanksgiving, and guard our worship by his Word, refusing both to borrow the world’s methods and to invent our own.

13.title: Warning Against False Prophets: Guard the Heart's Allegiance
13.text: <sup>1</sup>"If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you and gives you a sign or a wonder,<sup>2</sup>and the sign or wonder that he tells you comes to pass, and if he says, 'Let us go after other gods,' which you have not known, 'and let us serve them,'<sup>3</sup>you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or that dreamer of dreams. For the LORD your God is testing you, to know whether you love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.<sup>4</sup>You shall walk after the LORD your God and fear him and keep his commandments and obey his voice, and you shall serve him and hold fast to him.<sup>5</sup>But that prophet or that dreamer of dreams shall be put to death, because he has taught rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you out of the house of slavery, to make you leave the way in which the LORD your God commanded you to walk. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>6</sup>"If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son or your daughter or the wife you embrace or your friend who is as your own soul entices you secretly, saying, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' which neither you nor your fathers have known,<sup>7</sup>some of the gods of the peoples who are around you, whether near you or far off from you, from the one end of the earth to the other,<sup>8</sup>you shall not yield to him or listen to him, nor shall your eye pity him, nor shall you spare him, nor shall you conceal him.<sup>9</sup>But you shall kill him. Your hand shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people.<sup>10</sup>You shall stone him to death with stones, because he sought to draw you away from the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.<sup>11</sup>And all Israel shall hear and fear and never again do any such wickedness as this among you.<sup>12</sup>"If you hear in one of your cities, which the LORD your God is giving you to dwell there,<sup>13</sup>that certain worthless fellows have gone out among you and have drawn away the inhabitants of their city, saying, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' which you have not known,<sup>14</sup>then you shall inquire and make search and ask diligently. And behold, if it be true and certain that such an abomination has been done among you,<sup>15</sup>you shall surely put the inhabitants of that city to the sword, devoting it to destruction, all who are in it and its cattle, with the edge of the sword.<sup>16</sup>You shall gather all its spoil into the midst of its open square and burn the city and all its spoil with fire, as a whole burnt offering to the LORD your God. It shall be a heap forever. It shall not be built again.<sup>17</sup>None of the devoted things shall stick to your hand, that the LORD may turn from the fierceness of his anger and show you mercy and have compassion on you and multiply you, as he swore to your fathers,<sup>18</sup>if you obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping all his commandments that I am commanding you today, and doing what is right in the sight of the LORD your God.
13.overview:
Chapter 13 deals with the gravest threat to the covenant community: enticement to idolatry, however attractive the source. Three cases are addressed: a prophet whose sign comes true, a beloved family member who whispers in secret, and a whole city that falls away.

Even a true wonder cannot validate a call to go after other gods, because God is testing whether his people love him with all their heart (13:3). No human bond outranks loyalty to God, and defection is not a private preference but covenant treason. The penalties belonged to Israel as a nation under God; the seriousness carries across to the church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The False Prophet Who Works Wonders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even a prophet whose sign comes true must be rejected if he calls Israel to other gods.
verseByVerse.theology: A message is tested by whether it is faithful to God’s word, not by signs and wonders, and the test shows whether we truly love him.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians test every teaching by Scripture, however impressive the teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you and gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or wonder that he tells you comes to pass, and if he says, 'Let us go after other gods,' which you have not known, 'and let us serve them,' you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or that dreamer of dreams. For the LORD your God is testing you, to know whether you love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter puts three cases, each closer to home than the last, and the first is deliberately the hardest to answer.

The sign comes true. God does not say the man is a fraud or that the wonder was a trick that will fail on inspection. The prediction lands, and the man is still to be rejected, because of what he is calling them to. That settles a question people still get wrong: supernatural power is not self-authenticating. Pharaoh’s magicians duplicated the first plagues; the Lord Jesus warned that false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect (Matt. 24:24); and Paul says the man of lawlessness comes with all power and false signs and wonders (2 Thess. 2:9). The test of a message has never been whether something remarkable accompanied it. It is what the message says about God.

The LORD is testing you. The false prophet is not an accident God is dealing with but an examination he is setting, and what is examined is not doctrinal knowledge but love, the Shema quoted directly. A man who loves God with all his heart is not moved by a wonder-worker, because he is not shopping.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall walk after the LORD your God and fear him and keep his commandments and obey his voice, and you shall serve him and hold fast to him. But that prophet or that dreamer of dreams shall be put to death, because he has taught rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you out of the house of slavery, to make you leave the way in which the LORD your God commanded you to walk. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against the seducer stands a chain of six verbs: walk, fear, keep, obey, serve, cling. Deuteronomy stacks them because it will not let life with God be reduced to any one, and the last is the strongest: hold fast, glued to.

The remedy for seduction is not suspicion but attachment. A man is not protected from a false teacher by being sceptical of everybody; he is protected by being fastened to somebody. That is the whole logic of Christian assurance, and why the New Testament answers false teaching so often with abide rather than argue: Abide in me, and I in you (John 15:4).

And the crime is measured by the rescue. The prophet has taught rebellion against the God who brought you out of the land of Egypt. To turn a redeemed people back is not a difference of religious opinion; it is an attempt to march them back into the house they were bought out of.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — When the Tempter Is a Loved One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even the closest relative or friend who entices to idolatry must not be heeded or shielded.
verseByVerse.theology: Allegiance to God comes before the closest human ties.
verseByVerse.examples: We love our families rightly only when we love God first.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son or your daughter or the wife you embrace or your friend who is as your own soul entices you secretly, saying, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' which neither you nor your fathers have known, some of the gods of the peoples who are around you, whether near you or far off from you, from the one end of the earth to the other, you shall not yield to him or listen to him, nor shall your eye pity him, nor shall you spare him, nor shall you conceal him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second case is the one that hurts. Not a stranger or a public figure, but a brother, the son of your mother, the closest tie; your own child; the wife you embrace; your friend who is as your own soul, the phrase used of David and Jonathan. These are the voices that carry most weight with any human being, the people we cannot say no to, and God knows it, which is why he lists them by relationship rather than saying anyone.

And it comes secretly: not a public challenge answered in the open, but a quiet conversation with someone who has access, the kind nobody else hears.

Then five refusals, because one would not be enough: do not yield, listen, pity, spare, or conceal him, which is what love usually wants to do. The Lord Jesus said the same about the same relationships, in one of the hardest sentences he ever spoke: Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matt. 10:37). He was not devaluing families. He was ranking them, as Deuteronomy 13 does. For a Christian, whose answer to false teaching is warning and not the sword, this means refusing to follow a loved one away from God, not ceasing to love him; many have gone on praying for a wandering son or husband, and seen him come home.

verseByVerse.quote: But you shall kill him. Your hand shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. You shall stone him to death with stones, because he sought to draw you away from the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. And all Israel shall hear and fear and never again do any such wickedness as this among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
