The penalty is death, carried out by the community, and the one who was enticed must strike first: nobody may lay a charge and then step back and let others do it. Modern readers recoil, and should. Three things need saying, and the third matters most.

First, what this is not. It is not a private killing; the next case (vv. 12–15) requires investigation (you shall inquire and make search and ask diligently), and Deuteronomy elsewhere demands two or three witnesses (19:15). This is judicial, in a nation where God was literally the king, and enticement to idolatry was treason against the head of state.

Second, the requirement that the accuser strike first is a restraint, not a cruelty. It makes it impossible to denounce a family member and keep your hands clean. Anyone who brought such a charge had to be prepared to do the thing himself, in public, which is a considerable deterrent against denunciation.

Third, and this must be said without hedging: no Christian, church or state holds this commission. Israel was a theocracy for a period that ended, and the New Testament transfers the penalty to a different sphere entirely. Paul faces teachers who draw people away, and the remedy he commands is warning and then exclusion from the fellowship, not execution (Titus 3:10; 2 John 10). The weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4). Anyone who has ever used this chapter to justify violence has read it against Christ. Christians, including some of the Reformers, once used chapters like this to execute heretics, and that was a grievous error.

What does carry across is the seriousness. God treats the person who draws his people away from him as doing something worse than any other crime in the code, worse than theft or assault, and a church that finds false teaching a matter of taste has lost something this chapter had.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A city that turns to other gods must be carefully investigated and, if guilty, devoted to destruction.
verseByVerse.theology: Corruption of a whole community is to be taken with the utmost seriousness, yet justice still requires careful inquiry into the facts.
verseByVerse.examples: The church guards its purity by dealing patiently and seriously with sin that spreads.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you hear in one of your cities, which the LORD your God is giving you to dwell there, that certain worthless fellows have gone out among you and have drawn away the inhabitants of their city, saying, 'Let us go and serve other gods,' which you have not known, then you shall inquire and make search and ask diligently. And behold, if it be true and certain that such an abomination has been done among you, you shall surely put the inhabitants of that city to the sword, devoting it to destruction, all who are in it and its cattle, with the edge of the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third case is a whole city, and what is striking is how much investigation comes first: inquire, search, ask diligently, and then true and certain, before a single step may be taken. That runs against every instinct in a crisis. The greater the outrage, the greater the pressure to act before the facts are in, and the law puts its heaviest demands for evidence precisely where feelings run hottest.

The blame falls on certain worthless fellows, literally sons of belial, men of no worth. A whole town does not go over at once. It is talked over by a few persuasive people with nothing to lose, and the rest follow because everybody else is.

Were children killed too? The plain answer is yes: the law as written included the whole city (v. 15), as the flood and Sodom did. The town had turned the whole covenant community to rebellion against God their King. The law belonged to Israel as a nation under God and was never a pattern for the church, which bears no sword (John 18:36). No state today has the right to punish anyone for false worship. But the law also demanded patient inquiry first, and Scripture records no clear case of it being carried out against an Israelite town for idolatry. And the God who gave it is the same God who pitied the children of Nineveh (Jonah 4:11) and sent his Son to bear judgment for sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall gather all its spoil into the midst of its open square and burn the city and all its spoil with fire, as a whole burnt offering to the LORD your God. It shall be a heap forever. It shall not be built again. None of the devoted things shall stick to your hand, that the LORD may turn from the fierceness of his anger and show you mercy and have compassion on you and multiply you, as he swore to your fathers, if you obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping all his commandments that I am commanding you today, and doing what is right in the sight of the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city’s plunder is burnt rather than kept, as a whole burnt offering, the same guard as in chapter 7: what survives a purge is rarely the idol, but some small associated thing that seemed harmless to keep.

Show you mercy. Verse 17 changes the tone of everything before it. Mercy, compassion, multiplication: three words of tenderness at the end of the harshest chapter in the book, and they are the purpose. The severity exists so that God can be merciful to the rest and a nation is still standing to receive what he swore to Abraham.

This is the hardest thing about Deuteronomy for a modern reader. The God of chapter 13 is not two Gods, one fierce and one kind, alternating. He is one God, whose fierceness against what destroys his people is a function of his commitment to them. A physician who will not cut is not gentle; he is negligent.

The last clause brings it back to the start: the whole chapter is about listening to the right voice. Three seducers speak, a prophet with a wonder, a brother in the dark, a townful of neighbours, and against all three there is one sentence: you shall walk after the LORD your God… and hold fast to him. And he holds fast to his own: the Lord Jesus promised that his sheep, who hear his voice, will never be snatched out of his hand (John 10:27–28).

13.theology:
Truth tested by God’s word. A wonder never validates a message that contradicts what God has said (13:1–3), for Satan can counterfeit signs (2 Thess 2:9). The lasting test of every teacher is faithfulness to Scripture.

God first. No bond, not spouse, child or friend, may rival our loyalty to God (13:6–8; Matt 10:37). Rightly ordered love holds even our dearest under the love of God, a love the Spirit pours into our hearts.

The seriousness of defection. The penalties belonged to Israel’s unique place as a nation under God and do not pass to the church, but the truth they guard remains: idolatry endangers the whole community, and God purges it in order to show mercy (13:17).
13.examples:
Israel was to refuse even a sign-working prophet, a beloved relative or a whole city that enticed her to idolatry, while inquiring carefully into the facts, so that God might show mercy to a faithful people.

We test every teaching by Scripture, let no relationship rival our allegiance to Christ, and deal seriously with sin in the church. And we rest in the gospel: the wrath against idolatry fell on Christ, who bore God’s fierce anger so that mercy and compassion might flow freely to all who hold fast to him with all their heart.

14.title: A Holy People: Clean Foods, the Tithe, and the Joy of Worship
14.text: <sup>1</sup>"You are the sons of the LORD your God. You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead.<sup>2</sup>For you are a people holy to the LORD your God, and the LORD has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.<sup>3</sup>"You shall not eat any abomination.<sup>4</sup>These are the animals you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat,<sup>5</sup>the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the mountain sheep.<sup>6</sup>Every animal that parts the hoof and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat.<sup>7</sup>Yet of those that chew the cud or have the hoof cloven you shall not eat these: the camel, the hare, and the rock badger, because they chew the cud but do not part the hoof, are unclean for you.<sup>8</sup>And the pig, because it parts the hoof but does not chew the cud, is unclean for you. Their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch.<sup>9</sup>"Of all that are in the waters you may eat these: whatever has fins and scales you may eat.<sup>10</sup>And whatever does not have fins and scales you shall not eat; it is unclean for you.<sup>11</sup>"You may eat all clean birds.<sup>12</sup>But these are the ones that you shall not eat: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture,<sup>13</sup>the kite, the falcon of any kind;<sup>14</sup>every raven of any kind;<sup>15</sup>the ostrich, the nighthawk, the sea gull, the hawk of any kind;<sup>16</sup>the little owl and the short-eared owl, the barn owl<sup>17</sup>and the tawny owl, the carrion vulture and the cormorant,<sup>18</sup>the stork, the heron of any kind; the hoopoe and the bat.<sup>19</sup>And all winged insects are unclean for you; they shall not be eaten.<sup>20</sup>All clean winged things you may eat.<sup>21</sup>"You shall not eat anything that has died naturally. You may give it to the sojourner who is within your towns, that he may eat it, or you may sell it to a foreigner. For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.<sup>22</sup>"You shall tithe all the yield of your seed that comes from the field year by year.<sup>23</sup>And before the LORD your God, in the place that he will choose, to make his name dwell there, you shall eat the tithe of your grain, of your wine, and of your oil, and the firstborn of your herd and flock, that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always.<sup>24</sup>And if the way is too long for you, so that you are not able to carry the tithe, when the LORD your God blesses you, because the place is too far from you, which the LORD your God chooses, to set his name there,<sup>25</sup>then you shall turn it into money and bind up the money in your hand and go to the place that the LORD your God chooses<sup>26</sup>and spend the money for whatever you desire—oxen or sheep or wine or strong drink, whatever your appetite craves. And you shall eat there before the LORD your God and rejoice, you and your household.<sup>27</sup>And you shall not neglect the Levite who is within your towns, for he has no portion or inheritance with you.<sup>28</sup>"At the end of every three years you shall bring out all the tithe of your produce in the same year and lay it up within your towns.<sup>29</sup>And the Levite, because he has no portion or inheritance with you, and the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your towns, shall come and eat and be filled, that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands that you do.
14.overview:
Chapter 14 binds mourning customs, food laws and the tithe with one cord: “you are a people holy to the LORD your God” (14:2). Israel’s whole life, down to what she eats and how she grieves, is to express her identity as God’s treasured possession.

The food laws marked Israel out from the nations at every meal. The tithe is not a grim tax but a feast eaten before the LORD with rejoicing, “that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always” (14:23), and every third year it feeds the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow. Holiness touches every corner of life, worship is meant to be joyful, and God’s people are marked by care for the vulnerable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — A Holy People, Distinct in Grief
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As God’s holy people, Israel must not adopt pagan mourning rites.
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness shapes the whole of life, grief included. God’s people mourn differently because they belong to him and have hope.
verseByVerse.examples: Believers weep at gravesides like anyone else, but with hope.

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the sons of the LORD your God. You shall not cut yourselves or make any baldness on your foreheads for the dead. For you are a people holy to the LORD your God, and the LORD has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Identity first, then conduct, an order the whole Bible never reverses. Israel is not told to behave well in order to become God’s sons. She is told to stop doing something because she already is.

The forbidden practice is Canaanite mourning: gashing the skin and shaving the front of the head for the dead. The prophets of Baal did it on Carmel to get their god’s attention (1 Kgs. 18:28), in a world where the dead had to be appeased and grief was expressed by damaging yourself.

God does not forbid grief. Israel mourned Aaron thirty days (Numbers 20:29) and will mourn Moses thirty more (34:8). What is forbidden is grief with no hope in it, which turns inward and does violence to the body because there is nothing else to do with the pain. Paul draws the same line without a word of rebuke to the bereaved: that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess. 4:13). Not "do not grieve," but not as others do. A believer at a graveside weeps as hard as anybody and is not doing the same thing, because he is a son of the living God: since we believe that Jesus died and rose again (1 Thessalonians 4:14). The Christian’s hope at a grave rests on another grave, found empty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–21 — Clean and Unclean: Holiness at the Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is taught to distinguish clean from unclean animals in the most ordinary part of life.
verseByVerse.theology: The food laws set Israel apart and trained her to live by God’s distinctions; in Christ they have done their work.
verseByVerse.examples: Holiness still reaches the ordinary parts of life, though Christians are no longer bound by the food laws.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not eat any abomination. These are the animals you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the mountain sheep. Every animal that parts the hoof and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat. Yet of those that chew the cud or have the hoof cloven you shall not eat these: the camel, the hare, and the rock badger, because they chew the cud but do not part the hoof, are unclean for you. And the pig, because it parts the hoof but does not chew the cud, is unclean for you. Their flesh you shall not eat, and their carcasses you shall not touch. "Of all that are in the waters you may eat these: whatever has fins and scales you may eat. And whatever does not have fins and scales you shall not eat; it is unclean for you. "You may eat all clean birds. But these are the ones that you shall not eat: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture, the kite, the falcon of any kind; every raven of any kind; the ostrich, the nighthawk, the sea gull, the hawk of any kind; the little owl and the short-eared owl, the barn owl and the tawny owl, the carrion vulture and the cormorant, the stork, the heron of any kind; the hoopoe and the bat. And all winged insects are unclean for you; they shall not be eaten. All clean winged things you may eat. "You shall not eat anything that has died naturally. You may give it to the sojourner who is within your towns, that he may eat it, or you may sell it to a foreigner. For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then nineteen verses of animals: which chew the cud, which part the hoof, which have fins and scales, which birds are out. Modern readers find it the least promising material in the Pentateuch, and ask why.

Scripture does not give a full answer, and it would be dishonest to manufacture one. Hygiene is the popular explanation and almost certainly not the point; the text never mentions health, and some permitted animals are no safer than forbidden ones. Other suggestions, that the unclean animals were used in Canaanite ritual, or that they do not fit cleanly into the created order of Genesis 1, have something to them, and none is stated.

What the text says, twice (vv. 2, 21), is you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The reason is separation. You could not eat dinner in Israel without remembering whose you were. And the table became a boundary: a man who could not eat what his neighbour ate could not easily dine in his house, and much of the intermingling that led to intermarriage and idolatry was headed off at the kitchen.

That is why the lifting of these laws was an earthquake. Peter, shown a sheet of unclean animals on a roof in Joppa, found himself in a Gentile’s house saying God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean (Acts 10:28), and Mark states it flatly: Thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). The wall came down at a dinner table, because that is where it had been built. The food laws were not a mistake later corrected but a fence for a season, keeping one nation distinct until the promised Seed of Abraham came, in whom the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile is broken down (Ephesians 2:14).

Why not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk? The likeliest reason is that it was a pagan rite, or that it turned what nourished life into the means of death. The Jewish separation of meat and dairy grew from this verse later; Christians are not bound by it (Mark 7:19).
verseByVerse.note: The identity of many birds is uncertain (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Tithe and the Joy of Worship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tithe is to be eaten before the LORD with rejoicing, so that Israel learns to fear him.
verseByVerse.theology: The tithe is joyful worship that teaches the fear of the Lord: giving and feasting before God train the heart to revere and trust him.
verseByVerse.examples: Giving is meant to be glad worship, not a grim duty.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall tithe all the yield of your seed that comes from the field year by year. And before the LORD your God, in the place that he will choose, to make his name dwell there, you shall eat the tithe of your grain, of your wine, and of your oil, and the firstborn of your herd and flock, that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always. And if the way is too long for you, so that you are not able to carry the tithe, when the LORD your God blesses you, because the place is too far from you, which the LORD your God chooses, to set his name there, then you shall turn it into money and bind up the money in your hand and go to the place that the LORD your God chooses and spend the money for whatever you desire—oxen or sheep or wine or strong drink, whatever your appetite craves. And you shall eat there before the LORD your God and rejoice, you and your household. And you shall not neglect the Levite who is within your towns, for he has no portion or inheritance with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the tithe, in a form that surprises everybody who has heard tithing preached. They eat it. This tithe is brought to the sanctuary and consumed there by the family who brought it, as a feast in God’s presence, and the stated purpose is that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always. The method of learning it is a good dinner.

If the journey is too far, sell the produce, take the money, and buy whatever your appetite craves, strong drink named among it, and rejoice before the LORD with your household. That is in a law about tithing. Anyone who has absorbed the idea that God is fundamentally against enjoyment should read verse 26 again. He is not merely permitting the feast; he is commanding it, specifying the drink, and calling it worship.

Then the guard against self-indulgence: you shall not neglect the Levite. Bring the man with no land to the party. Joy in God’s presence that leaves out the one who cannot fund his own is not what is commanded here.

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and they belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Cor 16:2; 2 Cor 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and it calls churches to support those who teach them (Gal 6:6; 1 Cor 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.

May a Christian drink alcohol? Wine is a gift to be enjoyed before God, as here. Drunkenness is condemned (Prov 23:29–35; Eph 5:18), and abstaining for conscience or for a weaker brother is right (Rom 14:21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–29 — The Third-Year Tithe for the Vulnerable
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every third year the tithe is stored in the towns for the landless and vulnerable.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s people are marked by generous care for those with no inheritance or protection.
verseByVerse.examples: The church is still called to care for the poor deliberately and regularly, not only when moved.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the end of every three years you shall bring out all the tithe of your produce in the same year and lay it up within your towns. And the Levite, because he has no portion or inheritance with you, and the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your towns, shall come and eat and be filled, that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands that you do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every third year the tithe stays home as a local store for the same four Deuteronomy always names: the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan, the widow. None of them owned land, and in an agricultural economy land was the only security; a man without a field could not survive a bad year or press a claim. So God builds provision for them into the nation’s system rather than leaving it to charity, every third year, automatically, whether anybody feels generous or not.

And it happens within your towns, not at the sanctuary, where everybody knew which widow and which foreigner was coming to collect. Israel’s care for the poor was designed to be face to face.

The promise attached, that the LORD your God may bless you, is not a transaction, for God is not for sale; it is a Father’s delight in children who share what he gave them, and the New Testament repeats it without embarrassment: Whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully (2 Cor. 9:6).

Were there three tithes? Some count three: the Levites’ tithe (Num 18), the festival tithe (vv. 22–27), and this third-year tithe for the poor. The likelier reading is two at most: in the third year the festival tithe went to the poor instead. Either way, the tithe belonged to Israel’s law.

14.theology:
A people holy to the LORD. The refrain of 14:2 and 21 binds the chapter together: holiness shapes how Israel grieves, eats, worships and gives. The food laws are fulfilled in Christ, but the call to holiness in every part of life remains: “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16).

The joy of worship. The tithe is a feast before the LORD (14:23), and the regular act of giving and rejoicing trains the heart to revere and trust him.

Care for the vulnerable. The third-year tithe built care for the landless into Israel’s life (14:28–29), reflecting the heart of God, who draws near to the lowly.
14.examples:
As God’s holy people, Israel let her identity shape how she grieved and what she ate, feasted on the tithe before the LORD, and made regular provision for the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow.

We grieve with hope, let holiness reach ordinary life without the food laws, give gladly, and care for the poor deliberately, reflecting the God who became poor for our sake.

15.title: The Year of Release: Open Wide Your Hand
15.text: <sup>1</sup>"At the end of every seven years you shall grant a release.<sup>2</sup>And this is the manner of the release: every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not exact it of his neighbor, his brother, because the LORD's release has been proclaimed.<sup>3</sup>Of a foreigner you may exact it, but whatever of yours is with your brother your hand shall release.<sup>4</sup>But there will be no poor among you; for the LORD will bless you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance to possess—<sup>5</sup>if only you will strictly obey the voice of the LORD your God, being careful to do all this commandment that I command you today.<sup>6</sup>For the LORD your God will bless you, as he promised you, and you shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow, and you shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you.<sup>7</sup>"If among you, one of your brothers should become poor, in any of your towns within your land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother,<sup>8</sup>but you shall open your hand to him and lend him sufficient for his need, whatever it may be.<sup>9</sup>Take care lest there be an unworthy thought in your heart and you say, 'The seventh year, the year of release is near,' and your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother, and you give him nothing, and he cry to the LORD against you, and you be guilty of sin.<sup>10</sup>You shall give to him freely, and your heart shall not be grudging when you give to him, because for this the LORD your God will bless you in all your work and in all that you undertake.<sup>11</sup>For there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, 'You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land.'<sup>12</sup>"If your brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, is sold to you, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you.<sup>13</sup>And when you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty-handed.<sup>14</sup>You shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, out of your threshing floor, and out of your winepress. As the LORD your God has blessed you, you shall give to him.<sup>15</sup>You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; therefore I command you this today.<sup>16</sup>But if he says to you, 'I will not go out from you,' because he loves you and your household, since he is well-off with you,<sup>17</sup>then you shall take an awl, and put it through his ear into the door, and he shall be your slave forever. And to your female slave you shall do the same.<sup>18</sup>It shall not seem hard to you when you let him go free from you, for at half the cost of a hired worker he has served you six years. So the LORD your God will bless you in all that you do.<sup>19</sup>"All the firstborn males that are born of your herd and flock you shall dedicate to the LORD your God. You shall do no work with the firstborn of your herd, nor shear the firstborn of your flock.<sup>20</sup>You shall eat it, you and your household, before the LORD your God year by year at the place that the LORD will choose.<sup>21</sup>But if it has any blemish, if it is lame or blind or has any serious blemish whatever, you shall not sacrifice it to the LORD your God.<sup>22</sup>You shall eat it within your towns. The unclean and the clean alike may eat it, as though it were a gazelle or a deer.<sup>23</sup>Only you shall not eat its blood; you shall pour it out on the ground like water.
15.overview:
Chapter 15 sets out an economy shaped by grace rather than greed. Every seventh year, the year of release, debts among Israelites are cancelled and Hebrew servants set free: the God who released Israel from Egypt builds release into the calendar.

The vision is that “there will be no poor among you” (15:4); the realism, that “there will never cease to be poor in the land” (15:11), and therefore Israel must open wide her hand, lending freely and never hardening against a brother in need. The freed servant leaves furnished liberally, because the master remembers his own redemption (15:14–15). Jesus proclaimed “the year of the Lord’s favor” (Luke 4:19), the true release from the debt of sin, and the God who commands open hands did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Year of Release: Canceling Debts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every seventh year debts between Israelites are released.
verseByVerse.theology: God builds release into the rhythm of his people’s life, and he blesses a people who share his open hand.
verseByVerse.examples: Debts are not cancelled by calendar now, but the generosity behind the law still marks those who have received grace.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the end of every seven years you shall grant a release. And this is the manner of the release: every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not exact it of his neighbor, his brother, because the LORD's release has been proclaimed. Of a foreigner you may exact it, but whatever of yours is with your brother your hand shall release. But there will be no poor among you; for the LORD will bless you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance to possess— if only you will strictly obey the voice of the LORD your God, being careful to do all this commandment that I command you today. For the LORD your God will bless you, as he promised you, and you shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow, and you shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every seventh year, debts between Israelites are cancelled: not rescheduled, not reduced, cancelled, by law, on a fixed date everybody knew was coming. (That is the usual reading; a few scholars think repayment was suspended for the year rather than written off, but the generosity demanded in verse 9 is the same either way.)

There is no clear parallel to it in the ancient world as a standing institution. Kings occasionally proclaimed a remission of debts on their accession as a gesture; Israel had one written into the calendar, independent of who was on the throne. And the reason is theological: because the LORD’s release has been proclaimed. It is his release, not the creditor’s generosity.

No poor, yet always poor. Verse 4 and verse 11 seem to contradict each other until the conditions are read. Verse 4 is what would happen if only you will strictly obey; verse 11 is what will happen, because they will not. One is the design, the other the forecast. And it is verse 11 the Lord Jesus quotes when the disciples object to the ointment poured on him: For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them (Mark 14:7). He is not shrugging off poverty; he is quoting the verse that commands open-handedness, and the second half of his sentence is the command.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must not harden her heart against a poor brother but open wide her hand.
verseByVerse.theology: Generosity begins in the heart: God asks for ungrudging care for the poor, not just the outward act.
verseByVerse.examples: Believers watch for the calculating thought that keeps a hand closed when giving would cost.

verseByVerse.quote: "If among you, one of your brothers should become poor, in any of your towns within your land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother, but you shall open your hand to him and lend him sufficient for his need, whatever it may be.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A hardened heart and a shut hand belong together, and God names the inward thing first, because the hand does not close on its own. The measure of giving is sufficient for his need: not a token or a fixed percentage but the other man’s need, which removes the ceiling and makes each case a judgment. And open wide your hand pictures a hand spread flat so that nothing is kept back in the palm.

John turns heart and hand into a test of whether a man is a Christian at all: But if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him? (1 John 3:17). The same anatomy: goods, sight, a brother, and a heart that shuts. What opens it is that love of God, poured into us by the Spirit (Rom. 5:5), not a resolve we summon.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care lest there be an unworthy thought in your heart and you say, 'The seventh year, the year of release is near,' and your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother, and you give him nothing, and he cry to the LORD against you, and you be guilty of sin. You shall give to him freely, and your heart shall not be grudging when you give to him, because for this the LORD your God will bless you in all your work and in all that you undertake. For there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, 'You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God knows exactly how a shrewd man will handle this law. It is year six; a neighbour needs a loan; in twelve months the debt will be void, so the loan is effectively a gift, and a man who does not want to give finds he is suddenly unable to help. He has broken no law. He has become prudent at the exact moment generosity would cost him.

God calls it an unworthy thought, literally a word of belial, and names it before it is spoken, because it never will be. It is a thought in a heart, followed by a regretful conversation about how things are tight this year. And the poor man, who does not know he has been calculated against, cries to the LORD, and God hears him, and the prudent man is guilty of a sin nobody witnessed and he could deny with a straight face.

The antidote is not about the amount: your heart shall not be grudging. The manner is commanded as well as the act, as in Paul centuries later: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A freed Hebrew servant is sent away liberally furnished, in memory of Israel’s own redemption.
verseByVerse.theology: Those who remember their own release set others free generously.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians, redeemed at great cost, give in the manner they were given to.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, is sold to you, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you. And when you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty-handed. You shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, out of your threshing floor, and out of your winepress. As the LORD your God has blessed you, you shall give to him. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; therefore I command you this today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The release extends from debts to people. A Hebrew who sold himself into service, the ancient world’s answer to unpayable debt, goes free in the seventh year, and the next provision lifts this above every comparable law in the ancient world: he is not to go empty-handed. He leaves loaded with animals, grain and wine, enough to start again. Otherwise freedom would be a formality; a man released with nothing is back in servitude within a year, and God closes that door.

Remember that you were a slave. Israel did not leave Egypt empty-handed either: Thus they plundered the Egyptians (Exod. 12:36). God tells every Israelite master to do for his servant precisely what God did for him, and the standard of the giving is set by the exodus, not the market. That is the pattern of Christian generosity everywhere: not "give because it is decent," but "give in the manner you were given to." You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Cor. 8:9) is Paul making the identical move about a collection for famine relief.

Does the Bible approve slavery? This was debt service: limited to six years, with release, provision and the right to choose to stay. It is very different from the man-stealing slave trade, which the law punished with death (Exod 21:16; 1 Tim 1:10). God regulated a practice that existed everywhere, and planted the truths that would end it: every person in God’s image, and in Christ neither slave nor free (Gal 3:28). It must be said honestly that the law treated foreign slaves less generously (Leviticus 25:44–46); yet even they were protected from brutality (Exodus 21:20, 26–27), and a runaway slave was not to be handed back (Deuteronomy 23:15–16), a rule unusual in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: But if he says to you, 'I will not go out from you,' because he loves you and your household, since he is well-off with you, then you shall take an awl, and put it through his ear into the door, and he shall be your slave forever. And to your female slave you shall do the same. It shall not seem hard to you when you let him go free from you, for at half the cost of a hired worker he has served you six years. So the LORD your God will bless you in all that you do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then one of the most affecting cases in the law: a servant, offered his freedom, declines it because he loves you and your household. Six years of service, and a man would rather stay than take his freedom and a herd of animals. It can only mean the house was good, the master kind, and he had come to love them. The law that requires generous release has also produced households servants do not want to leave.

The ceremony is public and permanent: an awl through the ear at the doorpost, a mark carried for life, saying this man belongs here by choice. The ear is the organ of hearing and obedience, pinned to the door of the house he has chosen. Many Christians have heard an echo of it in a psalm spoken by somebody else altogether: In sacrifice and offering you have not delighted, but you have given me an open ear… Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me: I delight to do your will, O my God (Ps. 40:6–8), a passage Hebrews applies directly to Christ (Heb. 10:5–7).

The link is an echo, not the meaning of the law, but the pattern is real. One servant in history was under no obligation at all, could have walked away at any point, and chose to stay and serve out of love, though it led him to a cross. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). He delighted to do the Father’s will perfectly, and he did it in our place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–23 — The Firstborn Devoted to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The firstborn of herd and flock belong to the LORD and are eaten before him.
verseByVerse.theology: The firstborn belongs to God, who claims the best; giving it back is an act of worship and trust.
verseByVerse.examples: We give God the first and best, not what is left over.

verseByVerse.quote: "All the firstborn males that are born of your herd and flock you shall dedicate to the LORD your God. You shall do no work with the firstborn of your herd, nor shear the firstborn of your flock. You shall eat it, you and your household, before the LORD your God year by year at the place that the LORD will choose. But if it has any blemish, if it is lame or blind or has any serious blemish whatever, you shall not sacrifice it to the LORD your God. You shall eat it within your towns. The unclean and the clean alike may eat it, as though it were a gazelle or a deer. Only you shall not eat its blood; you shall pour it out on the ground like water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with the firstborn of the herds and flocks, which belong to God and are eaten before him at the sanctuary.

Any blemish. The lame or blind animal is not offered, but neither is it wasted; it is eaten at home. God will not be given the substandard. An animal a buyer would reject is no gift for the Almighty, and Malachi will flay the priests for exactly this: When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil?… Present that to your governor; will he accept you? (Mal. 1:8). Yet the imperfect animal is still food and still God’s gift. The law distinguishes what may be offered from what may be enjoyed, and does not despise the second.

The whole chapter has been about open hands: debts released, the poor supplied, the servant sent away loaded, the best of the flock given back to God. Every command rests on one sentence in the middle: you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you. Generosity in Deuteronomy is never an abstract virtue. It is the behaviour of people who remember what was done for them, and when they forget and close their hands, the way back is to remember it again.

15.theology:
The economics of grace. The God who released Israel from Egypt builds release into the calendar (15:1–2, 12). The hope that there would be no poor (15:4) is the fruit of a community shaped by gratitude, and it foreshadows the gospel, in which those forgiven an unpayable debt are freed to release others.

Open heart, open hand. Generosity is a matter of the heart, ungrudging and cheerful (15:7–11; cf. 2 Cor 9:7). Because poverty persists in a fallen world, the call is lasting, and Jesus’ words about the poor (Mark 14:7) command compassion rather than excuse its absence.

Redemption remembered. Gratitude for our own redemption (15:15) is the engine of Christian giving: the more we grasp how freely Christ saved us, the more freely we give.
15.examples:
Israel was to cancel debts and free servants every seventh year, send the freed servant away well supplied, keep her hand open to the poor, and give the firstborn to the LORD, all because she remembered that she too had been redeemed from slavery.

We who have had the infinite debt of sin cancelled live with open hands, giving cheerfully and enough, and rejoice in Jesus, who proclaimed the true release from sin and death (Luke 4) and whose pierced hands were opened on the cross for our freedom.

16.title: The Three Pilgrimage Feasts: Rejoice Before the LORD
16.text: <sup>1</sup>"Observe the month of Abib and keep the Passover to the LORD your God, for in the month of Abib the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt by night.<sup>2</sup>And you shall offer the Passover sacrifice to the LORD your God, from the flock or the herd, at the place that the LORD will choose, to make his name dwell there.<sup>3</sup>You shall eat no leavened bread with it. Seven days you shall eat it with unleavened bread, the bread of affliction—for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste—that all the days of your life you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt.<sup>4</sup>No leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory for seven days, nor shall any of the flesh that you sacrifice on the evening of the first day remain all night until morning.<sup>5</sup>You may not offer the Passover sacrifice within any of your towns that the LORD your God is giving you,<sup>6</sup>but at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell in it, there you shall offer the Passover sacrifice, in the evening at sunset, at the time you came out of Egypt.<sup>7</sup>And you shall cook it and eat it at the place that the LORD your God will choose. And in the morning you shall turn and go to your tents.<sup>8</sup>For six days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a solemn assembly to the LORD your God. You shall do no work on it.<sup>9</sup>"You shall count seven weeks. Begin to count the seven weeks from the time the sickle is first put to the standing grain.<sup>10</sup>Then you shall keep the Feast of Weeks to the LORD your God with the tribute of a freewill offering from your hand, which you shall give as the LORD your God blesses you.<sup>11</sup>And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite who is within your towns, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are among you, at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there.<sup>12</sup>You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt; and you shall be careful to observe these statutes.<sup>13</sup>"You shall keep the Feast of Booths seven days, when you have gathered in the produce from your threshing floor and your winepress.<sup>14</sup>You shall rejoice in your feast, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are within your towns.<sup>15</sup>For seven days you shall keep the feast to the LORD your God at the place that the LORD will choose, because the LORD your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful.<sup>16</sup>"Three times a year all your males shall appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks, and at the Feast of Booths. They shall not appear before the LORD empty-handed.<sup>17</sup>Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you.<sup>18</sup>"You shall appoint judges and officers in all your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, according to your tribes, and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment.<sup>19</sup>You shall not pervert justice. You shall not show partiality, and you shall not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and subverts the cause of the righteous.<sup>20</sup>Justice, and only justice, you shall follow, that you may live and inherit the land that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>21</sup>"You shall not plant any tree as an Asherah beside the altar of the LORD your God that you shall make.<sup>22</sup>And you shall not set up a pillar, which the LORD your God hates.
16.overview:
Chapter 16 sets out Israel’s sacred calendar: the three pilgrimage feasts, Passover, Weeks (Pentecost) and Booths (Tabernacles), at which all the men appeared before the LORD at the chosen place. The whole year became a rehearsal of redemption.

A refrain runs through the feasts: rejoice before the LORD, with sons and daughters, servants, Levites, sojourners, the fatherless and widows, and remember that you were a slave in Egypt (16:11–12). Then the chapter turns to justice in the courts and purity at the altar. Each feast finds its fulfilment in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Passover: Remember the Night of Redemption
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Passover and unleavened bread are kept at the chosen place, in lifelong memory of the exodus.
verseByVerse.theology: Passover remembers redemption from slavery and points to Christ, by whose blood his people are delivered from death and bondage.
verseByVerse.examples: At the Lord’s Table the church remembers a greater exodus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Observe the month of Abib and keep the Passover to the LORD your God, for in the month of Abib the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt by night. And you shall offer the Passover sacrifice to the LORD your God, from the flock or the herd, at the place that the LORD will choose, to make his name dwell there. You shall eat no leavened bread with it. Seven days you shall eat it with unleavened bread, the bread of affliction—for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste—that all the days of your life you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt. No leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory for seven days, nor shall any of the flesh that you sacrifice on the evening of the first day remain all night until morning. You may not offer the Passover sacrifice within any of your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, but at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell in it, there you shall offer the Passover sacrifice, in the evening at sunset, at the time you came out of Egypt. And you shall cook it and eat it at the place that the LORD your God will choose. And in the morning you shall turn and go to your tents. For six days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a solemn assembly to the LORD your God. You shall do no work on it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The year opens with Passover, and Deuteronomy adds a phrase not in Exodus: unleavened bread is the bread of affliction. Flat bread is what you make when there is no time to let dough rise, the bread of people leaving in a hurry, and it tastes of the night they went. For seven days every year Israel ate poor food on purpose, so that the memory would go in through the mouth as well as the ear, and the aim is all the days of your life: the feast keeps a memory from wearing thin, the great preoccupation of this book.

It must be kept at the place that the LORD your God will choose. Passover began as a household meal behind a bloodstained door in Egypt; here it becomes a national gathering. Verse 7 says to cook the lamb, where Exodus 12:9 forbids boiling it; the Hebrew word covers cooking in general, and 2 Chronicles 35:13 uses the same word of roasting the Passover with fire according to the rule.

Paul applies leaven and lamb to a church in one sentence: Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump… For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor. 5:7). The order is fixed: the lamb first, then the sweeping out. Nobody removes the leaven in order to qualify for the lamb.

Must Christians keep these feasts? They were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17): Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor 5:7), and the Lord’s Supper has taken the Passover’s place. Keeping them is a matter of freedom, not obligation (Rom 14:5–6), and never a condition of standing with God (Gal 4:10–11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — The Feast of Weeks: Rejoice and Remember
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Feast of Weeks is kept with freewill offerings and an inclusive table.
verseByVerse.theology: The harvest feast is grateful joy for God’s provision, and its table includes the whole community, especially the vulnerable.
verseByVerse.examples: Pentecost, when the Spirit was poured out, began the gospel harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall count seven weeks. Begin to count the seven weeks from the time the sickle is first put to the standing grain. Then you shall keep the Feast of Weeks to the LORD your God with the tribute of a freewill offering from your hand, which you shall give as the LORD your God blesses you. And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite who is within your towns, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are among you, at the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there. You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt; and you shall be careful to observe these statutes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven weeks after the sickle is first put to the grain comes the Feast of Weeks, later called Pentecost, kept with a freewill offering as the LORD your God blesses you. No fixed amount; each man brings in proportion to what the harvest gave him.

The guest list is the heart of the paragraph. Nine people, counting the man himself, and after the first three they are all people with no claim on the food: servants, the landless Levite, the foreigner, the orphan, the widow. God commands the harvest celebration and then fills the table with people who did not own a field.

And the reason: remember that you were a slave in Egypt. The ground of Israelite generosity is never that the poor deserve it or that giving is admirable. It is that these people were slaves and somebody came and got them, and they are to treat the powerless as God treated them when they were powerless. A harvest festival where the landless eat with the landowners is not a charitable add-on to the worship. It is the worship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Feast of Booths: Joy in God's Provision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Feast of Booths is kept with full joy; no one appears before the LORD empty-handed.
verseByVerse.theology: Abundant joy in God’s provision marks true worship, and each gives in proportion to what he has received.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians worship with full and grateful joy, remembering the Son who came to dwell among us.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall keep the Feast of Booths seven days, when you have gathered in the produce from your threshing floor and your winepress. You shall rejoice in your feast, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are within your towns. For seven days you shall keep the feast to the LORD your God at the place that the LORD will choose, because the LORD your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful. "Three times a year all your males shall appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks, and at the Feast of Booths. They shall not appear before the LORD empty-handed. Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD your God that he has given you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Feast of Booths comes after everything is in, grain threshed, grapes pressed, barns full, and its one instruction above all is rejoice, with the same guest list, and then so that you will be altogether joyful. That is a command to be happy, given in God’s law and repeated three times in this short chapter (vv. 11, 14, 15). Whatever else Israel’s religion was, it was not grim. God appointed a week of eating and drinking at the point of maximum prosperity and told them to enjoy it thoroughly and make sure the widow was there.

Three journeys a year for every man in the nation was a considerable cost in time and in unguarded farms, and God evidently thought it worth it.

Not empty-handed. Nobody comes with nothing, and nobody is told how much. The measure is what God has given him, so the poor man who brings little has met the standard as fully as the rich man who brings much, and the rich man who brings little has not. It is the principle the Lord Jesus applied while watching a widow drop in two small coins (Mark 12:41–44), and the only measure of giving Scripture ever uses.

It was at this feast, on its last and greatest day, that Jesus stood up in the temple and invited anyone who was thirsty to come to him and drink (John 7:37–38). A festival that remembered God’s care for Israel in the wilderness, water from the rock included, found its meaning in a man who said the living water was his to give.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is to appoint judges who judge righteously, without partiality or bribes.
verseByVerse.theology: God demands impartial, incorruptible justice; the God of the feasts is the God of the courts.
verseByVerse.examples: Those justified by the righteous Judge uphold honesty and fairness in their own dealings.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall appoint judges and officers in all your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, according to your tribes, and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment. You shall not pervert justice. You shall not show partiality, and you shall not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and subverts the cause of the righteous. Justice, and only justice, you shall follow, that you may live and inherit the land that the LORD your God is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight out of the feasting, without a pause, come judges and officers in all your towns. The juxtaposition is deliberate. A people just commanded to rejoice before God is told to run honest courts, and the second is not a lesser subject than the first. Worship and justice are not separate departments; the prophets will spend centuries insisting that a nation cannot have the first while neglecting the second (Amos 5:21–24; Isa. 1:11–17).

A bribe blinds the wise. Not fools: the wise. Money does not corrupt only weak or stupid men; it disables good judgment in able ones, and it does it invisibly. Nobody who takes a bribe believes his verdict has been affected.

Justice, and only justice. The Hebrew simply repeats the word, tsedeq, tsedeq, and the verb is the word for pursuit, not drift. Justice is not something a society drifts into; it has to be run after, by a people whom God had already rescued from Pharaoh’s injustice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–22 — No Idolatrous Symbols Beside the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No Asherah or sacred pillar may stand beside the LORD’s altar.
verseByVerse.theology: The worship of God must be kept unmixed with idolatry.
verseByVerse.examples: We refuse to blend the worship of God with the idols of the age, however harmless they look.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not plant any tree as an Asherah beside the altar of the LORD your God that you shall make. And you shall not set up a pillar, which the LORD your God hates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with two short prohibitions that look like an afterthought and are not. An Asherah was a wooden pole or living tree representing the Canaanite mother-goddess; a pillar was a sacred stone. Both were ordinary furniture of worship in that world, and both were attractive: a tree is beautiful, and a standing stone looks ancient and serious.

Beside the altar. Not instead of it. Nobody proposes to replace the worship of God; the suggestion is to improve the setting with something the neighbours find moving. That is the warning of 12:30 again, Deuteronomy’s most persistent anxiety about worship. Israel’s great failure was rarely a straight swap of gods. It was addition, the altar of the LORD with an Asherah next to it, on the grounds that it could not do any harm.

And the reason is startlingly personal: which the LORD your God hates. Not "which is unwise," or "which will confuse the people." He hates it, because a wife who keeps a photograph of another man on the bedside table has not committed adultery, but she has done something. It is the jealousy of a husband who has given himself wholly, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph. 5:25).

16.theology:
The calendar of redemption. Passover, Weeks and Booths rehearsed God’s mighty acts each year. They find their fulfilment in Christ, the Passover Lamb, the giver of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2), and the Word who “dwelt among us” (John 1:14), literally pitched his tent. The believer keeps a feast of remembrance in the Lord’s Supper, recalling our greater exodus from sin and death.

Commanded joy. Worship is to be glad, abundant and inclusive, drawing in servants, sojourners, orphans and widows (16:11, 15). A joyless religion misrepresents the God of all delight.

Worship and justice together. Honest courts belong with joyful feasts, and the altar must be kept free of every idol God hates (16:18–22). The Spirit given at Pentecost forms such a people, and where we fail, Christ, the one man who always judged rightly, is our righteousness.
16.examples:
Israel’s year was a rhythm of remembering and rejoicing, with every household and every stranger at the table, while she pursued justice in the courts and kept God’s altar clear of idols.

We keep the feast of remembrance at Christ’s table. Our worship is to be joyful and to welcome the vulnerable, our public life marked by the pursuit of justice, and our devotion undivided.

17.title: Kings and Justice: The King Who Reads the Law
17.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall not sacrifice to the LORD your God an ox or a sheep in which is a blemish, any defect whatever, for that is an abomination to the LORD your God.<sup>2</sup>"If there is found among you, within any of your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, a man or woman who does what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God, in transgressing his covenant,<sup>3</sup>and has gone and served other gods and worshiped them, or the sun or the moon or any of the host of heaven, which I have forbidden,<sup>4</sup>and it is told you and you hear of it, then you shall inquire diligently, and if it is true and certain that such an abomination has been done in Israel,<sup>5</sup>then you shall bring out to your gates that man or woman who has done this evil thing, and you shall stone that man or woman to death with stones.<sup>6</sup>On the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses the one who is to die shall be put to death; a person shall not be put to death on the evidence of one witness.<sup>7</sup>The hand of the witnesses shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>8</sup>"If any case arises requiring decision between one kind of homicide and another, one kind of legal right and another, or one kind of assault and another, any case within your towns that is too difficult for you, then you shall arise and go up to the place that the LORD your God will choose.<sup>9</sup>And you shall come to the Levitical priests and to the judge who is in office in those days, and you shall consult them, and they shall declare to you the decision.<sup>10</sup>Then you shall do according to what they declare to you from that place that the LORD will choose. And you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you.<sup>11</sup>According to the instructions that they give you, and according to the decision which they pronounce to you, you shall do. You shall not turn aside from the verdict that they declare to you, either to the right hand or to the left.<sup>12</sup>The man who acts presumptuously by not obeying the priest who stands to minister there before the LORD your God, or the judge, that man shall die. So you shall purge the evil from Israel.<sup>13</sup>And all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again.<sup>14</sup>"When you come to the land that the LORD your God is giving you, and you possess it and dwell in it and then say, 'I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me,'<sup>15</sup>you may indeed set a king over you whom the LORD your God will choose. One from among your brothers you shall set as king over you. You may not put a foreigner over you, who is not your brother.<sup>16</sup>Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, 'You shall never return that way again.'<sup>17</sup>And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away, nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold.<sup>18</sup>"And when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself in a book a copy of this law, approved by the Levitical priests.<sup>19</sup>And it shall be with him, and he shall read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by keeping all the words of this law and these statutes, and doing them,<sup>20</sup>that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers, and that he may not turn aside from the commandment, either to the right hand or to the left, so that he may continue long in his kingdom, he and his children, in Israel.
17.overview:
Chapter 17 turns to the offices that govern God's people: the courts, the central tribunal, and most strikingly the king. It opens with integrity in worship (no blemished sacrifice) and in judgment (two or three witnesses, never rash condemnation), and sets up a central court for the hardest cases.

Then comes the “law of the king” (17:14–20). God permits Israel the king she will want “like all the nations,” but forbids him to multiply horses, wives, or silver and gold, and requires him to copy out God's law and read it all his life, so that his heart is not lifted up above his brothers. Israel's kings largely failed this calling. It points to the King who fulfilled it, Christ, who came not to be served but to serve.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Justice in Worship and the Courts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No blemished sacrifice may be offered, and one accused of idolatry is to be judged carefully on the testimony of two or three witnesses, never on the word of one alone.
verseByVerse.theology: God demands integrity in worship and rigorous justice in judgment; truth must be established by sufficient witnesses, guarding against false condemnation.
verseByVerse.examples: The church today should be just as slow to condemn: no one is disciplined on a single, unsupported accusation.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not sacrifice to the LORD your God an ox or a sheep in which is a blemish, any defect whatever, for that is an abomination to the LORD your God. "If there is found among you, within any of your towns that the LORD your God is giving you, a man or woman who does what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God, in transgressing his covenant, and has gone and served other gods and worshiped them, or the sun or the moon or any of the host of heaven, which I have forbidden, and it is told you and you hear of it, then you shall inquire diligently, and if it is true and certain that such an abomination has been done in Israel, then you shall bring out to your gates that man or woman who has done this evil thing, and you shall stone that man or woman to death with stones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No blemish. The temptation is obvious and eternal. A farmer with a flock has good animals and damaged ones, and the damaged one is worth less at market. Offering it to God costs him nothing he was going to keep. God calls that an abomination — a word Deuteronomy uses of idolatry and the occult — because giving God what you could not sell says something about what you think he is worth. Malachi will make the same charge unanswerable by asking one question: Present that to your governor; will he accept you? (Mal. 1:8).

Then the judicial case: a man or woman found serving other gods is to be executed — but only after you shall inquire diligently, and only if it is true and certain.

In the most inflammatory charge the law recognises, the first requirement is not action but investigation, and the standard is not suspicion or general report but certainty. Israel’s law consistently puts its heaviest evidentiary demands exactly where feeling runs hottest, which is the opposite of what mobs do.

Should the state execute idolaters today? No. The penalty belonged to Israel as a nation under God, and it does not pass to the church or to any state; Jesus forbade uprooting the weeds before the harvest (Matt 13:29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: On the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses the one who is to die shall be put to death; a person shall not be put to death on the evidence of one witness. The hand of the witnesses shall be first against him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two or three witnesses. Here is one of the foundation stones of biblical justice: no conviction on a single testimony, however sincere or respectable the witness.

The rule exists because one person can be mistaken, and one person can lie, and there is no way to tell the difference from inside the courtroom. Requiring two independent witnesses does not make error impossible; it makes malice expensive, because a false charge now needs a conspiracy.

The New Testament carries the principle straight over and applies it in three different settings: to church discipline — take one or two others along with you, that every charge may be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses (Matt. 18:16); to Paul’s own conduct (2 Cor. 13:1); and, most pointedly, to accusations against a minister — Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses (1 Tim. 5:19). God protects the reputation of the accused as carefully as he pursues the guilt of the offender.

And then the requirement that the witnesses cast the first stone. Nobody testifies and walks away. A man who has sworn away another man’s life must be the first to take it, in public, with his own hands — which is the strongest possible deterrent against casual testimony, and the exact provision the men who dragged a woman before Jesus were quietly hoping he would forget (John 8:7; the earliest manuscripts of John do not contain this story, though many believe it records a true event).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Central Court for Hard Cases
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cases too difficult for local courts are to be brought to the priests and the judge at the chosen place, whose verdict must be obeyed; presumptuous defiance of the court is a capital offense.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides ordered authority and final courts to maintain justice; submission to legitimate authority guards the community from anarchy.
verseByVerse.examples: God still gives ordered authority in church and society, so that hard disputes have somewhere to be settled.

verseByVerse.quote: "If any case arises requiring decision between one kind of homicide and another, one kind of legal right and another, or one kind of assault and another, any case within your towns that is too difficult for you, then you shall arise and go up to the place that the LORD your God will choose. And you shall come to the Levitical priests and to the judge who is in office in those days, and you shall consult them, and they shall declare to you the decision. Then you shall do according to what they declare to you from that place that the LORD will choose. And you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you. According to the instructions that they give you, and according to the decision which they pronounce to you, you shall do. You shall not turn aside from the verdict that they declare to you, either to the right hand or to the left. The man who acts presumptuously by not obeying the priest who stands to minister there before the LORD your God, or the judge, that man shall die. So you shall purge the evil from Israel. And all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets up an appeal court. Cases too difficult for you — the phrase is literally too wonderful, beyond your reach — go up from the local court to the central sanctuary, to the priests and the judge who is in office at the time.

Three things about that arrangement. It assumes local judges will meet cases they cannot settle, and provides for it in advance without shame. It combines priest and judge, so that the hardest questions are decided where worship and law meet rather than in a purely secular room. And its verdict is binding, with severe penalties for defying it, because a legal system with no final court is not a legal system.

Nor may anyone turn aside from the verdict to the right or to the left: a man may not evade a judgment either by brushing it aside or by inventing scruples against it.

A society in which every man is his own final court is exactly what chapter 12 warned about — everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes — and the remedy God provides is not less freedom but a settled place where hard questions can be brought and answered. God does not expect his people to carry everything alone, and he provides authority precisely so that they need not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — The King Like the Nations: God's Restrictions
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Israel desires a king like the nations, God permits one of his choosing from among the brothers, but forbids him to multiply horses, wives, or silver and gold.
verseByVerse.theology: Even the king is subject to God's law; the restrictions guard against military self-reliance, divided allegiance, and greed — the besetting sins of power.
verseByVerse.examples: Every kind of authority is still accountable to God, and every leader needs guarding against the same three temptations.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you come to the land that the LORD your God is giving you, and you possess it and dwell in it and then say, 'I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me,' you may indeed set a king over you whom the LORD your God will choose. One from among your brothers you shall set as king over you. You may not put a foreigner over you, who is not your brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like all the nations. Centuries before Israel has a king, God permits one, and quotes in advance the motive that will actually produce one, which is not a good motive at all.

When the day came, Israel used almost these exact words: appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations, and God said to Samuel, they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (1 Sam. 8:5, 7). God knew the request was a rejection of himself, and he had made provision for it centuries earlier anyway.

God does not only plan for his people’s obedience. He legislates in advance for their failures, so that what they insist on wrongly is less ruinous than it might have been.

Many critical scholars think this law was written after Solomon, because it fits his failures so closely. The question is debated. But horses, foreign wives and treasure were the standing temptations of every ancient king and easily foreseen, and Samuel wrote down the rights and duties of the kingship in a book at the very start of the monarchy (1 Samuel 10:25), which shows such terms were known early.

And the terms begin at once: whom the LORD your God will choose. One from among your brothers. Not a self-made man, and not a foreigner — a king given rather than seized, and one of them rather than over them.

verseByVerse.quote: Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, 'You shall never return that way again.' And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away, nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Horses. Horses meant chariots, and chariots meant military power. And the reason attached is pointed: or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since Egypt was the horse market of the region. A king building an army would end up trading with the house of slavery — and the text adds God’s own comment: You shall never return that way again.

Wives. Royal marriages in the ancient world were treaties; a wife was a sealed alliance. So this is a prohibition on foreign policy conducted by marriage, and the danger named is not political but personal — lest his heart turn away.

Silver and gold. Great wealth buys a king independence from his people and, he may come to feel, from God.

Set that list beside the reign of Solomon: Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen… And Solomon’s import of horses was from Egypt (1 Kgs. 10:26, 28); he had 700 wives… and his wives turned away his heart (1 Kgs. 11:3); and the silver he made as common in Jerusalem as stone (1 Kgs. 10:27).

The wisest king Israel ever had broke all three clauses of this law, in order, and the historian who records it uses Deuteronomy’s own phrase to explain the ruin: his wives turned away his heart. God had named the exact failure centuries in advance, and it happened anyway, to the man best equipped to know better.
verseByVerse.note: For the whole record, read 1 Kings 10:14–11:8.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–20 — The King Who Reads the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king must copy out God's law for himself and live under it.
verseByVerse.theology: The true king is a humble student of God's word, subject to the law, a brother among brothers; this points to Christ, the King who perfectly embodies the law.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone given authority, at home, at work or in the church, needs the same daily correction from Scripture that the king did.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself in a book a copy of this law, approved by the Levitical priests. And it shall be with him, and he shall read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God by keeping all the words of this law and these statutes, and doing them, that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers, and that he may not turn aside from the commandment, either to the right hand or to the left, so that he may continue long in his kingdom, he and his children, in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A copy of this law. The king must copy out the law by hand. Not commission a scribe — write for himself — and have the copy checked by the priests against the original, so it cannot quietly drift. Then he is to keep it with him and read it every day for as long as he lives.

In Egypt the king was a god. In Mesopotamia he was the one who issued the law. In Israel he is the one man in the nation required to write the law out longhand and read it daily, because he is under it. The most powerful person in the country is the most thoroughly governed.

And the stated purposes are two. First, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God — the king is a learner. Second, that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers.

His brothers. That is what the law is meant to prevent him forgetting — not the technicalities of temple procedure, but that the people he rules are his own family. Power’s characteristic sin is not cruelty; it is the slow, unnoticed conviction that you are of a different kind from the people you govern. A daily hour in the Scriptures is God’s prescription against it.

And there was one King who fulfilled this. He was born under the law, knew it well enough to answer the devil out of it three times, said I have kept my Father’s commandments (John 15:10), and whose heart was never lifted up above his brothers — he is not ashamed to call them brothers (Heb. 2:11). Every other king in Israel’s history read this chapter and broke it. He read it and kept it, and then took the curse the breakers had earned.

17.theology:
The king under the Word. In a world of god-kings, Israel's king must write and read Scripture “all the days of his life” and never let his heart be “lifted up above his brothers” (17:18–20). The law stands above the throne.

The temptations of power restrained. Horses, wives, and silver and gold (17:16–17) name military self-reliance, divided allegiance and greed. Solomon broke every clause, which shows the need for a King whose heart would never turn away.

Rigorous, ordered justice. Unblemished worship (17:1), corroborated testimony (17:6), and courts whose verdicts are obeyed (17:8–13): God's justice is careful and protective of truth, and his gift of authority guards the community from anarchy.
17.examples: We give God our best, for we have been given Christ the unblemished Lamb; we require corroborated evidence and honor legitimate authority.
