And we look to the King who kept the law of the king in our place, our brother whose heart was never lifted up, who trusted God rather than horses, whose love was undivided, who became poor for our sake, and whose Spirit forms in his people the same humble love of God's word. Israel's kings failed; Christ alone is the righteous King we long for.

18.title: Prophets, Priests, and the Prophet to Come
18.text: <sup>1</sup>"The Levitical priests, all the tribe of Levi, shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel. They shall eat the LORD's food offerings as their inheritance.<sup>2</sup>They shall have no inheritance among their brothers; the LORD is their inheritance, as he promised them.<sup>3</sup>And this shall be the priests' due from the people, from those offering a sacrifice, whether an ox or a sheep: they shall give to the priest the shoulder and the two cheeks and the stomach.<sup>4</sup>The firstfruits of your grain, of your wine and of your oil, and the first fleece of your sheep, you shall give him.<sup>5</sup>For the LORD your God has chosen him out of all your tribes to stand and minister in the name of the LORD, him and his sons for all time.<sup>6</sup>"And if a Levite comes from any of your towns out of all Israel, where he lives—and he may come when he desires — to the place that the LORD will choose,<sup>7</sup>and ministers in the name of the LORD his God, like all his fellow Levites who stand to minister there before the LORD,<sup>8</sup>then he may have equal portions to eat, besides what he receives from the sale of his patrimony.<sup>9</sup>"When you come into the land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall not learn to follow the abominable practices of those nations.<sup>10</sup>There shall not be found among you anyone who burns his son or his daughter as an offering, anyone who practices divination or tells fortunes or interprets omens, or a sorcerer<sup>11</sup>or a charmer or a medium or a necromancer or one who inquires of the dead,<sup>12</sup>for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD. And because of these abominations the LORD your God is driving them out before you.<sup>13</sup>You shall be blameless before the LORD your God,<sup>14</sup>for these nations, which you are about to dispossess, listen to fortune-tellers and to diviners. But as for you, the LORD your God has not allowed you to do this.<sup>15</sup>"The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen—<sup>16</sup>just as you desired of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, 'Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die.'<sup>17</sup>And the LORD said to me, 'They are right in what they have spoken.<sup>18</sup>I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him.<sup>19</sup>And whoever will not listen to my words that he shall speak in my name, I myself will require it of him.<sup>20</sup>But the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die.'<sup>21</sup>And if you say in your heart, 'How may we know the word that the LORD has not spoken?'—<sup>22</sup>when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You need not be afraid of him.
18.overview:
Chapter 18 deals with spiritual leadership in Israel: the support of the Levitical priests, the ban on every occult practice of the nations, and the promise of the Prophet to come. It is one of the great messianic chapters of the Old Testament.

The Levites have no land, “for the LORD is their inheritance,” and live on what Israel brings to God. Israel is not to seek hidden knowledge from the dead but to listen to the Prophet God will raise up like Moses. The chapter closes with the test of a true prophet: his words come to pass.
18.theology:
The Prophet like Moses. The promise of 18:15 is fulfilled in Jesus, the mediator in whose mouth God put his words and to whom all must listen.

The God who speaks. Israel must shun all occult practices (18:9–14), humanity's attempt to gain hidden knowledge apart from God. We need not peer into forbidden darkness, for in Christ God has spoken his final word.

The LORD is the minister's inheritance. The Levites have no land and are supported by the people (18:2), the principle Paul applies to gospel ministers (1 Cor 9:14). God's servants find their true portion in God himself.
18.examples: We support those who labor in the Word, refuse every quest for forbidden knowledge, and listen to Jesus, the Prophet greater than Moses. To refuse him is to incur judgment; to listen to him is life. Our calling is the glad obedience of listening to the beloved Son in whom the Father is well pleased.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Priests and Their Portion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tribe of Levi is given no land. They live on what Israel brings to God, receiving specified portions from every sacrifice and the firstfruits of every harvest — and any Levite from any town may come and serve on equal terms.
verseByVerse.theology: The provision rests on a promise (v. 2). Levi has no acres because Levi has God, and the arrangement is a pledge God made and keeps. Paul reasons from this statute to the support of gospel ministers (1 Cor. 9:13–14).
verseByVerse.examples: A whole tribe lived without land on what the nation carried to God, so that Israel’s worship never depended on somebody having a free week. A congregation that supports those who labour in the Word is therefore not so much being generous as keeping an arrangement God made, and it frees them to give themselves to the work.

verseByVerse.quote: "The Levitical priests, all the tribe of Levi, shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel. They shall eat the LORD's food offerings as their inheritance. They shall have no inheritance among their brothers; the LORD is their inheritance, as he promised them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he promised them. Moses is preaching now, not legislating, and the phrase he adds is the one that matters. Levi’s landlessness is not an oversight or a penalty. It is the discharge of an undertaking God gave, and Moses reminds a tribe with nothing that God said he would do this.

Consider what it meant week to week. Every other Israelite could walk to the edge of his ground and see where it stopped. He could work it badly and be poorer, or work it well and be richer, and either way it was his and his son’s after him. The Levite had no such line to walk. What he had instead was a sentence — and a sentence is only worth as much as the person who said it.

That is why God ties it to a promise rather than to a policy. He is asking a tribe to live its entire history on his word, in public, in front of eleven brothers who can point at their fields. Every generation of Levites was a standing demonstration that the word of God will actually feed a family. And it is the same arrangement every Christian is on, whether he notices or not: your heavenly Father knows that you need them all (Matt. 6:32).

verseByVerse.quote: And this shall be the priests' due from the people, from those offering a sacrifice, whether an ox or a sheep: they shall give to the priest the shoulder and the two cheeks and the stomach. The firstfruits of your grain, of your wine and of your oil, and the first fleece of your sheep, you shall give him. For the LORD your God has chosen him out of all your tribes to stand and minister in the name of the LORD, him and his sons for all time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shoulder, cheeks and stomach. The specifics are startlingly domestic: named cuts from every sacrifice, and the first of the grain, wine, oil and fleece.

First, the priest received specified parts rather than whatever was left. A worshipper could not decide on the day what he felt like handing over; the shoulder was the priest’s before the animal was killed. There is no room in the arrangement for a man to be generous or grudging, and therefore none for the priest to be either flattered or slighted.

Second, the word first. The firstfruits of the grain, the wine and the oil, and the first fleece. Not the tenth after the household had taken what it needed — the first, before anybody knew whether the rest of the harvest would come in. Israel was asked to give away the earliest evidence that the year would be all right, while it was still the only evidence.

Chosen to minister. The support is not a wage for services rendered. It is the practical shape of a choice God made (v. 5), and the nation’s part in it was simply to honour what he had decided.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if a Levite comes from any of your towns out of all Israel, where he lives—and he may come when he desires — to the place that the LORD will choose, and ministers in the name of the LORD his God, like all his fellow Levites who stand to minister there before the LORD, then he may have equal portions to eat, besides what he receives from the sale of his patrimony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Equal portions. A Levite from the country may come and serve at the sanctuary when he desires, and eat the same as everyone else: no reduced allowance for the newcomer, no better share for the men who had been there longest.

Anyone in a church will recognise what this guards against. Wherever people serve together, an inner circle forms — the ones who have been here longest, who know how things are done, who are consulted. It happens without anybody deciding it should, and the man who arrives from outside can serve for years without ever quite getting in.

God legislated against it in the eighth verse of a chapter about priests’ dinners. And the New Testament raises the same guard in the plainest possible terms, over a matter as small as where a visitor sits: if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place”… have you not then made distinctions among yourselves? (Jas. 2:3–4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — No Traffic with the Occult
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nine practices are named and forbidden — child sacrifice heading the list, then every method by which the nations tried to reach the future or the dead. Israel is to be whole before the LORD instead, because she has something the nations do not: a God who speaks.
verseByVerse.theology: The prohibition is not a demand to manage without knowing. It is the near half of an argument whose far half is v. 15: the occult is forbidden and a Prophet is promised, in one breath. God does not shut a door without opening a better one.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel was surrounded by nations who read livers and consulted the dead, and was told to want none of it. The appetite has not changed, and neither has the answer. Horoscopes, mediums and the hunt for hidden knowledge all assume God is silent. He is not, and the reason we may leave the future alone is that it is held by a Father who has already told us what we need. Anyone who has dabbled is not shut out: the Prophet speaks pardon to all who come back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you come into the land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall not learn to follow the abominable practices of those nations. There shall not be found among you anyone who burns his son or his daughter as an offering, anyone who practices divination or tells fortunes or interprets omens, or a sorcerer or a charmer or a medium or a necromancer or one who inquires of the dead, for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD. And because of these abominations the LORD your God is driving them out before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It opens with the darkest practice of all: anyone who burns his son or his daughter as an offering. That is what heads the list of Canaanite religion — not a metaphor, not a scholarly dispute, but parents putting children in a fire to secure a harvest or a battle. Every line that follows should be read in the shadow of that one.

Then eight more, and English blurs them, so take them one at a time. To practise divination is to seek a decision by casting or reading signs. To tell fortunes is to forecast a person’s future. To interpret omens is to read meaning in ordinary events — a bird, a spill, a shape in the fire. A sorcerer works with potions and spells. A charmer binds by incantation. A medium and a necromancer and one who inquires of the dead all traffic with the dead. Nine practices, and they cover every route by which the ancient world tried to get at what it could not otherwise know or control.

And then verse 12 gives the reason the Canaanites are losing their land: because of these abominations the LORD your God is driving them out before you. That is a direct answer to the question every honest reader of the conquest asks. God is not clearing a country for a favourite. He is judging a civilisation that had been burning its children for centuries, after four hundred years of waiting for it to stop (Gen. 15:16).
verseByVerse.note: “Burns his son or his daughter” is literally “makes them pass through the fire” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: You shall be blameless before the LORD your God, for these nations, which you are about to dispossess, listen to fortune-tellers and to diviners. But as for you, the LORD your God has not allowed you to do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word behind blameless is tamim — whole, entire, all of a piece, the word used of a sacrificial animal without blemish. It does not primarily mean sinless. It means undivided: not a man who consults God on Sunday and a horoscope on Thursday, keeping a second channel open in case the first one goes quiet.

And the promise of a Prophet that follows matters, because the appetite behind the occult is not wickedness so much as fear. People consult mediums because somebody has died and they cannot bear the silence; they read horoscopes because next year is dark and they want a handhold. Saul went to the witch at Endor on the night before he died, and the text says exactly why: when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him (1 Sam. 28:6). He wanted a word from God and would not wait for one. The alternative God offers here is not stoicism. It is a voice.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises a Prophet from among Israel’s own brothers, in whose mouth he will put his words, and to whom the whole nation must listen. The promise answers the people’s own terrified request at Horeb — and God says their fear was right.
verseByVerse.theology: Outside Genesis, this is the clearest promise of the coming Messiah in the five books of Moses. A Prophet like Moses means a mediator of a covenant, an intercessor, and one rejected by his own brothers.
verseByVerse.examples: A people who could not bear to hear God directly were given a man to stand between them and the fire. Now the Mediator has come, and the God whose voice would have killed us has spoken to us in a human voice, at a carpenter’s bench and on a hillside and from a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen— just as you desired of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, 'Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die.' And the LORD said to me, 'They are right in what they have spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Horeb. Moses explains where the promise came from, and it is not where anyone would guess: the day the people begged never to hear God’s voice again, lest they die.

The mountain was burning to the heart of heaven, the trumpet was sounding, God was speaking the Ten Commandments in an audible voice, and the entire nation backed away and begged Moses to make it stop. They asked never to hear God again. On the face of it that is the low point of Israel’s history — a people offered the direct voice of God and asking to be spared it.

They are right. God agrees with them. He does not tell them to be braver, or rebuke them for cowardice, or insist that they would manage if they tried. He says they are correct — unmediated contact between the holy God and sinners would kill them, and they were right to say so. And then, out of that agreement, comes the promise of a Prophet.

Which means the greatest messianic prophecy in the book of Deuteronomy grew out of a frightened crowd telling God they could not survive him. He took their terror seriously, called it accurate, and answered it — not by turning down the fire but by providing somebody to stand in it on their behalf.

Is the “prophet like me” one person or the line of prophets? Many Jewish readers took it as the prophetic office. But by Jesus’ day many were waiting for one particular Prophet (John 1:21; 6:14), and Deuteronomy itself says no prophet like Moses had yet arisen (34:10), and Peter names him: Jesus (Acts 3:22–23). The prophets who followed were partial fulfilments; Christ is the Prophet.

verseByVerse.quote: I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. And whoever will not listen to my words that he shall speak in my name, I myself will require it of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two phrases carry the weight. The first is like you — like Moses. Israel had many prophets afterwards and none of them was that. Moses was not merely a man who delivered messages; he mediated a covenant, interceded for a nation under sentence and offered to be blotted out in its place, spoke with God face to face, and was rejected by the brothers he came to rescue. A prophet like Moses is a very particular thing, and the description is uncomfortably specific.

The second is from among their brothers. Not an angel, not a voice out of the fire — one of them. The mediator has to be one of the people he is standing for, which is exactly the argument Hebrews makes about the incarnation: he had to be made like his brothers in every respect (Heb. 2:17).

I myself will require it. Not the prophet will require it. God will. To ignore this Prophet is to be dealt with by God personally.

Peter stood in Solomon’s Portico with a healed lame man beside him and quoted this passage to a Jerusalem crowd, and then said who it was about: God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness (Acts 3:22–26). Stephen quoted it too, minutes before they killed him (Acts 7:37). And on a high mountain the cloud came down and the Father said the one thing this promise had been waiting centuries to hear said out loud: This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him (Matt. 17:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — The Test of a True Prophet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A prophet who speaks presumptuously in the LORD’s name, or in the name of other gods, is to die. And Israel is given a plain test for telling the difference: does what he says come true?
verseByVerse.theology: God does not leave his people at the mercy of a confident speaker: his word can be checked. The final answer, though, is not a better test but a better Prophet.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians must still test the spirits (1 John 4:1), weighing every claim to speak for God against what he has already said.

verseByVerse.quote: But the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name that I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die.' And if you say in your heart, 'How may we know the word that the LORD has not spoken?'— when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously. You need not be afraid of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A word that does not come true. Israel will hear men claiming to speak for God, so the chapter gives her a way to tell, and names two capital offences: speaking presumptuously in the LORD’s name, and speaking in the name of other gods.

Is that workable, when some prophecies take centuries? It is, because of how false prophets operate: the man inventing a message in God’s name is nearly always predicting something near — peace this year, victory in this battle, Babylon will not come. Jeremiah faced exactly that and Hananiah was dead within two months (Jer. 28). The test bites where the lying is done.

And read it alongside chapter 13, which supplies the other half: a prophet whose sign does come true but who says let us go after other gods is to be rejected anyway. So Israel had two criteria — does it come true, and does it agree with what God has already said — and a claimant had to pass both. God does not leave his people at the mercy of anyone confident enough to say thus says the LORD.

Verse 20 should also make anybody who stands up to preach go quiet for a moment. It is a capital matter to say God has spoken when he has not. The safety of a preacher lies entirely in staying inside what is written, and the man who wanders outside it is not being bold.

But the chapter’s last word is not a test; it is a Person. Israel was given a succession of prophets, and every one of them died and had to be replaced and could be got wrong. Then the succession stopped, because the promise was kept in full: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things (Heb. 1:1–2). The nations strained after the dead for a whisper. Israel was told to wait for a voice. And the voice, when it came, had a face, and ate with sinners, and wept at a grave, and said I am the resurrection and the life.

Does this condemn modern “prophets” whose predictions fail? Yes. Revelation of new words from God ended with the apostles (Eph 2:20; Heb 1:1–2), so no one today speaks with that authority, and one who claims to and is wrong has spoken presumptuously. Some prophecies in Scripture were conditional, such as Jonah’s against Nineveh (Jon 3:4, 10; Jer 18:7–10); that is not the same as a prediction that simply fails. This commentary holds that the prophetic gift ceased with the apostles, and faithful Christians differ on that; but continuationist brothers also hold that any prophecy today is subordinate to Scripture and must be tested (1 Corinthians 14:29; 1 Thessalonians 5:20–21), and all should agree that a failed prediction announced as God’s word is a serious matter.

19.title: Cities of Refuge and the Law of Witnesses
19.text: <sup>1</sup>"When the LORD your God cuts off the nations whose land the LORD your God is giving you, and you dispossess them and dwell in their cities and in their houses,<sup>2</sup>you shall set apart three cities for yourselves in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.<sup>3</sup>You shall measure the distances and divide into three parts the area of the land that the LORD your God gives you as a possession, so that any manslayer can flee to them.<sup>4</sup>"This is the provision for the manslayer, who by fleeing there may save his life. If anyone kills his neighbor unintentionally without having hated him in the past—<sup>5</sup>as when someone goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut wood, and his hand swings the axe to cut down a tree, and the head slips from the handle and strikes his neighbor so that he dies—he may flee to one of these cities and live,<sup>6</sup>lest the avenger of blood in hot anger pursue the manslayer and overtake him, because the way is long, and strike him fatally, though the man did not deserve to die, since he had not hated his neighbor in the past.<sup>7</sup>Therefore I command you, You shall set apart three cities.<sup>8</sup>And if the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as he has sworn to your fathers, and gives you all the land that he promised to give to your fathers—<sup>9</sup>provided you are careful to keep all this commandment, which I command you today, by loving the LORD your God and by walking ever in his ways— then you shall add three other cities to these three,<sup>10</sup>lest innocent blood be shed in your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, and so the guilt of bloodshed be upon you.<sup>11</sup>"But if anyone hates his neighbor and lies in wait for him and attacks him and strikes him fatally so that he dies, and he flees into one of these cities,<sup>12</sup>then the elders of his city shall send and take him from there, and hand him over to the avenger of blood, so that he may die.<sup>13</sup>Your eye shall not pity him, but you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood from Israel, so that it may be well with you.<sup>14</sup>"You shall not move your neighbor's landmark, which the men of old have set, in the inheritance that you will hold in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.<sup>15</sup>"A single witness shall not suffice against a person for any crime or for any wrong in connection with any offense that he has committed. Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established.<sup>16</sup>If a malicious witness arises to accuse a person of wrongdoing,<sup>17</sup>then both parties to the dispute shall appear before the LORD, before the priests and the judges who are in office in those days.<sup>18</sup>The judges shall inquire diligently, and if the witness is a false witness and has accused his brother falsely,<sup>19</sup>then you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>20</sup>And the rest shall hear and fear, and shall never again commit any such evil among you.<sup>21</sup>Your eye shall not pity. It shall be life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.
19.overview:
Chapter 19 is bound together by the protection of innocent blood and the integrity of justice. Israel is to set apart cities of refuge where one who kills unintentionally may flee from the avenger of blood until a fair trial, while the deliberate murderer is handed over. A single command guards the neighbour's boundary stone, and the law of witnesses deals severely with the false accuser, who suffers the punishment he sought to inflict.

The church has long seen in the cities of refuge a shadow of Christ. The one who has shed blood, pursued by the avenger, flees for his life to the appointed place of safety, and within its walls he is secure. So the sinner, pursued by the just demands of the law, flees to Christ, “the hope set before us,” to which we “have fled for refuge” (Heb. 6:18).
19.theology:
Christ our refuge. The refuge does not deny guilt but shelters from judgment; Christ bears the wrath, so that within him we are safe. As the roads were kept clear, the gospel makes him near to all who flee to him.

Justice balanced with mercy. The law shelters the one who killed without intent and refuses refuge to the murderer, to “purge the guilt of innocent blood” (19:13). God's law is neither careless nor cruel.

The integrity of testimony. No one may be condemned on a single witness (19:15), and the false accuser bears what he intended (19:19). The God of refuge is the God of truth, who will not have his courts corrupted by lies.
19.examples: We flee to Christ, our refuge from the wrath we deserve, secure in him though guilty; we uphold careful justice and abhor false witness, marvelling that the innocent One condemned by false witnesses has become the only refuge for sinners.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three cities, centrally placed with the roads kept clear, where a man who kills without intent may flee from the avenger of blood and stand trial. The deliberate murderer finds no shelter there; the elders hand him over.
verseByVerse.theology: The refuge does not pretend the manslayer is innocent of the death; it shelters him from a vengeance that cannot tell accident from murder until the facts are heard.
verseByVerse.examples: The cities were placed, and the roads kept clear, so that a frightened man could reach one in time. The refuge now is a Person, and preaching the gospel is the road-clearing: our business is to make him reachable, not to make him respectable.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD your God cuts off the nations whose land the LORD your God is giving you, and you dispossess them and dwell in their cities and in their houses, you shall set apart three cities for yourselves in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess. You shall measure the distances and divide into three parts the area of the land that the LORD your God gives you as a possession, so that any manslayer can flee to them. "This is the provision for the manslayer, who by fleeing there may save his life. If anyone kills his neighbor unintentionally without having hated him in the past— as when someone goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut wood, and his hand swings the axe to cut down a tree, and the head slips from the handle and strikes his neighbor so that he dies—he may flee to one of these cities and live, lest the avenger of blood in hot anger pursue the manslayer and overtake him, because the way is long, and strike him fatally, though the man did not deserve to die, since he had not hated his neighbor in the past. Therefore I command you, You shall set apart three cities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Measure the distances. The country is to be surveyed and the cities placed so that nobody is ever too far from one, and Jewish tradition adds that the roads to them were kept cleared and signposted, which is exactly what verse 3 implies.

The axe head. Two men working side by side on an ordinary afternoon. A loose axe head. One is dead and the other is a killer, and neither of them did anything wrong. Scripture does not deal in abstract categories here; it puts a specific accident in front of us, with two friends and a tool, because the man this law exists for is not a criminal and needs to be seen clearly.

The avenger of blood. In a society without police, the dead man’s nearest relative had the duty of pursuit. He was not a vigilante; he was the only enforcement there was. But he would be setting out on the day of the funeral, in hot anger, and grief cannot tell an accident from a murder at speed.

So the whole institution exists to put distance and time between a death and a killing — long enough for the facts to be heard. That is what God’s justice looks like when it is written into a map: not indifference to blood, but an absolute refusal to let a man die before anyone has found out what he did.

Is the city of refuge a picture of Christ? Hebrews calls believers those who have fled for refuge, to hold fast to the hope set before us (Heb 6:18). The difference is that the manslayer was innocent of murder; we come guilty, and find refuge because Christ bore the penalty. Numbers adds that the manslayer went free when the high priest died (Numbers 35:25, 28), and many Christians have seen there a hint of the great High Priest whose death sets the guilty free (Hebrews 9:15).

verseByVerse.quote: And if the LORD your God enlarges your territory, as he has sworn to your fathers, and gives you all the land that he promised to give to your fathers— provided you are careful to keep all this commandment, which I command you today, by loving the LORD your God and by walking ever in his ways— then you shall add three other cities to these three, lest innocent blood be shed in your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, and so the guilt of bloodshed be upon you. "But if anyone hates his neighbor and lies in wait for him and attacks him and strikes him fatally so that he dies, and he flees into one of these cities, then the elders of his city shall send and take him from there, and hand him over to the avenger of blood, so that he may die. Your eye shall not pity him, but you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood from Israel, so that it may be well with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God provides for expansion — three more cities if the territory grows — and then the limit. The three here are west of the Jordan, besides the three Moses had already set apart east of it (4:41–43), six in all (Joshua 20:7–8); the further three were apparently never needed, because Israel never held the full borders promised.

The refuge is not a loophole. A murderer who runs there is fetched out. And the three marks of murder are named: hates, lies in wait, attacks — motive, premeditation, and act. The law is asking what was in the man, not merely what happened.

No pity. That is a hard sentence and it is aimed at the judges, not the family. A community that will not carry out a just sentence because it finds the sentence distasteful has stopped protecting the next victim.

Innocent blood. The land itself is at stake. Unavenged blood, in Deuteronomy, defiles a country. A nation that shrugs at murder becomes complicit in it.

Hold the two halves of this paragraph together, because they are the same justice. The man who killed by accident is sheltered even from a grieving family; the man who killed on purpose is taken out of sanctuary and handed over. Mercy that cannot distinguish is not mercy, and severity that cannot distinguish is not justice.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One short command against moving a neighbour’s landmark — the stone that marked where his God-given inheritance began and ended.
verseByVerse.theology: Because God allotted the land, a moved boundary stone was theft from God as well as from the neighbour. Proverbs returns to it more than once, and ties it to the widow and the fatherless (Prov. 15:25; 22:28; 23:10-11).
verseByVerse.examples: Whoever has quietly lost out to someone stronger may take comfort here: God still takes the side of those who cannot fight back.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not move your neighbor's landmark, which the men of old have set, in the inheritance that you will hold in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The landmark. In a chapter about killing it looks like a change of subject, and it is not. Israel’s land was allotted by God, tribe by tribe and family by family, and the boundary stones marked what he had given. To shift one was to steal from a neighbour and to redraw God’s map.

And consider the crime itself, because it is the quietest one in the law. No violence. No confrontation. A man goes out at dusk and moves a stone eighteen inches, and does it again in a few years, and there are no witnesses and nothing to report. Meanwhile a family who cannot afford a surveyor is a little poorer every harvest and cannot say why.

That is why Scripture keeps returning to it, and see who turns up in the company each time: Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless, for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you (Prov. 23:10–11). The people this is done to are the ones who cannot fight back, and God appoints himself their advocate.

The modern version needs no stone. It is done in contracts, in invoices, in a fee structure a client cannot follow, in a margin quietly taken from somebody who will never audit it. Nobody calls it theft, and no one is ever charged. The verse is in the Bible for exactly that reason.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — Two Witnesses, and the False One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No charge may stand on one testimony. A malicious witness is investigated by priests and judges, and if he is proved false, the punishment he intended for his brother falls on him.
verseByVerse.theology: God guards the accused as carefully as he pursues the guilty, and turns the false accuser’s own weapon back on him.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone tempted to use the courts, or gossip, to ruin a neighbour should reckon with receiving the same sentence. And it is worth remembering that Christ himself was condemned by false witnesses (Matt. 26:59-60).

verseByVerse.quote: "A single witness shall not suffice against a person for any crime or for any wrong in connection with any offense that he has committed. Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established. If a malicious witness arises to accuse a person of wrongdoing, then both parties to the dispute shall appear before the LORD, before the priests and the judges who are in office in those days. The judges shall inquire diligently, and if the witness is a false witness and has accused his brother falsely, then you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother. So you shall purge the evil from your midst. And the rest shall hear and fear, and shall never again commit any such evil among you. Your eye shall not pity. It shall be life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A single witness. One witness is never enough, not because one person always lies, but because one person cannot be checked. The rule has already been given at 17:6 for capital cases; here it is widened to any crime or for any wrong, so that no dispute in Israel at all turns on a single voice.

A malicious witness. The procedure is careful. Both parties present, before God and the court, with diligent investigation — and the burden falls on the accuser to make his charge stand rather than on the accused to disprove it.

As he had meant. The penalty is the most exact in the law. The false witness receives precisely the sentence he was trying to obtain. A man who swore away his neighbour’s life loses his own; a man who tried to have him fined pays the fine. The lie comes back down the same road it went out on.

Eye for eye. Verse 21 is one of the most misunderstood in the Bible. It is not permission for revenge; it is a ceiling on it. In a world where a slight could start a feud that killed a family, the law says: one eye, no more. The punishment may not exceed the crime. Jewish interpreters came to apply it as fixing compensation of equal value rather than literal maiming (compare Exodus 21:26–27). It is a limit written to restrain vengeance, not to license it — which is exactly why the Lord Jesus could take it further in the same direction without contradicting it: You have heard that it was said, “An eye for an eye”… But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil (Matt. 5:38–39). Moses capped retaliation at one eye. Christ asks his people to give it up altogether, and then went to a court where false witnesses were heard and an innocent man was sentenced to die, and said nothing.

20.title: Laws of War: The LORD Goes With You to Fight
20.text: <sup>1</sup>"When you go out to war against your enemies, and see horses and chariots and an army larger than your own, you shall not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God is with you, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.<sup>2</sup>And when you draw near to the battle, the priest shall come forward and speak to the people<sup>3</sup>and shall say to them, 'Hear, O Israel, today you are drawing near for battle against your enemies: let not your heart faint. Do not fear or panic or be in dread of them,<sup>4</sup>for the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.'<sup>5</sup>Then the officers shall speak to the people, saying, 'Is there any man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man dedicate it.<sup>6</sup>And is there any man who has planted a vineyard and has not enjoyed its fruit? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man enjoy its fruit.<sup>7</sup>And is there any man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her.'<sup>8</sup>And the officers shall speak further to the people, and say, 'Is there any man who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go back to his house, lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own.'<sup>9</sup>And when the officers have finished speaking to the people, then commanders shall be appointed at the head of the people.<sup>10</sup>"When you draw near to a city to fight against it, offer terms of peace to it.<sup>11</sup>And if it responds to you peaceably and it opens to you, then all the people who are found in it shall do forced labor for you and shall serve you.<sup>12</sup>But if it makes no peace with you, but makes war against you, then you shall besiege it.<sup>13</sup>And when the LORD your God gives it into your hand, you shall put all its males to the sword,<sup>14</sup>but the women and the little ones, the livestock, and everything else in the city, all its spoil, you shall take as plunder for yourselves. And you shall enjoy the spoil of your enemies, which the LORD your God has given you.<sup>15</sup>Thus you shall do to all the cities that are very far from you, which are not cities of the nations here.<sup>16</sup>But in the cities of these peoples that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes,<sup>17</sup>but you shall devote them to complete destruction, the Hittites and the Amorites, the Canaanites and the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, as the LORD your God has commanded,<sup>18</sup>that they may not teach you to do according to all their abominable practices that they have done for their gods, and so you sin against the LORD your God.<sup>19</sup>"When you besiege a city for a long time, making war against it in order to take it, you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them. You may eat from them, but you shall not cut them down. Are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you?<sup>20</sup>Only the trees that you know are not trees for food you may destroy and cut down, that you may build siegeworks against the city that makes war with you, until it falls.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 sets out Israel's laws of war, and they are unlike the war manuals of any other ancient nation. The priest, not the general, addresses the troops first, and his message is trust: the LORD goes with you to fight for you (20:3–4). Generous exemptions reduce the army to those who will fight in faith, so that the victory is plainly God's.

Distant cities must first be offered peace. The Canaanite nations within the land fall under God's unique and unrepeatable judgment. Even in war the fruit trees are spared. The chapter points to the God who fights for his people, and to Christ, who has won the decisive victory over sin, death and the devil.
20.theology:
The LORD fights for his people. Before battle the priest preaches faith, not strategy (20:4). Holy war rests on God's presence, not human strength, and so does the believer's warfare (Rom. 8:31).

God saves by a believing remnant. The exemptions reduce the army (20:5–8), for God is not impressed by numbers or resources; he delights to save by the few who trust him, that the glory may be his alone.

Justice tempered by restraint. Terms of peace precede the siege (20:10), and even the fruit trees are spared (20:19). The judgment of the Canaanites was God's unique act on a people whose wickedness was complete, pointing to the cross, where judgment fell on Christ, and to the gospel's offer of peace.
20.examples: We face our battles knowing the Lord goes with us; we rejoice that the God of holy war offers peace to the world in the gospel, having borne his own judgment against sin at the cross; and in Christ, who has triumphed over sin, death and the devil, we are more than conquerors.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Before the Battle: the Priest and the Exemptions
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priest, not the general, speaks first, and his word is not tactics but faith. Then the officers send men home — the one with a new house, the one with a new vineyard, the newly betrothed, and anyone who is afraid.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel goes to war on the ground of who is with her: the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you (v.4). And the army is deliberately reduced rather than maximised, so that the victory can belong to nobody else.
verseByVerse.examples: God is not served by people driven past what he asked of them, and the church’s strength has never lain in its numbers. A believer who has had to step back from some work for a season has not left the Lord’s army.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you go out to war against your enemies, and see horses and chariots and an army larger than your own, you shall not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God is with you, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. And when you draw near to the battle, the priest shall come forward and speak to the people and shall say to them, 'Hear, O Israel, today you are drawing near for battle against your enemies: let not your heart faint. Do not fear or panic or be in dread of them, for the LORD your God is he who goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God grants the facts first. The enemy does have horses and chariots, and the army is larger. Israel had no cavalry and no chariot corps; against a chariot force on open ground an infantry army was at a severe disadvantage, and everybody involved knew it.

The priest shall speak. Not the general. The priest addresses the army on the morning of a battle, and what he delivers is not a strategy or a rallying speech but a sermon, and it opens with the words of the Shema: Hear, O Israel. The same call that opens the confession of faith opens the briefing before combat.

Do not fear. The priest uses four different words for fear, because fear comes in more than one form and God addresses all of them. And against them, not an argument about Israel’s capability but a single fact about God’s presence. That is the pattern of every battle speech in Scripture, and it is the shape of Paul’s question when he has finished eight chapters of argument: If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom. 8:31). And the battle that decided everything was fought by one man with no army at all, when Christ disarmed the powers of evil on the cross (Colossians 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the officers shall speak to the people, saying, 'Is there any man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man dedicate it. And is there any man who has planted a vineyard and has not enjoyed its fruit? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man enjoy its fruit. And is there any man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her.' And the officers shall speak further to the people, and say, 'Is there any man who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go back to his house, lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own.' And when the officers have finished speaking to the people, then commanders shall be appointed at the head of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new house, a young vineyard, a fiancée. God releases men from military service so that they will not die before enjoying the good things he has given them. A vineyard takes four or five years before its fruit may be eaten; a man who had planted one and not yet tasted it is sent home. That is not military logic. It is a Father protecting his children’s joy in a war he intends to win himself.

The fearful. Then an exemption few armies would ever grant: anyone who is frightened may leave, publicly, without penalty. The stated reason is practical — lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own, because fear is contagious and travels faster than courage. But the effect is that the army is deliberately reduced to men who actually believe God will do what he said.

God does not want the largest possible force. He wants a believing one, and he will strip the numbers down to make sure nobody can misattribute the result — which is exactly what he says to Gideon: The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, “My own hand has saved me” (Judg. 7:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — Terms of Peace, and the Cities of Canaan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Distant cities must first be offered peace, and only besieged if they refuse. The six nations named in v. 17 are under a different and unrepeatable command. (Chapter 7 names seven; the Hebrew list here leaves out the Girgashites, whom the Greek Old Testament includes, and both lists stand for the whole.)
verseByVerse.theology: Two régimes are set side by side deliberately. War outside Canaan begins with an offer of peace and spares women and children — a striking restraint by ancient standards. The herem (the ban, devoting a people wholly to God for destruction) inside Canaan is judicial, bounded by a named list, and given a stated protective reason in v.18. It is a model for nobody; the New Testament forecloses it (John 18:36; 2 Cor. 10:3-4).
verseByVerse.examples: Judgment fell only where peace had been refused, and that is still the order of God’s dealings: the gospel’s terms come first, and they are far better than any city in Canaan was offered.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you draw near to a city to fight against it, offer terms of peace to it. And if it responds to you peaceably and it opens to you, then all the people who are found in it shall do forced labor for you and shall serve you. But if it makes no peace with you, but makes war against you, then you shall besiege it. And when the LORD your God gives it into your hand, you shall put all its males to the sword, but the women and the little ones, the livestock, and everything else in the city, all its spoil, you shall take as plunder for yourselves. And you shall enjoy the spoil of your enemies, which the LORD your God has given you. Thus you shall do to all the cities that are very far from you, which are not cities of the nations here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terms of peace. Israel’s wars are to begin with an offer. Not a demand for surrender after a siege has already starved a city, but terms extended before a blow is struck. If the city accepts, its people become subject labourers; if it refuses and fights, then the siege follows, and the men are killed — but the women and the little ones, the livestock, and everything else in the city… you shall take as plunder.

Modern readers find that harsh, and by our standards it is. Measured against the actual practice of the ancient Near East it is a remarkable restraint. Assyrian kings recorded, with pride, the flaying of prisoners and the building of pillars from severed heads; total annihilation of a resisting city was common and boasted about. Israel is required to offer peace first, and is forbidden to kill the women and children even of a city that chose war.

And the offer of peace preceding judgment is not merely a rule of engagement here. It is how God himself operates throughout Scripture. Nineveh got forty days and a preacher. Judah got centuries of prophets. And the shape of the gospel is the same: we implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God (2 Cor. 5:20) — terms offered, freely, before anything falls.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the cities of these peoples that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes, but you shall devote them to complete destruction, the Hittites and the Amorites, the Canaanites and the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, as the LORD your God has commanded, that they may not teach you to do according to all their abominable practices that they have done for their gods, and so you sin against the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing that breathes. Then comes the exception, and the text marks it as one.

Everything in the previous paragraph applies to all the cities that are very far from you. This is different, and the difference is the whole point. What is commanded here is not Israel’s foreign policy; it is a bounded judicial act inside one territory, against six named nations, at one moment in history.

Lest they teach you. The stated purpose (v. 18) is protective. Not conquest, not land-hunger, not racial superiority — containment of a religion that burned children (12:31), so that it would not be taught to Israel. And the tragic footnote is that Israel did not carry it out, and it was taught to her, and within a few centuries Israelites were burning their own children in the valley of Hinnom (Jer. 7:31). The thing God said would happen is exactly what happened.

Three things must be said and held together. This is judgment, executed after four centuries of divine patience (Gen. 15:16). It is unrepeatable, and no nation, church or person has ever held this commission since; the New Testament removes the possibility (John 18:36). And it remains hard, and Scripture does not remove the difficulty — what it does is put alongside it a God who, when judgment finally fell on sin in earnest, arranged for it to fall on himself.

But women and children? This is the hardest question in the chapter, and it should be felt, not brushed aside. Scripture answers it from God’s side: the whole people fell under judgment, as the world did in the flood and Sodom did in the fire, and the Judge of all the earth, who gives every life, has the right to take any life (Gen 18:25). It shows mercy at the edges: Rahab and her household turned to the LORD and were spared (Josh 6:25). And it fences the command off as unique to that moment, never a pattern: in Israel’s own courts the law forbids punishing children for their fathers’ crimes (24:16). What happens to little children before God is in hands kinder and wiser than ours; the God who commanded this is the God who pitied the children of a pagan city (Jonah 4:11).

Was it carried out literally? The language of total destruction is the idiom of war; Joshua says he left none remaining (Josh 10:40), yet Canaanites remained (Josh 15:63; Judg 1). The command was real, and so was Israel’s partial obedience.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–20 — Do Not Destroy the Trees
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a long siege, Israel may cut timber for siegeworks but may not touch the fruit trees. The question God asks is unanswerable: are the trees in the field human, that you should besiege them?
verseByVerse.theology: Even a war God has authorised is fenced. What sustains life is not to be destroyed to win a battle, and the restraint is grounded in the nature of the thing itself rather than in Israel’s advantage.
verseByVerse.examples: An army under orders left the olive groves standing, and the same God still asks whether the thing we are about to destroy in order to win was ever the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you besiege a city for a long time, making war against it in order to take it, you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them. You may eat from them, but you shall not cut them down. Are the trees in the field human, that they should be besieged by you? Only the trees that you know are not trees for food you may destroy and cut down, that you may build siegeworks against the city that makes war with you, until it falls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scorched earth was standard practice. An army besieging a city cut down the orchards — for timber, for siege ramps, and to ruin the district so it could not recover. An olive tree can take many years to bear well and decades to reach full yield; destroying the groves meant a generation of poverty for whoever was left.

God forbids it. Israel may cut any tree that does not bear food, and must leave the fruit trees standing, even while starving out the city they belong to.

Are the trees human? This is one of the most humane sentences in the Pentateuch. The KJV reads for the tree of the field is man’s life; the Hebrew can be read either way, and both make the same point: the trees feed people and are not the enemy.

The tree has done nothing, it cannot fight, and it will still be feeding people long after this quarrel is settled. War does not license the destruction of everything within reach; there is a distinction between the combatant and the field he stands in, and God draws it in the middle of a manual on siegecraft.

That single verse stands near the root of later principles of restraint in war, and it comes from a God whose care runs down into things nobody thought to protect. He notices the sparrow and he notices the olive grove, and he asks the men with the axes a question they cannot answer.

21.title: Various Laws: A Hanged Man Is Cursed by God
21.text: <sup>1</sup>"If in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess someone is found slain, lying in the open country, and it is not known who killed him,<sup>2</sup>then your elders and your judges shall come out, and they shall measure the distance to the surrounding cities.<sup>3</sup>And the elders of the city that is nearest to the slain man shall take a heifer that has never been worked and that has not pulled in a yoke.<sup>4</sup>And the elders of that city shall bring the heifer down to a valley with running water, which is neither plowed nor sown, and shall break the heifer's neck there in the valley.<sup>5</sup>Then the priests, the sons of Levi, shall come forward, for the LORD your God has chosen them to minister to him and to bless in the name of the LORD, and by their word every dispute and every assault shall be settled.<sup>6</sup>And all the elders of that city nearest to the slain man shall wash their hands over the heifer whose neck was broken in the valley,<sup>7</sup>and they shall testify, 'Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it shed.<sup>8</sup>Accept atonement, O LORD, for your people Israel, whom you have redeemed, and do not set the guilt of innocent blood in the midst of your people Israel, so that their blood guilt be atoned for.'<sup>9</sup>So you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood from your midst, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD.<sup>10</sup>"When you go out to war against your enemies, and the LORD your God gives them into your hand and you take them captive,<sup>11</sup>and you see among the captives a beautiful woman, and you desire to take her to be your wife,<sup>12</sup>and you bring her home to your house, she shall shave her head and pare her nails.<sup>13</sup>And she shall take off the clothes in which she was captured and shall remain in your house and lament her father and her mother a full month. After that you may go in to her and be her husband, and she shall be your wife.<sup>14</sup>But if you no longer delight in her, you shall let her go where she wants. But you shall not sell her for money, nor shall you treat her as a slave, since you have humiliated her.<sup>15</sup>"If a man has two wives, the one loved and the other unloved, and both the loved and the unloved have borne him children, and if the firstborn son belongs to the unloved,<sup>16</sup>then on the day when he assigns his possessions as an inheritance to his sons, he may not treat the son of the loved as the firstborn in preference to the son of the unloved, who is the firstborn,<sup>17</sup>but he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the unloved, by giving him a double portion of all that he has, for he is the firstfruits of his strength. The right of the firstborn is his.<sup>18</sup>"If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son who will not obey the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and, though they discipline him, will not listen to them,<sup>19</sup>then his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city at the gate of the place where he lives,<sup>20</sup>and they shall say to the elders of his city, 'This our son is stubborn and rebellious; he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton and a drunkard.'<sup>21</sup>Then all the men of the city shall stone him to death with stones. So you shall purge the evil from your midst, and all Israel shall hear, and fear.<sup>22</sup>"And if a man has committed a crime punishable by death and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree,<sup>23</sup>his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God. You shall not defile your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 gathers laws for hard cases in community life: the unsolved murder, the captive woman taken as a wife, the rights of the unloved wife's firstborn, the incorrigibly rebellious son, and the body of an executed criminal. Through them runs a concern for the value of human life, the purging of bloodguilt, and the protection of people with no advocate.

The chapter's crown, for the Christian, is verses 22–23: a hanged man is “cursed by God,” the verse Paul uses to explain the cross (Gal. 3:13).
21.theology:
Christ became a curse for us. On the tree of Calvary the sinless Son bore the curse we deserved (21:23; Gal. 3:13), so that the verse which once made a crucified Messiah unthinkable became the reason for the church's hope.

The preciousness of innocent blood. Even an unsolved murder must be solemnly addressed (21:9); no bloodshed is too obscure to matter to God. Hebrews sets such rites beside the blood of Christ, which cleanses the conscience as no animal could (Heb. 9:13–14).

Justice for the vulnerable. The law guards the captive woman and the unloved wife's firstborn (21:10–17), and takes rebellion against God-given authority seriously (21:18–21), a rebellion the gospel answers by Christ bearing our judgment, that rebels might become beloved children.
21.examples: We rest in the gospel proclaimed from this chapter: Christ became a curse for us, so that the God who would not overlook a single drop of innocent blood has dealt fully with all our guilt at the cross, where the blessed One was cursed that the cursed might be blessed. So we honor human life and defend the vulnerable.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A body is found in open country and nobody knows who did it. The elders of the nearest town measure the distance, break a heifer’s neck in an untilled valley, wash their hands over it and swear they neither shed the blood nor saw it shed.
verseByVerse.theology: Innocent blood pollutes the land, and God will not let an unsolved killing be quietly forgotten. The ritual is a corporate confession that a death has occurred which the community cannot account for. Even where no one can be charged, atonement is sought.
verseByVerse.examples: A whole town stopped work over a stranger nobody could name, because his blood mattered to God. A society that can absorb unexplained deaths without flinching has lost something this ritual existed to protect, and the blood that finally answers for all of it was not a heifer’s.

verseByVerse.quote: "If in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess someone is found slain, lying in the open country, and it is not known who killed him, then your elders and your judges shall come out, and they shall measure the distance to the surrounding cities. And the elders of the city that is nearest to the slain man shall take a heifer that has never been worked and that has not pulled in a yoke. And the elders of that city shall bring the heifer down to a valley with running water, which is neither plowed nor sown, and shall break the heifer's neck there in the valley. Then the priests, the sons of Levi, shall come forward, for the LORD your God has chosen them to minister to him and to bless in the name of the LORD, and by their word every dispute and every assault shall be settled. And all the elders of that city nearest to the slain man shall wash their hands over the heifer whose neck was broken in the valley, and they shall testify, 'Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it shed. Accept atonement, O LORD, for your people Israel, whom you have redeemed, and do not set the guilt of innocent blood in the midst of your people Israel, so that their blood guilt be atoned for.' So you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood from your midst, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A body is found in open country, and nobody knows who did it. In most societies, ancient or modern, that is where the matter ends — no suspect, no evidence, no case.

Measure the distance. In Israel it triggers a ceremony: grown men with measuring lines, walking out into a field to establish which town is nearest to a corpse nobody can name.

The heifer. The heifer has never worked, the valley has never been ploughed, and water runs through it: everything in the scene is untouched. Over the dead animal the elders wash their hands and swear.

Two things are happening. The first is a denial of responsibility, made under oath by the men who bear authority nearest the scene — which also means that if anyone in that town knew anything, the ceremony would give him a very uncomfortable morning.

Accept atonement. The second is the prayer, and it is the heart of the passage. They ask for atonement for a crime they did not commit and cannot solve, because blood shed in the land defiles the land, and somebody must deal with it before God whether or not anybody can be charged.

What that whole ritual says is that no human life is too obscure to matter. A man nobody could identify, killed by somebody nobody could find, in a field outside a town that had nothing to do with him — and the entire leadership of that town stops work, walks out, and stands before God about it. Set that beside a world that scrolls past a body on the news, and you can measure the distance between two views of what a human being is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — The Captive Woman and the Unloved Wife’s Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two laws protecting people with no advocate: a woman taken in war, who must be given a month to mourn and may never be sold or treated as a slave; and the firstborn of a wife her husband does not love, whose double portion may not be given to a favourite’s son.
verseByVerse.theology: Neither law describes God’s ideal; both restrain a fallen practice and put a floor under the powerless. The captive is given time, dignity and — if the marriage fails — freedom rather than sale. The unloved wife’s son is protected from a father’s partiality, because justice may not be bent by affection.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel’s law named the two people least able to defend themselves and gave them rights. The test of any household, church or company is still what happens to the person in it who cannot appeal to anyone.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you go out to war against your enemies, and the LORD your God gives them into your hand and you take them captive, and you see among the captives a beautiful woman, and you desire to take her to be your wife, and you bring her home to your house, she shall shave her head and pare her nails. And she shall take off the clothes in which she was captured and shall remain in your house and lament her father and her mother a full month. After that you may go in to her and be her husband, and she shall be your wife. But if you no longer delight in her, you shall let her go where she wants. But you shall not sell her for money, nor shall you treat her as a slave, since you have humiliated her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This law troubles modern readers, and it should be read for what it does rather than for what it permits. A soldier sees a captive woman and wants to marry her. In every other army of the ancient world, that is the end of the story and she has no say in any of it; captured women were spoil, and what happened to them needs no describing.

Here it is stopped. You bring her home to your house — home, not the camp. She shaves her head, pares her nails and must take off the clothes in which she was captured, which are the signs of mourning, and then she shall remain in your house and lament her father and her mother a full month.

The law does not say that she chose this marriage, and that silence is part of why the passage is hard to read; what it does is take from the soldier everything it can. A full month. He may not touch her for thirty days, while she grieves for parents who are almost certainly dead in the battle he fought. He has to live in the same house as her sorrow, and watch it, before anything can happen at all.

She shall be your wife. A wife and not a concubine, with a wife’s standing. And then the provision that closes the last door.

She cannot be sold. She cannot be demoted. If the marriage fails she walks out free, and the law says plainly why — you have humiliated her, which is God taking her side in the statute book against the man who owns everything.

This is not God’s picture of marriage and nobody should pretend it is. It is God regulating a brutal practice in a brutal world and putting a floor beneath a woman who had no advocate, no family and no rights. He does the same thing repeatedly in the law — meeting people where they are, restraining the worst, and protecting the person nobody else will protect. The Lord Jesus said as much about divorce: Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you… but from the beginning it was not so (Matt. 19:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man has two wives, the one loved and the other unloved, and both the loved and the unloved have borne him children, and if the firstborn son belongs to the unloved, then on the day when he assigns his possessions as an inheritance to his sons, he may not treat the son of the loved as the firstborn in preference to the son of the unloved, who is the firstborn, but he shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the unloved, by giving him a double portion of all that he has, for he is the firstfruits of his strength. The right of the firstborn is his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Loved and unloved. The second law protects the son of a wife whose husband does not love her. God does not endorse the situation. Polygamy in Genesis and the histories is uniformly a source of misery, and the phrase the one loved and the other unloved is lifted almost directly from the household of Jacob, where Leah was the unloved one and Reuben was her firstborn (Gen. 29:31). (Reuben later lost his birthright through his own sin, not his father’s preference: Gen. 35:22; 1 Chron. 5:1.) The law is written about a mess God did not design.

And it protects the boy. He gets a double portion of all that he has — not because he is better, or preferred, or even liked, but because he is the firstborn and the law says so. A father’s affection may not rewrite an inheritance.

That is a very particular kind of justice: the sort that protects somebody precisely where he is least likely to be defended, in his own home, from his own father. There is no court a boy can appeal to against being loved less. So God writes it into the law instead.

And see what God repeatedly does with unloved sons. The unloved wife’s firstborn in Jacob’s house was Reuben — and it was Leah, the unloved one, through whose son Judah the Messiah came. God’s habit of preferring the overlooked is not a sentimental idea about him. It runs through the genealogies.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph’s two sons, each counted as a tribe, show the double portion at work (Gen. 48:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–21 — The Stubborn and Rebellious Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An incorrigible adult son, a glutton and a drunkard who has rejected all discipline, is brought by his own parents to the elders at the gate and stoned by the men of the city.
verseByVerse.theology: Rebellion against authority in the home is serious because the home is where every person first meets authority. The civil penalty belonged to Israel as a nation under God and is not carried into the church age; the seriousness of the sin is.
verseByVerse.examples: Parents grieving over a grown child who has rejected everything they taught may notice that the law took the matter out of their hands alone. They are not asked to carry it by themselves, and no child is beyond the reach of the Son who bore the rebel’s sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son who will not obey the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and, though they discipline him, will not listen to them, then his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city at the gate of the place where he lives, and they shall say to the elders of his city, 'This our son is stubborn and rebellious; he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton and a drunkard.' Then all the men of the city shall stone him to death with stones. So you shall purge the evil from your midst, and all Israel shall hear, and fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This law should be read carefully rather than either dismissed or brandished. Start with who is described. Not a small child: he is a glutton and a drunkard — which is not a description of a toddler in a tantrum but of an adult with an established way of life. Discipline has already been tried, repeatedly, and has failed.

His father and his mother. The safeguards are formidable. Both parents. The charge must be brought by the two people in the world least likely to want their son executed, and no parent brings such a case lightly or in a temper — which rules out the abusive father using the law as a weapon.

Then it goes to the elders of his city at the gate, in public, and the community judges. It is not a family matter settled at home, and the parents do not carry out the sentence.

Some later rabbis held that this law was never actually applied, and that the safeguards were designed to make it nearly impossible to apply. That may or may not be so; what is certain is that its stated purpose is deterrent: all Israel shall hear, and fear.

And the theology underneath it is what the fifth commandment already established: the home is where a person first meets authority at all. A society in which that collapses in one generation has nothing to govern the next one with.

The civil penalty belonged to Israel as a theocracy, a nation ruled directly under God’s law, which has ended, and no church or parent holds it now. But do not miss where the chapter is going. Israel is told to bring the rebellious son out to be stoned — and two verses later we are told what happens to a man hung on a tree. There is a rebellious son in this story, and it is every one of us; and there was a Son who was not rebellious at all, and he is the one who was taken outside the city and executed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–23 — A Hanged Man Is Cursed by God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The body of an executed criminal hung on a tree must not stay there overnight. It is to be buried the same day, for a hanged man is under the curse of God, and the land must not be defiled.
verseByVerse.theology: Paul uses this verse to explain what happened on the cross. The law’s severest sentence becomes the gospel’s deepest comfort.
verseByVerse.examples: A body on a tree was the visible sign of God’s curse. Christians look at a man on a tree and see the curse they had earned, borne by someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if a man has committed a crime punishable by death and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God. You shall not defile your land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hanged on a tree. This is not execution by hanging; Israel usually executed by stoning. The body was hung up afterwards, on a pole or a tree, as a public display — and the display meant one thing: this man is under the curse of God. Everybody who walked past knew it.

And even that had a limit. The body must come down before sunset, because a corpse left hanging defiles the land. Even a cursed man is not to be left up overnight in a country where God lives.

Now hold that verse in one hand and a Friday afternoon outside Jerusalem in the other.

Every Jew watching a crucifixion knew this text. It is why a crucified Messiah was not merely implausible to them but blasphemous — the one place a man could hang and prove he was under God’s curse was the last place the Christ could ever be. Paul had thought exactly that, and had persecuted the church over it.

And then, converted, he took the verse that had made Christianity impossible and made it the centre of the gospel (quoting it in a shortened form close to the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint): Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (Gal. 3:13).

The logic is exact. The law pronounces a curse on everyone who does not keep it (27:26), which is everybody. The curse had to fall somewhere. And on a hill outside the city, the one man who had never earned it took the position the law reserved for the cursed, and hung there in public, so that the sentence would land on him. He was not merely killed. He was, in the terms of this statute, a curse for us — and Paul chooses that appalling phrase deliberately, as he chooses he made him to be sin (2 Cor. 5:21).

And they took him down before dark. Since it was the day of Preparation… the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away (John 19:31) — men keeping Deuteronomy 21:23 to the letter while the Son of God hung under its curse for them.

The chapter that begins with a murder nobody could atone for ends with the atonement for everything. Israel washed her hands over a heifer and asked God to accept it. He accepted something else instead.

22.title: Laws on Community Life: Love Your Neighbor in the Details
22.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall not see your brother's ox or his sheep going astray and ignore them. You shall take them back to your brother.<sup>2</sup>And if he does not live near you and you do not know who he is, you shall bring it home to your house, and it shall stay with you until your brother seeks it. Then you shall restore it to him.<sup>3</sup>And you shall do the same with his donkey or with his garment, or with any lost thing of your brother's, which he loses and you find; you may not ignore it.<sup>4</sup>You shall not see your brother's donkey or his ox fallen down by the way and ignore them.
