You shall help him to lift them up again.<sup>5</sup>"A woman shall not wear a man's garment, nor shall a man put on a woman's cloak, for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD your God.<sup>6</sup>"If you come across a bird's nest in any tree or on the ground, with young ones or eggs and the mother sitting on the young or on the eggs, you shall not take the mother with the young.<sup>7</sup>You shall let the mother go, but the young you may take for yourself, that it may go well with you, and that you may live long.<sup>8</sup>"When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, that you may not bring the guilt of blood upon your house, if anyone should fall from it.<sup>9</sup>"You shall not sow your vineyard with two kinds of seed, lest the whole yield be forfeited, the crop that you have sown and the yield of the vineyard.<sup>10</sup>You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together.<sup>11</sup>You shall not wear cloth of wool and linen mixed together.<sup>12</sup>"You shall make yourself tassels on the four corners of the garment with which you cover yourself.<sup>13</sup>"If any man takes a wife and goes in to her and then hates her<sup>14</sup>and accuses her of misconduct and brings a bad name upon her, saying, 'I took this woman, and when I came near her, I did not find in her evidence of virginity,'<sup>15</sup>then the father of the young woman and her mother shall take and bring out the evidence of her virginity to the elders of the city in the gate.<sup>16</sup>And the father of the young woman shall say to the elders, 'I gave my daughter to this man to marry, and he hates her;<sup>17</sup>and behold, he has accused her of misconduct, saying, "I did not find in your daughter evidence of virginity." And yet this is the evidence of my daughter's virginity.' And they shall spread the cloak before the elders of the city.<sup>18</sup>Then the elders of that city shall take the man and whip him,<sup>19</sup>and they shall fine him a hundred shekels of silver and give them to the father of the young woman, because he has brought a bad name upon a virgin of Israel. And she shall be his wife. He may not divorce her all his days.<sup>20</sup>But if the thing is true, that evidence of virginity was not found in the young woman,<sup>21</sup>then they shall bring out the young woman to the door of her father's house, and the men of her city shall stone her to death with stones, because she has done an outrageous thing in Israel by whoring in her father's house. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>22</sup>"If a man is found lying with the wife of another man, both of them shall die, the man who lay with the woman, and the woman. So you shall purge the evil from Israel.<sup>23</sup>"If there is a betrothed virgin, and a man meets her in the city and lies with her,<sup>24</sup>then you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city, and you shall stone them to death with stones, the young woman because she did not cry for help though she was in the city, and the man because he violated his neighbor's wife. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>25</sup>"But if in the open country a man meets a young woman who is betrothed, and the man seizes her and lies with her, then only the man who lay with her shall die.<sup>26</sup>But you shall do nothing to the young woman; she has committed no offense punishable by death. For this case is like that of a man attacking and murdering his neighbor,<sup>27</sup>because he met her in the open country, and though the betrothed young woman cried for help there was no one to rescue her.<sup>28</sup>"If a man meets a virgin who is not betrothed, and seizes her and lies with her, and they are found,<sup>29</sup>then the man who lay with her shall give to the father of the young woman fifty shekels of silver, and she shall be his wife, because he has violated her. He may not divorce her all his days.<sup>30</sup>"A man shall not take his father's wife, so that he does not uncover his father's nakedness.
22.overview:
Chapter 22 works out the command to love your neighbor in the details of daily life: lost animals, fallen burdens, a parapet on the roof, the distinctions woven into creation, and a series of laws protecting marriage and the vulnerable in sexual matters.

Love does not look away. And the sexual laws, read carefully, consistently protect the person who cannot protect herself.
22.theology:
Love your neighbor in the details. Returning a lost animal, lifting a fallen burden, building a safe roof (22:1–8): love sees, stops and helps.

Honoring God's created order. The laws of distinction (22:5–12) trained Israel to honor the order God has woven into creation, for he is a God of order, not confusion (1 Corinthians 14:33); the ceremonial details are fulfilled in Christ, but his people still reverence the good distinctions he has made.

The sanctity of marriage and sexual integrity. These laws (22:13–30) protect the vulnerable and assess guilt justly, because marriage reflects Christ and his church (Eph. 5:31–32). None of us is clean here, in deed or in thought (Matt. 5:28); but Christ was faithful in our place and his purity is counted ours, so the fallen may confess and be washed (1 Cor. 6:11), and the Spirit who now dwells in us makes holiness possible.
22.examples: We are called to the same seeing love, stooping to serve as Christ our Good Samaritan stooped to bind our wounds, and we treasure sexual holiness not as joyless restriction but as God's wise design, reflecting Christ's covenant love for his bride.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Do Not Ignore Your Brother’s Loss
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A stray ox, a lost cloak, a donkey collapsed under its load. In every case the command is the same and it is negative: you shall not ignore it. If you do not know the owner, keep the animal until he comes looking.
verseByVerse.theology: It is not enough to refrain from theft; a man who walks past his neighbour’s loss has broken this command.
verseByVerse.examples: The sin these verses name is still the easiest one to commit and the hardest to notice, because it looks exactly like minding your own business.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not see your brother's ox or his sheep going astray and ignore them. You shall take them back to your brother. And if he does not live near you and you do not know who he is, you shall bring it home to your house, and it shall stay with you until your brother seeks it. Then you shall restore it to him. And you shall do the same with his donkey or with his garment, or with any lost thing of your brother's, which he loses and you find; you may not ignore it. You shall not see your brother's donkey or his ox fallen down by the way and ignore them. You shall help him to lift them up again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Hebrew is more pointed than ignore. It says: you shall not hide yourself from them. The picture is of a man who sees, and then arranges not to have seen — who looks the other way, walks a different route, and is home before he has to think about it.

That is the sin being legislated against, and it is the most respectable sin there is. Nothing has been stolen. Nobody has been struck. A man has simply declined to be involved in somebody else’s problem, and there is no law in most countries against that.

Bring it home. The demands are not small. You feed and water somebody else’s ox, at your own cost, for as long as it takes him to come looking. The inconvenience is unlimited and unreimbursed.

Fallen down by the way. A loaded animal collapsed on a road, and a man who happens to be passing. That is heavy, filthy work, and the law does not make it optional.

Many centuries later a lawyer asked And who is my neighbor?, and the Lord Jesus told him about a man lying by a road, and a priest and a Levite who, when he saw him he passed by on the other side (Luke 10:31–32). He was not inventing a new ethic. He was telling the story of Deuteronomy 22:4 with a man in the ditch instead of a donkey.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–12 — Distinctions, and the Guilt of Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A cluster of short laws: build a wall round every flat roof, let the mother bird go when you take her young, keep seeds, animals and fabrics unmixed, and wear tassels on the corners of your cloak.
verseByVerse.theology: Life is to be safeguarded before an accident happens, and a man who does not build a parapet bears the guilt of blood. And the distinctions woven into creation are to be respected rather than blurred; Israel is to live in a world with edges.
verseByVerse.examples: Every new roof had a wall round it because somebody’s child might fall. A small precaution taken for other people’s safety is a way of loving them before they know they need it.

verseByVerse.quote: "A woman shall not wear a man's garment, nor shall a man put on a woman's cloak, for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD your God. "If you come across a bird's nest in any tree or on the ground, with young ones or eggs and the mother sitting on the young or on the eggs, you shall not take the mother with the young. You shall let the mother go, but the young you may take for yourself, that it may go well with you, and that you may live long. "When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, that you may not bring the guilt of blood upon your house, if anyone should fall from it. "You shall not sow your vineyard with two kinds of seed, lest the whole yield be forfeited, the crop that you have sown and the yield of the vineyard. You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together. You shall not wear cloth of wool and linen mixed together. "You shall make yourself tassels on the four corners of the garment with which you cover yourself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A parapet. Two threads run through this cluster, and the first is the safeguarding of life before anything goes wrong. Flat roofs in Israel were living space — people slept, worked and ate up there. A low wall round the edge costs money and materials and prevents a funeral that has not happened yet. And the phrase is startling: a man who does not build one may bring the guilt of blood upon his house. He has not pushed anybody. He has simply not spent the money, and God calls the resulting death his.

That is a category modern law took centuries to recover, and it should be put to anyone who employs, builds, drives or has children in the house. The question God asks is not whether harm was intended. It is whether it was foreseeable and cheap to prevent.

The second thread is distinction. Fields not sown with two kinds of seed; ox and donkey not yoked together; wool and linen not woven into one cloth. These have puzzled readers for centuries, and the honest answer is that no reason is given. What can be said is that Israel was being taught, in the most ordinary things she touched, that God has made a world with edges in it, and that the instinct to blur every line is not a neutral one.

Let the mother go. In the middle sits the tenderest law in the chapter. Take the eggs if you are hungry; let the mother fly. It costs nothing and it preserves the future, and God attaches to this smallest of kindnesses the promise he elsewhere attaches to honouring your parents — that it may go well with you, and that you may live long.

Does this forbid women wearing trousers? No: the verse concerns what is the distinctive dress of the other sex in a given culture, and trousers are worn by both today. It does forbid deliberately presenting oneself as the other sex, which God calls an abomination, because he made us male and female (Gen 1:27). That bears directly on transgender identity: the body God gave is part of who he made us. The church should say so with compassion for those who struggle, and welcome them to Christ.

Must Christians avoid blended fabrics? No. These were signs of Israel’s separateness, fulfilled in Christ (Eph 2:14–15; Acts 10:15).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A husband who tires of his wife and slanders her publicly is tried by the elders, whipped, fined a hundred shekels paid to her father, and forbidden ever to divorce her.
verseByVerse.theology: The law puts the burden of proof on the accuser and treats a woman’s reputation as something that can be stolen. Where the charge is true, the penalty is grave; but the paragraph is weighted toward the woman being lied about.
verseByVerse.examples: A man who tried to ruin his wife’s name found the court, the money and the law all on her side. Before passing on a damaging story about anyone, especially someone with less power than you, ask whether it has been proved.

verseByVerse.quote: "If any man takes a wife and goes in to her and then hates her and accuses her of misconduct and brings a bad name upon her, saying, 'I took this woman, and when I came near her, I did not find in her evidence of virginity,' then the father of the young woman and her mother shall take and bring out the evidence of her virginity to the elders of the city in the gate. And the father of the young woman shall say to the elders, 'I gave my daughter to this man to marry, and he hates her; and behold, he has accused her of misconduct, saying, "I did not find in your daughter evidence of virginity." And yet this is the evidence of my daughter's virginity.' And they shall spread the cloak before the elders of the city. Then the elders of that city shall take the man and whip him, and they shall fine him a hundred shekels of silver and give them to the father of the young woman, because he has brought a bad name upon a virgin of Israel. And she shall be his wife. He may not divorce her all his days. But if the thing is true, that evidence of virginity was not found in the young woman, then they shall bring out the young woman to the door of her father's house, and the men of her city shall stone her to death with stones, because she has done an outrageous thing in Israel by whoring in her father's house. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man marries a woman, tires of her, and tries to be rid of her by destroying her name in public — accusing her of not having been a virgin when he married her.

Note what the law does with that. It does not accept the charge. The girl’s parents bring the evidence to the elders of the city in the gate, and the father speaks for her: I gave my daughter to this man to marry, and he hates her. That single word — he hates her — tells the court what is really going on, and the court is required to hear it.

And if the man is lying, the penalty is severe. He is whipped. He is fined a hundred shekels of silver, paid to her father — twice the bride-price of verse 29, an enormous sum, and it goes to her family rather than to the state. And then: she shall be his wife. He may not divorce her all his days.

Read that last provision carefully, because it is not a punishment of her. He has publicly tried to destroy her and failed; she now has a permanent claim on his house and income that he can never revoke. In a society where a discarded woman had nothing, the law makes her untouchable — by the very man who wanted her gone.

What the whole paragraph assumes is that a reputation is a real possession and that stealing one is a matter for the courts. It is the cheapest thing in the world to take and the hardest to restore, and God treats slander against a woman’s honour with the same seriousness as theft of livestock and rather more seriousness than most churches manage.

The evidence of virginity was most likely the bedding or garment of the wedding night, kept by the bride’s family. The law put the burden of proof on the accuser and punished false accusation. Verses 20–21 are stern, and belonged to Israel’s civil law, which ended with the theocracy. What remains is the moral principle: sexual faithfulness before and in marriage (Heb 13:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–30 — Sexual Sin, and the Cry That Was Not Heard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A series of cases distinguishing adultery from rape, turning on whether the woman cried out and whether anyone could have heard her.
verseByVerse.theology: The distinctions are the point. Where consent was given, both are guilty; where a woman is overpowered in open country, only the man dies, and the law compares her to a murder victim. In a world where a violated woman was routinely blamed, God writes her innocence into the statute.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who has been assaulted and then blamed, by others or by herself, should hear what this law says: God put the guilt on the attacker, and any church that assumes otherwise is not reading its own Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man is found lying with the wife of another man, both of them shall die, the man who lay with the woman, and the woman. So you shall purge the evil from Israel. "If there is a betrothed virgin, and a man meets her in the city and lies with her, then you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city, and you shall stone them to death with stones, the young woman because she did not cry for help though she was in the city, and the man because he violated his neighbor's wife. So you shall purge the evil from your midst. "But if in the open country a man meets a young woman who is betrothed, and the man seizes her and lies with her, then only the man who lay with her shall die. But you shall do nothing to the young woman; she has committed no offense punishable by death. For this case is like that of a man attacking and murdering his neighbor, because he met her in the open country, and though the betrothed young woman cried for help there was no one to rescue her. "If a man meets a virgin who is not betrothed, and seizes her and lies with her, and they are found, then the man who lay with her shall give to the father of the young woman fifty shekels of silver, and she shall be his wife, because he has violated her. He may not divorce her all his days. "A man shall not take his father's wife, so that he does not uncover his father's nakedness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where a man and a betrothed woman are found together in a town, both are guilty — because she did not cry for help though she was in the city (v. 24), where a cry would have been heard.

Like murder. In open country only the man shall die, and the law explains why with a comparison nobody expects. She is treated as a murder victim. That is the category God puts her in — not a participant in a shared sin, not a woman with questions to answer, but somebody who was attacked. And the presumption runs in her favour: she cried for help, and there was no one to hear. The law assumes it, because in open country it could not be disproved either way, and God gives the benefit of the doubt to the person who was overpowered.

Set that against how such women have been treated in most of human history — and in some churches within living memory — and the distance is enormous. Where the law of Moses could not establish the facts, it decided in favour of the victim and said so in writing.

Verse 29 is harder for modern readers: a man who violates an unbetrothed girl must pay her father fifty shekels and marry her, and he may not divorce her all his days. That reads as monstrous unless the situation is understood. Such a woman had no marriage prospects and no means of support; the law makes the man permanently liable for the woman he has ruined, with no possibility of walking away. It is not a reward for him. It is a life sentence of provision, and in that world it was the only protection available to her.

Did she have to marry him? Not necessarily. The parallel law in Exodus 22:16–17 lets her father refuse the marriage outright while the man still pays in full, and most interpreters read the two laws together: the marriage was a protection her family could claim, not a sentence passed on her. Some also note that the verb in verse 28 is milder than the one for the overpowering in verse 25, so that the case may include seduction as well as force. Either way the law binds the man, never the woman, and nothing here gives cover to anyone who presses a victim to stay with the one who harmed her. Today she should be brought to safety at once, and the crime reported.
verseByVerse.note: “Uncover his father’s nakedness” is literally “uncover his father’s skirt” (ESV note).

23.title: The Assembly of the LORD: Holiness and Compassion
23.text: <sup>1</sup>"No one whose testicles are crushed or whose male organ is cut off shall enter the assembly of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>"No one born of a forbidden union may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation, none of his descendants may enter the assembly of the LORD.<sup>3</sup>"No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation, none of them may enter the assembly of the LORD forever,<sup>4</sup>because they did not meet you with bread and with water on the way, when you came out of Egypt, and because they hired against you Balaam the son of Beor from Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse you.<sup>5</sup>But the LORD your God would not listen to Balaam; instead the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because the LORD your God loved you.<sup>6</sup>You shall not seek their peace or their prosperity all your days forever.<sup>7</sup>"You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother. You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you were a sojourner in his land.<sup>8</sup>Children born to them in the third generation may enter the assembly of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>"When you are encamped against your enemies, then you shall keep yourself from every evil thing.<sup>10</sup>"If any man among you becomes unclean because of a nocturnal emission, then he shall go outside the camp. He shall not come inside the camp,<sup>11</sup>but when evening comes, he shall bathe himself in water, and as the sun sets, he may come inside the camp.<sup>12</sup>"You shall have a place outside the camp, and you shall go out to it.<sup>13</sup>And you shall have a trowel with your tools, and when you sit down outside, you shall dig a hole with it and turn back and cover up your excrement.<sup>14</sup>Because the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give up your enemies before you, therefore your camp must be holy, so that he may not see anything indecent among you and turn away from you.<sup>15</sup>"You shall not give up to his master a slave who has escaped from his master to you.<sup>16</sup>He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him.<sup>17</sup>"None of the daughters of Israel shall be a cult prostitute, and none of the sons of Israel shall be a cult prostitute.<sup>18</sup>You shall not bring the fee of a prostitute or the wages of a dog into the house of the LORD your God in payment for any vow, for both of these are an abomination to the LORD your God.<sup>19</sup>"You shall not charge interest on loans to your brother, interest on money, interest on food, interest on anything that is lent for interest.<sup>20</sup>You may charge a foreigner interest, but you may not charge your brother interest, that the LORD your God may bless you in all that you undertake in the land that you are entering to take possession of it.<sup>21</sup>"If you make a vow to the LORD your God, you shall not delay fulfilling it, for the LORD your God will surely require it of you, and you will be guilty of sin.<sup>22</sup>But if you refrain from vowing, you will not be guilty of sin.<sup>23</sup>You shall be careful to do what has passed your lips, for you have voluntarily vowed to the LORD your God what you have promised with your mouth.<sup>24</sup>"If you go into your neighbor's vineyard, you may eat your fill of grapes, as many as you wish, but you shall not put any in your bag.<sup>25</sup>If you go into your neighbor's standing grain, you may pluck the ears with your hand, but you shall not put a sickle to your neighbor's standing grain.
23.overview:
Chapter 23 gathers laws on who may enter “the assembly of the LORD,” the holiness of the war camp, and a range of community matters: the runaway slave, lending, vows, and a neighbor's field. The unifying theme is the holiness fitting a people in whose midst God walks (23:14).

The exclusions from the assembly are ceremonial, and the gospel breaks through them: the eunuch and the foreigner are brought near (Isa 56; Acts 8). And holiness here walks with compassion: the runaway slave is given refuge, the poor brother is lent to without interest, and the hungry traveler may eat from any field.
23.theology:
The holiness of God's dwelling place. “The LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp” (23:14), so no corner of life is too ordinary to be touched by his presence. Now God's people are themselves his temple (1 Cor. 6:19; Eph. 2:21–22).

Barriers broken in Christ. The exclusions taught the gravity of approaching a holy God; in Christ the ones once shut out are brought near (Eph. 2:13–14). Christ has opened a new and living way into God's presence for all who come by faith.

Holiness wedded to compassion. Refuge for the runaway (23:15–16), no interest from the poor brother (23:19), vows kept (23:21–23), the hungry fed (23:24–25): the people among whom God walks reflect his holiness and his mercy alike.
23.examples: We are God's temple, indwelt by the Spirit; we rejoice that in Christ the far-off are brought near; and we join holiness with open-handed compassion, keeping our word and refusing to profit from a brother's poverty, for the God among us is both holy and merciful.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Who May Enter the Assembly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Restrictions on entry to the worshipping assembly — the emasculated, those of forbidden birth, Ammonites and Moabites — and then two surprising inclusions: the Edomite is a brother, and the Egyptian is not to be abhorred.
verseByVerse.theology: The exclusions are ceremonial, not a verdict on anyone’s soul, and Scripture itself dissolves them. The door that this chapter narrows, the prophets and then the gospel throw open.
verseByVerse.examples: No one need fear that something in their birth or their body, which they never chose, shuts them out from Christ. The eunuch who asked what prevented his baptism was baptised that same day (Acts 8:36).

verseByVerse.quote: "No one whose testicles are crushed or whose male organ is cut off shall enter the assembly of the LORD. "No one born of a forbidden union may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation, none of his descendants may enter the assembly of the LORD. "No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation, none of them may enter the assembly of the LORD forever, because they did not meet you with bread and with water on the way, when you came out of Egypt, and because they hired against you Balaam the son of Beor from Pethor of Mesopotamia, to curse you. But the LORD your God would not listen to Balaam; instead the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because the LORD your God loved you. You shall not seek their peace or their prosperity all your days forever. "You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother. You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you were a sojourner in his land. Children born to them in the third generation may enter the assembly of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The assembly of the LORD. The list of people barred makes modern readers uncomfortable, as it should, and two things need saying. These exclusions are from the assembly, the formal gathering, not from the covenant or from God’s mercy; and the Ammonite and Moabite exclusion is national and historical rather than personal: nobody is turned away for something he has done.

Bread and water, and Balaam. The grounds given for the Ammonite and Moabite are entirely historical: a judgment on two nations for what they did at a particular moment, written into Israel’s liturgy.

Because the LORD your God loved you. Verse 5 is one of the loveliest asides in the book. Israel did not even know at the time that it was happening. Balak paid a fortune, Balaam climbed three mountains, and out came blessing every time, while the people in the valley below slept through the whole thing.

Edomite and Egyptian. Then the surprises. The Edomite is a brother, and even the Egyptian may not be abhorred: the nation that enslaved them, drowned their sons and pursued them to the sea — and Israel is forbidden to hate them, with a reason that reads almost as a kindness toward Egypt: you were a sojourner in his land. Whatever else Egypt did, it fed them in a famine. God will not let the wrong be forgotten and he will not let it become hatred either, and the grandchildren of Egyptians may enter the assembly.

And the barred door does not stay barred. Ruth the Moabite becomes the great-grandmother of David. How, if Moabites were barred? Many Jewish and Christian readers have answered that the law shut out Moab the hostile nation, not the Moabite who took Israel’s God as her own (Ruth 1:16) and came to shelter under his wings (Ruth 2:12); faith brought her in. Isaiah promises the eunuch a monument and a name better than sons and daughters (Isa. 56:3–5).

Who is “born of a forbidden union” (v. 2)? Most likely a child of an incestuous or forbidden marriage, not simply one born outside marriage. Like the exclusion of eunuchs, it was ceremonial, and in Christ it is gone (Isa 56:3–5; Acts 8:27–39).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rules for an army in the field, down to burying human waste with a trowel — because God himself walks in the camp.
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness reaches into the latrine arrangements, not because God is fastidious but because he is present (v. 14).
verseByVerse.examples: A soldier carried a trowel among his weapons. The God who walks among his people is present in the most ordinary hours of the day, not only in the hour of worship.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you are encamped against your enemies, then you shall keep yourself from every evil thing. "If any man among you becomes unclean because of a nocturnal emission, then he shall go outside the camp. He shall not come inside the camp, but when evening comes, he shall bathe himself in water, and as the sun sets, he may come inside the camp. "You shall have a place outside the camp, and you shall go out to it. And you shall have a trowel with your tools, and when you sit down outside, you shall dig a hole with it and turn back and cover up your excrement. Because the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give up your enemies before you, therefore your camp must be holy, so that he may not see anything indecent among you and turn away from you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A trowel with your tools. Every soldier carries a trowel alongside his weapons. It is the most undignified verse in the Pentateuch and one of the most instructive, and everything depends on the reason attached.

God walks in the camp. That is the ground: not hygiene, not military discipline, but the presence of God. He walks about in that camp — the Hebrew verb is the one used of God walking in Eden in the cool of the day — he is not merely overhead, he is moving among the tents. And a camp with God walking through it cannot be arranged like a camp without him.

See what that does to the idea of holiness. We tend to file it under religion — worship, prayer, morality. This chapter files it under the latrine trench. There is no zone of ordinary life too undignified to be touched by the fact that God is present, and a man who thinks holiness begins at the sanctuary door has not read verse 13.

Paul makes the identical move for Christians, and grounds sexual purity in exactly the same fact: do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you? (1 Cor. 6:19). The camp has moved. God still walks in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–20 — The Runaway Slave and the Brother’s Loan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An escaped slave is not to be handed back but given refuge and allowed to settle wherever he chooses. And no interest may be charged on a loan to a fellow Israelite.
verseByVerse.theology: A nation God freed from slavery must be a refuge for the enslaved, and a people God provided for must not profit from a brother’s ruin.
verseByVerse.examples: A runaway arriving in Israel was told to choose a town and live there. The test of a Christian community is still what happens to the person who arrives with nothing and nothing to offer.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not give up to his master a slave who has escaped from his master to you. He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him. "None of the daughters of Israel shall be a cult prostitute, and none of the sons of Israel shall be a cult prostitute. You shall not bring the fee of a prostitute or the wages of a dog into the house of the LORD your God in payment for any vow, for both of these are an abomination to the LORD your God. "You shall not charge interest on loans to your brother, interest on money, interest on food, interest on anything that is lent for interest. You may charge a foreigner interest, but you may not charge your brother interest, that the LORD your God may bless you in all that you undertake in the land that you are entering to take possession of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An escaped slave. Set this law beside the rest of the ancient world and the contrast is total. The legal codes and treaties we know from the period, such as Hammurabi’s laws and Hittite treaties, required the return of fugitive slaves, and Hammurabi prescribed death for harbouring one. International treaties were signed specifically to guarantee extradition. It was one of the fixed points of ancient civilisation.

Israel, so far as we know alone, reverses it. (Most think the law has in view a slave fleeing into Israel from a foreign master.) The runaway is not returned. He is not detained, not registered, not assigned. He chooses where he lives — in the place that he shall choose… wherever it suits him — and it is a criminal matter to mistreat him.

Israel could hardly have been given a law more calculated to remind her what she was. A nation of escaped slaves is told to be, permanently, the country where escaped slaves are safe.

Interest from a brother. The distinction is between commerce and need. A foreigner borrowing in Israel was probably, as a rule, a merchant borrowing to trade, and interest on a commercial loan is ordinary business. A brother borrowing was a farmer who had lost a harvest, and to profit from that is to build your income on your neighbour’s disaster. God permits the first and forbids the second, and the line he draws is not between kinds of people but between kinds of transaction.

Cult prostitutes, male and female, probably served in Canaanite fertility worship; “dog” (v. 18) was most likely a term for the male prostitute. Money gained by sin cannot be offered to God.

Is charging interest sin? The law forbade interest on relief loans to a poor brother, and allowed it in trade with foreigners (v. 20). Jesus assumes interest on money with bankers (Matt 25:27). Ordinary lending is not sin; exploiting the needy is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–25 — Vows, and a Neighbour’s Field
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A vow is voluntary, but once made it binds and must not be delayed. And a hungry traveller may eat his fill from a neighbour’s vineyard or standing grain — but may put nothing in a basket or a sickle to it.
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody is required to vow; if you refrain from vowing, you will not be guilty of sin (v.22). God asks only that the promises we make be kept. And his law makes room for hunger without making room for greed.
verseByVerse.examples: The same line runs through every kind of generosity: the difference between meeting a need and exploiting an opening.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you make a vow to the LORD your God, you shall not delay fulfilling it, for the LORD your God will surely require it of you, and you will be guilty of sin. But if you refrain from vowing, you will not be guilty of sin. You shall be careful to do what has passed your lips, for you have voluntarily vowed to the LORD your God what you have promised with your mouth. "If you go into your neighbor's vineyard, you may eat your fill of grapes, as many as you wish, but you shall not put any in your bag. If you go into your neighbor's standing grain, you may pluck the ears with your hand, but you shall not put a sickle to your neighbor's standing grain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Vows. Nobody has to vow. There is no obligation, no expectation, no spiritual advantage in making one. The whole institution is voluntary from beginning to end — and the moment a man opens his mouth, it binds him absolutely, and God will require it.

That combination is the point. It is not the vow God is exacting about; it is the word. A promise freely made to God is not a gesture of enthusiasm to be revisited when the mood has passed. Ecclesiastes puts it bluntly: It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay (Eccl. 5:5). And the Lord Jesus, rather than tightening the law of vows, cut underneath it: Let what you say be simply “Yes” or “No” (Matt. 5:37) — because a man whose ordinary word is reliable has no need of the apparatus.

No basket, no sickle. A hungry traveller may eat as much as he wants, on the spot, from any field in Israel. He may not take a basket or a sickle. The line is between meeting a need and starting a harvest, and it is drawn with an exactness that makes it usable: the moment you reach for a tool, you are a thief.

That is the law the disciples were keeping when they walked through the grainfields on a Sabbath, plucking heads of grain and rubbing them in their hands (Luke 6:1). The Pharisees who objected were not accusing them of theft — Deuteronomy 23:25 made that impossible. They were accusing them of harvesting on the wrong day.

24.title: Laws Protecting the Vulnerable: Remember You Were a Slave
24.text: <sup>1</sup>"When a man takes a wife and marries her, if then she finds no favor in his eyes because he has found some indecency in her, and he writes her a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand and sends her out of his house, and she departs out of his house,<sup>2</sup>and if she goes and becomes another man's wife,<sup>3</sup>and the latter man hates her and writes her a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand and sends her out of his house, or if the latter man dies, who took her to be his wife,<sup>4</sup>then her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after she has been defiled, for that is an abomination before the LORD. And you shall not bring sin upon the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.<sup>5</sup>"When a man is newly married, he shall not go out with the army or be liable for any other public duty. He shall be free at home one year to be happy with his wife whom he has taken.<sup>6</sup>"No one shall take a mill or an upper millstone in pledge, for that would be taking a life in pledge.<sup>7</sup>"If a man is found stealing one of his brothers of the people of Israel, and if he treats him as a slave or sells him, then that thief shall die. So you shall purge the evil from your midst.<sup>8</sup>"Take care, in a case of leprous disease, to be very careful to do according to all that the Levitical priests shall direct you. As I commanded them, so you shall be careful to do.<sup>9</sup>Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam on the way as you came out of Egypt.<sup>10</sup>"When you make your neighbor a loan of any sort, you shall not go into his house to collect his pledge.<sup>11</sup>You shall stand outside, and the man to whom you make the loan shall bring the pledge out to you.<sup>12</sup>And if he is a poor man, you shall not sleep in his pledge.<sup>13</sup>You shall restore to him the pledge as the sun sets, that he may sleep in his cloak and bless you. And it shall be righteousness for you before the LORD your God.<sup>14</sup>"You shall not oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers or one of the sojourners who are in your land within your towns.<sup>15</sup>You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets (for he is poor and counts on it), lest he cry against you to the LORD, and you be guilty of sin.<sup>16</sup>"Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. Each one shall be put to death for his own sin.<sup>17</sup>"You shall not pervert the justice due to the sojourner or to the fatherless, or take a widow's garment in pledge,<sup>18</sup>but you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt and the LORD your God redeemed you from there; therefore I command you to do this.<sup>19</sup>"When you reap your harvest in your field and forget a sheaf in the field, you shall not go back to get it. It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands.<sup>20</sup>When you beat your olive trees, you shall not go over them again. It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow.<sup>21</sup>When you gather the grapes of your vineyard, you shall not strip it afterward. It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow.<sup>22</sup>You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt; therefore I command you to do this.
24.overview:
Chapter 24 is held together by one thread: the protection of the vulnerable and the remembrance of redemption. The refrain, “you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt” (24:18, 22), grounds every law of mercy in grace received. The God who remembered Israel in her slavery calls her to remember the vulnerable in her midst.

The chapter opens by regulating divorce, limiting it and protecting the woman. Then it guards the poor: a year at home for the newlywed, no millstone taken in pledge, the cloak returned at sunset, wages paid the same day, and the edges of the harvest left for the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow.
24.theology:
Compassion grounded in redemption. Every law of mercy here rests on “the LORD your God redeemed you” (24:18). Having been shown mercy in Christ, we leave generous margin for the poor.

God defends the defenseless. The poor man's cloak (24:13), the worker's wages (24:15), the gleaner's portion (24:19–21): God hears their cry (cf. James 5:4), and his people may never use legal rights to crush the weak.

Marriage and merciful accommodation. The divorce law limited the damage of hard hearts; God's design was always the lifelong union of Genesis 2:24, and the year for the newlywed (24:5) shows his delight in the joy of marriage, pointing to Christ, who heals hard hearts and restores marriage as a picture of his unbreakable covenant love.
24.examples: Redeemed from a slavery deeper than Egypt's, we deal justly and generously with the poor and the worker, looking to Christ, who became poor that we might become rich. Where we have been hard-hearted, he who kept these laws perfectly in our place forgives, and his Spirit makes us open-handed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man divorces his wife with a written certificate; she remarries; the second marriage ends. The one thing forbidden is that the first husband should take her back.
verseByVerse.theology: The law regulates a practice already happening rather than approving it, and puts two limits round it.
verseByVerse.examples: A husband or wife in a hard marriage should not read this passage as an exit sign: Jesus read it as evidence of hard hearts, and sent his hearers back to what God made marriage to be.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man takes a wife and marries her, if then she finds no favor in his eyes because he has found some indecency in her, and he writes her a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand and sends her out of his house, and she departs out of his house, and if she goes and becomes another man's wife, and the latter man hates her and writes her a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand and sends her out of his house, or if the latter man dies, who took her to be his wife, then her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after she has been defiled, for that is an abomination before the LORD. And you shall not bring sin upon the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the passage the Pharisees brought to Jesus. Look at the structure. Verses 1–3 are a long conditional clause — when a man does this and if she does that and if the second husband does the other. The command does not arrive until verse 4, and when it comes it is a single prohibition: then her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife.

So the law does not institute divorce, does not command it and does not approve it. It describes a practice already going on and legislates one thing about it: a woman may not be passed out and taken back like property.

And within the description there is a protection that is easily missed. The man in the case writes a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand. In the surrounding world a man could send his wife away with a sentence at the door and later deny it, leaving her unable to remarry and unable to return. A document in her hand made her status legally clear and her freedom provable. It is not much. It was more than anyone else gave her.

When they asked Jesus about this text, they framed it as a permission — why then did Moses command one to give a certificate of divorce and to send her away? — and he corrected the verb: Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so (Matt. 19:7–8). Not commanded; allowed. And he sent them back past Deuteronomy to Genesis 2, to what marriage was before anything went wrong.

If you are reading this from inside a marriage that has ended, hear what he heard in it. This chapter is not a loophole and it is not a verdict on you. It is God putting a fence round a wound he never wanted, in a world of hard hearts, to keep the damage from spreading further than it already had.

What is “some indecency”? In Jesus’ day Hillel’s school read it as anything displeasing, Shammai’s as a sexual or shameful fault. Jesus reads it on the narrow side: Moses permitted divorce because of your hardness of heart (Matt 19:8). The first husband may not take her back because the second marriage was real; the law kept marriage from being treated as a revolving door.

May a divorced person remarry? Some Christians hold that remarriage is never allowed while the first spouse lives. The Reformed confessions, such as the Westminster Confession (24.5–6), hold that adultery (Matt 19:9) and desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Cor 7:15) free the innocent party to remarry. That is the better reading, and this commentary holds it, while honouring brothers who hold the stricter view out of reverence for Christ’s words. Persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion: the abuser has abandoned the marriage in all but name. Anyone in danger should seek safety at once, without waiting for any ruling, and the elders of the church help judge each case. Divorce on other grounds is sin, but it is not beyond forgiveness, and those who have sinned here find mercy in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–13 — A Year at Home, and the Cloak Returned at Sunset
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A newly married man is exempt from war and public duty for a full year. A creditor may not enter a house to seize a pledge, and must return a poor man’s cloak before dark.
verseByVerse.theology: God cares for the joy of a young marriage and for the dignity of a debtor, and writes both into the nation’s law. A millstone may not be taken at all, for that would be taking a life in pledge.
verseByVerse.examples: A debtor kept his dignity at his own door and slept warm. The way a strong party collects from a weak one is still, in God’s reckoning, a spiritual matter.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man is newly married, he shall not go out with the army or be liable for any other public duty. He shall be free at home one year to be happy with his wife whom he has taken. "No one shall take a mill or an upper millstone in pledge, for that would be taking a life in pledge. "If a man is found stealing one of his brothers of the people of Israel, and if he treats him as a slave or sells him, then that thief shall die. So you shall purge the evil from your midst. "Take care, in a case of leprous disease, to be very careful to do according to all that the Levitical priests shall direct you. As I commanded them, so you shall be careful to do. Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam on the way as you came out of Egypt. "When you make your neighbor a loan of any sort, you shall not go into his house to collect his pledge. You shall stand outside, and the man to whom you make the loan shall bring the pledge out to you. And if he is a poor man, you shall not sleep in his pledge. You shall restore to him the pledge as the sun sets, that he may sleep in his cloak and bless you. And it shall be righteousness for you before the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A year at home. No war, no civic office, no committee. God writes into the national law of Israel that a young husband is to stay home for twelve months, and the stated purpose is not household management or childbearing but that he should be happy with his wife.

There is little like it in ancient legislation, and there is a rebuke in it for every culture that treats a young marriage as something to be fitted around a career. The state has no claim on that first year. God says so.

Then three laws about lending, and each of them guards a poor man’s dignity as carefully as his property.

The millstone. The handmill was how a family made its daily bread. Taking it as security is not debt collection; it is starvation with paperwork, and God calls it what it is.

Stand outside. The creditor waits at the door. He does not walk through a poor man’s home choosing what to take, and the debtor brings out what he can spare. A man who owes money has not forfeited the privacy of his house.

The cloak at sunset. The outer cloak was a labourer’s blanket. So the security is handed over each morning and given back each evening, every day, for as long as the debt runs — which makes it almost useless as security and entirely effective as a daily reminder of who this man is.

Righteousness for you. Handing a coat back at sunset is called righteousness. God does not reserve that word for the sanctuary.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprous disease” covers several skin diseases (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The poor labourer must be paid the same day. Justice may not be perverted for the sojourner or the fatherless, and a widow’s garment may not be taken in pledge.
verseByVerse.theology: God makes the worker’s need, not the employer’s convenience, the measure of when wages are due.
verseByVerse.examples: The delayed invoice, the withheld payment and the squeezed subcontractor are all in this verse, and God hears the same cry.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers or one of the sojourners who are in your land within your towns. You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets (for he is poor and counts on it), lest he cry against you to the LORD, and you be guilty of sin. "Fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. Each one shall be put to death for his own sin. "You shall not pervert the justice due to the sojourner or to the fatherless, or take a widow's garment in pledge, but you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt and the LORD your God redeemed you from there; therefore I command you to do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He counts on it. The reason God gives is not a principle but a picture, and it is what a day-labourer’s life was. No savings, no contract, no reserve: he worked, he was paid at sunset, and his family ate that night. A day’s delay in payment is not an administrative matter to such a man; it is a hungry evening, and the employer who delays may not even notice he has caused one.

Brother or sojourner. The foreign labourer gets the identical protection, which in most economies then and since is precisely where the corner is cut.

Lest he cry against you. The worker has no recourse. He cannot sue, cannot organise, cannot afford to lose the work. So he prays — and God says that prayer reaches him and the employer is guilty.

James takes this verse and makes it terrifying: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts (Jas. 5:4). Now it is not merely the man crying. The wages cry.

Remember you were a slave. Verse 18 gives the ground of the whole paragraph, as it does throughout this book. Israel is to treat her workers as God treated her when she was the labour force.

Does this contradict “visiting the iniquity of the fathers” (Exod. 20:5) or Achan’s family (Josh 7)? Human courts may punish only the guilty, and Amaziah obeyed this law (2 Kgs 14:6). Exodus speaks of God’s providence, as children suffer the consequences of their parents’ sin and repeat it; Achan’s case was God’s own judgment.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The forgotten sheaf stays where it fell; the olive trees are not gone over twice; the vineyard is not stripped. What is left belongs to the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow.
verseByVerse.theology: The margin is not charity administered by the owner but a standing right of the poor, gathered by their own work with their own hands, and its ground is Israel's own slavery (v. 22).
verseByVerse.examples: The question these verses put to any Christian is not what he gives away but whether his margins are set to catch anybody at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you reap your harvest in your field and forget a sheaf in the field, you shall not go back to get it. It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands. When you beat your olive trees, you shall not go over them again. It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow. When you gather the grapes of your vineyard, you shall not strip it afterward. It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt; therefore I command you to do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three provisions, and they all work the same way. The forgotten sheaf stays where it fell. The olive trees are beaten once and not gone over again. The vineyard is picked and not stripped.

Israel is commanded to farm inefficiently. Every instinct of a working farmer — go back for it, shake the branch again, get the last cluster — is overruled, and what is left is not the owner’s to give. It already belongs to somebody else.

That is the genius of the arrangement, and it should be seen clearly. This is not charity. A widow did not queue at a landowner’s door, or explain her situation, or be assessed, or thank anybody. She walked into the field and worked, with her own hands, and took home what she gathered — and she owed nobody anything for it. The system provided food without requiring humiliation, which is more than most welfare has ever managed.

And it is the law under which the loveliest book in the Old Testament happens. A Moabite widow with nothing goes out to glean in a field that turns out to belong to Boaz, and he tells his young men to pull out extra stalks and leave them for her (Ruth 2:16) — a man going beyond the margin the law required, which is exactly what the law was training him to want to do.

Therefore I command you. The reason is the one already given in verse 18. Not because the poor deserve it, and not because generosity is admirable. Because these people were once the ones with nothing, and somebody came and got them.

A Christian reads that sentence with a larger Exodus behind it. We were the ones with nothing, and the Lord Jesus, though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). Many Christians have also seen in Boaz, who went beyond the margin and then redeemed the widow gleaning in his field, a picture of that greater Redeemer from his own line.

25.title: Levirate Marriage and Honest Weights: Justice in the Details
25.text: <sup>1</sup>"If there is a dispute between men and they come into court and the judges decide between them, acquitting the innocent and condemning the guilty,<sup>2</sup>then if the guilty man deserves to be beaten, the judge shall cause him to lie down and be beaten in his presence with a number of stripes in proportion to his offense.<sup>3</sup>Forty stripes may be given him, but not more, lest, if one should go on to beat him with more stripes than these, your brother be degraded in your sight.<sup>4</sup>"You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain.<sup>5</sup>"If brothers dwell together, and one of them dies and has no son, the wife of the dead man shall not be married outside the family to a stranger. Her husband's brother shall go in to her and take her as his wife and perform the duty of a husband's brother to her.<sup>6</sup>And the first son whom she bears shall succeed to the name of his dead brother, that his name may not be blotted out of Israel.<sup>7</sup>And if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife, then his brother's wife shall go up to the gate to the elders and say, 'My husband's brother refuses to perpetuate his brother's name in Israel; he will not perform the duty of a husband's brother to me.'<sup>8</sup>Then the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him, and if he persists, saying, 'I do not wish to take her,'<sup>9</sup>then his brother's wife shall go up to him in the presence of the elders and pull his sandal off his foot and spit in his face. And she shall answer and say, 'So shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother's house.'<sup>10</sup>And the name of his house shall be called in Israel, 'The house of him who had his sandal pulled off.'<sup>11</sup>"When men fight with one another and the wife of the one draws near to rescue her husband from the hand of him who is beating him and puts out her hand and seizes him by the private parts,<sup>12</sup>then you shall cut off her hand. Your eye shall have no pity.<sup>13</sup>"You shall not have in your bag two kinds of weights, a large and a small.<sup>14</sup>You shall not have in your house two kinds of measures, a large and a small.<sup>15</sup>A full and fair weight you shall have, a full and fair measure you shall have, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>16</sup>For all who do such things, all who act dishonestly, are an abomination to the LORD your God.<sup>17</sup>"Remember what Amalek did to you on the way as you came out of Egypt,<sup>18</sup>how he attacked you on the way when you were faint and weary, and cut off your tail, those who were lagging behind you, and he did not fear God.<sup>19</sup>Therefore when the LORD your God has given you rest from all your enemies around you, in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance to possess, you shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven; you shall not forget.
25.overview: Chapter 25 brings the body of covenant law toward its close with laws on justice in the practical details of life: a limit on judicial beating so that the guilty man remains “your brother,” the ox not muzzled as it treads, levirate marriage to preserve a dead brother's name (the background of Ruth and Boaz, in the line of Christ), honest weights and measures, and the command to remember Amalek, who preyed on the weak.
25.theology:
Integrity in the marketplace. “All who act dishonestly are an abomination to the LORD” (25:16); the rigged scale stands in the same category as idolatry (cf. Prov 11:1). Redeemed by a Kinsman who paid in full, the believer is called to scrupulous honesty in every transaction.

The dignity of persons and the worker. Even the guilty are not to be degraded (25:3), and the working ox eats (25:4), which Paul applies to gospel laborers (1 Cor. 9:9).

The kinsman-redeemer. Levirate marriage preserved a dead brother's name and protected his widow (25:5–10), and something like it is at work in Ruth and Boaz. It points to Jesus, our great Redeemer, who gives us his name and secures our inheritance forever.
25.examples: We pursue honesty in all our dealings, support those who labor for the gospel, rejoice in Christ our kinsman-Redeemer, and trust the God who remembers every wrong done to the weak.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Forty Stripes, and the Ox That Treads
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A guilty man may be beaten in proportion to his offence and never more than forty strokes, lest he be degraded. And the ox treading out grain is not to be muzzled.
verseByVerse.theology: Both laws protect the party who cannot protect himself: the cap on strokes keeps a criminal under sentence your brother, and the muzzle law lets even a working animal eat from what it is producing.
verseByVerse.examples: The sentence stopped short of stripping a man of his humanity, and the ox ate as it worked. It is still fair to ask whether the people who do the work in our churches and businesses are allowed to eat from what they produce.

verseByVerse.quote: "If there is a dispute between men and they come into court and the judges decide between them, acquitting the innocent and condemning the guilty, then if the guilty man deserves to be beaten, the judge shall cause him to lie down and be beaten in his presence with a number of stripes in proportion to his offense. Forty stripes may be given him, but not more, lest, if one should go on to beat him with more stripes than these, your brother be degraded in your sight. "You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forty stripes. The first law is a cap on judicial flogging: in proportion to the offence, and never more than forty.

Your brother. The man is guilty, sentenced and being punished, and God still calls him that. The limit exists so that a legal penalty does not turn into the destruction of a human being, and so that the watching community never comes to see him as something less than one of them.

The Jews later reduced it to thirty-nine, counting carefully in case of a miscount — which is why Paul says, Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one (2 Cor. 11:24). He knew this law from the wrong end of it.

The ox that treads. The ox walks in circles over the threshing floor all day, and the grain is under its feet. Muzzling it costs the farmer nothing and gains him a little; the law forbids it. The animal that does the work may eat from the work.

Paul quotes that verse twice, and both times about paying people. Arguing for the support of those who preach, he cites it and asks: Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does he not certainly speak for our sake? (1 Cor. 9:9–10). And again, on elders: “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain,” and, “The laborer deserves his wages” (1 Tim. 5:18) — where he sets this verse alongside a saying of Jesus and calls both of them Scripture.
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish law had the man assessed first, so that he received only as many strokes as he could bear (Mishnah, Makkot 3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–10 — Levirate Marriage, and the Sandal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A widow left without a son is to be married by her late husband’s brother, and their first son carries the dead man’s name. A brother who refuses is publicly shamed — his sandal pulled off and spat before, his house renamed.
verseByVerse.theology: The provision keeps a widow inside a family rather than destitute outside it, and keeps a dead man’s name in Israel. The refusal is not criminal, only shameful; the law will not compel a marriage, and so it shames instead.
verseByVerse.examples: Taking up a duty that costs us and earns no credit is rare. Christ is the Kinsman who did not decline: he had to be made like his brothers in every respect (Heb. 2:17).

verseByVerse.quote: "If brothers dwell together, and one of them dies and has no son, the wife of the dead man shall not be married outside the family to a stranger. Her husband's brother shall go in to her and take her as his wife and perform the duty of a husband's brother to her. And the first son whom she bears shall succeed to the name of his dead brother, that his name may not be blotted out of Israel. And if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife, then his brother's wife shall go up to the gate to the elders and say, 'My husband's brother refuses to perpetuate his brother's name in Israel; he will not perform the duty of a husband's brother to me.' Then the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him, and if he persists, saying, 'I do not wish to take her,' then his brother's wife shall go up to him in the presence of the elders and pull his sandal off his foot and spit in his face. And she shall answer and say, 'So shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother's house.' And the name of his house shall be called in Israel, 'The house of him who had his sandal pulled off.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man dies childless. Under the law of levirate marriage — from the Latin levir, brother-in-law — his brother is to marry the widow, and their first son shall succeed to the name of his dead brother, that his name may not be blotted out of Israel.

Two people are being protected. The widow, who in that society had no income, no inheritance and no standing without a husband or a son, and who would otherwise leave the family with nothing. And the dead man, whose name and portion in Israel would simply disappear.

It is a costly duty. The brother takes on a wife and raises a son who will not count as his own and who will inherit the dead man’s land rather than his. The law is asking him to spend part of his life and his estate on somebody who cannot thank him.

And if he refuses, the law does not compel him. It shames him. The widow brings him to the elders at the gate and says My husband’s brother refuses to perpetuate his brother’s name in Israel; and then she pulls his sandal off his foot and spits in his face, and his household is known ever afterwards as The house of him who had his sandal pulled off.

The sandal is not incidental. Putting a foot on land was how possession was claimed, and taking a man’s sandal off publicly declared that he had walked away from a claim he should have taken up.

All of which is the background to Ruth 4, where a nearer kinsman is offered Naomi’s field, and takes it — until he hears that Ruth comes with it. I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance, he says, and takes off his sandal (Ruth 4:6–8). And Boaz, who has more to lose and less to gain, steps forward. The love story of Ruth turns on Deuteronomy 25, and behind it stands the Kinsman-Redeemer who did not calculate what it would do to his own inheritance.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A brief law on proportion in a fight, and then the demand for honest weights and measures: no large stone and small stone in the same bag, no big measure and little measure in the same house.
verseByVerse.theology: God cares about the scales on a market stall as much as about the altar in the sanctuary: fraud is theft dressed as trade.
verseByVerse.examples: Whoever handles other people’s money, in a shop, an office or a church treasury, is handling something God watches closely.

verseByVerse.quote: "When men fight with one another and the wife of the one draws near to rescue her husband from the hand of him who is beating him and puts out her hand and seizes him by the private parts, then you shall cut off her hand. Your eye shall have no pity. "You shall not have in your bag two kinds of weights, a large and a small. You shall not have in your house two kinds of measures, a large and a small. A full and fair weight you shall have, a full and fair measure you shall have, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you. For all who do such things, all who act dishonestly, are an abomination to the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a brief and startling law about a woman who intervenes in a fight by seizing a man’s genitals — a case about proportion and about protecting a man’s capacity to father children — the chapter reaches its ethical centre.

Two kinds of weights. In the ancient world commerce ran on stone weights carried in a pouch and measuring vessels kept at home. A dishonest trader had two sets: the heavy stone for buying, so that he received more than he paid for, and the light one for selling, so that he gave less than he charged for. Nobody could tell. The customer had no scales of his own.

And the theft is invisible, small each time, and falls hardest on the people least able to notice — the poor buying in small quantities, who cannot afford to check and would not be believed if they complained.

God calls it an abomination. That word is used in Deuteronomy for idolatry, the occult, and child sacrifice. A rigged set of scales is put in the same category, because to practise fraud on people who trust you is not a lesser sin because it is quiet.

Proverbs returns to it repeatedly — A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight (Prov. 11:1) — and the modern equivalents need no imagination. The fee that is not explained, the estimate written to be exceeded, the contract clause the other party will not understand. Two weights in one bag, and nobody will ever check. Where we have used them, the way back is the one Zacchaeus took, confession and restitution, and it ends at the table of Christ, who came for him first (Luke 19:5–9).

Why “cut off her hand”? It is the only mutilation in the law, and the injury it punished threatened the man’s ability to have children, which the law guarded carefully (cf. vv. 5–10). It belonged to Israel’s civil law and does not apply today. Some read it as a lesser shaving or shaming rather than amputation.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is to remember what Amalek did on the way out of Egypt — attacking the faint and weary and cutting off the stragglers at the back — and, once God gives rest, to blot out the memory of Amalek.
verseByVerse.theology: Amalek attacked the people least able to defend themselves, and he did not fear God. This is judgment on a particular nation for a particular cruelty, delayed until Israel has rest: God settling an account the victims could not.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who was hurt when they were weakest, and has never seen justice done, may take this passage to heart: God keeps such accounts open, and he does not forget.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember what Amalek did to you on the way as you came out of Egypt, how he attacked you on the way when you were faint and weary, and cut off your tail, those who were lagging behind you, and he did not fear God. Therefore when the LORD your God has given you rest from all your enemies around you, in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance to possess, you shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven; you shall not forget.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faint and weary. Picture the column. A nation of former slaves walking out of Egypt — women, children, old people, animals — strung out over miles, and at the back the ones who cannot keep up: the sick, the elderly, the mothers with small children. That is where Amalek attacked. Not the front, where the fighting men were. The tail.

They were not defending territory or resisting an invasion. They picked off the weakest people in a refugee column because it was easy, and the text adds the diagnosis in five words: he did not fear God. Cruelty toward the defenceless is, in Scripture, the surest sign that a man believes nobody is watching.

Blot out the memory. The sentence is deferred. Not now; later, when Israel is safe. God is in no hurry, and centuries pass before Saul is sent to carry it out (1 Sam. 15).

Here is what that provision says about God. The people at the back of that column had nobody. They could not fight, could not report it, and most of them died without anyone learning their names. God saw it, wrote it into the law of the nation, and kept the account open for generations. No cruelty done to the weak is ever finally unrecorded, however unwitnessed it was, and the God who notices the ox on the threshing floor and the widow at the gate has never once looked away from the back of the column.

Did God really command the destruction of a whole people? When the sentence came, it included everyone (1 Sam. 15:3), and that is among the hardest things in the Old Testament. Three things can be said honestly. It was a judgment by the Judge of all the earth on a people who kept up this cruelty for generations (1 Sam. 15:33), not a licence for ethnic hatred: the same law forbids Israel to abhor the Egyptian (23:7). It was a single command for one moment in Israel’s history; no nation or Christian may take it up, and Christ commands his people to love their enemies (Matt. 5:44). And it looks ahead to the last judgment, when God himself will deal with every unrepented cruelty, and the Judge will be the One who bore judgment for his enemies (Acts 17:31). Questions remain, especially about the children, and we leave them with the God who will do what is just (Gen. 18:25).

26.title: Firstfruits and Covenant Affirmation: You Are His Treasured Possession
26.text: <sup>1</sup>"When you come into the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance and have taken possession of it and live in it,<sup>2</sup>you shall take some of the first of all the fruit of the ground, which you harvest from your land that the LORD your God is giving you, and you shall put it in a basket, and you shall go to the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name to dwell there.<sup>3</sup>And you shall go to the priest who is in office at that time and say to him, 'I declare today to the LORD your God that I have come into the land that the LORD swore to our fathers to give us.'<sup>4</sup>Then the priest shall take the basket from your hand and set it down before the altar of the LORD your God.<sup>5</sup>"And you shall make response before the LORD your God, 'A wandering Aramean was my father. And he went down into Egypt and sojourned there, few in number, and there he became a nation, great, mighty, and populous.<sup>6</sup>And the Egyptians treated us harshly and humiliated us and laid on us hard labor.<sup>7</sup>Then we cried to the LORD, the God of our fathers, and the LORD heard our voice and saw our affliction, our toil, and our oppression.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, with great deeds of terror, with signs and wonders.<sup>9</sup>And he brought us into this place and gave us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>10</sup>And behold, now I bring the first of the fruit of the ground, which you, O LORD, have given me.' And you shall set it down before the LORD your God and worship before the LORD your God.<sup>11</sup>And you shall rejoice in all the good that the LORD your God has given to you and to your house, you, and the Levite, and the sojourner who is among you.<sup>12</sup>"When you have finished paying all the tithe of your produce in the third year, which is the year of tithing, giving it to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, so that they may eat within your towns and be filled,<sup>13</sup>then you shall say before the LORD your God, 'I have removed the sacred portion out of my house, and moreover, I have given it to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, according to all your commandment that you have commanded me. I have not transgressed any of your commandments, nor have I forgotten them.<sup>14</sup>I have not eaten of the tithe while I was mourning, or removed any of it while I was unclean, or offered any of it to the dead. I have obeyed the voice of the LORD my God. I have done according to all that you have commanded me.<sup>15</sup>Look down from your holy habitation, from heaven, and bless your people Israel and the ground that you have given us, as you swore to our fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey.'<sup>16</sup>"This day the LORD your God commands you to do these statutes and rules. You shall therefore be careful to do them with all your heart and with all your soul.<sup>17</sup>You have declared today that the LORD is your God, and that you will walk in his ways, and keep his statutes and his commandments and his rules, and will obey his voice.<sup>18</sup>And the LORD has declared today that you are a people for his treasured possession, as he has promised you, and that you are to keep all his commandments,<sup>19</sup>and that he will set you in praise and in fame and in honor high above all nations that he has made, and that you shall be a people holy to the LORD your God, as he promised."
26.overview:
Chapter 26 brings the body of covenant law (chs. 12–26) to its climax with two liturgies, the offering of firstfruits and the declaration of the third-year tithe, and a solemn affirmation of the covenant bond.

As the Israelite brings the first of his harvest, he recites the story of his redemption: “A wandering Aramean was my father” (26:5). The tithe liturgy confirms his care for the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow. And the chapter closes with mutual belonging: Israel declares that the LORD is her God, and the LORD declares Israel his treasured possession. God is theirs, and they are his, a bond fulfilled in Christ, in whom we become God's own people forever.
26.theology:
Worship rooted in redemption. As the offering is presented, the worshiper recites the story of grace (26:5–9). True worship rehearses God's saving acts and makes them personal; the gift in the hand and the gospel on the lips belong together.

Worship inseparable from compassion. The worshiper declares before God that he has cared for the Levite, sojourner, fatherless and widow (26:12–13); worship is hollow without it (James 1:27).

Mutual belonging. Israel declares the LORD her God, and the LORD declares her his “treasured possession” (26:17–18). The covenant is a bond of love, and in Christ every believer belongs to “a people for his own possession” (1 Pet. 2:9).
26.examples: We give God our first and best in gratitude, rehearsing our own redemption: enslaved, we cried out, and Christ delivered us. Our worship overflows in care for the poor, and we rest in the deepest joy of the redeemed: in Christ, God says over us, “You are mine.”
