verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Basket at the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first Israelite to bring in a harvest from his own land takes some of it in a basket to the sanctuary, hands it to the priest, and makes a declaration.
verseByVerse.theology: The offering is small and the words are everything. A man standing in a field his great-grandfather was promised says out loud that God has kept his word, and the fruit in the basket is the evidence.
verseByVerse.examples: The first harvest of a lifetime went to God before any of it was eaten. Christian giving keeps the same shape: the first and best, brought before the rest is enjoyed, with words attached that say why.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you come into the land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance and have taken possession of it and live in it, you shall take some of the first of all the fruit of the ground, which you harvest from your land that the LORD your God is giving you, and you shall put it in a basket, and you shall go to the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name to dwell there. And you shall go to the priest who is in office at that time and say to him, 'I declare today to the LORD your God that I have come into the land that the LORD swore to our fathers to give us.' Then the priest shall take the basket from your hand and set it down before the altar of the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Picture the man this law is written for. He is the first in his family for centuries to harvest a crop from ground that belongs to him. His father may have been born in a tent in the wilderness. His grandfather was a slave.

Some of the first. This is not the tithe, which comes later in the chapter, but simply some of the first of the harvest, in a basket, carried by hand, before anything is eaten or stored or sold.

I declare today. The one sentence he says to the priest is a verdict on God. Not "I have worked hard," not even "thank you" — but: "you said you would do this, and here is the fruit of it in my hands." Somewhere behind him stands a childless old man being told to count the stars, and this basket of figs is the receipt.

And the order matters. The words come before the worship and the basket is set down before the altar, not on it. This is not payment. It is testimony with something in a bag to prove it.

Do firstfruits apply to Christians? The law ended with the sanctuary and the land, but the principle remains: give to God first and gratefully, not from what is left over (Prov 3:9; 1 Cor 16:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — A Wandering Aramean Was My Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The worshipper recites the whole story of redemption — a wandering ancestor, slavery in Egypt, a cry, a rescue, a land — and only then sets down his basket and worships.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel’s confession of faith is a story of rescue, and it ends in joy shared with the Levite and the sojourner, who have no harvest of their own.
verseByVerse.examples: Asked why he had come with a basket, a farmer told the story of the exodus. A Christian has the same kind of answer and no other: not our standards or our tradition, but that we were slaves and somebody came for us.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you shall make response before the LORD your God, 'A wandering Aramean was my father. And he went down into Egypt and sojourned there, few in number, and there he became a nation, great, mighty, and populous. And the Egyptians treated us harshly and humiliated us and laid on us hard labor. Then we cried to the LORD, the God of our fathers, and the LORD heard our voice and saw our affliction, our toil, and our oppression. And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, with great deeds of terror, with signs and wonders. And he brought us into this place and gave us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey. And behold, now I bring the first of the fruit of the ground, which you, O LORD, have given me.' And you shall set it down before the LORD your God and worship before the LORD your God. And you shall rejoice in all the good that the LORD your God has given to you and to your house, you, and the Levite, and the sojourner who is among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wandering Aramean. This confession, counted among the oldest creeds in the Bible, begins at the bottom. Not "my father was a patriarch" — a wandering Aramean, a landless nomad from Syria with no country and no standing. Israel’s national confession opens by admitting that her origins were nothing worth boasting about.

Then watch the pronouns move, because it is the most important thing in the passage. It starts with my father and he went down — third person, history, somebody else. And then, without warning: And the Egyptians treated us harshly and humiliated us… Then we cried to the LORD… and the LORD brought us out of Egypt.

The man saying this was not in Egypt. Neither was his father. He is standing in a vineyard centuries later with a basket of grapes — and he says us, and we cried, and he brought us out. Every Israelite was taught to place himself inside a rescue that happened long before he existed, and to speak of it in the first person.

That is exactly what a Christian does at the Lord’s Table. Not "he died for people" — who loved me and gave himself for me (Gal. 2:20). The events are historical and the pronoun is personal, and a faith that cannot make that move has not yet become anybody’s.

And see the shape of the confession: a wanderer, a descent into slavery, a cry, a hearing, a rescue, a land. There is no doctrine stated and no proposition defended. It is a story, told in six verses, and it was the answer every Israelite child was given when he asked why his family lived the way it did.

Which you have given me. Then, at last, the basket. Even the harvest he grew himself is described as a gift. And the scene ends where Deuteronomy always ends, in rejoicing shared with the Levite and the sojourner. The man with no land is at the table.
verseByVerse.note: The “wandering Aramean” is most likely Jacob, whose mother and wives came from Aram.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having given the third-year tithe to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow, the worshipper states before God that he has done it and has kept nothing back.
verseByVerse.theology: Giving to the poor is a sacred trust, not an optional kindness. The declaration is not a claim to sinlessness but a redeemed man's honest account, and it ends not in self-congratulation but in a request for blessing.
verseByVerse.examples: The account is still asked for, and vague good intentions will not survive the question. Where honesty shows a shortfall, Christ's faithfulness covers it and the way back is open.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you have finished paying all the tithe of your produce in the third year, which is the year of tithing, giving it to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, so that they may eat within your towns and be filled, then you shall say before the LORD your God, 'I have removed the sacred portion out of my house, and moreover, I have given it to the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, according to all your commandment that you have commanded me. I have not transgressed any of your commandments, nor have I forgotten them. I have not eaten of the tithe while I was mourning, or removed any of it while I was unclean, or offered any of it to the dead. I have obeyed the voice of the LORD my God. I have done according to all that you have commanded me. Look down from your holy habitation, from heaven, and bless your people Israel and the ground that you have given us, as you swore to our fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second liturgy concerns the third-year tithe, which stayed in the local towns for the Levite, the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow — and the worshipper must now stand before God and say whether he has actually done it.

Read what that declaration assumes. That God will ask. That the money reaching the widow in your town is a matter he takes an account of. And that a man ought to be able to state plainly whether it happened, rather than offering a general impression of himself as a generous person.

There is a searching quality in having to say it out loud at a sanctuary. Most of us can maintain a comfortable vagueness about what we actually give and to whom. This liturgy makes it specific, spoken, and addressed to God — and the four categories are named, so the man knows exactly which faces he is being asked about.

Look down from heaven. The ending is not what a modern reader expects after a recitation of good conduct. He does not ask for a reward. He asks for a blessing on the nation.

The man who has just given away a tenth of his income to people who cannot repay him ends by asking God to bless everybody else.

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and they belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Cor 16:2; 2 Cor 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and it calls churches to support those who teach them (Gal 6:6; 1 Cor 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.

Verse 14, offered any of it to the dead, refers to pagan rites of feeding the dead, which had no place in what was holy to the LORD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law closes with a mutual affirmation. Israel declares that the LORD is her God and that she will walk in his ways; and the LORD declares that Israel is his treasured possession.
verseByVerse.theology: The declaring in vv. 17–18 is mutual and formal, as at a wedding, and God’s half is the larger one.
verseByVerse.examples: The same exchange stands at the centre of the Christian faith: I will be their God, and they shall be my people (Heb. 8:10).

verseByVerse.quote: "This day the LORD your God commands you to do these statutes and rules. You shall therefore be careful to do them with all your heart and with all your soul. You have declared today that the LORD is your God, and that you will walk in his ways, and keep his statutes and his commandments and his rules, and will obey his voice. And the LORD has declared today that you are a people for his treasured possession, as he has promised you, and that you are to keep all his commandments, and that he will set you in praise and in fame and in honor high above all nations that he has made, and that you shall be a people holy to the LORD your God, as he promised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have declared today. The law ends as a wedding does: a formal, public, mutual declaring, and both parties are on the record.

Everything since chapter 12 has been building to this exchange. The whole body of the law — the sanctuary, the feasts, the courts, the king, the gleaning, the weights — turns out to be the terms of a relationship, and the terms are now being said aloud by both sides.

Treasured possession. Israel’s half is to walk in his ways. God’s half is larger: his segullah, the private hoard a king keeps apart from the state treasury.

God commits to something Israel cannot deliver. Her half is obedience, which she will fail at within a generation. His half is glory, and it does not depend on her.

Which is why this passage does not stay in Deuteronomy. The prophets take the same mutual formula and promise it again on the far side of the failure — I will be their God, and they shall be my people (Jer. 31:33) — and Hebrews quotes it of the new covenant, and the last chapter of the Bible says it once more with nothing left to go wrong: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man… they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God (Rev. 21:3).

And Paul says how the treasured possession was secured: Christ gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession (Titus 2:14). It was bought.

The law of Moses ends with two parties declaring what they are to each other. One of them kept his word.

27.title: The Covenant at Shechem and the Curses
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Moses and the elders of Israel commanded the people, saying, "Keep the whole commandment that I command you today.<sup>2</sup>And on the day you cross over the Jordan to the land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall set up large stones and plaster them with plaster.<sup>3</sup>And you shall write on them all the words of this law, when you cross over to enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you, a land flowing with milk and honey, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you.<sup>4</sup>And when you have crossed over the Jordan, you shall set up these stones, concerning which I command you today, on Mount Ebal, and you shall plaster them with plaster.<sup>5</sup>And there you shall build an altar to the LORD your God, an altar of stones. You shall wield no iron tool on them;<sup>6</sup>you shall build an altar to the LORD your God of uncut stones. And you shall offer burnt offerings on it to the LORD your God,<sup>7</sup>and you shall sacrifice peace offerings and shall eat there, and you shall rejoice before the LORD your God.<sup>8</sup>And you shall write on the stones all the words of this law very plainly."<sup>9</sup>Then Moses and the Levitical priests said to all Israel, "Keep silence and hear, O Israel: this day you have become the people of the LORD your God.<sup>10</sup>You shall therefore obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping his commandments and his statutes, which I command you today."<sup>11</sup>That day Moses charged the people, saying,<sup>12</sup>"When you have crossed over the Jordan, these shall stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin.<sup>13</sup>And these shall stand on Mount Ebal for the curse: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali.<sup>14</sup>And the Levites shall declare to all the men of Israel in a loud voice:<sup>15</sup>"'Cursed be the man who makes a carved or cast metal image, an abomination to the LORD, a thing made by the hands of a craftsman, and sets it up in secret.' And all the people shall answer and say, 'Amen.'<sup>16</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who dishonors his father or his mother.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>17</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who moves his neighbor's landmark.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>18</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who misleads a blind man on the road.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>19</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who perverts the justice due to the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>20</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who lies with his father's wife, because he has uncovered his father's nakedness.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>21</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who lies with any kind of animal.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>22</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who lies with his sister, whether the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>23</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who lies with his mother-in-law.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>24</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who strikes down his neighbor in secret.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>25</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who takes a bribe to shed innocent blood.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'<sup>26</sup>"'Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'
27.overview:
Chapter 27 turns from the giving of the law to its ratification. Once Israel enters the land, the law is to be written on plastered stones, an altar built on Mount Ebal, and the tribes set on Gerizim and Ebal. The Levites proclaim curses on specific violations, most of them sins done in secret, and to each the whole nation answers “Amen.”

The last curse covers the whole law (27:26). Here the law shuts every mouth and drives us to Christ, who bore the curse pronounced from Ebal for us on the tree. The mountain of cursing points to Calvary, where the curse was exhausted and the blessing secured.
27.theology:
The curse of the law drives us to Christ. The law demands a whole obedience no sinner can render (27:26), and so it cannot justify; Christ redeemed us from its curse by becoming a curse for us (Gal. 3:10, 13).

The altar at the mountain of cursing. The altar of uncut stones stands on Ebal, the mountain of curse (27:5–7). Where the curse falls, there the sacrifice stands, because at the cross the curse and the sacrifice met in the body of Christ.

Identity precedes obedience. “This day you have become the people of the LORD your God. You shall therefore obey” (27:9–10). Israel obeys because she is God's people, not to become them, and the believer's obedience is the joyful working out of an identity freely given by grace.
27.examples: The curse of verse 26 drives us out of self-righteousness into the arms of Christ, who bore in our place the curse we earned by failing to keep the whole law, so that the blessing of Abraham flows to all who believe. We obey not to become God's people, but because, in Christ, we already are, and his Spirit now works that obedience in us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Law on Stones, and an Altar of Uncut Stone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On crossing the Jordan Israel is to set up large plastered stones and write the law on them very plainly, and to build an altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal — and there to offer sacrifices, eat, and rejoice.
verseByVerse.theology: Beside the written law God sets an altar, and beside the altar a meal and rejoicing.
verseByVerse.examples: The same two things still stand together, in the same order: the law that shows us what we are, and beside it a sacrifice we did not shape.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses and the elders of Israel commanded the people, saying, "Keep the whole commandment that I command you today. And on the day you cross over the Jordan to the land that the LORD your God is giving you, you shall set up large stones and plaster them with plaster. And you shall write on them all the words of this law, when you cross over to enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you, a land flowing with milk and honey, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you. And when you have crossed over the Jordan, you shall set up these stones, concerning which I command you today, on Mount Ebal, and you shall plaster them with plaster. And there you shall build an altar to the LORD your God, an altar of stones. You shall wield no iron tool on them; you shall build an altar to the LORD your God of uncut stones. And you shall offer burnt offerings on it to the LORD your God, and you shall sacrifice peace offerings and shall eat there, and you shall rejoice before the LORD your God. And you shall write on the stones all the words of this law very plainly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Large plastered stones. Two structures are to be built on Mount Ebal, and they belong together. Plastered stone takes writing well and can be read at a distance. The law is to be published, put up in the open, where anybody walking past can read the terms of the covenant for himself.

No iron tool. Field stones, taken as they were found, with no chisel work and no dressing. And the reason is given in Exodus: if you wield your tool on it you profane it (Exod. 20:25). A shaped stone is a stone a man has contributed to. The altar where atonement is made must contain nothing of human workmanship at all.

So on one hill there stand two things: a written law, produced with great care and human craft, so that everyone knows exactly what is required — and an altar that no human hand has improved, where the blood goes. That is the whole architecture of the Bible on a single hillside.

The Hebrew text names Mount Ebal here (v. 4); the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Samaritans’ own copy of the five books, reads Mount Gerizim, their holy mountain, and most scholars think it was changed to suit them. A large ancient structure on Mount Ebal has been identified by some archaeologists as an early altar, though that remains debated.

You shall rejoice. At that altar Israel is to sacrifice, eat and rejoice, on Mount Ebal, the mountain of the curse. Before a word of the curses has been read, there is an altar on that hill, and a meal, and gladness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–10 — This Day You Have Become the People of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses and the priests call for silence and tell Israel that today she has become the people of the LORD — and that she must therefore obey.
verseByVerse.theology: Each generation must take the covenant as its own: nobody inherits it like an heirloom.
verseByVerse.examples: Every command in the New Testament stands on the same footing — you are a chosen race… therefore (1 Pet. 2:9-11).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and the Levitical priests said to all Israel, "Keep silence and hear, O Israel: this day you have become the people of the LORD your God. You shall therefore obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping his commandments and his statutes, which I command you today."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This day. An odd thing to say. Israel had been the people of the LORD since the night of the Passover forty years earlier — since Abraham, in a sense. What can Moses mean by this day?

He means what he meant in 5:3: the covenant is not an heirloom. The generation standing in front of him did not come out of Egypt; most of them were born in the wilderness. Today, as they hear these words, they become the people of God for themselves, and not merely the children of people who were.

Therefore. This is the pulse of the entire book. Not "obey, and you will become his people." You have become his people; now obey. Peter writes to scattered Christians in exactly that order — you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation… Beloved, I urge you (1 Pet. 2:9, 11).

Reverse the two and you have a different religion. It is the commonest mistake made about the Bible, and it is made most often by people who are trying hardest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–25 — The Twelve Curses from Mount Ebal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six tribes on Gerizim for the blessing and six on Ebal for the curse, with the Levites in the valley proclaiming twelve curses — and the whole nation answering Amen to each.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s law reaches the places no one else can see.
verseByVerse.examples: God is the only witness who has never missed anything. That is why the altar was built on Ebal before the first curse was read: the sins nobody saw have a sacrifice provided for them too.

verseByVerse.quote: That day Moses charged the people, saying, "When you have crossed over the Jordan, these shall stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin. And these shall stand on Mount Ebal for the curse: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali. And the Levites shall declare to all the men of Israel in a loud voice: "'Cursed be the man who makes a carved or cast metal image, an abomination to the LORD, a thing made by the hands of a craftsman, and sets it up in secret.' And all the people shall answer and say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who dishonors his father or his mother.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who moves his neighbor's landmark.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who misleads a blind man on the road.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who perverts the justice due to the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who lies with his father's wife, because he has uncovered his father's nakedness.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who lies with any kind of animal.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who lies with his sister, whether the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who lies with his mother-in-law.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who strikes down his neighbor in secret.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.' "'Cursed be anyone who takes a bribe to shed innocent blood.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gerizim and Ebal. Two hillsides facing each other with a valley between, natural acoustics that carry a voice across, and hundreds of thousands of people arranged on the slopes. (The blessings from Gerizim are not recited here; chapter 28 supplies them.) A single sentence goes up from the valley floor, and a nation answers as one word: Amen — so be it, let it stand, we agree.

The twelve curses. They have something in common that is easy to miss. The idol a man sets up in secret. Dishonouring a father or mother. Moving a boundary stone. Misleading a blind man on the road. Perverting the justice due to the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow. A series of sexual sins committed inside families. Striking a neighbour in secret. Taking a bribe to kill an innocent person.

Almost every one of them is a sin nobody would see. The idol is hidden. The stone is moved at dusk. The blind man never knows who turned him the wrong way. The widow cannot prove that the verdict was bought. The incest happens in a house. Twice the text says in secret outright.

This is deliberate. The blessings and curses of chapter 28 will deal with a nation’s public life. Chapter 27 deals with what a man does when there is no witness — and it makes an entire nation stand on a hillside and say Amen to a curse on exactly those things.

Because that is where a man actually lives. Anyone can keep the law where he can be seen. The list on Mount Ebal is a list of the places where a person’s real character is, and where God is the only one watching.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 26 — Cursed Be Everyone Who Does Not Keep the Whole Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The twelfth curse gathers up all the rest: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them. And all the people said, Amen.
verseByVerse.theology: The law’s last word over the whole nation is a curse, but it is not the Bible’s last word.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel pronounced a curse on herself and said Amen to it. That curse was carried off by a man on a tree, and the believer’s Amen now belongs to a different sentence (2 Cor. 1:20).

verseByVerse.quote: "'Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them.' And all the people shall say, 'Amen.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole law. The first eleven curses name particular sins. The twelfth names the whole law and requires all of it, the entire body of it, without exception.

And a nation stood on a mountainside and said Amen to that. They agreed to it. They put themselves under it, out loud, with their own voices, as the last word of the ceremony.

Centuries later, Paul is arguing with churches in Galatia who have been persuaded that keeping the law is how a person gets right with God, and he reaches for this exact verse: For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them” (Gal. 3:10). He quotes the wording of the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, which spells out the word all; the Hebrew already means the whole law.

The logic is devastating. If the law could bless the man who keeps it, it must curse the man who does not. And the standard is all things. So the moment a person puts himself under the law as a way of being accepted, he has put himself under a sentence that will certainly fall — because nobody has ever kept all of it, and the law has no provision for partial obedience.

Which is why Mount Ebal is not the end of the story, and why the sentence Paul writes three verses later is among the sweetest in the New Testament: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal. 3:13).

Israel said Amen to her own curse on a hillside in Canaan. It was a true and honest Amen, and it fell — and it fell on somebody else, on a hill outside a city, centuries after the last Israelite who shouted it was dust. Every promise of God now has a different word attached to it, and Paul says so with the same Hebrew syllable: For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory (2 Cor. 1:20).

28.overview:
Chapter 28 is the longest chapter in Deuteronomy, the great chapter of covenant consequences: fourteen verses of blessing (vv. 1–14) and fifty-four of escalating curse (vv. 15–68). The blessings are a Father's gifts to the people he has already made his own (28:9), reaching city and field, womb and harvest, coming in and going out. The curses turn each blessing over and end in siege, exile and scattering, and they read like a prophecy of Israel's history.

The chapter confronts us with the holiness of God, who will not be mocked. Yet every curse here was borne by Christ, so that the blessings might fall on us.
28.theology:
Christ bore the covenant curse. The catalogue of curse reveals what sin deserves. On the cross Christ absorbed the full weight of the broken covenant, even God-forsakenness (Matt. 27:46), so that all who trust him might receive the covenant blessing instead (Gal. 3:13–14).

The holiness and justice of God. God will not be mocked (Gal. 6:7). The severity of the curses, and their fulfillment in Israel's exile, vindicate the truthfulness of his word.

The peril of joyless prosperity. The root of the curse was failing to serve God “with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things” (28:47). Ingratitude amid blessing is the seedbed of ruin.
28.examples: We read this chapter as a measure of what our sin deserves, a backdrop against which the cross blazes all the brighter: here is what Christ bore, so that we might never be forsaken and might receive every spiritual blessing in him. Let us serve our God with gladness of heart, the joy his Spirit gives, never taking his grace for granted.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Blessings That Overtake You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: City and field, womb and ground and herd, basket and kneading bowl, coming in and going out — and enemies who come out one way and flee seven ways. Israel will be the head and not the tail.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s blessing reaches the most ordinary parts of life, and it is the gift of a Father to children already his, not wages earned.
verseByVerse.examples: God’s people may look for his kindness in the kitchen and on the doorstep, not only in church, though the note below warns against turning these national promises into a private formula.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if you faithfully obey the voice of the LORD your God, being careful to do all his commandments that I command you today, the LORD your God will set you high above all the nations of the earth. And all these blessings shall come upon you and overtake you, if you obey the voice of the LORD your God. Blessed shall you be in the city, and blessed shall you be in the field. Blessed shall be the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground and the fruit of your cattle, the increase of your herds and the young of your flock. Blessed shall be your basket and your kneading bowl. Blessed shall you be when you come in, and blessed shall you be when you go out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Overtake. The word is used of an army running down a fleeing enemy. God is describing his own goodness as something that chases his people and catches them.

That is not how most people imagine blessing. We picture it as something to be sought, worked toward, perhaps deserved. Here it is behind Israel on the road, gaining on her.

Basket and bowl. Look at what the blessings actually are. A basket. A kneading bowl. The doorway of a house. There is not one religious item in the list. God’s blessing is promised over the bowl a woman makes bread in and the threshold a man crosses twice a day, which is where almost the whole of any life is actually lived.

The pairs are total: city and field, coming in and going out, the beginning and the end of every journey. Between them there is nowhere left. And the same picture turns up in the best-loved line in the Psalter — surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life (Ps. 23:6), where the Hebrew behind follow is the word for pursue. David may well have had this chapter in mind, and the pursuit has not slackened.

Does this national covenant apply to modern nations? It was made with Israel as God’s covenant nation; no other nation stands in that relation to him. God does judge nations for injustice (Prov 14:34), but no country can claim these promises as its own. And verse 12 is a picture of national blessing, not a ban on borrowing; Scripture warns against debt (Prov 22:7) but does not forbid it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD will cause your enemies who rise against you to be defeated before you. They shall come out against you one way and flee before you seven ways. The LORD will command the blessing on you in your barns and in all that you undertake. And he will bless you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you. The LORD will establish you as a people holy to himself, as he has sworn to you, if you keep the commandments of the LORD your God and walk in his ways. And all the peoples of the earth shall see that you are called by the name of the LORD, and they shall be afraid of you. And the LORD will make you abound in prosperity, in the fruit of your womb and in the fruit of your livestock and in the fruit of your ground, within the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give you. The LORD will open to you his good treasury, the heavens, to give the rain to your land in its season and to bless all the work of your hands. And you shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow. And the LORD will make you the head and not the tail, and you shall only go up and not down, if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God, which I command you today, being careful to do them, and if you do not turn aside from any of the words that I command you today, to the right hand or to the left, to go after other gods to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One way, seven ways. The blessing widens from the household to the nation.

One road in and seven roads out: it is a picture of a rout, an army that arrived in formation and left in every direction at once, scattering across the countryside.

Two things need saying about all this, because it is the raw material of a great deal of bad preaching.

First, these are national promises under a specific covenant, attached to a land, and they are not a formula that a Christian can apply to his own finances. The New Testament nowhere transfers them in that form, and several of its own authors were poor, and several were martyred. Job’s friends reasoned exactly that way about prosperity and suffering, and God said at the end that they had not spoken of me what is right (Job 42:7).

Second, what does carry over is the disposition behind them. God is not stingy; the language here is extravagant, and it is his own. Whatever a believer’s circumstances, he is dealing with a God whose instinct toward his people is to give — He who did not spare his own Son… how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Rom. 8:32).

If you obey. The blessing has a hinge, and the next verse swings on it. Only one Israelite ever kept every word without turning aside, and in him, whose obedience is counted as ours, the blessing reaches those who fail (Rom. 5:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–46 — The Curses That Overtake You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The same pursuing language returns, reversed: each blessing is turned over one by one, and disease, drought, defeat, madness and captivity are added.
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue is deliberately relentless: a covenant with terms has terms on both sides.
verseByVerse.examples: A nation heard its own blessings read back to it as threats. The New Testament does not repeal these curses; it shows where they finally fell.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you will not obey the voice of the LORD your God or be careful to do all his commandments and his statutes that I command you today, then all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you. Cursed shall you be in the city, and cursed shall you be in the field. Cursed shall be your basket and your kneading bowl. Cursed shall be the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground, the increase of your herds and the young of your flock. Cursed shall you be when you come in, and cursed shall you be when you go out. "The LORD will send on you curses, confusion, and frustration in all that you undertake to do, until you are destroyed and perish quickly on account of the evil of your deeds, because you have forsaken me. The LORD will make the pestilence stick to you until he has consumed you off the land that you are entering to take possession of it. The LORD will strike you with wasting disease and with fever, inflammation and fiery heat, and with drought and with blight and with mildew. They shall pursue you until you perish. And the heavens over your head shall be bronze, and the earth under you shall be iron. The LORD will make the rain of your land powder. From heaven dust shall come down on you until you are destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Overtake you. The same verb returns, because the curses pursue too, and they are the blessings turned over, one at a time, in nearly the same order and the same words.

Every clause of verses 3 to 6 is read back inverted. The basket, the bowl, the doorway — the identical ordinary things, now under the identical pursuing power, running the other way.

That structure is the theology of the chapter. These are not two unrelated lists. It is one covenant with two faces, and the same God stands behind both. What he gives he may withhold, and a relationship with terms has terms on both sides.

Then the catalogue begins — pestilence, wasting disease, fever, drought, blight, mildew, a sky like bronze and earth like iron, and dust for rain. The blessings took fourteen verses. The curses will take fifty-four, and the disproportion is deliberate. The reader is meant to be worn down.

Do these curses fall on Christians? Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13). Believers still suffer, and the Father disciplines them (Heb 12:6), but that is not the covenant curse; there are no “generational curses” on those in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD will cause you to be defeated before your enemies. You shall go out one way against them and flee seven ways before them. And you shall be a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth. And your dead body shall be food for all birds of the air and for the beasts of the earth, and there shall be no one to frighten them away. The LORD will strike you with the boils of Egypt, and with tumors and scabs and itch, of which you cannot be healed. The LORD will strike you with madness and blindness and confusion of mind, and you shall grope at noonday, as the blind grope in darkness, and you shall not prosper in your ways. And you shall be only oppressed and robbed continually, and there shall be no one to help you. You shall betroth a wife, but another man shall ravish her. You shall build a house, but you shall not dwell in it. You shall plant a vineyard, but you shall not enjoy its fruit. Your ox shall be slaughtered before your eyes, but you shall not eat any of it. Your donkey shall be seized before your face, but shall not be restored to you. Your sheep shall be given to your enemies, but there shall be no one to help you. Your sons and your daughters shall be given to another people, while your eyes look on and fail with longing for them all day long, but you shall be helpless. A nation that you have not known shall eat up the fruit of your ground and of all your labors, and you shall be only oppressed and crushed continually, so that you are driven mad by the sights that your eyes see. The LORD will strike you on the knees and on the legs with grievous boils of which you cannot be healed, from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head. "The LORD will bring you and your king whom you set over you to a nation that neither you nor your fathers have known. And there you shall serve other gods of wood and stone. And you shall become a horror, a proverb, and a byword among all the peoples where the LORD will lead you away. You shall carry much seed into the field and shall gather in little, for the locust shall consume it. You shall plant vineyards and dress them, but you shall neither drink of the wine nor gather the grapes, for the worm shall eat them. You shall have olive trees throughout all your territory, but you shall not anoint yourself with the oil, for your olives shall drop off. You shall father sons and daughters, but they shall not be yours, for they shall go into captivity. The cricket shall possess all your trees and the fruit of your ground. The sojourner who is among you shall rise higher and higher above you, and you shall come down lower and lower. He shall lend to you, and you shall not lend to him. He shall be the head, and you shall be the tail. "All these curses shall come upon you and pursue you and overtake you till you are destroyed, because you did not obey the voice of the LORD your God, to keep his commandments and his statutes that he commanded you. They shall be a sign and a wonder against you and your offspring forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The curses accumulate, and their range is what is most striking. They reach into every part of a national life: defeat in battle, bodies left unburied, madness and blindness, a wife taken by another man, a house built and not lived in, a vineyard planted and not enjoyed, children going into captivity while the parents watch and can do nothing.

No one to help. A phrase recurs through them (vv. 29, 32): loss, and no one to help, and parents watching their children taken.

Helplessness is the note. Not merely loss, but loss while watching and being unable to act, which is the particular cruelty of every disaster that happens to somebody else’s children.

You and your king. Verse 36 names the shape it will finally take: exile, with the monarchy dragged off with it. On the book’s own account it was spoken centuries before there was a king to drag. Many scholars date the book’s final form to the time of the kings and read these verses as written with exile in view; those who hold to Moses’ authorship see here God’s foreknowledge, and in either case the words stood as a warning that Israel did not heed.

A byword. The nation chosen to display God’s goodness to the world would end up as a cautionary tale told by the nations she was meant to attract.

Pursue and overtake. In the summary of verse 45, three verbs of pursuit stacked in a single sentence — come, pursue, overtake — and the reason given each time is the same, and it is not idolatry or violence. It is not listening.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 47–57 — Because You Did Not Serve Him with Gladness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hinge of the chapter names the cause of the ruin, and it is not idolatry or violence: because you did not serve the LORD your God with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things. Then the siege, in horrifying detail.
verseByVerse.theology: God cares not only whether he is served but how.
verseByVerse.examples: The same warning stands over any comfortable church: God notices the difference between obedience and gladness. The way back is not forced feeling but return to the Giver.

verseByVerse.quote: Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things, therefore you shall serve your enemies whom the LORD will send against you, in hunger and thirst, in nakedness, and lacking everything. And he will put a yoke of iron on your neck until he has destroyed you. The LORD will bring a nation against you from far away, from the end of the earth, swooping down like the eagle, a nation whose language you do not understand, a hard-faced nation who shall not respect the old or show mercy to the young. It shall eat the offspring of your cattle and the fruit of your ground, until you are destroyed; it also shall not leave you grain, wine, or oil, the increase of your herds or the young of your flock, until they have caused you to perish. "They shall besiege you in all your towns, until your high and fortified walls, in which you trusted, come down throughout all your land. And they shall besiege you in all your towns throughout all your land, which the LORD your God has given you. And you shall eat the fruit of your womb, the flesh of your sons and daughters, whom the LORD your God has given you, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemies shall distress you. The man who is the most tender and refined among you will begrudge food to his brother, to the wife he embraces, and to the last of the children whom he has left, so that he will not give to any of them any of the flesh of his children whom he is eating, because he has nothing else left, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemy shall distress you in all your towns. The most tender and refined woman among you, who would not venture to set the sole of her foot on the ground because she is so delicate and tender, will begrudge to the husband she embraces, to her son and to her daughter, her afterbirth that comes out from between her feet and her children whom she bears, because lacking everything she will eat them secretly, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemy shall distress you in your towns.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without joyfulness. Alongside forsaking him (v. 20) and not obeying (v. 45), the chapter names a cause nobody expects: they served God without joy, at a time when they had everything.

They were, on the face of it, still serving. The sacrifices were being offered and the feasts kept. What had gone was gladness — and God treats that absence as sufficient ground for the ruin of a nation.

That should stop anybody who has settled into a religion of duty. God is not indifferent to the difference between obedience and delight. A man can attend, give, serve and behave, and be under this verse the whole time, and never suspect it because nothing measurable is missing. And the way back is open: gladness is not manufactured but given, as the Spirit's fruit (Gal. 5:22), to those who return and remember what they have received.

And note the clause attached: because of the abundance of all things. The joylessness grew in the good years. Prosperity did not make them rebellious; it made them flat. They had so much that God became one item among many, and the thanking stopped, and then the gladness — and the serving went on with nothing inside it.

The sentence fits the crime exactly. They would not serve God with gladness while they had everything; they will serve enemies in hunger while they have nothing. And then comes the siege, described in the most harrowing verses in the Pentateuch — the refined and gentle among them turning on their own children for food (vv. 53–57), a horror that Scripture records as literally fulfilled twice over, in Samaria and in Jerusalem (2 Kgs. 6:28–29; Lam. 4:10).
verseByVerse.note: Josephus records the same horror in the Roman siege of Jerusalem in AD 70 (Jewish War 6.3.4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 58–68 — Scattered, and No Resting Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends in exile: plucked off the land, scattered from one end of the earth to the other, a trembling heart and failing eyes, and no resting place for the sole of the foot.
verseByVerse.theology: The specificity is extraordinary — a nation from far away with an unknown language, siege, cannibalism, dispersion, and a return to Egypt in ships. Israel’s later history reads like a commentary on these verses. And yet Deuteronomy has already said what lies past them: from there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him (4:29).
verseByVerse.examples: The last word of the covenant curse was a slave nobody would buy. But there is a rest for the people of God that no exile can reach (Heb. 4:9), and it was bought by a man who found no resting place either.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you are not careful to do all the words of this law that are written in this book, that you may fear this glorious and awesome name, the LORD your God, then the LORD will bring on you and your offspring extraordinary afflictions, afflictions severe and lasting, and sicknesses grievous and lasting. And he will bring upon you again all the diseases of Egypt, of which you were afraid, and they shall cling to you. Every sickness also and every affliction that is not recorded in the book of this law, the LORD will bring upon you, until you are destroyed. Whereas you were as numerous as the stars of heaven, you shall be left few in number, because you did not obey the voice of the LORD your God. And as the LORD took delight in doing you good and multiplying you, so the LORD will take delight in bringing ruin upon you and destroying you. And you shall be plucked off the land that you are entering to take possession of it. "And the LORD will scatter you among all peoples, from one end of the earth to the other, and there you shall serve other gods of wood and stone, which neither you nor your fathers have known. And among these nations you shall find no respite, and there shall be no resting place for the sole of your foot, but the LORD will give you there a trembling heart and failing eyes and a languishing soul. Your life shall hang in doubt before you. Night and day you shall be in dread and have no assurance of your life. In the morning you shall say, 'If only it were evening!' and at evening you shall say, 'If only it were morning!' because of the dread that your heart shall feel, and the sights that your eyes shall see. And the LORD will bring you back in ships to Egypt, a journey that I promised that you should never make again; and there you shall offer yourselves for sale to your enemies as male and female slaves, but there will be no buyer."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like the eagle. The chapter ends in exile, and the detail is unnerving: a hard-faced nation from far away, and then dispersion from one end of the earth to the other.

Verse 63 is the hardest sentence in the book: And as the LORD took delight in doing you good and multiplying you, so the LORD will take delight in bringing ruin upon you. It should not be softened. God is not indifferent when he judges; he is not a reluctant administrator of a system. What he is delighting in is the vindication of his own holiness, and Ezekiel insists that I have no pleasure in the death of anyone (Ezek. 18:32). Both stand, and any reader who finds them hard to hold together is reading correctly.

A trembling heart. Then the description of life in exile, one of the most psychologically exact passages in Scripture.

Anybody who has lived through a season of dread knows that last verse from the inside. The day is unbearable and so is the night, and each is longed for while the other is being endured, and neither brings anything when it comes. It is a description of anxiety written more than two and a half thousand years ago, on any dating, and it has not dated by a syllable.

If that verse describes your nights, it is not proof that you are under this curse. God’s own children have known dread like it (Ps. 88; 2 Cor. 1:8–9), and the curse has already fallen on Christ in their place. The one who said Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28) meets the anxious there, and there is no shame in seeking help from doctors and friends as well as in prayer.

No buyer. The very last line is the bitterest. Back to the house of slavery, by sea this time, so worthless that nobody will take them even for nothing.

That is where the covenant curse ends. And the only reason a Christian can read this chapter without despair is that Paul told us where the whole weight of it went — onto somebody who had never earned a line of it: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal. 3:13). Deuteronomy 28 is the size of what he absorbed. Read it to the end, and then read that sentence again, and you will not think the cross was a small thing.

29.title: The Covenant Renewed in Moab: The Secret Things Belong to God
29.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the words of the covenant that the LORD commanded Moses to make with the people of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant that he had made with them at Horeb.<sup>2</sup>And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: "You have seen all that the LORD did before your eyes in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land,<sup>3</sup>the great trials that your eyes saw, the signs, and those great wonders.<sup>4</sup>But to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear.<sup>5</sup>I have led you forty years in the wilderness. Your clothes have not worn out on you, and your sandals have not worn off your feet.<sup>6</sup>You have not eaten bread, and you have not drunk wine or strong drink, that you may know that I am the LORD your God.<sup>7</sup>And when you came to this place, Sihon the king of Heshbon and Og the king of Bashan came out against us to battle, but we defeated them.<sup>8</sup>We took their land and gave it for an inheritance to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of the Manassites.<sup>9</sup>Therefore keep the words of this covenant and do them, that you may prosper in all that you do.<sup>10</sup>"You are standing today, all of you, before the LORD your God: the heads of your tribes, your elders, and your officers, all the men of Israel,<sup>11</sup>your little ones, your wives, and the sojourner who is in your camp, from the one who chops your wood to the one who draws your water,<sup>12</sup>so that you may enter into the sworn covenant of the LORD your God, which the LORD your God is making with you today,<sup>13</sup>that he may establish you today as his people, and that he may be your God, as he promised you, and as he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.<sup>14</sup>It is not with you alone that I am making this sworn covenant,<sup>15</sup>but with whoever is standing here with us today before the LORD our God, and with whoever is not here with us today.<sup>16</sup>"You know how we lived in the land of Egypt, and how we came through the midst of the nations through which you passed.<sup>17</sup>And you have seen their detestable things, their idols of wood and stone, of silver and gold, which were among them.<sup>18</sup>Beware lest there be among you a man or woman or clan or tribe whose heart is turning away today from the LORD our God to go and serve the gods of those nations. Beware lest there be among you a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit,<sup>19</sup>one who, when he hears the words of this sworn covenant, blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart.' This will lead to the sweeping away of moist and dry alike.<sup>20</sup>The LORD will not be willing to forgive him, but rather the anger of the LORD and his jealousy will smoke against that man, and the curses written in this book will settle upon him, and the LORD will blot out his name from under heaven.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD will single him out from all the tribes of Israel for calamity, in accordance with all the curses of the covenant written in this Book of the Law.<sup>22</sup>And the next generation, your children who rise up after you, and the foreigner who comes from a far land, will say, when they see the afflictions of that land and the sicknesses with which the LORD has made it sick—<sup>23</sup>the whole land burned out with brimstone and salt, nothing sown and nothing growing, where no plant can sprout, an overthrow like that of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger and wrath—<sup>24</sup>all the nations will say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land? What caused the heat of this great anger?'<sup>25</sup>Then people will say, 'It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers, which he made with them when he brought them out of the land of Egypt,<sup>26</sup>and went and served other gods and worshiped them, gods whom they had not known and whom he had not allotted to them.<sup>27</sup>Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against this land, bringing upon it all the curses written in this book,<sup>28</sup>and the LORD uprooted them from their land in anger and fury and great wrath, and cast them into another land, as they are this day.'<sup>29</sup>"The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law.
29.overview:
Chapter 29 opens Moses' final address (chs. 29–30), in which the covenant is renewed on the plains of Moab with the whole nation, down to the woodcutter and the water-carrier, and with generations not yet born.

The chapter diagnoses the human condition: after forty years of wonders, “the LORD has not given you a heart to understand” (29:4). The problem is not lack of evidence but a blindness only God can heal, which sets up the promise of chapter 30. Moses warns against the man who blesses himself in his heart while walking in stubbornness, and closes with the great boundary of faith: the secret things belong to the LORD, and the revealed things to us (29:29).
29.theology:
The need for a new heart. Evidence cannot cure a heart that cannot perceive (29:4). This cries out for the new covenant promise (ch. 30) that God himself will give the heart we lack (John 3:3; 1 Cor. 2:14).

The danger of presumption. To presume on grace while clinging to sin (29:19) is the most dangerous spiritual condition; the all-seeing God knows every secret turning of the heart and calls us to genuine repentance.

The secret and the revealed. Mature faith trusts God's sovereignty over what we cannot understand and obeys what he has plainly revealed (29:29). Where God has spoken, we obey; where God is silent, we trust.
29.examples: We confess that we were blind until God gave us eyes to see, the gift of the new covenant given in the Spirit. We heed the warning against nursing secret sin, trust God's goodness over all that is hidden, and by that same Spirit devote ourselves to what he has plainly revealed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — You Have Seen, and You Do Not See
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses rehearses forty years of miracle — Egypt, the signs, clothes and sandals that did not wear out — and then says something startling: to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear.
verseByVerse.theology: The heart to understand is God’s to give, and the answer to its lack is the promise of 30:6.
verseByVerse.examples: Nobody argues himself into faith, which is why Christians pray for eyes to be opened as well as offering arguments.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the words of the covenant that the LORD commanded Moses to make with the people of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant that he had made with them at Horeb. And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: "You have seen all that the LORD did before your eyes in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land, the great trials that your eyes saw, the signs, and those great wonders. But to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear. I have led you forty years in the wilderness. Your clothes have not worn out on you, and your sandals have not worn off your feet. You have not eaten bread, and you have not drunk wine or strong drink, that you may know that I am the LORD your God. And when you came to this place, Sihon the king of Heshbon and Og the king of Bashan came out against us to battle, but we defeated them. We took their land and gave it for an inheritance to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of the Manassites. Therefore keep the words of this covenant and do them, that you may prosper in all that you do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not given a heart. Moses sets forty years of wonders beside verse 4. They saw everything — the plagues, the sea, the mountain, forty years of bread on the ground — and Moses says they still cannot see. He does not say they refused to look, but that they have not been given the faculty.

That single sentence demolishes a very common assumption about faith. Israel’s problem was never a shortage of evidence. No generation in history has had more, and it did not produce a heart to understand, because evidence and understanding are two different things and the second is a gift.

Which is why Paul quotes this same language about the Israel of his own day: God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear (Rom. 11:8). And why he says of everyone, without exception: The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God… because they are spiritually discerned (1 Cor. 2:14).

Nobody has ever been argued into the kingdom. Which does not make argument useless — Moses is arguing at this very moment — but it does change what we pray for. We ask God to open eyes, because he is the one who has them.

And the gift Moses could not hand over arrived in person. The Lord Jesus opened the eyes of the blind as a sign of what he had come to do, and said to his disciples, blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear (Matt. 13:16). The same God who said Let light shine out of darkness now shines in hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor. 4:6). The heart to understand is given by the Son, through his Spirit.

Your sandals have not worn off. Verse 5, tucked in beside all that, is as tender as anything in the book. They could not see, and he kept their shoes on their feet for forty years anyway.

If God had not given them a heart to understand, how can they be blamed? The inability is real, and only God can cure it (30:6); but it is the inability of a will that does not want to obey, not an excuse. Moses at once commands obedience (v. 9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — All of You Are Standing Here Today
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole nation is drawn up to enter the covenant — leaders and elders, men, women and little ones, and the foreigner who cuts your wood and draws your water — and with them whoever is not here with us today.
verseByVerse.theology: The list goes deliberately to the bottom, and the covenant reaches past the people present to generations unborn.
verseByVerse.examples: A slave drawing water stood in the same covenant as the head of a tribe, and the ground at the foot of the cross is no less level: there is neither slave nor free… for you are all one in Christ Jesus (Gal. 3:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "You are standing today, all of you, before the LORD your God: the heads of your tribes, your elders, and your officers, all the men of Israel, your little ones, your wives, and the sojourner who is in your camp, from the one who chops your wood to the one who draws your water, so that you may enter into the sworn covenant of the LORD your God, which the LORD your God is making with you today, that he may establish you today as his people, and that he may be your God, as he promised you, and as he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. It is not with you alone that I am making this sworn covenant, but with whoever is standing here with us today before the LORD our God, and with whoever is not here with us today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woodcutter and water-carrier. Read the list from the bottom up. The last two named are the woodcutter and the water-carrier — the lowest jobs in the camp, done by resident foreigners, the people nobody would have thought to mention.

They are standing in the same covenant as the heads of the tribes. Not in an annexe, not on different terms, not as observers. The same covenant, entered on the same day, with the same God — and the text takes the trouble to name their trades so that nobody can miss it.

And the women and the little ones are there too, which ancient treaty ceremonies did not usually trouble to record. This is not a covenant between God and the men of standing, with everybody else covered by association. Everybody is present and everybody is party to it.

Whoever is not here. Verse 15 stretches it further still: people not yet born are included in a covenant made on one day in Moab. Which is why Deuteronomy insists so hard that each generation must make it its own (5:3). The covenant reaches forward; the entering into it has to be done by every person for himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A warning against the man who hears the covenant curses and privately reassures himself that he will be fine — and against the hidden turning of a heart that spreads like a bitter root.
verseByVerse.theology: Unbelief nursed in secret does not stay private; what one person hides can spread to many.
verseByVerse.examples: The person in most danger in any church is rarely the one who is worried about himself, and the one who is worried may take the warning straight to Christ, who casts out no one who comes (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: "You know how we lived in the land of Egypt, and how we came through the midst of the nations through which you passed. And you have seen their detestable things, their idols of wood and stone, of silver and gold, which were among them. Beware lest there be among you a man or woman or clan or tribe whose heart is turning away today from the LORD our God to go and serve the gods of those nations. Beware lest there be among you a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit, one who, when he hears the words of this sworn covenant, blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart.' This will lead to the sweeping away of moist and dry alike. The LORD will not be willing to forgive him, but rather the anger of the LORD and his jealousy will smoke against that man, and the curses written in this book will settle upon him, and the LORD will blot out his name from under heaven. And the LORD will single him out from all the tribes of Israel for calamity, in accordance with all the curses of the covenant written in this Book of the Law. And the next generation, your children who rise up after you, and the foreigner who comes from a far land, will say, when they see the afflictions of that land and the sicknesses with which the LORD has made it sick— the whole land burned out with brimstone and salt, nothing sown and nothing growing, where no plant can sprout, an overthrow like that of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger and wrath— all the nations will say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land? What caused the heat of this great anger?' Then people will say, 'It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers, which he made with them when he brought them out of the land of Egypt, and went and served other gods and worshiped them, gods whom they had not known and whom he had not allotted to them. Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against this land, bringing upon it all the curses written in this book, and the LORD uprooted them from their land in anger and fury and great wrath, and cast them into another land, as they are this day.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the warning, and the danger is located with great precision. It is not an idolater in the open; it is a man or woman or clan or tribe whose heart is turning away today — turning, present tense, while the ceremony is going on.

I shall be safe. Such a man is present. He hears the curses read out. He says Amen with everybody else. And privately, at that moment, he reassures himself that none of it applies to him.

That is the most dangerous condition described anywhere in Deuteronomy, and it is dangerous precisely because it is comfortable. The man is not anxious. He is not under conviction. He has performed a small internal act of self-blessing and is now settled, and nothing in the service touched him.

Moses calls it a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit — something underground, invisible, and spreading. Hebrews takes the image and hands it to the church without alteration: See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled (Heb. 12:15).

The consequences described are national and terrible — a land like Sodom, burned and salted, so that passing travellers ask Why has the LORD done thus to this land? But the origin of it is one person, in a crowd, quietly deciding that the warnings are for other people.

Can a believer lose salvation? Arminian Christians, many of them godly and earnest, read this as a warning that true believers can fall away. The man described here blesses himself while walking in stubbornness, a hypocrite who was never truly the LORD’s. The warning is real, aimed at everyone in the covenant community, and it is one of the means by which God keeps his own (Heb 3:12–14).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One of the great verses of Scripture: the secret things belong to the LORD, and the things revealed belong to us and to our children — that we may do them.
verseByVerse.theology: There is a line, and God draws it. Some things he has kept; some he has given, and what is given is for obedience, not speculation.
verseByVerse.examples: The same discipline saves a great deal of anguish about providence, election and the future: the hidden half belongs to God.

verseByVerse.quote: "The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The secret things. The verse draws a line that saves an enormous amount of grief.

There are things God has not told us. Why this and not that; why now and not then; how his sovereignty and our choices fit together; what he is doing in a particular providence that has broken somebody’s life. Those are the secret things, and Moses says plainly that they belong to the LORD. They are not withheld information we are entitled to and have been denied. They are his property.

And there are things he has told us, and they are described in the warmest possible terms: they belong to us and to our children forever. Revelation is not a loan. What God has said is ours, permanently, and our children’s after us.

That we may do. The purpose clause is the part usually left off when this verse is quoted. The revealed things are not given for speculation but for obedience. God has told us what he has told us so that we would act on it.

And the two halves tend to be confused in the same person. It is remarkably easy to spend years worrying at the hidden things — the questions that have no answer this side of glory — while leaving the plain ones undone. A man can hold strong opinions about the decrees of God and not have forgiven his brother.

The New Testament adds a glorious turn. It speaks of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed (Rom. 16:25–26), and the mystery is Christ, and Christ in his people (Col. 1:26–27). The greatest of God’s secret things has been carried across the line and given to us.

The comfort in it is real. When you cannot understand what God is doing, you are not failing. You are standing at a boundary he drew on purpose, and on this side of it there is quite enough to be getting on with.

30.title: The Promise of Restoration: God Will Circumcise Your Heart
30.text: <sup>1</sup>"And when all these things come upon you, the blessing and the curse, which I have set before you, and you call them to mind among all the nations where the LORD your God has driven you,<sup>2</sup>and return to the LORD your God, you and your children, and obey his voice in all that I command you today, with all your heart and with all your soul,<sup>3</sup>then the LORD your God will restore your fortunes and have mercy on you, and he will gather you again from all the peoples where the LORD your God has scattered you.<sup>4</sup>If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there the LORD your God will gather you, and from there he will take you.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD your God will bring you into the land that your fathers possessed, that you may possess it. And he will make you more prosperous and numerous than your fathers.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live.<sup>7</sup>And the LORD your God will put all these curses on your foes and enemies who persecuted you.<sup>8</sup>And you shall again obey the voice of the LORD and keep all his commandments that I command you today.<sup>9</sup>The LORD your God will make you abundantly prosperous in all the work of your hand, in the fruit of your womb and in the fruit of your cattle and in the fruit of your ground. For the LORD will again take delight in prospering you, as he took delight in your fathers,<sup>10</sup>when you obey the voice of the LORD your God, to keep his commandments and his statutes that are written in this Book of the Law, when you turn to the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.<sup>11</sup>"For this commandment that I command you today is not too hard for you, neither is it far off.<sup>12</sup>It is not in heaven, that you should say, 'Who will ascend to heaven for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?'<sup>13</sup>Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, 'Who will go over the sea for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?'<sup>14</sup>But the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it.<sup>15</sup>"See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil.<sup>16</sup>If you obey the commandments of the LORD your God that I command you today, by loving the LORD your God, by walking in his ways, and by keeping his commandments and his statutes and his rules, then you shall live and multiply, and the LORD your God will bless you in the land that you are entering to take possession of it.<sup>17</sup>But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away to worship other gods and serve them,<sup>18</sup>I declare to you today, that you shall surely perish. You shall not live long in the land that you are going over the Jordan to enter and possess.<sup>19</sup>I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live,<sup>20</sup>loving the LORD your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life and length of days, that you may dwell in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them."
30.overview:
Chapter 30 is the turning point of Deuteronomy's final addresses. After the curses and the diagnosis of Israel's heartlessness, Moses looks beyond the coming failure and exile to restoration: when Israel returns to the LORD, he will have mercy and gather her from wherever she has been scattered (30:1–5).

The heart of the chapter is verse 6: “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart.” What the law commanded (10:16) but could not produce, God promises to do himself, the new covenant at the heart of the gospel. The word is near, in the mouth and in the heart (30:14). And Moses sets before Israel life and death, and pleads with her to choose life, for the LORD is her life.
30.theology:
The new covenant: God circumcises the heart. God promises to do what the law commanded but could not produce (30:6), working in us by his Spirit what we could never do (Ezek. 36:26; Rom. 2:29). Salvation is God's sovereign work from first to last.

The word is very near. Paul applies 30:14 to the gospel of faith (Rom. 10:6–8): we need not ascend to heaven or descend to the depths, for Christ has done it all, and in him God has come near to us.

Choose life. God's work in the heart does not cancel human responsibility but enables it; the God who commands the choice gives the new heart that makes it possible (30:19–20). The call still sounds to all: hold fast to the Lord, who is himself our life.
30.examples: The promise is fulfilled in the new covenant: God has given us by his Spirit a new heart that loves him, and where our love still falls short, Christ, who loved the Father with all his heart in our place, is our righteousness. The word of faith is as near as our mouths and hearts, and the call still sounds: choose life; hold fast to him, for he is your life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — From the Uttermost Parts of Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses looks past the curses of chapter 28 to what lies on the far side of them: exile remembered, hearts turned, and God gathering his scattered people home from wherever they have been driven.
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is made before the failure has happened, and its reach is unlimited (v. 4): God undertakes to cross any distance to gather his people.
verseByVerse.examples: No one reading this has wandered beyond God’s reach: there is no far country in Scripture that has ever been out of range.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when all these things come upon you, the blessing and the curse, which I have set before you, and you call them to mind among all the nations where the LORD your God has driven you, and return to the LORD your God, you and your children, and obey his voice in all that I command you today, with all your heart and with all your soul, then the LORD your God will restore your fortunes and have mercy on you, and he will gather you again from all the peoples where the LORD your God has scattered you. If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there the LORD your God will gather you, and from there he will take you. And the LORD your God will bring you into the land that your fathers possessed, that you may possess it. And he will make you more prosperous and numerous than your fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 28 ended with a nation scattered to the ends of the earth and offering itself for sale with no buyer. Chapter 30 begins on the far side of that.

When, not if. Moses is not describing a possibility. He is telling a people standing on the border of the promised land what will happen after they have lost it, and what God will do next.

The uttermost parts of heaven. Verse 4 sets the reach of it.
