The phrase is Hebrew for as far as anything can be, and it is put in deliberately as an extreme case — you can imagine an Israelite in Babylon reading it and thinking, but what about the ones nobody knows about, the ones taken further, the ones we have lost track of? The verse is written for exactly that objection, and it closes it.

There is no distance in this sentence that God does not undertake to cross. The same reach turns up in the mouth of the Lord Jesus about a single sheep out of a hundred, and in the running father of Luke 15 who sees his son while he was still a long way off. Nobody in Scripture has ever gone too far to be fetched back.

Is this regathering fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. Dispensationalists see a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel. But the circumcised heart of verse 6 is the work of the new covenant, and Christ died to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad (John 11:52). The fullest fulfilment is Christ gathering his people from every nation, including, as many believe, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Rom 11:26). Faithful Christians differ on these details, and charity becomes them; all agree that no one is gathered home except through Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises to do the thing he commanded in 10:16 and wished for in 5:29 — to circumcise the heart of his people and of their offspring, so that they will love him with all their heart and live.
verseByVerse.theology: The law commands a love nobody can produce; the covenant exposes the failure; and here God undertakes to work in his people what he demands from them.
verseByVerse.examples: A people who could not change their own hearts were told God would change them, and that same promise is what makes anyone a Christian: born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God (John 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live. And the LORD your God will put all these curses on your foes and enemies who persecuted you. And you shall again obey the voice of the LORD and keep all his commandments that I command you today. The LORD your God will make you abundantly prosperous in all the work of your hand, in the fruit of your womb and in the fruit of your cattle and in the fruit of your ground. For the LORD will again take delight in prospering you, as he took delight in your fathers, when you obey the voice of the LORD your God, to keep his commandments and his statutes that are written in this Book of the Law, when you turn to the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Circumcise your heart. This is the sentence the whole book has been building toward. Set three verses side by side and you have the argument of Deuteronomy in miniature.

At 5:29 God says, Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear me and to keep all my commandments. That is the wish — God longing for something his people do not have.

At 10:16 he commands it: Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn. That is the demand — and, as that verse showed, it asks of a man precisely the one operation he cannot perform on himself.

And here, at 30:6, the subject of the verb changes. What he wished for, and then commanded, he now promises to do himself.

That is the gospel, in the fifth book of Moses, centuries before Jeremiah and long before Christ. God requires of us what we cannot produce, and then undertakes to produce it in us. The law was never a ladder; it was a mirror, and this verse is what God does about what the mirror shows.

So that you will love. The command of 6:5 — the greatest commandment, the one no sinner has ever kept for an hour, and only one Man ever kept at all — is here promised as the result of God’s work rather than the condition of it.

The prophets take this verse and make it the definition of the new covenant. I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer. 31:33). I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezek. 36:26). And the Lord Jesus told a religious teacher who knew all of this that he must be born again, and was astonished he did not recognise it: Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things? (John 3:10). It was in his Bible. It is here.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — The Word Is Very Near You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The commandment is not too hard for Israel, nor hidden in heaven or beyond the sea; nobody has to fetch it, because it is already in their mouth and heart.
verseByVerse.theology: God has already brought his word down and put it within reach.
verseByVerse.examples: The excuse that God’s will is out of reach is closed off for us too, and more firmly: the Word himself came down.

verseByVerse.quote: "For this commandment that I command you today is not too hard for you, neither is it far off. It is not in heaven, that you should say, 'Who will ascend to heaven for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?' Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, 'Who will go over the sea for us and bring it to us, that we may hear it and do it?' But the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not far off. Moses is closing off an excuse before it is made. Nobody in Israel will be able to say that God’s will was inaccessible, that it required an expedition, that somebody would have had to climb into heaven or cross an ocean to find out what he wanted. God has brought it down and said it out loud and put it within reach. The word is already in their mouths, because they have just heard it and can repeat it.

And then Paul does something extraordinary with this passage. Writing about the righteousness that comes by faith, he takes these verses and reads them of Christ: Do not say in your heart, “Who will ascend into heaven?” (that is, to bring Christ down) or “Who will descend into the abyss?” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim) (Rom. 10:6–8).

His logic is exact. Deuteronomy’s point is that nobody has to fetch God’s word from an inaccessible place because God has already delivered it. Paul’s point is that nobody has to fetch Christ from heaven or from the grave, because God has already done both — he came down, and he came up, and the work is finished and the news is at your elbow.

Which means the gospel asks nothing of a man except that he receive what has been brought. Not an ascent, not a voyage, not a search. If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved (Rom. 10:9) — mouth and heart, the two words Moses used, and nothing else required.

Can anyone keep the law, if it is “not too hard”? The command was near and plain, not hidden in heaven; and God promised the heart to obey it (v. 6). Paul reads these verses of the word of faith in Christ (Rom 10:6–8): the law as a way to earn life is beyond sinners (Rom 8:3), but Christ has come near, and believing in him is not beyond anyone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sets life and death, blessing and curse, before the whole nation, calls heaven and earth as witnesses, and tells them to choose — because he is your life and length of days.
verseByVerse.theology: The book’s great either-or reaches its climax, and there is no third option. To choose life is to choose a Person.
verseByVerse.examples: A nation stood on the plain and was told to choose. Anyone still undecided about Christ is being asked the same question, and it is asked in love.

verseByVerse.quote: "See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil. If you obey the commandments of the LORD your God that I command you today, by loving the LORD your God, by walking in his ways, and by keeping his commandments and his statutes and his rules, then you shall live and multiply, and the LORD your God will bless you in the land that you are entering to take possession of it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away to worship other gods and serve them, I declare to you today, that you shall surely perish. You shall not live long in the land that you are going over the Jordan to enter and possess. I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live, loving the LORD your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life and length of days, that you may dwell in the land that the LORD swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Choose life. Everything since chapter 11 has been coming to this. Two ways, two outcomes, and no third option — no comfortable middle where a person can live without deciding. Moses summons the sky and the ground as legal witnesses, and puts it to them.

He is your life. Then the definition, which is the most important thing in the paragraph: verse 20 says the life to be chosen is loving the LORD, obeying his voice and holding fast to him.

It is not a lifestyle, nor even a set of blessings: the thing being chosen is a Person, and the three verbs are the ones this book has used from the beginning — love, obey, cling.

Two things guard this from misuse. The first: the command to choose comes after the promise of verse 6. God does not tell Israel to produce a new heart and then choose. He promises to circumcise their hearts, and then calls them to choose — and the calling is the very means by which he does it. Nobody has ever had to work out how divine sovereignty and human choosing fit together in order to obey a verse like this. Moses did not explain it; he simply said choose.

The second: it is addressed to people who have been listening for thirty chapters to how badly they will fail. This is not a call to the confident. It is a call to a nation whose exile has just been predicted in detail, and it is made anyway, and it is meant.

The same call is still being made in the same terms. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly (John 10:10). And the one who says it is not offering a way to life; he told Martha, on the way to her brother’s grave, what he actually is — I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25). Moses said he is your life to a crowd on a plain in Moab, and did not know how completely he was right.

Does “choose life” teach that fallen people can choose God by their own power? Arminian readers, many of them earnest Christians, say the command implies the ability. But a command shows what is right, not what we are able to do (Rom 8:7–8). The choice is real and must be made; and God gives the heart that chooses (v. 6; Phil 2:12–13). The verse is about life with God in the covenant; the sanctity of unborn life rests on other texts (Ps 139:13–16).

31.title: Moses' Farewell and the Law Deposited
31.text: <sup>1</sup>So Moses continued to speak these words to all Israel.<sup>2</sup>And he said to them, "I am 120 years old today. I am no longer able to go out and come in. The LORD has said to me, 'You shall not go over this Jordan.'<sup>3</sup>The LORD your God himself will go over before you. He will destroy these nations before you, so that you shall dispossess them, and Joshua will go over at your head, as the LORD has spoken.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD will do to them as he did to Sihon and Og, the kings of the Amorites, and to their land, when he destroyed them.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD will give them over to you, and you shall do to them according to the whole commandment that I have commanded you.<sup>6</sup>Be strong and courageous. Do not fear or be in dread of them, for it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you."<sup>7</sup>Then Moses summoned Joshua and said to him in the sight of all Israel, "Be strong and courageous, for you shall go with this people into the land that the LORD has sworn to their fathers to give them, and you shall put them in possession of it.<sup>8</sup>It is the LORD who goes before you. He will be with you; he will not leave you or forsake you. Do not fear or be dismayed."<sup>9</sup>Then Moses wrote this law and gave it to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and to all the elders of Israel.<sup>10</sup>And Moses commanded them, "At the end of every seven years, at the set time in the year of release, at the Feast of Booths,<sup>11</sup>when all Israel comes to appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose, you shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing.<sup>12</sup>Assemble the people, men, women, and little ones, and the sojourner within your towns, that they may hear and learn to fear the LORD your God, and be careful to do all the words of this law,<sup>13</sup>and that their children, who have not known it, may hear and learn to fear the LORD your God, as long as you live in the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess."<sup>14</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, the days approach when you must die. Call Joshua and present yourselves in the tent of meeting, that I may commission him." And Moses and Joshua went and presented themselves in the tent of meeting.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD appeared in the tent in a pillar of cloud. And the pillar of cloud stood over the entrance of the tent.<sup>16</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, you are about to lie down with your fathers. Then this people will rise and whore after the foreign gods among them in the land that they are entering, and they will forsake me and break my covenant that I have made with them.<sup>17</sup>Then my anger will be kindled against them in that day, and I will forsake them and hide my face from them, and they will be devoured. And many evils and troubles will come upon them, so that they will say in that day, 'Have not these evils come upon us because our God is not among us?'<sup>18</sup>And I will surely hide my face in that day because of all the evil that they have done, because they have turned to other gods.<sup>19</sup>"Now therefore write this song and teach it to the people of Israel. Put it in their mouths, that this song may be a witness for me against the people of Israel.<sup>20</sup>For when I have brought them into the land flowing with milk and honey, which I swore to give to their fathers, and they have eaten and are full and grown fat, they will turn to other gods and serve them, and despise me and break my covenant.<sup>21</sup>And when many evils and troubles have come upon them, this song shall confront them as a witness (for it will live unforgotten in the mouths of their offspring). For I know what they are inclined to do even today, before I have brought them into the land that I swore to give."<sup>22</sup>So Moses wrote this song the same day and taught it to the people of Israel.<sup>23</sup>And the LORD commissioned Joshua the son of Nun and said, "Be strong and courageous, for you shall bring the people of Israel into the land that I swore to give them. I will be with you."<sup>24</sup>When Moses had finished writing the words of this law in a book to the very end,<sup>25</sup>Moses commanded the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD,<sup>26</sup>"Take this Book of the Law and put it by the side of the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, that it may be there for a witness against you.<sup>27</sup>For I know how rebellious and stubborn you are. Behold, even today while I am yet alive with you, you have been rebellious against the LORD. How much more after my death!<sup>28</sup>Assemble to me all the elders of your tribes and your officers, that I may speak these words in their ears and call heaven and earth to witness against them.<sup>29</sup>For I know that after my death you will surely act corruptly and turn aside from the way that I have commanded you. And in the days to come evil will befall you, because you will do what is evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger through the work of your hands."<sup>30</sup>Then Moses spoke the words of this song until they were finished, in the ears of all the assembly of Israel:
31.overview:
Chapter 31 begins the closing scenes of Moses' life. At a hundred and twenty he commissions Joshua, deposits the written law beside the ark, and hears God foretell Israel's apostasy after his death.

The thread running through it is God's faithful presence, which outlasts both Moses' death and Israel's foreseen unfaithfulness.
31.theology:
God's faithful presence is the ground of courage. “Be strong and courageous… for it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you” (31:6, 8). Biblical courage is God-confidence, not self-confidence. The promise reverberates to every believer (Heb 13:5–6) and is fulfilled in Christ, Immanuel, who pledged, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

The written, preserved, proclaimed Word. Moses writes the law down and has it read to every generation, children and sojourners included (31:11–13). Scripture is God's enduring, authoritative witness, the means by which faith is passed from generation to generation (Rom 10:17; 1 Tim 4:13).

God's foreknowledge and grace. God foretells Israel's apostasy before they enter the land (31:16), yet covenants with them still and provides, in advance, the Song as a witness to recall them. The God who foreknew the full depth of our sin set his love on us anyway and provided in Christ the remedy for the very unfaithfulness he foresaw.
31.examples: Moses faced his own death and Israel's coming failure with the same confidence he gave Joshua. We face every uncertain future on the same ground: Christ is Immanuel, with us always, and his Spirit in us is the strength the command calls for. We treasure the Word read aloud as the means by which faith passes to our children.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses tells the nation he will not cross the Jordan: God himself will go before them, and Joshua will lead them. Then he charges Joshua in front of everybody with the words he has just given the people.
verseByVerse.theology: The command is given twice in eight verses, and its ground is never Israel’s strength: it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you. God repeats the whole charge to Joshua himself after Moses dies (Josh. 1:5-9).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a dying man told his successor to be brave, in public, and gave him the reason. Now: the same promise is the ground of every Christian’s courage, and we hold it with more light than Joshua had.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses continued to speak these words to all Israel. And he said to them, "I am 120 years old today. I am no longer able to go out and come in. The LORD has said to me, 'You shall not go over this Jordan.' The LORD your God himself will go over before you. He will destroy these nations before you, so that you shall dispossess them, and Joshua will go over at your head, as the LORD has spoken. And the LORD will do to them as he did to Sihon and Og, the kings of the Amorites, and to their land, when he destroyed them. And the LORD will give them over to you, and you shall do to them according to the whole commandment that I have commanded you. Be strong and courageous. Do not fear or be in dread of them, for it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you." Then Moses summoned Joshua and said to him in the sight of all Israel, "Be strong and courageous, for you shall go with this people into the land that the LORD has sworn to their fathers to give them, and you shall put them in possession of it. It is the LORD who goes before you. He will be with you; he will not leave you or forsake you. Do not fear or be dismayed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go out and come in is the language of leading in war and public life. Moses says he can no longer do it, though at his death his eye was still undimmed (34:7); the real reason is that the LORD has said he will not cross. What follows is the measure of him: no complaint, no revisiting of Meribah, straight into encouragement.

The command is to be brave; the reason is that somebody else is going. Moses then charges Joshua in the sight of all Israel, so the whole nation hears what its new leader has been promised. It is the last kindness of a leader who will not see the outcome.

Moses, the giver of the law, can bring the people to the border but not across it; another must lead them in. Hebrews observes that even Joshua did not give them the final rest (Heb. 4:8), and points to the One who does. In Greek the two names are the same: Jesus is the greater Joshua, who brings his people into a rest no river or grave can keep them from.

When Hebrews quotes the promise, it applies it, unexpectedly, to money: Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Heb. 13:5). The word given to a man about to invade a country is handed to Christians worrying about the bills, on the grounds that it is the same promise and the same God.

The conquest was God’s unique judgment through Israel at one moment in history. It gives no warrant for violence in God’s name today (John 18:36).
verseByVerse.note: Moses' 120 years fall into three forties: in Egypt, in Midian, and in the wilderness (Acts 7:23, 30, 36).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — Read This Law Every Seven Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses writes the law down and gives it to the priests and elders, with instructions: at the Feast of Booths every seventh year, read it aloud to the whole assembly — men, women, little ones, and the sojourner.
verseByVerse.theology: The reason for gathering everybody is stated twice: that they may hear and learn to fear the LORD, and that their children, who have not known it, may hear and learn. Faith is passed on by hearing long before it is grasped.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a nation gathered every seven years and simply listened to Scripture read from beginning to end. Now: the public reading of the Word is still commanded (1 Tim. 4:13) and is still the thing most easily crowded out of a service.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses wrote this law and gave it to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and to all the elders of Israel. And Moses commanded them, "At the end of every seven years, at the set time in the year of release, at the Feast of Booths, when all Israel comes to appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose, you shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing. Assemble the people, men, women, and little ones, and the sojourner within your towns, that they may hear and learn to fear the LORD your God, and be careful to do all the words of this law, and that their children, who have not known it, may hear and learn to fear the LORD your God, as long as you live in the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The harvest festival, when the nation is gathered anyway, becomes a long reading in the open to an enormous crowd. The striking part is who must be there: the little ones, who will fidget and understand almost nothing, are required to come. A child who has sat under Scripture from before he could follow it has something in him that a child who arrived at fifteen does not, and God builds that into the national calendar.

And the sojourner is there too — the foreigner living among them, who has no covenant claim and is included anyway, hearing the law of a God who was not his by birth.

Nehemiah 8 is this command being kept, centuries later, after the exile: Ezra standing on a wooden platform from early morning until midday, reading the Book of the Law to the assembly, both men and women and all who could understand what they heard, and the people weeping as they listened. They simply read the Bible aloud, and it broke them.

Did Moses write Deuteronomy? Many scholars hold that it was written in the seventh century BC and “found” in the temple under Josiah (2 Kgs 22) to support his reforms. The book itself says Moses wrote this law (31:9, 24), and Jesus speaks of it as Moses’ (Mark 10:3–5). Its covenant shape resembles treaties of the second millennium BC, though scholars also point to likenesses with seventh-century Assyrian treaties, so that argument is not decisive either way. The book also has a narrator who speaks of Moses in the third person (1:1–5), and the account of Moses’ death (ch. 34) was added by a later inspired hand, perhaps Joshua; how much editing there was, and when, is still debated among faithful scholars. This commentary holds that the substance is Moses’, as the book and our Lord say, and that what Josiah found was a neglected copy of an old book, which is why its words terrified him (2 Kgs 22:11–13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–23 — A Song for a Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Moses plainly that Israel will forsake him after Moses dies — and commissions a song to be taught to the nation, so that when the evils come the words will already be in their mouths.
verseByVerse.theology: God plants the testimony before the sin: it will live unforgotten in the mouths of their offspring, so that when they need it they will find they already know it by heart.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God buried the truth in a tune because he knew where they were going. Now: he still gives his people songs to carry them where sermons cannot reach.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, the days approach when you must die. Call Joshua and present yourselves in the tent of meeting, that I may commission him." And Moses and Joshua went and presented themselves in the tent of meeting. And the LORD appeared in the tent in a pillar of cloud. And the pillar of cloud stood over the entrance of the tent. And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, you are about to lie down with your fathers. Then this people will rise and whore after the foreign gods among them in the land that they are entering, and they will forsake me and break my covenant that I have made with them. Then my anger will be kindled against them in that day, and I will forsake them and hide my face from them, and they will be devoured. And many evils and troubles will come upon them, so that they will say in that day, 'Have not these evils come upon us because our God is not among us?' And I will surely hide my face in that day because of all the evil that they have done, because they have turned to other gods. "Now therefore write this song and teach it to the people of Israel. Put it in their mouths, that this song may be a witness for me against the people of Israel. For when I have brought them into the land flowing with milk and honey, which I swore to give to their fathers, and they have eaten and are full and grown fat, they will turn to other gods and serve them, and despise me and break my covenant. And when many evils and troubles have come upon them, this song shall confront them as a witness (for it will live unforgotten in the mouths of their offspring). For I know what they are inclined to do even today, before I have brought them into the land that I swore to give." So Moses wrote this song the same day and taught it to the people of Israel. And the LORD commissioned Joshua the son of Nun and said, "Be strong and courageous, for you shall bring the people of Israel into the land that I swore to give them. I will be with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not "may" but "will": on the day he commissions Joshua, God states that this nation will abandon him, and when. The cause is the diagnosis of chapter 8: not persecution but prosperity, when they are full and grown fat.

Facing certain betrayal, God does not withdraw the covenant or reduce the promises. He commissions a song and has it memorised, because songs last: sermons are forgotten and laws shelved, but a tune learned in childhood comes back unbidden.

Anyone who has sat with a dying believer whose memory has largely gone, and heard them join in a hymn they learned as a child, knows that God was right about this. What we sing in health is what we will have in the dark — which is a serious argument for being careful about what the church sings.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — The Book Beside the Ark
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The finished book is placed beside the ark as a witness, and Moses tells the elders bluntly what he expects of them after his death.
verseByVerse.theology: Moses’ farewell assessment is unsparing: even today while I am yet alive with you, you have been rebellious… How much more after my death!
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the last act of Israel’s greatest leader was to leave a written record that would outlive and outrank him. Now: the same book is still beside us, and still says what it said whether we like it or not.

verseByVerse.quote: When Moses had finished writing the words of this law in a book to the very end, Moses commanded the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, "Take this Book of the Law and put it by the side of the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, that it may be there for a witness against you. For I know how rebellious and stubborn you are. Behold, even today while I am yet alive with you, you have been rebellious against the LORD. How much more after my death! Assemble to me all the elders of your tribes and your officers, that I may speak these words in their ears and call heaven and earth to witness against them. For I know that after my death you will surely act corruptly and turn aside from the way that I have commanded you. And in the days to come evil will befall you, because you will do what is evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger through the work of your hands." Then Moses spoke the words of this song until they were finished, in the ears of all the assembly of Israel:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tablets went inside the ark; the book goes alongside, where it can be taken out, read, and produced in evidence. Israel now has a written record of the terms, kept at the holiest place in the nation, that will outlive every person present.

There is no flattery in his farewell. He tells them it will be worse when he is gone, and he leaves a book so that nobody can say they were not told. There is a hard love in that: what they need is not his good opinion but the truth in writing.

And the book is still here. It has outlived Moses, and Joshua, and the monarchy, and the exile, and every empire that has handled it since.

The same verdict stands over us: none of us keeps this book as it deserves (Eccl. 7:20). But the God who foresaw Israel's rebellion and kept his covenant anyway has given his Son, who kept the law perfectly in our place and whose obedience is counted ours (Rom. 5:19). So the witness that accuses us also sends us back by confession to the mercy it promised (30:1–3; 1 John 1:9).

A God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is he.<sup>5</sup>They have dealt corruptly with him; they are no longer his children because they are blemished; they are a crooked and twisted generation.<sup>6</sup>Do you thus repay the LORD, you foolish and senseless people? Is not he your father, who created you, who made you and established you?<sup>7</sup>Remember the days of old; consider the years of many generations; ask your father, and he will show you, your elders, and they will tell you.<sup>8</sup>When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance, when he divided mankind, he fixed the borders of the peoples according to the number of the sons of God.<sup>9</sup>But the LORD's portion is his people, Jacob his allotted heritage.<sup>10</sup>"He found him in a desert land, and in the howling waste of the wilderness; So I will make them jealous with those who are no people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.<sup>22</sup>For a fire is kindled by my anger, and it burns to the depths of Sheol, devours the earth and its increase, and sets on fire the foundations of the mountains.<sup>23</sup>"'And I will heap disasters upon them;
