for the day of their calamity is at hand, and their doom comes swiftly.'<sup>36</sup>For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants, when he sees that their power is gone and there is none remaining, bond or free.<sup>37</sup>Then he will say, 'Where are their gods, the rock in which they took refuge,<sup>38</sup>who ate the fat of their sacrifices and drank the wine of their drink offering? Let them rise up and help you; let them be your protection!<sup>39</sup>"'See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me; I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand.<sup>40</sup>For I lift up my hand to heaven and swear, As I live forever,<sup>41</sup>if I sharpen my flashing sword and my hand takes hold on judgment, I will take vengeance on my adversaries and will repay those who hate me.<sup>42</sup>I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh— with the blood of the slain and the captives, from the long-haired heads of the enemy.'<sup>43</sup>"Rejoice with him, O heavens; bow down to him, all gods, for he avenges the blood of his children and takes vengeance on his adversaries. He repays those who hate him and cleanses his people's land."<sup>44</sup>Moses came and recited all the words of this song in the hearing of the people, he and Joshua the son of Nun.<sup>45</sup>And when Moses had finished speaking all these words to all Israel,<sup>46</sup>he said to them, "Take to heart all the words by which I am warning you today, that you may command them to your children, that they may be careful to do all the words of this law.<sup>47</sup>For it is no empty word for you, but your very life, and by this word you shall live long in the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess."<sup>48</sup>That very day the LORD spoke to Moses,<sup>49</sup>"Go up this mountain of the Abarim, Mount Nebo, which is in the land of Moab, opposite Jericho, and view the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the people of Israel for a possession.<sup>50</sup>And die on the mountain which you go up, and be gathered to your people, as Aaron your brother died in Mount Hor and was gathered to his people,<sup>51</sup>because you broke faith with me in the midst of the people of Israel at the waters of Meribah-kadesh, in the wilderness of Zin, and because you did not treat me as holy in the midst of the people of Israel.<sup>52</sup>For you shall see the land before you, but you shall not go there, into the land that I am giving to the people of Israel."
32.overview:
Chapter 32 is the Song of Moses, a poem rehearsing God's faithfulness and Israel's unfaithfulness. Commanded as a witness (ch. 31), it was to be learned by heart, so that even in apostasy the truth about God and about themselves would remain on Israel's lips.

It moves from God's character and care, through Israel's ingratitude and the judgment it brings, to the hope that God will atone for his land and people (32:43).
32.theology:
The Rock whose work is perfect. “The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice” (32:4). When we cannot trace his hand in trial or judgment, we trust his character: the Rock does not move (32:39).

The tender love of God and the tragedy of ingratitude. God kept Israel as the apple of his eye (32:10–11), yet Jeshurun grew fat and kicked (32:15). Prosperity, not affliction, turned them away, and God's lavish love makes ingratitude the basest folly.

Vengeance belongs to God; the song of Moses and the Lamb. “Vengeance is mine, and recompense” (32:35): the righteous Judge will settle every account. Yet the song ends with God atoning for his people (32:43), and the redeemed will sing it with the song of the Lamb (Rev 15:3), celebrating the final exodus victory secured by Christ.
32.examples: Israel was given this song to learn by heart; so, in a sense, are we. We rest on the Rock when we cannot trace his hand, marvel that he found us in our lostness, guard against the prosperity that breeds ingratitude, and leave vengeance to the righteous Judge. One day, in Christ, we will sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Rock, and the Eagle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song opens by calling heaven and earth to listen, names God the Rock whose work is perfect, and then tells the story of how he found Israel in a howling waste and carried her like an eagle carrying its young.
verseByVerse.theology: The Rock is the song’s controlling name for God and appears five times. Against it stands the tenderness of vv. 10-11, the eye guarded and the eagle catching its young: strength and tenderness in one God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a nation was told what it had been found as and what had carried it. Now: the same two things are still true of every believer, and both are needed — a Rock that does not move, and wings underneath when the nest is stirred.

verseByVerse.quote: "Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak, and let the earth hear the words of my mouth. May my teaching drop as the rain, my speech distill as the dew, like gentle rain upon the tender grass, and like showers upon the herb. For I will proclaim the name of the LORD; ascribe greatness to our God! "The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is he. They have dealt corruptly with him; they are no longer his children because they are blemished; they are a crooked and twisted generation. Do you thus repay the LORD, you foolish and senseless people? Is not he your father, who created you, who made you and established you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song opens by summoning the universe as an audience — and as witnesses, since Moses has already called heaven and earth to testify against Israel (4:26; 30:19; 31:28). Everything that exists is told to listen.

His image for his own preaching is rain, not a hammer: after a chapter telling this nation exactly what it is, he wants his words to soak in slowly and make something grow.

A rock does not move, does not erode in a season, does not give under pressure; in a desert it is also the only shade there is. And Paul, recalling the wilderness, says of the rock that followed Israel, the Rock was Christ (1 Cor. 10:4): the name this song gives God is a name the New Testament gives the Son.

The song establishes God’s character before a word of accusation is spoken, so Israel’s corruption is measured against a standard already set. Then the question of verse 6 is a father’s, not a judge’s: the language of a parent who cannot understand what has happened.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember the days of old; consider the years of many generations; ask your father, and he will show you, your elders, and they will tell you. When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance, when he divided mankind, he fixed the borders of the peoples according to the number of the sons of God. But the LORD's portion is his people, Jacob his allotted heritage. "He found him in a desert land, and in the howling waste of the wilderness; he encircled him, he cared for him, he kept him as the apple of his eye. Like an eagle that stirs up its nest, that flutters over its young, spreading out its wings, catching them, bearing them on its pinions, the LORD alone guided him, no foreign god was with him. He made him ride on the high places of the land, and he ate the produce of the field, and he suckled him with honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock. Curds from the herd, and milk from the flock, with fat of lambs, rams of Bashan and goats, with the very finest of the wheat— and you drank foaming wine made from the blood of the grape.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The story of how God got them is told in two images to be held together.

The first is that God found him. He did not choose the best of the nations; he found him in a howling waste, where you find things nobody is looking for. Then three verbs of protection, as a man guards the pupil of his own eye, the most instinctively defended thing on a human body.

The eagle stirs the nest deliberately. It makes the comfortable place uncomfortable so the young will fly, and then it hovers underneath — and when a fledgling drops, it goes below and takes the weight on its own back.

Both halves of that are God. The stirring of the nest is his; so are the wings underneath. Any believer who has had a settled situation broken up and could not see why should read verse 11 slowly. The disturbance and the catching are done by the same bird.

Verses 13–14 describe a feast. This is what Israel had, and the next verse is what she did with it.

Who are the “sons of God”? The standard Hebrew text reads “sons of Israel”; the ESV follows the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek translation, which read “sons of God”. The latter is most likely original. Many think the sense is that God set the nations under heavenly powers, while keeping Israel as the LORD’s portion (v. 9), and that such powers stand behind the gods the nations worshipped (v. 17; 1 Cor 10:20); others take the sons of God as angels appointed to serve. The details are debated. In Christ the nations are being reclaimed for their true King (Col 2:15).
verseByVerse.note: On the two readings, “sons of God” and “sons of Israel”, see above.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–25 — Jeshurun Grew Fat, and Kicked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The turn of the song. Israel — here called Jeshurun — grows fat, sleek and prosperous, and kicks the God who fed her, sacrificing to demons and forgetting the Rock that bore you.
verseByVerse.theology: Paul quotes v.21 — God provoking Israel to jealousy with those who are no people — to explain the Gentile mission (Rom. 10:19).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the nation called by a pet name grew sleek and kicked. Now: the danger is the same. Almost nobody is argued out of faith; a great many are fed out of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked; you grew fat, stout, and sleek; then he forsook God who made him and scoffed at the Rock of his salvation. They stirred him to jealousy with strange gods; with abominations they provoked him to anger. They sacrificed to demons that were not God, to gods they had never known, to new gods that had come recently, whom your fathers had never dreaded. You were unmindful of the Rock that bore you, and you forgot the God who gave you birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeshurun is a pet name for Israel, probably meaning “upright one”, used only four times in the Bible. God calls his people by a name of affection at the exact moment he describes their worst behaviour.

The image is a beast fed until it is sleek and strong, which then kicks the man with the bucket. Not corrupt, not oppressed, not deceived: well fed. It is the diagnosis of chapters 6, 8 and 31, and the repetition is the point: Deuteronomy’s great warning is not about persecution.

There is a sneer in new gods that had come recently: they left the Rock, which is old and does not move, for gods that had only just arrived. And in the saddest line of the song the verb is a mother’s: God describes himself as the one who went through labour to give them birth, and says they forgot him — which is a thing you can do to a person without ever deciding to.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD saw it and spurned them, because of the provocation of his sons and his daughters. And he said, 'I will hide my face from them; I will see what their end will be, for they are a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness. They have made me jealous with what is no god; they have provoked me to anger with their idols. So I will make them jealous with those who are no people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation. For a fire is kindled by my anger, and it burns to the depths of Sheol, devours the earth and its increase, and sets on fire the foundations of the mountains. "'And I will heap disasters upon them; I will spend my arrows on them; they shall be wasted with hunger, and devoured by plague and poisonous pestilence; I will send the teeth of beasts against them, with the venom of things that crawl in the dust. Outdoors the sword shall bereave, and indoors terror, for young man and woman alike, the nursing child with the man of gray hairs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The punishment mirrors the crime exactly. They went after a nothing-god; God will go after a no-people. Paul quotes this verse in Romans as the Old Testament’s own prediction of the Gentile mission — First Moses says, “I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation” (Rom. 10:19). The church of the nations was in the Song of Moses before it was in anybody’s plan but God’s.

The judgment itself is described without flinching. The song does not spare the reader, because the God who inspired it did not spare the nation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–43 — I Would Have Wiped Them Out, But…
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God says he would have scattered them entirely, except that he would not give their enemies the satisfaction of saying Our hand is triumphant, it was not the LORD who did all this.
verseByVerse.theology: At the centre of the section stands v.35, Vengeance is mine, and recompense, which the New Testament quotes twice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a nation was spared for the sake of God’s reputation rather than its own record. Now: that is still the only ground any of us stands on, and it is a far steadier one than merit.

verseByVerse.quote: I would have said, "I will cut them to pieces; I will wipe them from human memory," had I not feared provocation by the enemy, lest their adversaries should misunderstand, lest they should say, "Our hand is triumphant, it was not the LORD who did all this."' "For they are a nation void of counsel, and there is no understanding in them. If they were wise, they would understand this; they would discern their latter end! How could one have chased a thousand, and two have put ten thousand to flight, unless their Rock had sold them, and the LORD had given them up? For their rock is not as our Rock; our enemies are by themselves. For their vine comes from the vine of Sodom and from the fields of Gomorrah; their grapes are grapes of poison; their clusters are bitter; their wine is the poison of serpents and the cruel venom of asps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses stop the judgment in mid-sentence, and they are the reason Israel survived. Not her repentance — the song does not mention any. Not her value. God will not destroy her because he will not have his enemies draw the wrong conclusion and credit themselves.

That is a mercy grounded entirely outside its object, and it is exactly the ground Moses had pleaded at Sinai (9:28). It looks like a lesser reason for sparing somebody, and is in fact the sturdiest, because it does not depend on the person spared.

The bleak verdict on the nations (vv. 32–33) stops anyone imagining the alternative to Israel was better.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Is not this laid up in store with me, sealed up in my treasuries? Vengeance is mine, and recompense, for the time when their foot shall slip; for the day of their calamity is at hand, and their doom comes swiftly.' For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants, when he sees that their power is gone and there is none remaining, bond or free. Then he will say, 'Where are their gods, the rock in which they took refuge, who ate the fat of their sacrifices and drank the wine of their drink offering? Let them rise up and help you; let them be your protection!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The New Testament uses these words twice, in two directions. Paul quotes them to forbid personal revenge: Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord” (Rom. 12:19). The logic is not that the wrong does not matter. It is that it matters far too much to be left to us. Vengeance belongs to somebody with perfect information and no personal stake, and that is none of us. The God who will repay has already borne the wrong done by us in his Son, and by his Spirit he enables the wronged to bless instead of curse (Rom. 12:14, 21).

Hebrews quotes the same words as a warning to the church: For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.”… It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb. 10:30–31).

The same sentence comforts the wronged and warns the presumptuous, and both uses are right.

Verse 36 is the turn of the whole song, and its timing matters. God moves when their strength is gone: not while they still had options, reserves, or a plan. He waits until there is nothing left of them at all, and then he has compassion. That is his characteristic timing throughout Scripture. He is not slow. He is waiting for the point at which nobody, including you, will be able to attribute the rescue to anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: "'See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me; I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand. For I lift up my hand to heaven and swear, As I live forever, if I sharpen my flashing sword and my hand takes hold on judgment, I will take vengeance on my adversaries and will repay those who hate me. I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh— with the blood of the slain and the captives, from the long-haired heads of the enemy.' "Rejoice with him, O heavens; bow down to him, all gods, for he avenges the blood of his children and takes vengeance on his adversaries. He repays those who hate him and cleanses his people's land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The summit of the song is spoken by God himself, and few sentences in the Old Testament are more absolute. Two pairs, held in one hand: killing and making alive, wounding and healing. God does not divide the world between his sphere and somebody else’s. There is no rival deity operating the bad half, and no accident outside his reach.

That is a hard doctrine and it is also the only real comfort available, and Job understood both halves of it at the worst hour of his life: Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil? (Job 2:10). A God who is sovereign only over the pleasant things could not be trusted with the rest.

And none that can deliver out of my hand reads as a threat until you hear it in the mouth of the Son: no one will snatch them out of my hand… and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand (John 10:28–29). The same grip, from the inside.

The New Testament will not leave the final call alone. Paul quotes it to prove that the Gentiles were always meant to be included — Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people (Rom. 15:10) — and Hebrews takes the line about worship and applies it to Christ: Let all God’s angels worship him (Heb. 1:6).

The last time this song appears in Scripture, it is being sung beside a sea of glass: the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb (Rev. 15:3). The piece God commissioned because he knew his people would forget him turns out to be one of the two songs of heaven.

Is God bloodthirsty? Lines about arrows drunk with blood are hard to read, and they should be. This is the poetry of judgment on enemies who persist against him, written so that wrong is not simply passed over. Revelation shows Christ coming in the same way, clothed in a robe dipped in blood (Rev 19:13); the church leaves vengeance to him (Rom 12:19).
verseByVerse.note: The Masoretic Hebrew text lacks “bow down to him, all gods” (ESV note); the longer wording is quoted in Hebrews.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 44–52 — The Song Taught, and the Mountain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses recites the whole song to Israel with Joshua beside him, calls it your very life, and is told the same day to climb Mount Nebo, look at the land, and die there.
verseByVerse.theology: His last verdict on Scripture is that it is no empty word for you, but your very life. Then the sentence of Meribah is restated without softening (see 3:26).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a man finished the song, handed over the book, and climbed a mountain to die outside the land. Now: the sentence was not the last word, as the end of the chapter shows.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses came and recited all the words of this song in the hearing of the people, he and Joshua the son of Nun. And when Moses had finished speaking all these words to all Israel, he said to them, "Take to heart all the words by which I am warning you today, that you may command them to your children, that they may be careful to do all the words of this law. For it is no empty word for you, but your very life, and by this word you shall live long in the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess." That very day the LORD spoke to Moses, "Go up this mountain of the Abarim, Mount Nebo, which is in the land of Moab, opposite Jericho, and view the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the people of Israel for a possession. And die on the mountain which you go up, and be gathered to your people, as Aaron your brother died in Mount Hor and was gathered to his people, because you broke faith with me in the midst of the people of Israel at the waters of Meribah-kadesh, in the wilderness of Zin, and because you did not treat me as holy in the midst of the people of Israel. For you shall see the land before you, but you shall not go there, into the land that I am giving to the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is Moses' verdict on Scripture, given on the last day he will ever teach: not important, not helpful, not a resource, but life. The word is life because it comes from the God who redeemed them, and the same God would one day write it on the heart by his Spirit (Jer. 31:33).

The same day God sends him up Nebo to die. The reason, Meribah, is restated in God's own words, and Moses lets it stand without defence. He has asked once (3:25) and been told not to raise it again, and he does not. Then the last, aching clause: he will see the land but not go there.

That is the sentence he lives under and dies under, and the book does not resolve it. It is resolved somewhere else entirely, on a different mountain, where two men appeared in glory and talked with Jesus about his departure — and one of them was Moses, standing on a mountain inside the land (Luke 9:30–31). He got there in the end. He came in with the Christ he had been writing about, and by then the Jordan was not the point.

33.title: The Blessing of Moses: The Eternal God Is Your Dwelling Place
33.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the blessing with which Moses the man of God blessed the people of Israel before his death.<sup>2</sup>He said, "The LORD came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon us; he shone forth from Mount Paran; he came from the ten thousands of holy ones, with flaming fire at his right hand.<sup>3</sup>Yes, he loved his people, all his holy ones were in his hand; so they followed in your steps, receiving direction from you,<sup>4</sup>when Moses commanded us a law, as a possession for the assembly of Jacob.<sup>5</sup>Thus the LORD became king in Jeshurun, when the heads of the people were gathered, all the tribes of Israel together.<sup>6</sup>"Let Reuben live, and not die, but let his men be few."<sup>7</sup>And this he said of Judah: "Hear, O LORD, the voice of Judah, and bring him in to his people. With your hands contend for him, and be a help against his adversaries."<sup>8</sup>And of Levi he said, "Give to Levi your Thummim, and your Urim to your godly one, whom you tested at Massah, with whom you quarreled at the waters of Meribah;<sup>9</sup>who said of his father and mother, 'I regard them not'; he disowned his brothers and ignored his children. For they observed your word and kept your covenant.<sup>10</sup>They shall teach Jacob your rules and Israel your law; they shall put incense before you and whole burnt offerings on your altar.<sup>11</sup>Bless, O LORD, his substance, and accept the work of his hands; crush the loins of his adversaries, of those who hate him, that they rise not again."<sup>12</sup>Of Benjamin he said, "The beloved of the LORD dwells in safety. The High God surrounds him all day long, and dwells between his shoulders."<sup>13</sup>And of Joseph he said, "Blessed by the LORD be his land, with the choicest gifts of heaven above, and of the deep that crouches beneath,<sup>14</sup>with the choicest fruits of the sun and the rich yield of the months,<sup>15</sup>with the finest produce of the ancient mountains and the abundance of the everlasting hills,<sup>16</sup>with the best gifts of the earth and its fullness and the favor of him who dwells in the bush. May these rest on the head of Joseph, on the pate of him who is prince among his brothers.<sup>17</sup>A firstborn bull —he has majesty, and his horns are the horns of a wild ox; with them he shall gore the peoples, all of them, to the ends of the earth; they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh."<sup>18</sup>And of Zebulun he said, "Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar, in your tents.<sup>19</sup>They shall call peoples to their mountain; there they offer right sacrifices; for they draw from the abundance of the seas and the hidden treasures of the sand."<sup>20</sup>And of Gad he said, "Blessed be he who enlarges Gad! Gad crouches like a lion; he tears off arm and scalp.<sup>21</sup>He chose the best of the land for himself, for there a commander's portion was reserved; and he came with the heads of the people, with Israel he executed the justice of the LORD, and his judgments for Israel."<sup>22</sup>And of Dan he said, "Dan is a lion's cub that leaps from Bashan."<sup>23</sup>And of Naphtali he said, "O Naphtali, sated with favor, and full of the blessing of the LORD, possess the lake and the south."<sup>24</sup>And of Asher he said, "Most blessed of sons be Asher; let him be the favorite of his brothers, and let him dip his foot in oil.<sup>25</sup>Your bars shall be iron and bronze, and as your days, so shall your strength be.<sup>26</sup>"There is none like God, O Jeshurun, who rides through the heavens to your help, through the skies in his majesty.<sup>27</sup>The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms. And he thrust out the enemy before you and said, 'Destroy.'<sup>28</sup>So Israel lived in safety, Jacob lived alone, in a land of grain and wine, whose heavens drop down dew.<sup>29</sup>Happy are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD, the shield of your help, and the sword of your triumph! Your enemies shall come fawning to you, and you shall tread upon their backs."
33.overview:
Chapter 33 is the Blessing of Moses, his last words over the tribes, in the manner of Jacob's blessing (Gen 49). After the song of Israel's failure, he blesses each tribe in hope of their life in the land.

A prologue celebrates the LORD's coming at Sinai and his kingship over Jeshurun (33:5). The tribes are then blessed one by one, each according to its character and calling. The close (33:26–29) is among the most comforting passages in Scripture.
33.theology:
The eternal God is our dwelling place. Our true home is not a place but a Person; the eternal God is our secure, unchanging refuge (cf. Ps 90:1), and there is none like him (33:26).

God's majesty and intimate love. The God who rides through the heavens (33:26) is the God who loved his people and holds them in his hand (33:3), carrying his beloved on his shoulders (33:12). Transcendent majesty and tender, intimate love meet in the God who reigns as King over his people (33:5).

Strength proportioned to each day. God supplies grace sufficient for each day's need, mercies new every morning (33:25; Lam 3:23; 2 Cor 12:9).
33.examples: Our home is the eternal God himself, who upholds us beneath every weakness and fall, as he upheld the tribes Moses blessed. We trust his grace for each day as it comes, and rejoice that we are a people saved by the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The LORD Came from Sinai
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses opens his last words with a picture of God coming from Sinai in fire and holy ones — and then the reason for all of it: Yes, he loved his people.
verseByVerse.theology: The blessing begins where Deuteronomy began, at the mountain, and states the ground of the covenant in five words. Verse 5 names what came of it: the LORD became king in Jeshurun.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a nation was told, before a single tribe was blessed, that the whole thing rested on God’s love for them. Now: the order is unchanged — we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: This is the blessing with which Moses the man of God blessed the people of Israel before his death. He said, "The LORD came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon us; he shone forth from Mount Paran; he came from the ten thousands of holy ones, with flaming fire at his right hand. Yes, he loved his people, all his holy ones were in his hand; so they followed in your steps, receiving direction from you, when Moses commanded us a law, as a possession for the assembly of Jacob. Thus the LORD became king in Jeshurun, when the heads of the people were gathered, all the tribes of Israel together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last thing Moses does is bless them. After forty years of grumbling, rebellion, a golden calf, a refused land and a sentence on himself that they caused, the final act of his life is to go round the tribes one at a time and speak good over each of them.

The verbs of the opening are sunrise verbs, dawned and shone forth: God coming over the horizon with an army of angels behind him. Then, in the middle of all that fire, five plain words: Yes, he loved his people. That is the ground of everything that follows, stated before a single tribe is named; not their record, which the previous chapter has just demolished in verse. He loved them.

Verse 5 is Israel’s constitution in a line. Israel’s first form of government was not a monarchy. God was king, and every human king afterwards ruled as a deputy under a law he had to copy out by hand (17:18). When Israel later asked for a king like all the nations, God told Samuel exactly what had happened: they have rejected me from being king over them (1 Sam. 8:7). This verse is what they gave up.

But the King they set aside came back in person. The Son of David, who is also David’s Lord, rode into Jerusalem as its king and was crucified under the title King of the Jews (John 19:19), and he now reigns over a people gathered from every tribe and nation. In him the LORD is king in Jeshurun again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–25 — The Tribes Blessed One by One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Each tribe is named and given a word, from Judah brought to his people to Asher dipping his foot in oil.
verseByVerse.theology: The blessings differ as the tribes differ: some are brief, one tribe is missing, and the fullest words go to Levi and Joseph.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a dying man went round the family one by one and had something to say to each. Now: the God who turned Levi’s curse into a calling has not changed his habits with people whose history is against them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let Reuben live, and not die, but let his men be few." And this he said of Judah: "Hear, O LORD, the voice of Judah, and bring him in to his people. With your hands contend for him, and be a help against his adversaries." And of Levi he said, "Give to Levi your Thummim, and your Urim to your godly one, whom you tested at Massah, with whom you quarreled at the waters of Meribah; who said of his father and mother, 'I regard them not'; he disowned his brothers and ignored his children. For they observed your word and kept your covenant. They shall teach Jacob your rules and Israel your law; they shall put incense before you and whole burnt offerings on your altar. Bless, O LORD, his substance, and accept the work of his hands; crush the loins of his adversaries, of those who hate him, that they rise not again." Of Benjamin he said, "The beloved of the LORD dwells in safety. The High God surrounds him all day long, and dwells between his shoulders." And of Joseph he said, "Blessed by the LORD be his land, with the choicest gifts of heaven above, and of the deep that crouches beneath, with the choicest fruits of the sun and the rich yield of the months, with the finest produce of the ancient mountains and the abundance of the everlasting hills, with the best gifts of the earth and its fullness and the favor of him who dwells in the bush. May these rest on the head of Joseph, on the pate of him who is prince among his brothers. A firstborn bull —he has majesty, and his horns are the horns of a wild ox; with them he shall gore the peoples, all of them, to the ends of the earth; they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reuben, the firstborn who lost his place, gets a prayer that he will not disappear altogether. And Simeon is not mentioned at all, perhaps because the tribe was already fading: a Simeonite chief had sinned openly at Peor (Num. 25:14), its numbers had fallen from 59,300 to 22,200 in a generation, and it would later be absorbed into Judah (Josh. 19:1, 9).

Judah gets a soldier’s blessing. But the astonishing one is Levi. On Jacob’s deathbed the same tribe heard this: Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of violence are their swords… Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce… I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel (Gen. 49:5–7). Levi was cursed by his own father, for a massacre at Shechem, and sentenced to be scattered.

Here he is blessed, holding the Urim and Thummim, teaching the law and standing at the altar, and scattered, exactly as Jacob said, into forty-eight cities in every tribe, which turned out to be how the whole nation got taught.

God did not cancel the sentence. He kept it and converted it. The scattering that was a punishment became the mechanism of Israel’s instruction, and the tribe with the worst family history in the nation ended up carrying the ark. Anybody whose past is genuinely against him should hold on to that.

The Thummim and Urim were the sacred lots in the high priest’s breastpiece, used to seek God’s decision (Exod 28:30; Num 27:21).

verseByVerse.quote: And of Zebulun he said, "Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar, in your tents. They shall call peoples to their mountain; there they offer right sacrifices; for they draw from the abundance of the seas and the hidden treasures of the sand." And of Gad he said, "Blessed be he who enlarges Gad! Gad crouches like a lion; he tears off arm and scalp. He chose the best of the land for himself, for there a commander's portion was reserved; and he came with the heads of the people, with Israel he executed the justice of the LORD, and his judgments for Israel." And of Dan he said, "Dan is a lion's cub that leaps from Bashan." And of Naphtali he said, "O Naphtali, sated with favor, and full of the blessing of the LORD, possess the lake and the south." And of Asher he said, "Most blessed of sons be Asher; let him be the favorite of his brothers, and let him dip his foot in oil. Your bars shall be iron and bronze, and as your days, so shall your strength be.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessings are full of the physical goodness of the land, exactly what a dying man in a desert would want to say to people about to inherit a country. Asher gets the most homely: olive oil so plentiful you could paddle in it, and then the promise that has comforted more people than anything else in this chapter.

The strength is issued to match the days, as they come. It is not a reservoir handed over in advance, which is what most of us would prefer and would certainly misuse; it is enough for today, and then enough for tomorrow when tomorrow arrives. The strength is not in you and it is not stockpiled anywhere you can inspect. It is issued daily, and it has never yet failed to arrive. That is the same arrangement as the manna, and the same as give us this day our daily bread.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–29 — Underneath Are the Everlasting Arms
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The blessing closes with God riding through the heavens to help his people, the eternal God as their dwelling place, and everlasting arms underneath.
verseByVerse.theology: Three images in one breath: a God who rides to the rescue, a God who is himself the house they live in, and arms beneath them that do not tire.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a nation with no home of its own was told that God was the dwelling place. Now: the arms are still underneath, and in Christ the eternal God has shown how far they will reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "There is none like God, O Jeshurun, who rides through the heavens to your help, through the skies in his majesty. The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms. And he thrust out the enemy before you and said, 'Destroy.' So Israel lived in safety, Jacob lived alone, in a land of grain and wine, whose heavens drop down dew. Happy are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD, the shield of your help, and the sword of your triumph! Your enemies shall come fawning to you, and you shall tread upon their backs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last words of Moses are among the loveliest in Scripture. He calls them by the affectionate name one final time — Jeshurun — the same name the Song used when it said they grew fat and kicked. Both are true, and the last time Moses uses it, it is in a sentence about God riding to their rescue.

Verse 27's two images work in opposite directions. God is the dwelling place — the house you live in, which is around you and over you. And underneath there are everlasting arms — which is the picture of a father carrying a child, the same image as 1:31, returning at the very end.

After forty years in tents, the men listening had never had an address. Moses tells them that the God they have been following is the house, and that he was underneath them the whole time.

And the arms are everlasting. Arms tire; a father carrying a sleeping child eventually has to put him down. These do not, which is why the verse has been read beside so many deathbeds.

After all the curses and the song and the sentence on himself, the final word of the man who gave Israel the law is a beatitude, not a warning. Happy are you. Not because of what they are — the last thirty chapters have settled that — but because of whose they are. A people saved by the LORD. That is his last public sentence, and there is nothing else in it about them at all.

34.title: The Death of Moses: The Law Could Not Bring Them In
34.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho. And the LORD showed him all the land, Gilead as far as Dan,<sup>2</sup>all Naphtali, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah as far as the western sea,<sup>3</sup>the Negeb, and the Plain, that is, the Valley of Jericho the city of palm trees, as far as Zoar.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD said to him, "This is the land of which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, 'I will give it to your offspring.' I have let you see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there."<sup>5</sup>So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD,<sup>6</sup>and he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab opposite Beth-peor; but no one knows the place of his burial to this day.<sup>7</sup>Moses was 120 years old when he died. His eye was undimmed, and his vigor unabated.<sup>8</sup>And the people of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days. Then the days of weeping and mourning for Moses were ended.<sup>9</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him. So the people of Israel obeyed him and did as the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>10</sup>And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face,<sup>11</sup>none like him for all the signs and the wonders that the LORD sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land,<sup>12</sup>and for all the mighty power and all the great deeds of terror that Moses did in the sight of all Israel.
34.overview:
Chapter 34 closes Deuteronomy and the whole Pentateuch with the death of Moses. The greatest prophet Israel had known sees the Promised Land from Mount Nebo and dies in Moab without setting foot in it; God buries him in an unknown grave.

The mediator of the old covenant cannot bring the people into the inheritance; Joshua, whose name (Yehoshua, later Yeshua) is the Hebrew name behind Jesus, will do what Moses could not.
34.theology:
The law cannot bring us in; only the Savior can. Moses, the law-giver and mediator of the old covenant, sees the land but cannot enter it (34:4). The law shows us the inheritance and our inability to reach it, because none of us keeps it; Christ kept it perfectly in our place, and his obedience is counted ours (Rom 5:19). Joshua leads the people in (34:9), for “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). Where the law fails, Christ saves.

The servant of the LORD. Moses' deepest identity, even in death, was “the servant of the LORD” (34:5), faithful to the end. God's purposes did not die with his servant.

The Prophet greater than Moses. Moses himself foretold the Prophet to come (18:15), so the book ends in longing, pointing to Jesus, faithful over God's house as a Son (Heb 3:5–6), the radiance of God's glory (Heb 1:3), everything Moses foreshadowed and more.
34.examples: The law brings us to the border and shows us the promise, but cannot carry us home; only Jesus, the Prophet greater than Moses, leads his people through death into the inheritance and the rest of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses climbs Nebo, and God shows him the whole land he will not enter.
verseByVerse.theology: The tour is God’s own doing; he takes his servant up and points out the country he has been walking toward for forty years. Seeing is all he is given, and it is given as a kindness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a man saw everything he had worked for and was told he would not enter it. Now: the sight was not a consolation prize — these all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Heb. 11:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho. And the LORD showed him all the land, Gilead as far as Dan, all Naphtali, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah as far as the western sea, the Negeb, and the Plain, that is, the Valley of Jericho the city of palm trees, as far as Zoar. And the LORD said to him, "This is the land of which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, 'I will give it to your offspring.' I have let you see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He climbs alone and will not come down. Then God gives him not a glance but a tour, region by region, north, west and south: every place somewhere Moses will never walk.

Both halves of verse 4 stand in one sentence, and neither cancels the other. The promise to Abraham is being kept — Moses is looking at the evidence. And the crossing is refused to the man who brought them this far.

There is real kindness in the seeing. God did not have to show him anything; he could have let him die in his tent. Instead he took him up and let him look at what forty years had been for. Hebrews puts a whole company in this position and does not treat it as failure: These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth (Heb. 11:13). Seeing and greeting from a distance is not a lesser form of faith. It is what faith normally looks like from inside a life.

Why was Moses kept out? Because at Meribah he did not honour God as holy before the people (Num 20:12; 32:51). He was disciplined, not rejected: the God who kept him out of Canaan brought him into it at last, as the end of this chapter shows (Luke 9:30–31).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses dies according to the word of the LORD, and God buries him in a valley opposite Beth-peor — and nobody has ever known the place. Israel weeps thirty days.
verseByVerse.theology: The text says God buried him, which is said of nobody else in Scripture. The greatest man in Israel’s history has no tomb, no shrine and no site of pilgrimage.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the man who spoke with God face to face was laid in unmarked ground by God’s own hands. Now: the grave that changes every other grave, including the ones we stand beside, is one that was marked, guarded, and found empty.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD, and he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab opposite Beth-peor; but no one knows the place of his burial to this day. Moses was 120 years old when he died. His eye was undimmed, and his vigor unabated. And the people of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days. Then the days of weeping and mourning for Moses were ended.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three things in these verses are remarkable.

First, the title: not lawgiver, prophet, or deliverer, but servant. It is among the highest titles the Old Testament gives anybody, and it is the word on his gravestone.

Second, who buried him. The Hebrew text most naturally says God did (the Greek and Samaritan texts read they buried him). The Almighty attending to the body of his friend on a mountainside, alone, is tender beyond anything the ancient world imagined about its gods.

Third, the anonymity. Given what this nation did with a bronze snake, making offerings to it until Hezekiah smashed it (2 Kgs. 18:4), a known grave of Moses would have been a shrine within a generation.

Verse 7 means he was not worn out: his eye was undimmed and his strength unabated. He was stopped, which makes the mountain an act of God rather than the end of a decline. The nation weeps thirty days, as for Aaron, and then the book moves on because the people had to.

Jude says that Michael disputed with the devil over Moses’ body (Jude 9). Jude draws on a Jewish tradition not recorded in the Old Testament; one later form of it says the devil claimed the body because Moses had killed the Egyptian. Jude’s point is that even the archangel left judgment to God: The Lord rebuke you.
verseByVerse.note: On who wrote this closing account, see the question at vv. 9–12.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — There Has Not Arisen a Prophet Like Moses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua takes up the leadership, full of the spirit of wisdom, and the book closes with an epitaph: no prophet has arisen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face.
verseByVerse.theology: The Pentateuch ends incomplete: the greatest prophet is dead, the land is unentered, and the epitaph is written in the negative, there has not arisen.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the law ended with an open question and a fresh grave. Now: the Father has named the Prophet we were waiting for, and told us to listen to him (Matt. 17:5).

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him. So the people of Israel obeyed him and did as the LORD had commanded Moses. And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face, none like him for all the signs and the wonders that the LORD sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land, and for all the mighty power and all the great deeds of terror that Moses did in the sight of all Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The handover works. The man Moses commissioned in public (31:7) is followed, and the nation does not fall apart at the funeral, which is the best thing that can be said of any succession. The wisdom that fills Joshua is the Spirit's gift, not his own store.

Because the epitaph is negative, the Pentateuch, from the creation of the world to this hillside, ends on a note of waiting. Sixteen chapters ago God had promised something: The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers — it is to him you shall listen (18:15). And the last paragraph of the book says, in effect: not yet. Nobody like him has come.

Who wrote these verses? Not Moses, and the text does not pretend he did. Phrases such as to this day (v. 6) and there has not arisen a prophet since (v. 10) read like the words of someone writing well after the event. Jewish tradition credited Joshua with them; many Christians think a later inspired editor completed the book, and how much later is debated. Either way, an account of Moses’ death by another hand does not undercut the book’s claim that Moses wrote the law (31:9). It is what any book finished after its author died would contain.

Centuries later, on a high mountain, Moses stood inside the land at last, in glory, in the country he had only seen from Pisgah, talking with Jesus (Matt. 17:3), and he was not the point of the scene. A cloud came down, and a voice said the sentence Deuteronomy 18 had been waiting for: This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him.

When they looked up, they saw no one but Jesus only (Matt. 17:8). The law had led them as far as the bank of the river and stopped; the one who takes people across is not a law but a Person, named Jesus because he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21).
